editorialDecl.p: New English translation produced by the Falsafa project (Thothica) using an in-house agentic AI translation system, rendered from the Perseus source edition and reviewed by the project. Contributed to provide a translation for a work that previously had no English translation in the corpus.

div.p: Procopius of Caesarea has written the history of the wars which Justinian, Emperor of the Romans, waged against the barbarians of the East and of the West, recording each of them as it happened to come about, so that the great course of time might not, by mastering deeds of surpassing magnitude and leaving them bereft of record, surrender them to oblivion and render them altogether lost—deeds whose memory he himself believed would prove a great thing and most useful both to those now living and to those who shall come after, should time at any point again bring men into some like necessity.

Not long afterward Chosroes, learning that Belisarius had begun to win Italy too for the Emperor Justinian, was no longer able to restrain his mind, but wished to devise pretexts by which he might break the treaty under some specious word.

The Median war, then, came for the Emperor Justinian to this end; but I now go on to tell what he wrought against the Vandals and the Moors. And it shall first be told whence the army of the Vandals attacked the land of the Romans.

When Gelimer saw that all the Vandals had gathered into one place, he led his army against Carthage. 1.2. And when they had come close to it, they broke apart the aqueduct, a thing well worth seeing, which conducted the water into the city; and after encamping there for some time they withdrew, since none of the enemy came out against them. 1.3. Then, going about the country thereabouts, they kept watch over the roads and supposed that by this they were besieging Carthage; yet they neither plundered anything nor laid waste the land, but laid claim to it as their own. 1.4. At the same time they cherished a hope that some treachery would come to their aid, both from the Carthaginians themselves and from those Roman soldiers who held to the Arian faith. 1.5. They sent also to the leaders of the Huns, and, promising that many good things would come to them from the Vandals, begged them to become their friends and allies. 1.6. But these men, who even before were not well disposed toward the affairs of the Romans, inasmuch as they had not come as their allies of their own free will (for they said that the Roman general Peter, after swearing oaths and then disregarding what he had sworn, had thus carried them off to Byzantium), received the proposals of the Vandals and agreed that, as soon as they came to actual battle, they would join with them against the Roman army. 1.7. Now Belisarius, holding all this in suspicion (for he had heard of it from deserters, and at the same time the whole circuit-wall had not yet been completed), thought that for the present he ought not to go out against the enemy, and he set in order the situation within as well as possible. 1.8. And a certain Carthaginian, Laurus by name, who had been convicted of treachery and proved guilty by his own secretary, he impaled upon a hill before the city; and from this the rest, falling into an irresistible fear, abstained from the attempt at treachery. 1.9. As for the Massagetae, he won them over with gifts and a share at his table and with all other manner of flattery, and persuaded them to disclose to him each day all that Gelimer had promised them, 1.10. on condition that they should prove cowardly in the encounter. And these barbarians said that they had no eagerness for the fight; for they feared lest, when the Vandals had been defeated, the Romans would not send them back to their native haunts, but they would be compelled to grow old and die there in Libya; and moreover they were anxious about the booty, lest it should be taken from them. 1.11. Then indeed Belisarius gave them pledges that, if the Vandals were defeated by force of arms, they should be sent at once with all their plunder to their own homes; and thus he bound them by oaths, that they would in very truth carry through the war with all eagerness in his support. 1.12. And when everything had been prepared by him as well as possible and the circuit-wall was now finished, he called together the whole army and spoke as follows: 1.13. "An exhortation, Romans, I do not know that I need make to you, who have lately so conquered the enemy that this Carthage and the whole of Libya are a possession won by your valour, and for this reason you will have need of no counsel to spur you on to courage. For the spirits of victors are by no means wont to be diminished. 1.14. But this one thing only I think it not out of season to remind you of: that, if in the present struggle you play the man as you yourselves have done before, the hopes of the Vandals will straightway come to an end, and so too your fighting. 1.15. Wherefore it is reasonable that you should enter upon this encounter with the greatest eagerness. For toil that is coming to an end and moving toward its conclusion is always sweet to men. Let none of you reckon up the host of the Vandals. 1.16. For war is wont to be decided not by the multitude of men nor by the measure of bodies, but by valour of soul. And let there enter into you the strongest of all things among men, the shame felt over one's deeds. 1.17. For to men of sense it is a disgrace to be worsted by themselves and to be seen falling short of their own valour. As for the enemy, I know well that dread and the memory of their misfortunes encompass them and compel them to become worse: the one dismaying them with what has already befallen, the other driving away the hope of success. 1.18. For fortune, the moment she is seen to be malignant, enslaves the spirit of those who have fallen under her power. And that the struggle now is for us over greater stakes than before, I shall make clear. 1.19. For in the former battle, when our affairs were not going well, the danger lay in our not taking the land of another; but now, if we do not prevail in the struggle, we shall lose our own. 1.20. By as much, then, as to possess nothing is lighter than to be deprived of what one has, by so much greater now than before is the fear in matters of the utmost necessity. 1.21. And yet, though formerly we were left without our infantry, we still chanced to win the victory; whereas now, entering the encounter with God propitious and with the whole army, I have hope that we shall master the camp of the enemy, men and all. 1.22. Having, then, the conclusion of the war ready at hand, do not by any heedlessness put it off to another time, lest, when the opportunity has slipped past, you be compelled to seek it. 1.23. For the fortune of war, when it is put off, is not wont to proceed as it stood before, especially if it is prolonged by the will of those concerned in it. 1.24. For the divine power is ever wont to be jealous of those who throw away the prosperity at hand. And if anyone supposes that the enemy, seeing their children and wives and most precious possessions in our hands, will dare beyond their judgment and will run risks beyond the strength they have, he does not think rightly. 1.25. For excessive passion, growing in the soul on behalf of one's dearest, is wont to break down even the strength one has and does not permit a man to use the means at his disposal. All this, then, you ought to reckon, and to go against the enemy with great contempt for them." 2.1. After Belisarius had thus exhorted them, he sent forth that same day all his horsemen except five hundred, entrusting to John the Armenian both the guardsmen and the standard, which the Romans call a 'bandum,' and bidding him skirmish, should occasion arise. 2.2. And he himself on the following day followed with the infantry and the five hundred horsemen. 2.3. Now the Massagetae, taking counsel among themselves, decided, in order that they might seem to be keeping faith with both Gelimer and Belisarius, neither to begin battle on behalf of the Romans nor to go over to the Vandals before the action, but, whenever the affairs of either army should be in a bad way, then to join the victors in the pursuit of the vanquished. This, then, had been decided by the barbarians in this manner. 2.4. And the Roman army came upon the Vandals encamped at Tricamarum, distant one hundred and forty stades from Carthage. 2.5. There each side bivouacked at a considerable distance from the other. But when the night was far advanced, a portent of the following kind occurred in the Roman camp. 2.6. The tips of their spears were lit up with a bright fire, and the points of them seemed to most of them to be burning. This was not visible to many, but it astonished the few who beheld it, since they did not know how it would turn out. 2.7. This same thing befell the Romans again in Italy a long time afterward; and then indeed, knowing it by experience, they believed it to be a symbol of victory. But at this time, as has been said, since it had happened for the first time, they were dismayed and passed the night in great fear. 2.8. On the following day Gelimer commanded the Vandals to place their children and wives and all their goods in the middle of the encampment, although it had no fortification whatever, and, calling them all together, he spoke as follows: 2.9. "Not for glory, Vandals, nor for the loss of empire only is our struggle, so that even by playing the coward and giving these up it would be possible for us to live, sitting at home and keeping what is our own; 2.10. but you see surely to what fortune our affairs have come round, so that, if we do not master the enemy, we shall, in dying, leave them masters of these our children and wives and our land and all our possessions, while to us, if we survive, there will be added the lot of being slaves and of looking upon all this; 2.11. but if we come safely through the war against the foe, both while we live we shall pass our days amid all good things, and after the seemly close of life happiness will have been left to our children and wives, and to the name of the Vandals the survival of their race and the preservation of their empire. 2.12. For if it has ever fallen to any other men to contend for their all, we ourselves now most of all men know that, bearing upon ourselves the hopes of all, we are entering into the line of battle. 2.13. The fear, then, is not for our bodies, nor is the danger in dying, but in being worsted by the enemy. For to those who have been left without victory, death will be a gain. 2.14. Since, then, these things are so, let no one of the Vandals be soft, but let each give up his body to his spirit, and out of shame at the evils that follow defeat let him be eager for the close of life. 2.15. For to the man who is ashamed of base things it is always possible not to fear danger. And let no memory of the battle that took place before come upon you. 2.16. For it was not by our own cowardice that we were defeated, but, dashing against the obstacles of fortune, we were tripped up. But the current of fortune is not wont always to be borne in the same direction, but, for the most part, is apt to shift each day. 2.17. And in courage we boast that we surpass the enemy, and in numbers we far exceed them; 2.18. for in measure we think to be superior to them by not less than tenfold. And why should I add that there are many great things which now most of all urge us on to valour, both the glory of our forefathers and the empire handed down to us by them? 2.19. For the one, on our part, is veiled by our being unlike our kin, and the other declares that it will flee from us as unworthy. 2.20. And I pass over in silence the lamentations of these women and the tears of our children, for whom now, as you see, being overcome with grief, I am unable to prolong my speech. 2.21. But this one thing only I shall say and then cease: that there will be no return for us to these our dearest unless we master the enemy. 2.22. Bearing these things in mind, be good men and do not disgrace the glory of Gizeric." 2.23. When Gelimer had said this, he commanded his brother Tzazon to make an exhortation in private to the Vandals who had come with him from Sardinia. 2.24. And he, gathering them a little apart from the camp, spoke as follows: "For all the Vandals, fellow-soldiers, the struggle is over those things which you have just now heard the king describe; but for you it happens that, besides all the rest, you must vie with your own selves. 2.25. For you lately conquered while contending for the leadership, and you won back the island for the empire of the Vandals; it is reasonable, therefore, that you should make a greater display of your valour. 2.26. For those whose danger is for the greatest stakes must of necessity have also the greatest eagerness for the fight. For those who contend for the leadership, if they should chance to be defeated, have not stumbled in matters of the utmost necessity; 2.27. but those whose battle is for their all have their whole life shaped by the conclusion of the war. Besides, if you prove good men in the present, you confirm for yourselves that the overthrow of the tyrant Goda was a deed of valour; but if you now play the coward, you will be deprived even of the good repute won by those deeds, as though it in no way belonged to you. 2.28. And yet on other grounds also it is reasonable that you above the rest of the Vandals should have the advantage in this battle. 2.29. For those who have been tripped up the fortune that has gone before strikes with dismay, but those who have stumbled in nothing enter the struggle with their courage unimpaired. 2.30. And this too, I think, will not be said amiss: that if we master the enemy, you will bind on yourselves the greatest part of the victory, and all will call you the saviours of the Vandal nation. 2.31. For those who win glory along with men who have previously been unfortunate reasonably appropriate to themselves the better fortune. 2.32. Reckoning, then, all these things, I say that you must bid your children and wives, who are lamenting, to take courage now, and must call upon God for alliance, and go against the enemy with spirit, and lead the way for your kinsmen into this battle." 3.1. When Gelimer and Tzazon had thus exhorted them, they led out the Vandals, and about the time of the midday meal, when the Romans were not expecting them but were preparing their meal, they were at hand and arrayed themselves for battle along the banks of the river. 3.2. Now the river that flows there is perennial, but so scanty in its stream that it does not even receive a special name from the people of the country, but is reckoned as a brook. 3.3. To the other bank of this river the Romans came, after making such preparation as the circumstances allowed, and arrayed themselves thus. 3.4. The left wing was held by Martinus and Valerianus and John and Cyprian and Althias and Marcellus and the other commanders of the foederati; the right by Pappus and Barbatus and Aïgan and all who commanded the cavalry detachments. 3.5. And in the centre John was stationed, leading the guardsmen and spearmen of Belisarius and the general's standard. 3.6. There too Belisarius arrived in good time with his five hundred horsemen, leaving the infantry behind to come up at a walking pace. 3.7. For the Huns had all arrayed themselves in another place, it being their custom even before not to mingle much with the Roman army, and at this time too, since they had in mind what has been disclosed, they were unwilling to be ranged with the rest of the army. Thus, then, stood the array of the Romans. 3.8. As for the Vandals, the chiliarchs held each wing, and each one led the company about himself, while in the centre was Tzazon the brother of Gelimer, and behind were arrayed the Moors. 3.9. Gelimer himself, going about everywhere, kept urging them on and rousing them to courage. And word had been passed to all the Vandals to use neither spear nor any other weapon in this engagement except their swords. 3.10. When a long time had passed and no one began the battle, John, picking out a few of those about him, with the consent of Belisarius crossed the river and dashed against the centre, where Tzazon, using a thrust, drove them back. 3.11. And they fled to their own camp, while the Vandals, pursuing, came as far as the river, but did not cross it. 3.12. Again John, taking with him a larger number of the guardsmen of Belisarius, leaped against the forces of Tzazon, and again, beaten off from there, withdrew to the Roman camp. 3.13. And the third time, taking with him almost all the spearmen and guardsmen of Belisarius and the general's standard, he made the attack with much shouting and din. 3.14. And as the barbarians manfully withstood them and used only their swords, the battle became fierce, and many of the Vandals fell, the best of them, and Tzazon himself the brother of Gelimer. 3.15. Then indeed the whole Roman army was set in motion, and crossing the river they advanced against the enemy, and the rout, beginning from the centre, became brilliant; for each contingent turned to flight those opposed to them with no trouble. 3.16. And seeing this, the Massagetae, according to their agreement, joined the Roman army in the pursuit; not for long, however, did this pursuit continue. 3.17. For the Vandals, entering their own camp in haste, kept quiet, and the Romans, not supposing that they would be able to fight against them within the rampart, stripped those of the dead who wore gold and withdrew to their own camp. 3.18. And there perished in this battle of the Romans fewer than fifty, but of the Vandals about eight hundred. 3.19. But Belisarius, when his infantry arrived about late afternoon, setting out with all the army as fast as he could, went against the camp of the Vandals. 3.20. And Gelimer, learning that Belisarius with the infantry and the rest of the army was coming straight against him, without saying or commanding anything, leaped upon his horse and fled along the road leading to Numidia. 3.21. And there followed him his kinsmen and a few of his servants, panic-stricken and keeping silence about the present situation. 3.22. And for some time Gelimer escaped the notice of the Vandals as he stole away; but when all perceived that he had fled and the enemy were already in sight, then indeed the men raised a tumult, and the children cried out, and the women wailed. 3.23. And they neither laid hold of the goods that were at hand nor cared for their dearest ones who were lamenting, but each one fled in no order wherever he could. 3.24. And the Romans, coming up, took the camp, empty of men, with all its goods, and pursuing through the whole night, killed all the men they met, and made the children and women slaves. 3.25. And they found in this camp such an abundance of money as has never before chanced to be in one place. 3.26. For the Vandals, having plundered the Roman empire of old, had carried off much money to Libya; and since their land was exceedingly good and abounded most plentifully in the most necessary crops, it came about that the revenues of money, which were gathered from the good things produced there, were not spent upon any other country in the importing of provisions, but those who possessed the lands always added to their store for ninety-five years, during which the Vandals ruled Libya. 3.27. And from this their wealth, having grown to a very great sum, on that day passed back again into the hands of the Romans. 3.28. This battle and pursuit, then, and the capture of the camp of the Vandals took place three months after the Roman army came to Carthage, about the middle of the last month, which the Romans call December. 4.1. At that time Belisarius, seeing the Roman army borne along in disorder and with much confusion, was distressed, fearing throughout the whole night lest the enemy, coming to an understanding and uniting against them, should work irreparable harm upon them. 4.2. And if this had in any way then come to pass, I think that not one of the Romans would have escaped to enjoy this booty. 4.3. For the soldiers, being men utterly poor, and having become of a sudden masters of exceedingly great wealth and of women young and surpassingly fair, were no longer able to restrain their minds nor to find any satiety in the things at hand, but were so intoxicated, drenched as they were in their good fortune, that each one wished to bring everything off to Carthage with him. 4.4. And they went about not in companies, but singly or two together, wherever hope might lead them, searching out everything round about, in glens and rugged places and wherever a cave chanced to be, or anything else that led to danger or ambush. 4.5. For neither did fear of the enemy enter them, nor respect for Belisarius, nor anything else at all except the desire for plunder; and this, overmastering them, turned them to disregard of all else. 4.6. Considering all this in his mind, Belisarius was at a loss how to deal with the present situation. 4.7. And at daybreak he stationed himself upon a certain hill near the road, recalling the good order that was no longer present and abusing both soldiers and commanders alike. 4.8. Then indeed all who chanced to be somewhere near, and especially those of the household of Belisarius, sent to Carthage the money and slaves they had, together with their tent-mates and table-companions, while they themselves, going to the general, gave heed to the commands given them. 4.9. He commanded John the Armenian, with two hundred men, to follow Gelimer, and, slackening neither by night nor by day, to pursue him until they should take him alive or dead. 4.10. And to the friendly people in Carthage he sent orders, with regard to the Vandals who were sitting as suppliants in the sanctuaries about the city, to take their pledges and their arms, that they might attempt no revolt, and to bring them into the city and keep them, 4.11. until he himself should come. And with those who were left he went about everywhere and zealously roused the soldiers, and to the Vandals who were continually being found he gave pledges of safety. For it was no longer possible to take any Vandal except as a suppliant in the sanctuaries. 4.12. And taking away their arms, he sent them to Carthage with soldiers to guard them, giving them no opportunity to unite against the Romans. 4.13. And when everything was in the best of order for him, he himself with the greater part of the army went in haste against Gelimer. 4.14. Now John, having pursued for five days and nights, was now not far from Gelimer, but on the following day he was about to come to grips with him. But since it was not fated that Gelimer should be taken by John, an adverse stroke of fortune fell out as follows. 4.15. Among those pursuing with John there chanced to be Uliaris, the guardsman of Belisarius. 4.16. Now this man was high-spirited and well endowed by nature for vigour of soul and body, but not very serious, taking pleasure for the most part in wine and jests. 4.17. This Uliaris, on the sixth day of the pursuit, being drunk about sunrise, saw a bird sitting on a tree, and quickly drawing his bow, let fly the arrow at the bird. 4.18. And he missed the bird, but hit John behind in the neck, by no means willingly. 4.19. And he, smitten by a mortal wound, a little later passed from among men, leaving great longing for himself to the Emperor Justinian and to Belisarius the general and to all the Romans and Carthaginians. 4.20. For he was well endowed with manliness and all other virtue, and showed himself gentle to those who met him, and most reasonable, inferior to none. So John fulfilled his destiny in this way. 4.21. And Uliaris, when he came to himself, fled to a certain village near by and sat as a suppliant in the sanctuary there. 4.22. But the soldiers were no longer eager to pursue Gelimer; instead, they tended John while he lived, and when he died they performed the customary rites for his burial, and, after disclosing the whole matter to Belisarius, they remained there. 4.23. And he, as soon as he heard it, came to the tomb of John and bewailed his fate. 4.24. And when he had bewailed him and grieved deeply over the whole calamity, he honoured the tomb of John with many things and especially with the revenue of money. 4.25. To Uliaris, however, he did nothing dreadful, since the soldiers said that John had enjoined upon them by the most terrible oaths that no vengeance should be taken upon him, inasmuch as he had wrought the defilement not from forethought. 4.26. In this way, then, Gelimer escaped falling under the hand of the enemy on that day. And Belisarius thereafter pursued him, and arriving at a strong city of the Numidians, lying upon the sea, distant ten days' journey from Carthage, which they call Hippo Regius, he learned that Gelimer, having gone up to Mount Papua, was no longer to be captured by the Romans. 4.27. Now this mountain is at the extreme limits of Numidia, exceedingly steep and dreadfully hard to traverse (for lofty rocks rise on every side toward it), and on it dwell barbarian Moors who were friends and helpers of Gelimer; and an ancient city, Medeus by name, lies at the extremity of the mountain. 4.28. There Gelimer with those who followed him kept quiet. But Belisarius (since he was not able to attempt the mountain, especially in the winter season, and since, moreover, with his affairs still in suspense, he thought it inexpedient to be away from Carthage), picking out soldiers and a commander, Pharas, established them in the blockade of the mountain. 4.29. Now this Pharas was energetic and exceedingly serious and well endowed with valour, although he was an Erulian by race. 4.30. And for an Erulian not to be given over to faithlessness and drunkenness, but to lay claim to valour, is both difficult and worthy of much praise. 4.31. And Pharas was not the only one who held to good order, but also all the Eruli who followed him. This Pharas, then, Belisarius commanded to sit at the foot of the mountain during the winter season and to keep strict guard, so that it should be impossible either for Gelimer to leave the mountain or for any necessaries to be brought in to him. 4.32. And Pharas did accordingly. But Belisarius caused the Vandals who were sitting as suppliants at the sanctuaries in Hippo Regius, many and of the best, to rise up after receiving pledges, and sent them to Carthage under guard. And there it chanced that something of the following sort befell him. 4.33. In the house of Gelimer there was a secretary, Boniface, a Libyan, coming from Byzacium, exceedingly faithful to Gelimer. 4.34. This Boniface Gelimer, at the beginning of this war, had embarked upon a ship that was a most excellent sailer, and, placing in it all the royal treasure, commanded him to anchor in the harbour of Hippo Regius, and, if he should see that affairs were not turning out well for them, to sail in haste to Spain with the money and come to Theudis the ruler of the Visigoths, where Gelimer himself also expected to find safety, should the fortune of the war prove evil for the Vandals. 4.35. And Boniface, so long as he had hope in the affairs of the Vandals, remained there; but as soon as the battle at Tricamarum and the other events that have been told had taken place, he set sail and sailed as Gelimer had directed him. 4.36. But a contrary wind carried him back, against his will, to the harbour of Hippo Regius. And when he heard that the enemy were now somewhere near, he promised much to the sailors and begged them to go by force to some other mainland or island. 4.37. But they (for they were unable, since a very severe storm had fallen upon them and the surge of the sea, being in the Tyrrhenian deep, was rising to a great height), then indeed both they and Boniface came to the thought that God, wishing to give the money to the Romans, would not permit the ship to put out. 4.38. With difficulty, however, getting outside the harbour, they held the ship at sea amid great danger. 4.39. And when Belisarius came to Hippo Regius, Boniface sent some men to him. These he bade sit in a sanctuary and say that they had been sent by Boniface, who had the money of Gelimer, but to conceal where it might be, until they should receive pledges that, by giving the money of Gelimer, he should himself depart unharmed and free from evil, keeping whatever was his own. 4.40. And they did this, and Belisarius was glad at the good tidings and did not refuse to swear. 4.41. And sending some of his friends, he took the wealth of Gelimer and let Boniface go with his own money, of which he had stolen a very great amount from the wealth of Gelimer. 5.1. When Belisarius returned to Carthage, he set about preparing all the Vandals, so that he might send them to Byzantium at the opening of spring, and he sent out an army to recover for the Romans all the territory which the Vandals had ruled. 5.2. He sent Cyril, then, with a great force to Sardinia, carrying the head of Tzazon, since these islanders by no means wished to come over to the Romans, both fearing the Vandals and not supposing that what was said to have befallen them at Tricamarum was true. 5.3. And to this Cyril he gave orders to send a part of the army to Corsica and to recover the island for the Roman empire, since it had formerly been subject to the Vandals; it was in ancient times called Cyrnus, and is not far from Sardinia. 5.4. And he, coming to Sardinia, showed the head of Tzazon to those who dwelt there, and recovered both islands for the Roman empire to pay tribute. 5.5. And to Caesarea in Mauretania Belisarius sent John with a company of infantry of which he himself was leader; this city is distant from Carthage a journey of thirty days for an unencumbered man, as one goes toward Gadira and the setting sun; and it lies on the sea, being great and populous from of old. 5.6. And another John, one of his own guardsmen, he sent to the strait at Gadira and the other of the Pillars of Heracles, to hold the fortress there which they call Septem. 5.7. And to the islands which are near the entrance of the Ocean, called by the natives Ebusa and Majorica and Minorica, he sent Apollinarius, who came originally from Italy, but while still a youth had come to Libya. 5.8. And having been presented with much money by Ilderic, who was then ruling the Vandals, when Ilderic had been deposed from the kingship and was being held in prison, as has been told in the previous narrative, he came to the Emperor Justinian with the other Libyans who supported the cause of Ilderic, to make supplication. 5.9. And taking the field with the Roman fleet against Gelimer and the Vandals, he proved himself a good man in this war and above all others at Tricamarum. And on account of this deed Belisarius entrusted these islands to him. 5.10. And afterward, sending an army to Tripolis, to Pudentius and Tattimuth, who were being hard pressed by the Moors there, he strengthened the Roman power in that quarter. 5.11. And sending some men also to Sicily, in order that they might hold the fortress in Lilybaeum, on the ground that it belonged to the dominion of the Vandals, he was repulsed from there, the Goths by no means consenting to yield any part of Sicily, on the ground that this fortress in no way belonged to the Vandals. 5.12. And he, when he heard this, wrote to the commanders who were there as follows: "You are robbing us of Lilybaeum, the fortress of the Vandals, who are slaves of the emperor, doing what is neither just nor expedient for yourselves, and you wish to make hostile toward your ruler, who is neither willing for it nor present at what is being done, the great emperor, whose goodwill he has gained with much toil. 5.13. And yet how would you not seem to act contrary to the manner of mankind, if you lately consented that Gelimer should hold the fortress, but have decided to deprive the emperor, the master of Gelimer, of the possessions of his slave? 5.14. Do not so, most excellent men. But consider that friendship is wont to cover many grievances, while enmity does not endure even the smallest wrongs, but searches everything out from the beginning, and does not overlook the enemy growing rich on things that in no way belong to them. 5.15. Then it fights over things for which it says its forefathers were wronged; and if it stumbles in the danger, it has lost nothing of what it had, but if it prospers, it makes the vanquished unlearn forgiveness. 5.16. Do you, then, neither do us any further harm nor suffer it yourselves, nor make the great emperor an enemy to the Gothic race, for whom it is your prayer that he should be propitious to you. 5.17. For know well that, if you lay claim to this fortress, war will be at hand for you, not over Lilybaeum only, but over all the things to which, though none of them belongs to you, you nevertheless cling." 5.18. Such was the import of the letter. But the Goths referred these matters to the mother of Atalaric, and as the woman had directed them, answered thus: 5.19. "The letter which you have written, most excellent Belisarius, brings a true exhortation, but one that has come to certain other men, not to us Goths. 5.20. For we hold nothing that we have taken belonging to the Emperor Justinian — may we never be so mad! — but we claim that the whole of Sicily is ours, of which one promontory is the fortress in Lilybaeum. 5.21. And if Theoderic permitted his sister, who was the wife of the king of the Vandals, to use one of the market-towns of Sicily, this is no matter. 5.22. For it would bring you no claim of right whatever. You, however, O general, would be doing what is just toward us, if you should be willing to make the settlement of the matters in dispute between us not as an enemy but as a friend. And there is this difference, 5.23. that friends are wont to decide their differences by arbitration, but enemies by battle. 5.24. We, then, shall entrust to the Emperor Justinian the arbitration concerning these matters, in whatever way may seem to him lawful and just. And we wish you to deliberate in the best way rather than the quickest, and to await the decision of your emperor." Such was the import of the writing of the Goths. 5.25. And Belisarius, referring everything to the emperor, kept quiet until the emperor should send him word as to what was his pleasure. 6.1. But Pharas, already distressed by the blockade, especially in the winter season, and at the same time not supposing that the Moors there were able to stand in his way, attempted the ascent to Papua with great eagerness. So he armed all his followers very well and began the ascent. 6.2. But as the Moors came to the rescue, since the place was steep and exceedingly hard to traverse, the hindrance came easily upon those ascending. 6.3. And as Pharas forced the ascent vigorously, one hundred and ten of his men perished in this action, and he himself, beaten back with the survivors, withdrew; and as a result he no longer ventured to attempt the ascent, the thing being against him, but established a most zealous guard, as strict as possible, so that those in Papua, being hard pressed by famine, should give themselves up, and he neither allowed them to escape nor permitted anything from outside to be brought in to them. 6.4. There it befell Gelimer and those about him, his nephews and cousins and other men of good birth, to undergo such suffering as, however one might describe it, one could not set forth in a way to match the reality. 6.5. For of all the nations whom we know, the most luxurious is that of the Vandals, and the most wretched that of the Moors. 6.6. For the Vandals, from the time they took Libya, used baths, all of them, every day, and a table abounding in all things, the sweetest and best that earth and sea produce. 6.7. And they wore gold for the most part, and clothed themselves in Median garments, which they now call silken, and passed their time in theatres and hippodromes and in other pleasures, and above all in hunting. 6.8. And they had dancers and mimes and all manner of things to hear and to see that are accounted musical or otherwise worth seeing among men. 6.9. And most of them dwelt in parks, well supplied with water and trees; and they held very many banquets, and all the pursuits of love were practised by them with great zeal. 6.10. But the Moors dwell in stifling huts, both in winter and in the summer season and at every other time, removing thence neither for snows nor for the heat of the sun nor for any other compulsion of evil whatever. 6.11. And they sleep upon the ground, the prosperous among them, if it so happen, spreading a fleece under them. 6.12. And it is not their custom to change their garments with the seasons, but they wear a thick cloak and a rough shirt at all times. 6.13. And they have neither bread nor wine nor any other good thing, but the grain, either spelt or barley, neither boiling it nor grinding it to meal or barley-groats, they eat in no way different from the other animals. 6.14. Among such Moors, then, the followers of Gelimer, having dwelt for a long time, and having changed their accustomed manner of life to this wretchedness, when even the very necessaries had now failed them, no longer held out, but to them death seemed sweetest and slavery by no means shameful. 6.15. When Pharas perceived this, he wrote to Gelimer as follows: "I too am myself a barbarian, and I am neither accustomed to letters and speech nor otherwise experienced in them. 6.16. But what it is necessary for me, being a man, to know, I have written, having learned it from the nature of things. 6.17. Why ever, dear Gelimer, have you suffered such a thing as to cast not yourself only but your whole race into this pit, that you may not, forsooth, become a slave? 6.18. For I think that in this you are playing the youthful boaster, and holding forth liberty, as though it were worth exchanging all hardships for it. 6.19. And then, do you not think that you are now a slave to the most unfortunate of the Moors, you who hold your hope of safety, if the best should come, in them? 6.20. And yet how would it not in every way be better to be a slave among the Romans and a beggar than to play the monarch in Papua and among the Moors? 6.21. But of course to you it seems the height of insolence even to be a fellow-slave with Belisarius. 6.22. Away with such thoughts, most excellent Gelimer. Or are not we too, sprung from noble fathers, proud now to serve the emperor? And indeed they say that it is the pleasure of the Emperor Justinian both to enroll you in the senate, sharing the highest honour, which they call the patriciate, and to present you with much good land and great wealth, and that Belisarius is willing to guarantee that all this shall be yours, giving pledges. 6.23. As for the hard things which fortune has brought, you are able to bear them all nobly, thinking that what comes from this source is necessary for a man. 6.24. But if it has been decided to mingle some good with these hard things, would you not deem it right to receive this of your own free will? Or are not the good things which come from fortune, no less than the base, to be reckoned by us as necessary? But this does not seem so even to the very foolish. 6.25. But for you now, plunged as you are in misfortunes, it happens, as is likely, that you are without understanding; 6.26. for despondency, striking with dismay, is wont to turn men to thoughtlessness. But if you are able to bear your own mind and not be vexed at fortune as it shifts, it will be possible for you straightway to choose all that is expedient and to be freed from the evils that press upon you." 6.27. When Gelimer had read this letter, he wept bitterly and wrote back thus: "For the counsel which you have given me I am very grateful to you, but to be a slave to an unjust enemy I think not endurable — to one from whom I would pray to obtain justice, if God should be propitious to me, since, though I had suffered nothing unpleasant from him either in deed nor heard it in word, he furnished a pretext for war when I gave no occasion, and brought me to this fortune, having from I know not where brought Belisarius against me. 6.28. And yet to him too, being a man and an emperor, it is not unlikely that something of what he would not choose may befall. 6.29. I, however, am not able to write anything further. For the present fortune has taken away my power of thought. 6.30. But farewell to me, dear Pharas, and send me, who beg it, a lyre and one loaf of bread 6.31. and a sponge." When this was brought to him and Pharas had learned it, he was for some time at a loss, unable to make out the conclusion of the letter, until the man who brought it explained to him that Gelimer was in need of one loaf, longing to come to the sight and the tasting of it, since from the time he had gone up to Papua he had seen no baked bread. 6.32. And a sponge was necessary to him, for one of his eyes, irritated by lack of washing, had become greatly swollen. 6.33. And being a good harpist, he had composed a song over his present misfortune, which he was eager to lament and bewail to the lyre. 6.34. When Pharas heard this, he grieved deeply and bewailed the lot of mankind, and did according to what was written and sent all the things of which Gelimer was in need. The blockade, however, he relaxed not at all, but kept guard even more strictly than before. 7.1. Now the time of three months had already been spent in this blockade, and the winter was coming to an end. And Gelimer was afraid, suspecting that the besiegers would before long ascend against him; and the bodies of most of the children of his kinsmen, in this wretchedness, were sending forth worms. 7.2. And he was in pain over all things, and ill-content with everything except dying; yet against his suffering he held out beyond expectation, until it befell him to see a sight of the following kind. 7.3. A certain Moorish woman, having somehow pounded a little grain, and made from it a very small cake, threw it into the hot ashes upon the hearth. For thus it is the custom among the Moors to bake their bread. 7.4. By this hearth two boys were sitting, exceedingly oppressed by hunger — one of them the son of the woman herself who had thrown in the cake, the other a nephew of Gelimer — and they wished to snatch this cake as soon as it should seem to them to be baked. 7.5. Of these two boys the Vandal, getting the start, seized the cake first, and, while it was still very hot and full of ashes, hunger overmastering him, thrust it into his mouth and was eating it; but the other, laying hold of him by the hair of his head, struck him on the temple and, striking him again, compelled him with much violence to throw out the cake which was already in his throat. 7.6. This calamity Gelimer could not bear (for he had followed all things from the beginning), and he was unmanned in his mind and wrote to Pharas as quickly as possible as follows: 7.7. "If it has ever fallen to any other man, after enduring dreadful things, to go contrary to what he had before resolved, count me too to be some such man, most excellent Pharas. 7.8. For your counsel has come into my mind, which I am by no means willing to disregard. For I would no longer strive against fortune nor wrestle with destiny, but will follow at once wherever it may seem good to her to lead; only let me receive the pledges, that Belisarius will guarantee that the emperor will do all that you lately promised me. 7.9. For I, as soon as you give the pledge, will deliver myself into your hands, and these kinsmen and the Vandals who are here with us." 7.10. Such was what Gelimer had written in this letter. And Pharas, making known both this and what had been previously written between them to Belisarius, begged him to disclose as quickly as possible what was his pleasure. 7.11. And Belisarius (for he had a great desire to bring Gelimer alive to the emperor), as soon as he had read the letter, was overjoyed and commanded Cyprian, a commander of the foederati, to go to Papua with certain others, and enjoined upon them to give oaths concerning the safety of Gelimer and those with him, and that he should be held in honour by the emperor and lack nothing. 7.12. And they, when they had come to Pharas, went with him to a place at the foot of the mountain, where Gelimer came at their summons, and, receiving the pledges as he wished, came with them to Carthage. 7.13. And it chanced that Belisarius was making a stay in the suburb of the city 7.14. which they call Aclas. There Gelimer came in to him, laughing a laugh that was neither slight nor able to be hidden; and some of those who beheld him suspected, by reason of the excess of his suffering, that he had departed from his natural state of mind and was already mad, and held his laughter for no reason at all. 7.15. His friends, however, wished the man to be shrewd, and held that, since he had been born of a royal house and had ascended to kingship, and had been clothed about with strong power and great wealth from boyhood even to old age, and then had fallen into flight and great fear and had endured the suffering in Papua, and had now come into the lot of captives, and had thus made trial of all the goods and ills that come from fortune — he thought that human affairs were worthy of nothing else but much laughter. 7.16. Now concerning the laughter with which Gelimer laughed, let each speak as he knows, 7.17. both foe and friend. But Belisarius, having reported to the emperor that Gelimer was a captive in Carthage, asked to come with him to Byzantium. Meanwhile he kept both him and all the Vandals under guard, not in dishonour, and made the fleet ready. 7.18. Now many other things in all the ages have come to pass beyond expectation, and ever will, so long as the fortunes of men are the same; 7.19. for things which seem in reasoning to be impossible are accomplished in deed, and things which often appeared impossible, 7.20. when they have come to pass, have seemed worthy of wonder. Whether, however, such deeds have ever before come to pass, I am not able to say — that the fourth descendant of Gizeric, and his kingdom flourishing in wealth and in the power of soldiers, should have been overthrown in so short a time by five thousand men who were newcomers and had no place to anchor. 7.21. For such was the number of the horsemen who followed Belisarius and who carried through the whole war against the Vandals. Whether, then, this came about by fortune or by some valour, one might justly marvel at it. But I shall return to the point from which I digressed. 8.1. The Vandalic war, then, ended thus. But envy, such as is wont to arise amid great prosperity, was now swelling against Belisarius, although he furnished it no occasion. 8.2. For some of the commanders slandered him to the emperor, charging him with aiming at a tyranny in no way belonging to him. 8.3. But the emperor did not bring this matter into the open at all, either making light of the slander, or because he thought it better so. 8.4. And sending Solomon, he gave Belisarius the choice of whichever of two courses he wished — either to come to Byzantium with Gelimer and the Vandals, or, remaining there, to send them. 8.5. But he (for the commanders who had brought the charge of tyranny did not escape his notice) was eager to come to Byzantium, that he might both clear himself of the accusation and be able to punish those who had slandered him. And in what manner he learned of the attempt of his accusers, I shall now tell. 8.6. When those who slandered him wished to make this slander, fearing lest he who was to carry the letter to the emperor should perish at sea and so prevent what they were doing, they wrote out the charge of tyranny on two documents and planned to send two messengers to the emperor in two ships. 8.7. Of these one set sail unobserved, but the other, falling under some suspicion, was caught at Mandracium, and, handing over the letter to those who seized him, made known what was being done. 8.8. And learning of this, Belisarius was eager, as has been said, to come into the presence of the emperor. These things, then, were going on at Carthage in this way. 8.9. But the Moors who dwelt in Byzacium and Numidia looked toward revolt for no cause whatever, and, dissolving the truce, suddenly resolved to raise their hands against the Romans. And this was done by them in no way alien to their character. 8.10. For among the Moors there is neither fear of God nor respect of men. For they care neither for oaths nor for hostages, even though the hostages chance to be the children or brothers of their leaders. 8.11. Nor is there any other peace among the Moors except that which is held secure by fear of the enemies opposed to them. And in what manner the truce with Belisarius was made by them, and in what manner it was dissolved, I shall now disclose. 8.12. When the fleet of the emperor was expected to come to Libya, the Moors, fearing lest they should suffer some harm from it, made use of the divinations of their women. 8.13. For it is not lawful for a man to give oracles in this nation, but women among them, becoming possessed by reason of a certain sacred rite, foretell the future, no less than any of the ancient oracles. 8.14. At that time, then, as they inquired, as has been said, the women declared: an army from the waters, the destruction of the Vandals, the ruin and defeat of the Moors, 8.15. when there should come to the Romans a beardless general. The Moors, hearing this, when they saw the emperor's army come from the sea, fell into great fear, and were by no means willing to ally themselves with the Vandals, but, sending to Belisarius and confirming the peace, as has been disclosed before, kept quiet and waited to see how the future would turn out. 8.16. But when the affairs of the Vandals had now come to an end, they sent to the Roman army, inquiring whether there was anyone among them beardless in command. 8.17. And when they saw all of them grown full of beard, they supposed that the oracle did not signify to them the present time, but many generations afterward, interpreting the prophecy in this way, as they themselves wished. 8.18. At once, then, they were eager for the dissolution of the truce, but the fear of Belisarius held them back. 8.19. For they had no hope of prevailing in war over the Romans while he was present. 8.20. But when they heard that he was departing with his own guardsmen and spearmen, and learned that the ships were now being filled by these men and the Vandals, suddenly taking up their arms they displayed every form of evil against the Libyans. 8.21. For the soldiers, being few in each extreme region and still unprepared, were unable to withstand the barbarians overrunning the land everywhere, nor to prevent their incursions, which were frequent and not made in the open. 8.22. But the men were slain in no order, and the women with the children were made slaves, and the goods from every borderland were carried off, and the whole country was filled with flight. These things were reported to Belisarius when he was now putting to sea. 8.23. And he was no longer able to turn back, but gave to Solomon the management of the dominion of Libya, picking out for him also the greater part of his own guardsmen and spearmen, so that the Moors who had revolted might as quickly as possible be punished by Solomon, with great eagerness, for their wrong against the Romans. 8.24. And the emperor too sent another army to Solomon, with Theodore the Cappadocian and Ildiger, who was the son-in-law of Antonina the wife of Belisarius. 8.25. And since it was no longer possible to find the taxes of the regions in Libya set down in writing, in the way in which the Romans had recorded them in former times — inasmuch as Gizeric had at the beginning thrown all into confusion and destroyed everything — Tryphon and Eustratius were sent by the emperor to assess the taxes for them according to each man's measure. These, however, seemed to the Libyans neither moderate nor bearable. 9.1. But Belisarius, coming with Gelimer and the Vandals to Byzantium, was deemed worthy of such honours as in former times had been appointed for those Roman generals who had won the greatest and most noteworthy victories. 9.2. And a period of about six hundred years had now passed since anyone had attained these honours, except indeed Titus and Trajan and such other emperors as had led armies against some barbarian nation and conquered. 9.3. For displaying the spoils and the captives of the war, he marched in procession in the midst of the city, the thing which the Romans call a triumph — not, however, in the ancient fashion, but going on foot from his own house to the hippodrome, and there again from the starting-line until he reached the place where the imperial throne is. 9.4. And there was booty — all that is wont to be set apart for the service of the emperor: thrones of gold and carriages in which it is customary for the wife of the emperor to ride, and much jewelry made of precious stones, and golden drinking-cups, and all the other things useful for the imperial banquet. 9.5. And there was also silver weighing many tens of thousands of talents, and all the royal treasure amounting to an exceedingly great sum (since Gizeric had despoiled the Palatium in Rome, as has been said in the previous narrative), among which were also the treasures of the Jews, which Titus the son of Vespasian, after the capture of Jerusalem, had brought to Rome together with certain others. 9.6. And one of the Jews, seeing these, approached one of those known to the emperor and said: "These treasures I think it inexpedient to carry into the palace in Byzantium. 9.7. For it is not possible for them to be anywhere except in the place where Solomon the king of the Jews formerly placed them. 9.8. For it was because of these that Gizeric captured the palace of the Romans, and now the Roman army has captured that of the Vandals." 9.9. When this had been reported and the emperor heard it, he became afraid and quickly sent everything to the sanctuaries of the Christians in Jerusalem. 9.10. And the captives of the triumph were Gelimer himself, wearing some purple garment upon his shoulders, and all his family, and those of the Vandals who were very tall and fair of body. 9.11. And when Gelimer came into the hippodrome and saw the emperor sitting upon a lofty seat and the people standing on either side, and perceived, as he looked about, in what evil case he was, he neither wept nor cried out, but ceased not saying, according to the Hebrew scripture, "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity." 9.12. And when he came before the emperor's seat, they stripped off the purple robe and compelled him to fall prone and do obeisance to the Emperor Justinian. This Belisarius also did, inasmuch as he had become a suppliant of the emperor along with him. 9.13. And the Emperor Justinian and the Empress Theodora presented the children and all the descendants of Ilderic, and all those of the lineage of the Emperor Valentinian, with sufficient money, and giving to Gelimer not despicable lands in Galatia, they permitted him to dwell there together with his kinsmen. 9.14. Gelimer, however, was by no means enrolled among the patricians, since he was not willing to change from the faith of Arius. 9.15. And a little later the triumph was celebrated for Belisarius also according to the ancient custom. For as he advanced to the consulship, it fell to him to be borne aloft by the captives, and, riding in the curule chair, to throw to the people those very spoils of the Vandalic war. 9.16. For the silver plate and golden girdles and a great amount of other Vandalic wealth the people seized from the consulship of Belisarius, and it seemed that something not customary was being renewed after a long time. These things, then, happened thus in Byzantium. 10.1. But Solomon, having taken over the army in Libya, with the Moors in revolt, as has been disclosed, and with the whole situation in suspense, was at a loss how to deal with the present state of affairs. 10.2. For it was reported that the barbarians had slain the soldiers in Byzacium and Numidia and were plundering and carrying off everything there. 10.3. And most of all, both him and all Carthage there confounded the events that befell Aïgan the Massagete and Rufinus the Thracian in Byzacium. 10.4. For both were exceedingly notable, both in the household of Belisarius and in the Roman army — the one of them, Aïgan, being ranked among the guardsmen of Belisarius, the other, being the most stout-hearted of all, accustomed to carry the general's standard in the battle-lines, which the Romans call a bandophorus. 10.5. For at that time these two men, leading cavalry detachments in Byzacium, when they saw the Moors plundering all that was at hand and making slaves of all the Libyans, watching for them in a narrow place with those who followed them, attacked the men who were escorting the booty, slew them, and took away all the captives. 10.6. But when this word came to the commanders of the barbarians — Cutzinas and Esdilasas and Iourphouthes and Medisinissas — who were not far from this narrow place, they advanced against them with their whole army about late afternoon. 10.7. And the Romans, being exceedingly few and shut up in a narrow space in the midst of many tens of thousands, were not able to defend themselves against the assailants. For wherever they turned, they were always struck in the rear. 10.8. Then indeed Rufinus and Aïgan with a few men ran up to a rock that was somewhere near and from there defended themselves against the barbarians. 10.9. So long, then, as they used their bows, the enemy did not dare to come straight to grips with them, but hurled their javelins; but when all their missiles had failed them, the Moors came to grips with them, and they too defended themselves with their swords as best they could from what they had. 10.10. But as the multitude of the barbarians pressed hard, Aïgan, his whole body cut to pieces, fell there, but Rufinus the enemy seized and led away. 10.11. And straightway one of the commanders, Medisinissas, fearing lest he should escape and cause them trouble again, cut off his head, and, taking it home, showed it to his women, since it was worth seeing for its exceeding size and the abundance of its hair. 10.12. But since the course of the history has brought us here, it is necessary to tell from the beginning whence the Moorish nations came to Libya and how they settled there. 10.13. When the Hebrews had departed from Egypt and had come near the borders of Palestine, Moses, a wise man, who had led them on the way, died, and the leadership was taken over by Joshua the son of Nun, who led this people into Palestine, and, displaying valour in war greater than that of human nature, won the land. 10.14. And overthrowing all the nations, he easily subdued the cities, and seemed to be altogether invincible. 10.15. At that time the whole coast-land from Sidon to the borders of Egypt was called Phoenicia. 10.16. And a single king of old presided over it, as is agreed by all who have written the most ancient history of the Phoenicians. 10.17. There dwelt nations exceedingly populous, the Gergesites and the Jebusites and others bearing certain other names, by which the history of the Hebrews calls them. 10.18. This people, when they saw that the invading general was an irresistible thing, rose up from their ancestral homes and went off to Egypt, which bordered upon them. 10.19. There, finding no place sufficient for them to settle in, since there was from of old a dense population in Egypt, they set out for Libya. 10.20. And settling many cities, they took possession of the whole of Libya as far as the Pillars of Heracles, and there, using the Phoenician tongue, they have dwelt even down to my time. 10.21. And they built a fortress in Numidia, where now is the city called Tigisis. 10.22. There are two columns made of white stones near the great spring, having Phoenician letters cut in them which say in the Phoenician tongue thus: "We are those who fled from before the face of Joshua 10.23. the robber, the son of Nun." And there were also other nations who had dwelt in Libya before, who, because they had been settled there from of old, were said to be sprung from the soil. 10.24. And from this they said that Antaeus, their king, who wrestled with Heracles at Clypea, was a son of the earth. 10.25. And at a later time those who removed from Phoenicia with Dido came to their kinsmen who were dwelling in Libya. And these of their own free will permitted them to found Carthage and to hold it. 10.26. And as time went on, the power of the Carthaginians became great and populous. 10.27. And when a battle took place between them and their neighbours, who had come earlier, as has been said, from Palestine, and are now called Moors, the Carthaginians defeated them and compelled them to dwell very far from Carthage. 10.28. Then the Romans, having become superior to all in war, settled the Moors at the extremities of the inhabited land of Libya, and made the Carthaginians and the other Libyans subject to themselves and tributary. 10.29. And later the Moors, winning many victories over the Vandals, took possession of what is now called Mauretania, extending from Gadira to the borders of Caesarea, and of most of the rest of Libya. So the matter of the settlement of the Moors in Libya was in this way. 11.1. But Solomon, hearing what had befallen Rufinus and Aïgan, set about preparing for war and wrote to the commanders of the Moors as follows: 11.2. "It has already fallen to certain other men to lose their senses and to perish, who had no means before of conjecturing how their madness would turn out for them. 11.3. But you, who have the example near at hand in the Vandals who dwelt beside you, what ever has happened to you that you have resolved to raise your hands against the great emperor and to throw away your own salvation, 11.4. and that too after giving the most terrible oaths in writing and offering your children as pledges of your agreements? 11.5. Or have you decided to make some demonstration that you have no regard for God or for faith or for kinship itself or for your safety or for anything else whatever? 11.6. And yet, if your dealings with the divine are thus, in what ally do you trust as you march against the emperor of the Romans? 11.7. And if you are about to destroy your children by taking the field, for what then have you resolved to run the risk? 11.8. But if any repentance for what has gone before has now entered you, write, that we may settle for you well what has been done; but if your madness has not yet abated, receive a Roman war coming against you together with the oaths you have outraged and the wrong done to your children." 11.9. So much Solomon wrote. But the Moors answered thus: "Belisarius, encompassing us with great promises, persuaded us to be subjects of the Emperor Justinian; but the Romans, giving us a share in none of their good things, while we were oppressed by famine, demanded to have us as friends and allies. 11.10. So that it is fitting that the name of faithless should belong rather to you than to the Moors. 11.11. For it is not those who, being wronged, openly accuse their neighbours and revolt who break the truce, but those who, claiming to hold others as allies, then do them violence. 11.12. And it is not those who go against others to recover their own who make God hostile to them, but those who lay claim to what belongs to others and so come into the danger of war. 11.13. As for children, that will be a concern to you, who must marry one wife each; for to us, who have wives, even fifty if it so happen, dwelling with us, the breed of children would never fail." 11.14. When Solomon had read this, he decided to lead his whole army against the Moors. And having set in order affairs in Carthage, he went with all his army to Byzacium. 11.15. And coming to the place called Mammes, where the four commanders of the Moors whom I mentioned a little before had encamped, he made a stockade. 11.16. Now there are lofty mountains there, and a level space about the foot of the mountains, where the barbarians, having made their preparation, set their array for battle thus. 11.17. Forming a circle of their camels — the very thing which Cabaon also was said in the previous narrative to have done — they made the depth of the front about twelve camels. 11.18. And the women with the children they placed within the circle (for it is the custom among the Moors to bring a few women with the children into the battle-line, who make for them their stockades and huts, and tend the horses skilfully, and have charge of the camels and the food; 11.19. and, sharpening the iron of their weapons, they relieve them of much of the toil in the battle-lines); and they themselves on foot stood in the middle, between the legs of the camels, having shields and swords and javelins, with which they are accustomed to hurl. And some of them, keeping their horses in the mountains, remained quiet. 11.20. But Solomon left untouched the half of the Moorish circle which chanced to be next to the mountain, stationing no one there. 11.21. For he feared lest the enemy in the mountain, coming down, and those in the circle, turning about, should put those arrayed there between two fires in the battle-line. 11.22. And arraying his whole army against the remaining part of the circle, when he saw that most of them were afraid and without courage on account of what had befallen Aïgan and Rufinus, wishing to make for them a reminder of courage, he spoke as follows: 11.23. "Men who took the field with Belisarius, let no fear of these men enter you, nor, if the Moors, gathered together to the number of fifty thousand, conquered five hundred Romans, let this become to you in the place of an example. 11.24. But remember your own valour, and reckon that the Vandals conquered the Moors, while you have become masters of the Vandals in war without an effort; and that for those who have mastered the greater to fear the lesser is not just. 11.25. And yet the nation of the Moors seems to be the most worthless of all men for a contest of war. 11.26. For the most of them are naked, and those of them who have shields hold before themselves shields which are small and not well made and unable to ward off what comes against them. 11.27. And after hurling these two javelins, if they accomplish nothing, 11.28. they turn of their own accord to flight. So that it is possible for you, after guarding against the first onset of the barbarians, to win the mastery in war with no trouble. 11.29. And how great the difference is between your equipment and that of the enemy you surely see. 11.30. And besides this, valour of soul and strength of body and experience of wars and confidence, by reason of having already conquered all the enemy, belong to you; but the Moors, deprived of all these things, trust in their own throng alone. 11.31. And it is easier for a few men, best equipped, to conquer in war a multitude of men who are not good, than to be defeated by them. 11.32. For to the good soldier confidence in himself is present, but for the cowardly the multitude of his fellows in array for the most part turns into a perilous straitness. 11.33. And indeed it is right that you should despise these camels too, which are neither able to defend their masters, and, when struck, as is likely, will be the cause to them of greater confusion and disorder. 11.34. And the rashness which the enemy have gained by their former success will fight on your side. 11.35. For daring, when measured to one's power, will perhaps even profit those who use it, 11.36. but when it overpasses this, it leads to danger. Bearing these things in mind, and despising the enemy, practise silence and good order; for taking care of these things, we shall master the disorder of the barbarians more easily and with less toil." Thus Solomon spoke. 11.37. But the commanders of the Moors, when they too saw the barbarians dismayed at the good order of the Romans, wishing to bring their multitude back to courage, exhorted them thus: 11.38. "That the Romans have human bodies and such as we have learned yield when struck with iron, fellow-soldiers — we who lately slew the best of them, partly by burying them under our spears, partly by seizing and making them our captives. 11.39. And these things being so, that we now far surpass them in multitude, it is possible to see. 11.40. And indeed our struggle is for the greatest stakes — either to be masters of all Libya, 11.41. or to be slaves to these braggarts. So that we must of necessity play the man now as much as possible. For those whose danger is for their all, not to be most stout-hearted is inexpedient. 11.42. And it is fitting that we despise the equipment of the enemy. For if they come against us on foot, they will not be nimble, but will be worsted by the swiftness of the Moors, and as for their cavalry, the sight of the camels, striking them with dismay, and the bellowing of these, drowning out the other tumult of war, will, as is likely, throw them into disorder. 11.43. And if anyone, reckoning up the victory over the Vandals, thinks that they are not to be contended with, he errs in judgment. 11.44. For the issue of war is wont to be decided by the valour or fortune of the general; and as for Belisarius, who was the cause of the conquest of the Vandals, the divine power has caused him now to stand out of our way. 11.45. Besides, we ourselves, having often conquered the Vandals and stripped them of their power, have made the mastery over them easier and less toilsome for the Romans. 11.46. And now too we have hope of mastering these enemy, if you play the man in the action." 11.47. When the commanders of the Moors had thus exhorted them, they began the encounter. And at first great disorder fell upon the Roman army. 11.48. For their horses, distressed by the bellowing and the sight of the camels, reared up, and, throwing off their riders, fled in no order, most of them. 11.49. And meanwhile the Moors, making sallies and hurling all the javelins they had in their hands, kept filling the army with confusion, and struck them as they neither defended themselves nor kept their array. 11.50. But afterward Solomon, perceiving what was being done, leaped down first from his horse and led all the rest to do the same. 11.51. And when they had dismounted, he commanded the others to remain quiet, holding their shields before them and receiving the missiles sent from the enemy, and to keep their array; while he himself, taking with him no fewer than five hundred soldiers, attacked a part of the circle. 11.52. These he commanded to draw their swords and kill the camels that stood there. 11.53. Then the Moors who were stationed there turned to flight, and those with Solomon killed about two hundred camels; and straightway the circle, when the camels had fallen, 11.54. became open to the Romans. And they ran at a run into the middle of the circle, where the women of the Moors sat; while the barbarians, dismayed, withdrew to the mountain which was nearest, and the Romans, pursuing them in their flight with all disorder, kept killing them. 11.55. And it is said that ten thousand of the Moors perished in this action; and the women, all of them, with the children, became slaves. 11.56. And the soldiers plundered all the camels, as many as they had not killed. And thus the Romans went with all the booty to Carthage to celebrate the festival of victory. 12.1. But the barbarians, with one accord using their fury against the Romans again, leaving none of themselves behind, took the field and began to overrun the regions in Byzacium, sparing no age among those who fell in their way. 12.2. And when Solomon had just arrived at Carthage, it was reported that barbarians in great multitude had come to Byzacium and were plundering everything there. So setting out in haste with all his army, he went against them. 12.3. And coming to Burgaon, where the enemy had encamped, for some days he sat opposite them, so that, as soon as the Moors should come down into the level ground, he might begin the encounter. 12.4. But as they remained in the mountain, he set his army in order as for battle and arrayed it; and the Moors planned by no means to go down henceforth into the plain to battle with the Romans (for already an irresistible fear came over them), but in the mountain they hoped to overcome them more easily in war. 12.5. Now the mountain Burgaon is for the most part precipitous, and the side toward the rising sun terribly hard to traverse, while the side toward the west is easy of approach and gently sloping. 12.6. And two lofty peaks rise up, making a glen between them, exceedingly narrow but stretching down to an unspeakable depth. 12.7. The barbarians left the summit of the mountain empty of men, thinking that no danger to them would come thence; and likewise they left the place about the foot, where Burgaon was easy of approach. 12.8. But encamping in the middle, they waited, so that, if the enemy, ascending against them, should begin the battle, they themselves, being already above them, might hurl missiles down upon their heads. 12.9. And there were with them in the mountain also many horses, made ready either for flight or for pursuit, if they should master the battle. 12.10. But Solomon, when he saw that the Moors no longer wished to fight it out in the level ground, and at the same time was distressed that the Roman army should sit idle in the blockade in a desolate place, was eager to come to grips with the enemy in Burgaon. 12.11. And seeing the soldiers dismayed at the throng of their opponents, many times greater than that which had appeared in the former battle, he called the multitude together and spoke as follows: 12.12. "The fear which the enemy feel toward you needs no other accuser, but is self-proclaimed and convicted, bringing the testimony from its own home. 12.13. For you see surely that the enemy, gathered together to so many tens of thousands, do not dare to come down into the plain and join battle with us, nor have confidence in themselves, but have taken refuge in the difficulty of this place. 12.14. So that there is no necessity even to exhort you at present. For those to whom the circumstances and the weakness of the enemy give confidence have no need, I think, of the help that comes from words. 12.15. But this much it will be necessary to remind you of: that, if we carry through this encounter too with good courage, it will be left to us, the Vandals having been conquered and the Moors having come to the same fortune, to enjoy all the good things of Libya, with nothing left that we can reckon as hostile. 12.16. And that the enemy may not hurl missiles down upon your heads, nor any harm come to us from the ground, I shall provide." 12.17. After Solomon had thus exhorted them, he commanded Theodore, who was leader of the excubitores (for thus the Romans call their guards), to take a thousand foot-soldiers, and about late afternoon, having with him one of the standards, to ascend secretly the side of Burgaon toward the rising sun, where the mountain was most difficult and almost impassable, charging him that, when they should come near the crest of the mountain, they should there remain quiet and pass the rest of the night, and at sunrise, appearing above the enemy and displaying the standards, should hurl their missiles. 12.18. And he did accordingly. And when the night was far advanced, ascending through the precipitous part near the peak, they escaped the notice not only of the Moors but of all the Romans as well; 12.19. for they were sent out, by way of pretext, as an advance-guard, lest anyone from outside should go to do mischief to the camp. And at deep dawn Solomon with all his army began to ascend against the enemy by the lower part of Burgaon. 12.20. And when day had come and the enemy were seen near at hand, the soldiers, no longer beholding the summit of the mountain bare, as before, but full of men and displaying Roman standards (for already some part of the day was showing), were perplexed. 12.21. But when those on the summit began the fight, and the Romans perceived that the army was their own and the barbarians perceived that they had come into the midst of the enemy, being struck from both sides and unable to defend themselves against the enemy, they no longer looked to defence, but all at once turned to flight. 12.22. And being unable to run up to the summit of Burgaon, held by the enemy, nor to go down to the level ground through the foot, where their opponents were pressing upon them, they went at a great run into the glen and to one of the two peaks, some on horseback, some on foot. 12.23. And since they were a great throng fleeing in fear and great tumult, they kept killing one another, and, falling into the glen, which was exceedingly deep, the first ones kept dying, but gave no perception of the disaster to those coming behind. 12.24. But when the glen, becoming full of dead horses and men, made a crossing from Burgaon to the other mountain, then those who were left were saved, making their way over the bodies. 12.25. And there perished in this action of the Moors fifty thousand, as the survivors among them maintained, but of the Romans not one at all, nor did anyone even receive a wound either from the enemy or by any chance befalling him, but all unhurt enjoyed this victory. 12.26. And all the leaders of the barbarians escaped, except indeed that Esdilasas, receiving pledges, delivered himself up to the Romans. 12.27. As for the booty of women and children, the Romans took so great a multitude that for the price of a sheep they sold a Moorish child to those who wished to buy. 12.28. And then there came over the survivors among the Moors the prophecy of their women, that their race should be destroyed by a beardless man. 12.29. So the Roman army with the booty and Esdilasas marched into Carthage; while of the barbarians who chanced not to have perished, it seemed impossible to be settled in Byzacium, lest, being few, they should suffer violence from the Libyans who bordered upon them; and going with their own commanders into Numidia, they became suppliants of Iaudas, who ruled the Moors in Aurasium. 12.30. Alone of the Moors there remained in Byzacium those whose leader was Antalas, who in this time, keeping faith with the Romans, remained free from harm with his own subjects. 13.1. While these things were happening in Byzacium, Iaudas, who ruled the Moors in Aurasium, leading more than thirty thousand fighting men, plundered the regions in Numidia and made slaves of many of the Libyans. 13.2. Now it chanced that Althias was holding the garrison of the fortresses there in Centuriae; he, being eager to take away some of the captives from the enemy, with the Huns who followed him, about seventy in number, got outside the fortress. 13.3. And reckoning that he was not able with seventy men to come to grips with so great a multitude of the Moors, he wished to seize some narrow place, so that, as the enemy went along the road through it, he might be able to snatch away some of the captives. 13.4.
