And (since there is no such road there, the regions thereabouts being level plains on every side) he devised the following. 13.5. There is a city near by, Tigisis by name, at that time unwalled, but having a certain great spring in a very narrow place. 13.6. This spring Althias decided to seize, reckoning that the enemy, compelled by thirst, would by all means come there; for there was no other water at all near by. 13.7. To all who reckoned up the multitude of the enemy, the thought seemed contrary to reason, and his plan to be madness. 13.8. But the Moors, having met with much toil and great suffocating heat in the summer season, and, as was likely, oppressed by very great thirst from this, came to the spring at a great run, with no thought of any obstacle in mind. 13.9. But when they found the water held by the enemy, they all stood in perplexity, the greatest part of their strength being already spent on their desire for the water. 13.10. Wherefore Iaudas, coming to a parley with Althias, agreed to give him the third part of the booty, on condition that all the Moors should drink. 13.11. But he by no means wished to accept the proposal, and demanded to fight a single combat with him over these things. 13.12. And when Iaudas had accepted this challenge, it was agreed that, if Althias should chance to be defeated, the Moors should drink. 13.13. And the whole army of the Moors rejoiced, being of good hope, since Althias was thin and not large of body, while Iaudas was the fairest and most warlike of all the Moors. 13.14. Both, then, chanced to be horsemen. And Iaudas hurled his javelin first, and Althias, as it came against him, succeeded beyond expectation in catching it with his right hand, and struck Iaudas and the enemy with dismay. 13.15. And drawing his bow with his left hand at once, since he was ambidextrous, he hit the horse of Iaudas and killed it. 13.16. And when it had fallen, the Moors brought another horse for their commander, upon which Iaudas leaped and straightway fled; and in no order the army of the Moors followed him. 13.17. And Althias, taking away the captives and all the booty, won a great name from this deed throughout all Libya. These things, then, went thus. 13.18. But Solomon, after spending a short time in Carthage, led his army against Mount Aurasium and Iaudas, bringing against him the charge that, when the Roman army had its occupation in Byzacium, he plundered many of the regions in Numidia. And so it was. 13.19. And other commanders of the Moors urged Solomon on against Iaudas — Massonas and Ortaïas — because of their own enmity: Massonas, because Iaudas, being his father Mephanias's son-in-law, had slain him by treachery; the other, because, along with Mastinas, who ruled the barbarians in Mauretania, he had planned to drive both him and the Moors he ruled out of the country where they had dwelt of old. 13.20. So the Roman army, with Solomon leading them, and the Moors who came to them as allies, encamped at the river Abigas, which, flowing past Aurasium, waters the regions there. 13.21. To Iaudas it seemed inexpedient to array himself against the enemy in the plain, but he set in order matters in Aurasium so that it should seem to him as difficult as possible for the assailants. 13.22. Now this mountain is distant from Carthage about thirteen days' journey, and it is the greatest of all we know. 13.23. For its circuit is a journey of three days for an unencumbered man. And to one wishing to go up into it, it is hard of access and terribly wild, but to one who has come up and reached the level ground there appear plains and many springs forming rivers, and a great number of parks, wonderful to behold. 13.24. And the grain which grows there and every kind of fruit is double the size of that which is wont to grow in all the rest of Libya. 13.25. There are also some fortresses there, neglected, because they seem not necessary to those who dwell there. 13.26. For from the time the Moors took Aurasium from the Vandals, no enemy ever came to it or put the barbarians in fear, but even the city of Tamougadis, which, lying at the mountain at the beginning of the plain toward the rising sun, was populous, the Moors made empty of men and razed to the ground, so that the enemy should not be able to encamp there, nor even, on the pretext of the city, to come near the mountain. 13.27. And the Moors there held also the country to the west of Aurasium, 13.28. which was large and good. And beyond these dwelt other nations of the Moors, whom Ortaïas ruled, who, 13.29. as has been said before, came as an ally to Solomon and the Romans. I myself heard this man saying that beyond the country which he ruled no men dwell, but a desert land stretches over a very great distance, and beyond this are men, not black-skinned like the Moors, but very white in body and fair-haired. So these things are thus. 13.30. But Solomon, having presented the allied Moors with great sums of money, and after much exhortation, with his whole army ascended Mount Aurasium arrayed as for battle, supposing that on that day he would both come to battle with the enemy and be parted from them, whichever way fortune should wish. 13.31. For the soldiers brought along for themselves and their horses only a little food. 13.32. And going on amid much rough country about fifty stades, they bivouacked. 13.33. And accomplishing so great a journey each day, on the seventh they arrived at a place where there was an old fortress and a perennial river. The Latins call the place 'Shield Mountain' in their own tongue. 13.34. There the enemy were reported to be encamping, and when they came to this place and no enemy met them, they encamped and, making preparation as for battle, remained there, and a period of three days was spent by them there. 13.35. But when the enemy stood altogether out of their way and provisions failed, it came into the mind of Solomon and the whole army that some plot against them was being formed by the allied Moors; 13.36. for these men, although they were not without practice in the journey through Aurasium, and knew, as was likely, all that the enemy had planned, hastening to them secretly each day, as was said, and often sent to them by the Romans for scouting, had decided to report nothing sound, so that the Romans, not learning beforehand, might not, having more provisions for a longer time, ascend Mount Aurasium and make their other preparations in the way that would be best. 13.37. And altogether suspecting that an ambush had been laid for them by their allies, they came into fear, reckoning that the Moors were said to be by nature faithless, especially when, fighting as allies of the Romans or any others, they take the field against Moors. 13.38. Bearing these things in mind, and at the same time oppressed by famine, they withdrew thence in haste without accomplishing anything, and, coming to the plain, made a stockade. 13.39. Afterward Solomon, stationing a part of the army for the sake of guard in Numidia (for it was now winter), with the rest went to Carthage. 13.40. There he managed and arranged everything, so that at the opening of spring he might take the field again against Aurasium with greater preparation and, if he should be able, without the alliance of the Moors. 13.41. And at the same time he was preparing generals and another army and a fleet of ships against the Moors who dwell in the island of Sardinia; 13.42. for this island is large and otherwise prosperous, extending toward the two parts of Sicily (for the circuit of its land is a journey of twenty days for an unencumbered man), and lying midway between Rome and Carthage, it is oppressed by the Moors who dwell there. 13.43. For the Vandals of old, using their anger against these barbarians, sent some few of them with their wives to Sardinia and shut them up there. 13.44. And as time went on, they seized the mountains which are somewhere near Caranalis, at first making robberies in secret upon their neighbours, but when they became no fewer than three thousand, overrunning the land openly too, and, deeming it not worth while to escape notice, plundered all the regions there, being called Barbaricini by the natives. 13.45. Against these Moors, then, Solomon was making ready a fleet during this winter. These things, then, were going on in Libya in this way. 14.1. In Italy during this same time the following things chanced to happen. Belisarius was being sent by the Emperor Justinian against Theudatus and the nation of the Goths, and, sailing to Sicily, he took this island with no trouble. 14.2. In what manner he did so will be told in the later part of my narrative, when the account brings me to the history of the affairs of Italy. 14.3. For now it has seemed to me not out of place, having recorded all that happened in Libya, thus to go on to the account concerning Italy and the Goths. 14.4. During this winter, then, Belisarius spent his time in Syracuse, and Solomon in Carthage. 14.5. And a most dread portent chanced to come to pass in this year. For the sun gave forth its light without brightness, like the moon, throughout the whole of this year, and it seemed exceedingly like the sun in eclipse, for the beams it shed were not clear nor such as it is accustomed to shed. 14.6. And from the time when this happened, men were free neither from war nor pestilence nor anything else leading to death. And it was the time when Justinian was in the tenth year of his reign. 14.7. And at the opening of spring, when the Christians were keeping the feast which they call Easter, a mutiny fell upon the soldiers in Libya. How it arose and to what end it came, I shall now tell. 14.8. When the Vandals had been defeated in the battle, as I have said before, the Roman soldiers took their daughters and wives in the place of married wives. 14.9. And each of these women kept urging her husband to lay claim to the possession of the lands of which she had previously been mistress, saying that it was not holy if, while dwelling with the Vandals, they had enjoyed these lands, but, having come in marriage to those who had conquered them, they should thus be deprived of what was theirs. 14.10. Bearing these things in mind, the soldiers did not think they ought to yield to Solomon, who wished to register the lands of the Vandals to the public treasury and the emperor's house, saying that it was not unreasonable for the slaves and all the other goods to go to the soldiers as plunder, but that the land itself belonged to the emperor and the Roman state, which had reared them and had made them to be called soldiers and to be such, not in order that they should acquire for themselves the lands which they had taken from barbarians who had usurped the empire of the Romans, but in order that these should go to the public treasury, from which both they and all others receive their pay. 14.11. This, then, was one cause of the mutiny. And another also chanced to come about of the following kind, which no less, if not more, had power to confound all the affairs in Libya. 14.12. In the Roman army it chanced that there were no fewer than a thousand soldiers of the Arian faith; of these the most were barbarians, and some of them of the Erulian nation. 14.13. These the priests of the Vandals urged most of all to mutiny. For it was not possible for them to perform the customary rites to God, but they were excluded from all mysteries and sacred things. 14.14. For the Emperor Justinian did not permit a Christian man who had not partaken of the orthodox faith to use either baptism or any other mystery. 14.15. And most of all the feast of Easter confounded them, at which they were unable to baptize their own children in the divine bath, or do anything else pertaining to this feast. 14.16. And as if these things were not enough for the divine power, which was eager to destroy the affairs of the Romans, something else also befell as a provision for those who were planning the mutiny. 14.17. The Vandals whom Belisarius had brought to Byzantium the emperor had organized into five cavalry detachments, so that they should be settled in the cities of the East for all time; and calling them the Justinianic Vandals, he commanded them to be conveyed with ships to the East. 14.18. Of these Vandal soldiers the most came to the East and, filling the detachments to which they had been assigned, take the field against the Persians even to this day; but the others, about four hundred in number, when they came to Lesbos, with their sails bellied out, forced the sailors and put in at the Peloponnesus. 14.19. And setting out thence, they sailed to Libya and landed at a desolate place, where, leaving the ships and gathering their gear, they went up to Mount Aurasium and into Mauretania. 14.20. Encouraged by these, the soldiers who had the mutiny in charge united among themselves still more. 14.21. And many words about this and oaths now took place in the camp. And when they were about to keep the feast, the Arians, distressed at the prohibition of their sacred rites, pressed exceedingly hard. 14.22. And it seemed good to their leaders, on the first day of the feast, which they call the Great Day, 14.23. to kill Solomon. And they escaped detection, no one having disclosed this plan. For inasmuch as those who were planning the dreadful deed were many, the talk, going round, fell upon no one hostile to them, and in this way they were able to escape notice, since indeed many of Solomon's own guardsmen and spearmen and most of his servants had been enrolled in this mutiny through their desire for the lands. 14.24. And when the appointed day was now at hand, Solomon was sitting in the sanctuary, far removed from his own danger. 14.25. And those who had resolved to kill this man went in and, urging one another on with nods, laid hold of their swords; yet they did nothing, either because they were ashamed before the rites then being performed in the sanctuary, or because they blushed before the general's reputation, or because something divine prevented them. 14.26. But when the sacred rites of that day had now been performed and each was being conveyed home, the mutineers blamed one another for having become soft when they ought not, and again put off the plan to the next day. 14.27. And in like manner on the following day too, having passed it without accomplishing anything, they withdrew from the sanctuary, and, coming to the market-place, abused one another openly, and each one, calling his neighbour a coward and a breaker of their fellowship, did not refuse to reproach him with his respect for Solomon. 14.28. Wherefore they no longer thought their stay in Carthage would be free from danger, inasmuch as they had brought the plan completely into the open. 14.29. So the most of them, going quickly outside the city, plundered the lands and treated as enemies the Libyans whom they met; but the others, remaining in the city, gave no perception of the purpose which they themselves held, but pretended to be ignorant of what had been planned. 14.30. But Solomon, hearing what was being done by the soldiers in the country, falling into great tumult, ceased not exhorting those in the city, calling upon them to be loyal to the emperor. 14.31. And they at first seemed to accept his words, but on the fifth day, when they heard that those who had gone out were firmly established in tyranny, gathering in the hippodrome, they outraged Solomon and the other commanders without restraint. 14.32. There Theodore the Cappadocian, sent by Solomon, undertook to console and tame them, but they paid no heed at all to what was said. 14.33. Now this Theodore had a grudge against Solomon and a suspicion of plotting against him. 14.34. Wherefore the mutineers straightway by acclamation voted him to be their general, and with him, bearing arms and using much tumult, they came quickly to the Palatium. 14.35. There they killed another Theodore, who was leader of the guards, a man who had attained the height of all virtue and was exceedingly good in matters of war. 14.36. And when they had tasted of this murder, they now killed everyone in their way, whether Libyan or Roman, who was an acquaintance of Solomon or who had money in his hands; and thence they withdrew to plunder, going up into the houses where soldiers did not defend them, and seized all the most precious things, until night, coming on, and drunkenness, succeeding their toil, made them cease. 14.37. But Solomon, taking refuge in the sanctuary which is great in the Palatium, escaped notice, and there Martinus too came to him about late afternoon. 14.38. And when all the mutineers were asleep, going out from the sanctuary they came to the house of Theodore the Cappadocian, who compelled them, though by no means eager, to dine, and, conveying them to the harbour, put them into a skiff of a certain ship which there chanced to have been made ready by Martinus. 14.39. And there followed them Procopius, who wrote these things, and about five men of the household of Solomon. 14.40. And accomplishing three hundred stades, they came to Misua, the port of the Carthaginians, and when they were in safety, straightway Solomon commanded Martinus to go to Numidia, to Valerianus and the other commanders, and to try, if in any way each one might be able, by money or in some other way, to come round some of the notable soldiers and bring them over to loyalty to the emperor. 14.41. And he sent a letter to Theodore, enjoining him to take charge of Carthage and to manage everything else as might seem to him possible; while he himself with Procopius came to Belisarius at Syracuse. 14.42. And reporting to him all that had chanced to happen in Libya, he begged him to go quickly to Carthage and to aid the emperor, who was suffering unholy things at the hands of his own soldiers. So Solomon did this. 15.1. But the mutineers, having plundered everything in Carthage, and gathering in the plain of Bulla, chose for themselves as tyrant Stotzas, one of the guardsmen of Martinus, a man high-spirited and energetic, in order that, after driving out the emperor's commanders, they might master all Libya. 15.2. And he, having armed his whole force, amounting to about eight thousand, led it against Carthage, intending to bring the city over to himself straightway with no trouble. 15.3. And he sent also to the Vandals who had run away from Byzantium with the ships and those who from the first had not followed Belisarius, either having escaped notice or because those who at that time were conveying the Vandals had made no account of them. 15.4. And there were no fewer than a thousand, who not long afterward came with eagerness to Stotzas in the camp. And there came to him also a great throng of slaves. 15.5. And when they were near Carthage, Stotzas sent a message, commanding them to surrender the city to him as quickly as possible, 15.6. on condition that they should remain free from harm. But those in Carthage and Theodore, refusing this outright, agreed with the emperor to guard Carthage. 15.7. And sending to him Josephius, who had become a not undistinguished secretary of the emperor's guards and was of the household of Belisarius, and had lately been sent to them in Carthage on some business, they begged him to use no further force against them. 15.8. But Stotzas, when he heard this, straightway killed Josephius and set about the siege. And those in the city, dreading the danger, planned to deliver themselves and Carthage to Stotzas by agreement. So the army of Libya was in this state. 15.9. But Belisarius, picking out a hundred men of his own guardsmen and spearmen and taking Solomon along, sailed to Carthage with a single ship at lamp-lighting time, when the besiegers expected the city to be delivered to them on the following day. And holding these things in hope, they bivouacked that night. 15.10. But when day had come and they learned that Belisarius was present, dissolving the camp as quickly as possible, shamefully and in no order, they turned to flight. 15.11. And Belisarius, gathering about two thousand of the army and urging them on to loyalty to the emperor by words, and strengthening them with much money, made the pursuit upon the fugitives. 15.12. And he overtook them at the city of Membresa, distant three hundred and fifty stades from Carthage. 15.13. There each side encamped and made ready for battle, those with Belisarius at the river Bagradas, the others making their stockade in a place lofty and difficult. 15.14. For into the city neither side decided to go, since it chanced to be unwalled. 15.15. And on the following day they joined the encounter, the mutineers trusting in their own multitude, those with Belisarius despising the enemy as senseless and without a general. 15.16. And Belisarius, wishing to fix these things firmly in the minds of the soldiers, called them all together and spoke as follows: "It is less than our hope and prayer, fellow-soldiers, that the affairs of the emperor and of the Romans stand. 15.17. For we have now come to an encounter from which we shall not even have the victory without tears, taking the field against kinsmen and those nurtured with us. 15.18. But we have this comfort for the evil, that we are not ourselves beginning the battle, but defending ourselves we come into the danger. 15.19. For he who has made the plot against his dearest and dissolved the kinship by what he has done, if he perishes, dies not at the hands of friends, but, having become as an enemy, pays the penalty to those whom he has wronged. 15.20. And that the enemy are foes and barbarians and whatever one might say more dreadful, not only does Libya show, which has come into plunder under their hands, nor those who dwell in it, slain by them without cause, but also the multitude of Roman soldiers whom these foes dared to kill, charging against them one accusation alone, their loyalty to the state. 15.21. Avenging whom, we have now come against them, having reasonably become foes to those once dearest. 15.22. For by nature none of all men would be friendly or hostile to one another, but the deeds of each, either joining men in alliance by likeness of character, or distinguishing them into enmity by difference of judgment, make them, as it may chance, either friends or enemies to one another. 15.23. That, then, we are taking the field against unholy and hostile men, you have enough; and that they are worthy to be despised by us, I shall show. 15.24. For a throng of men gathered together not by law but assembled out of injustice is by no means apt to play the man, since valour cannot in any way dwell with lawlessness, but ever withdraws from the unholy. 15.25. Nor will they keep good order, nor obey the commands of Stotzas. 15.26. For a tyranny lately established and not yet having received the power to feel confidence must of necessity be despised by the ruled. 15.27. For neither is it honoured by goodwill, since tyranny is wont to be hated, nor does it lead its subjects by fear; for fear has taken away from it its frankness. 15.28. And when the enemy are left without valour and good order, they are easily defeated. With much contempt, then, as I said, it is fitting for us to go against these enemy. 15.29. For the mastery in war is wont to be measured not by the multitude of the combatants, but by good order and courage." 15.30. Belisarius spoke thus. And Stotzas exhorted his men as follows: "Men who with me have got outside the slavery to the Romans, let none of you deem it not worth while to die for liberty, which you have won by courage and all other valour. 15.31. For it is not so dreadful, after growing old amid evils, to end one's life, as, after the freedom from hardships, to return to them again. 15.32. For the time in between, having given a taste of release, makes the calamity, as is likely, harder to bear. 15.33. These things being so, you must remember that, having conquered the Vandals and the Moors, you yourselves enjoyed the toils of the wars, while others became masters of all the spoils. 15.34. And reckon that, being soldiers, you must consort with the dangers of war for all time — either for the emperor's affairs, if you should again be his slaves, or for your own selves, if you preserve this liberty. 15.35. And which of the two is the more to be chosen, it is in your power to choose, either by playing the coward in the present, or by wishing to play the man. 15.36. And indeed this too it is fitting that you should consider: that, having taken up arms against the Romans, if you come to be under them, you will make trial of masters neither moderate nor forgiving, but you will suffer irreparable things, and there will be added to you the consolation of not having perished unjustly. Death, then, to whomsoever of you it may come in this battle, will plainly be glorious; 15.37. but life, for those who master the enemy, will be independent and otherwise happy, while for the defeated I would call it nothing else but bitter, having all its hope in the pity of those men." 15.38. And the encounter will not be on equal terms of power. 15.39. For in multitude the enemy fall far short of us, and they come against us with the least eagerness — men who, I think, even pray to share with us this liberty." Such things Stotzas also said. 15.40. As the armies were going to the encounter, a wind hard and dreadfully troublesome fell full in the face of the mutineers of Stotzas. 15.41. Wherefore they thought it inexpedient to make the battle there, fearing lest the wind, overpowering them, should both direct the missiles of the enemy upon them and check most of all the force of their own missiles. 15.42. Setting out, then, they went obliquely, reckoning that, if the enemy too, as was likely, should shift, so that they might not be harassed from behind by them, the wind would be in their faces. 15.43. But Belisarius, when he saw them leaving their array and going about in no order, straightway commanded the attack to begin. 15.44. And those with Stotzas, thrown into confusion by the unexpected, with much disorder, as each one could, turned to flight, and, coming into Numidia, gathered again. 15.45. Few of them, however, perished in this action, and most of these were Vandals. 15.46. For Belisarius made no pursuit at all upon them, since, his army being very small, it seemed enough to him if the enemy, being for the present defeated, should stand out of his way. 15.47. And he gave the soldiers the stockade of their opponents to plunder, and they took it empty of men. There were found there much money and many women, on account of whom this war had arisen. Having accomplished these things, Belisarius marched off to Carthage. 15.48. And someone, coming from Sicily, reported to him that a mutiny, having fallen upon the army, was about to throw affairs into confusion, unless he himself, returning quickly to them, should put a stop to it. 15.49. And he, after setting in order the affairs in Libya as best he could and handing over Carthage to Ildiger and Theodore, went to Sicily. 15.50. But the Roman commanders in Numidia, when they heard that the forces of Stotzas had come and were gathering there, made ready for battle. Now the leaders of the foederati were Marcellus and Cyril, of a cavalry detachment Barbatus, 15.51. and of infantry Terentius and Sarapis. To Marcellus, however, all gave heed, inasmuch as he held the command of Numidia. 15.52. He, when he heard that Stotzas was at a place called Gazophyla, distant about two days' journey from Constantina, with a few men, wishing to get the start before all the mutineers should gather, led his army quickly against them. 15.53. But when the armies had come near and the battle was about to be at hand, Stotzas alone, coming into the midst of his opponents, spoke as follows: 15.54. "Fellow-soldiers, you do not do what is just, taking the field against kinsmen and those nurtured with you, and raising arms against men who, distressed at your evils and at the wrongs done to you, have decided to make war upon the emperor and the Romans. 15.55. Or do you not remember that you have been deprived of the pay long owed to you, and robbed of the spoils of the enemy, which the law of war has set as the prizes of the dangers of battle? 15.56. And that, while others have thought it right to revel for all time in the good things of victory, you follow in the lot of servants? 15.57. If, then, you are angry with me, it is in your power to use your fury upon this body alone, but to escape the defilement against the rest; but if you have no accusation to bring against me, it is time for you, on behalf of your own selves, 15.58. to take up arms." So Stotzas said this much; and the soldiers accepted his words and greeted him with much goodwill. 15.59. And the commanders, seeing what was being done, withdrew in silence and took refuge in a sanctuary which was in Gazophyla. But Stotzas, gathering both armies into one, went against them, and, finding them in the sanctuary and giving them pledges, killed them all. 16.1. When the emperor learned this, he sent Germanus, his own nephew, a man of patrician rank, to Libya with a few men. 16.2. And there followed him Symmachus and Domnicus, men of the senate, the one to be prefect and steward of the expense, Domnicus to be in charge of the infantry. For John, upon whom this office had rested, had now died after falling sick. 16.3. And when they had sailed to Carthage, Germanus numbered the soldiers present with them and, going through the books of the secretaries, where are recorded all the names of the soldiers, found that the third part of the army was in Carthage and the other cities, but all the rest had ranged themselves with the tyrant against the Romans. 16.4. So for this reason he did not begin battle, but took care of the army as well as possible. And reckoning that those left in Carthage chanced to be kinsmen or tent-mates of the enemy, he uttered many things enticing to all, and said that he himself had been sent by the emperor to Libya to defend the wronged soldiers and to punish those who had begun any wrong against them. 16.5. When the mutineers learned this, they began to come over to him in small numbers. And Germanus received them into the city with kindness, and, giving pledges, held them in honour, and gave them their pay for the time during which they were in arms against the Romans. 16.6. And when the talk about this, going round, came to all, they now in great numbers, abandoning the tyrant, marched into Carthage. 16.7. And then indeed Germanus, hoping that the battle with his opponents would be on equal terms of power, made ready for the array. 16.8. Meanwhile Stotzas, now perceiving his trouble, and fearing lest, by the desertion of still more soldiers, his army should be still further diminished, was eager to run the risk at once and to take hold of the war more sharply. 16.9. And he had some hope from the soldiers in Carthage concerning desertion, and thought that they, if they should come near, would with no trouble desert, having spread the hope abroad to all; and especially encouraging them by this, he went quickly against Carthage with his whole army. 16.10. And coming within thirty-five stades of it, he encamped not far from the sea, and Germanus, arming his whole force and arraying it as for battle, led it out. 16.11. And when they had got outside the city — for he had heard what Stotzas was hoping for — calling all together, he spoke as follows: 16.12. "That you would not justly blame the emperor in anything, fellow-soldiers, nor find fault with anything that has been done by him toward you, no one, I think, of all men would gainsay; 16.13. seeing that he, having gathered you who came from the country with a wallet and a single tunic, and brought you to Byzantium, has made you to be so great that the affairs of the Romans now rest upon you. 16.14. But that he has chanced not only to be insulted, but also to suffer the most dreadful things of all at your hands, 16.15. you yourselves surely also know. Wishing the memory of these things to be preserved for you forever, he has remitted the grounds of complaint, deeming this debt alone to be owed him by you — the shame for what has been done. 16.16. Being led by this consideration, it is reasonable that you should unlearn your faithlessness and set right your former folly. 16.17. For repentance, coming upon those who have stumbled at the right time, is wont to make those who have been wronged forgiving toward them, and service, coming at the proper moment, is wont to change the name of the ungrateful." 16.18. "And this too it will be well for you to know: that, if in the present you become most loyal to the emperor, no memory of what has gone before will be left. 16.19. For every deed is ever wont to be named by men from its conclusion; and a fault once committed could not in all time be made undone, but, set right by deeds better than those which wrought it, it attains a seemly silence and for the most part comes round to oblivion. 16.20. And yet, if you now treat these accursed men with some negligence, and afterward, contending in many wars on behalf of the Romans, often win the mastery over the enemy, you would no longer seem to have rendered the like service to the emperor. 16.21. For those who win good repute in the very matters in which they erred bear forever a more seemly defence. So let each one of you reckon thus concerning the emperor. 16.22. And I, who have begun no wrong against you, and have shown by every means my goodwill toward you, and am now coming into this danger, have decided to ask this much of all: let no one go with us against the enemy contrary to his own judgment. 16.23. But if it is now the wish of any of you to range himself with them, let him, without delay, go with his arms to the camp of our opponents, granting us this one favour only, that he has decided to wrong us not secretly but openly. 16.24. For this is the reason that I make my speech not in Carthage but in the open space between the armies, so that I may be a hindrance to no one who wishes to desert to our opponents, it being possible for all, free from danger, to display 16.25. their purpose toward the state." Germanus said this much. And there was great commotion in the Roman army, since each one was eager to be first to display his goodwill toward the emperor to the general and to swear the most terrible oaths concerning these things. 17.1. For some time, then, each side remained, sitting opposite the other. But afterward the mutineers, seeing that nothing of what Stotzas had foretold was coming to pass, became afraid, inasmuch as their hope had been belied beyond expectation, and, dissolving their array, withdrew and marched off to Numidia, where their women and the goods of the booty were. 17.2. Thither Germanus too with his whole army came not long afterward, having made his other preparations as well as possible and bringing many wagons for the army. 17.3. And overtaking his opponents at a place which the Romans call Scalae Veteres, he made ready for the array in the following manner. 17.4. Placing the wagons in a line in front, he stationed all the infantry by them, of whom Domnicus was leader, so that, having their backs in safety, they might be the more confident. 17.5. And of the horsemen the best men, and those who had come with him from Byzantium, he himself held on the left of the infantry, but all the others he stationed on the right wing, not in one array, but in about three companies. 17.6. And of these Ildiger led one, Theodore the Cappadocian another, and the remaining one, which was the larger, John the brother of Pappus, himself the fourth in command. Thus, then, the Romans were arrayed. 17.7. And the mutineers stood facing them, not, however, arrayed in order, but scattered in barbarian fashion. 17.8. And there followed them at no great distance many tens of thousands of Moors, of whom, among many others, Iaudas and Ortaïas were leaders. 17.9. Not all, however, chanced to be faithful to the forces of Stotzas, but many, sending to Germanus beforehand, agreed that, when they should be in the action, they would range themselves with the emperor's army against the enemy. 17.10. Germanus, however, was not able to trust them altogether, since the nation of the Moors is by nature faithless toward all men. 17.11. Wherefore they did not even array themselves with the mutineers, but remained behind, watching for the outcome, so that with the victors they too might make the pursuit upon the defeated. 17.12. The Moors, then, with this purpose, not mingling with the mutineers, followed behind. 17.13. But Stotzas, when he had come very near the enemy, as soon as he saw the standard of Germanus, urging on those present, went against him. 17.14. But the Eruli who chanced to be arrayed as mutineers about him neither followed nor permitted it with all their might, saying that they did not know what the force of Germanus might be, but knew well that those who were arrayed on the right wing of the enemy would by no means withstand them. 17.15. If, then, they should go against those men, they themselves, not withstanding them, would turn to flight and would, as was likely, throw the rest of the army into confusion; but if Germanus, beating them off, should turn them, all their affairs would straightway be ruined. 17.16. Persuaded by these men, Stotzas left the others to fight with the forces of Germanus, while he himself with the best men went against John and those arrayed with him. 17.17. And they, not withstanding them, in no order turned to flight. And the mutineers straightway took all their standards, and pursued the fugitives with all their might, and some of them rode even against the infantry, 17.18. and the infantry now began to leave their array. But meanwhile Germanus himself, drawing his sword and rousing all the army there to the same, with much toil turned the mutineers opposed to him and at a run advanced against Stotzas. 17.19. And as the forces of Ildiger and Theodore joined him in this action, both sides became so mingled with one another that the mutineers, pursuing some of the enemy, were overtaken by others and slain. 17.20. And as the confusion advanced to a great pitch, the forces of Germanus, coming from behind, pressed on still more, while the mutineers, falling into great fear, no longer looked to defence. 17.21. Neither side, however, was distinguishable, either to themselves or to one another. For all used one tongue and the same fashion of arms, differing neither in form nor in dress nor in anything else whatever. 17.22. Wherefore, by the judgment of Germanus, the emperor's soldiers, whomsoever they should seize, asked who he was; then, if anyone said he was a soldier of Germanus, they bade him give the watchword of Germanus, and one who was in no way able to give this they straightway killed. 17.23. In this action one of the enemy, unobserved, killed the horse of Germanus, and Germanus himself, falling to the ground, came into danger, had not his guardsmen quickly saved him, fencing him round about and mounting him upon another horse. 17.24. So Stotzas in this tumult, with a few men, was able to escape. But Germanus, urging on his men, went straight against the camp of the enemy. 17.25. There those of the mutineers who had been stationed to guard the stockade met him. 17.26. And a fierce battle taking place about its entrance, the mutineers came within a little of beating off their opponents, but Germanus, sending some of those who followed him, commanded them to attempt another part of the camp. 17.27. And they, no one defending it there, got inside the stockade with little trouble. 17.28. And the mutineers, seeing them, turned to flight, and Germanus with all the rest of the army leaped into the camp of the enemy. 17.29. There the soldiers, plundering the goods with no trouble, made no account of their opponents nor any longer gave heed to the general as he exhorted them, the goods being at hand; wherefore Germanus, 17.30. fearing lest the enemy, coming to an understanding, should go against them, himself with a few men stood at the entrance of the stockade, lamenting much and calling those who paid no heed to good order. 17.31. And many of the Moors, the rout having thus come about, now pursued the mutineers and, ranging themselves with the emperor's army, plundered the camp of the defeated. 17.32. But Stotzas, at first having confidence in the army of the Moors, rode toward them, as if to renew the battle. 17.33. But perceiving what was being done, with a hundred men he was scarcely able to escape. 17.34. And again many, gathering about him, attempted to come to grips with the enemy, but, beaten off, no less, if not more, they all came over to Germanus. 17.35. And Stotzas alone, with a few Vandals, withdrew to Mauretania, and, taking as wife the daughter of one of the rulers, remained there. So this mutiny came to such an end. 18.1. Now there was among the guardsmen of Theodore the Cappadocian a certain Maximinus, an exceedingly wicked man. 18.2. This Maximinus, having with him very many of the soldiers who had sworn together against the state, 18.3. planned to make an attempt at tyranny. And being eager to win over still more to his fellowship, he disclosed the plan, among others, to Asclepiades, a man who came originally from Palestine, was well born, and was the first of the intimates of Theodore. 18.4. So Asclepiades, taking counsel with Theodore, straightway reported the whole matter to Germanus. 18.5. And he, not wishing, with his affairs still in suspense, to begin some other disturbance, decided to come round the man by flattery rather than by punishment, and to bind him by oaths to loyalty to the state. 18.6. Since, then, it was customary for all Romans from of old that no one should be appointed a guardsman of any commander unless he first, by providing the most terrible oaths, gave pledges of his loyalty toward him and toward the emperor of the Romans, Germanus, summoning Maximinus, praised his courage and bade him be henceforth his guardsman. 18.7. And he, overjoyed at the surpassing honour, and supposing that thereby his attack would proceed more easily for him, both submitted to the oath and thereafter, being ranged among the guardsmen of Germanus, thought it right straightway to disregard what he had sworn and to make his preparations for the tyranny much more strongly still. 18.8. Now the city was keeping a certain festival in full assembly, and many of the mutineers of Maximinus came about the time of the midday meal to the Palatium according to their agreement, where Germanus was entertaining his intimates, and Maximinus stood by the feast with the other guardsmen. 18.9. As the drinking went on, someone came in and reported to Germanus that many soldiers, in no order, were standing before the courtyard door, complaining that the public treasury owed them pay of a long time. 18.10. And he commanded the most faithful of the guardsmen secretly to keep Maximinus under guard, giving him by no means any perception of what was being done. 18.11. So the mutineers, with threat and tumult, went at a run to the hippodrome, and those of the senate who shared in their plan, gathering little by little out of the houses, streamed together there. 18.12. And if it had chanced that all were gathered into one place, no one, I think, 18.13. would easily have been able to break up their force; but as it was, Germanus, getting the start while the greater part of the throng was still left behind, sent against them at once all those who were loyal to him and to the emperor. 18.14. And these came to grips with the mutineers, who were not expecting them. And they, neither having Maximinus with them, whom they were expecting to lead them in the danger, nor seeing the multitude gathered to them as they thought, but beholding their fellow-soldiers fighting them beyond expectation, and from this falling into negligence, were easily defeated in the battle and in no order turned to flight. 18.15. And their opponents killed many of them and led many, taken alive, to Germanus. 18.16. But those who did not arrive at the hippodrome in time gave no perception of their share in the purpose concerning Maximinus. 18.17. Germanus, however, did not think it right to search these out further, but inquired whether Maximinus, after he had sworn, had practised plotting. 18.18. And when he was convicted of having, while ranged among his own guardsmen, made his attack still more, he impaled him very near the circuit-wall of Carthage, and thus was able to break up the mutiny altogether. So the plot of Maximinus came to such an end. 19.1. And the emperor, summoning Germanus with Symmachus and Domnicus, again entrusted to Solomon all the affairs of Libya, being in the thirteenth year of his reign as autocrat; and he furnished him an army and commanders, among others Rufinus and Leontius, the sons of Zaunas the son of Pharesmanes, and John the son of Sisiniolus. 19.2. For Martinus and Valerianus had already before come to Byzantium at the emperor's summons. 19.3. And Solomon, having sailed to Carthage and being freed from the mutiny of Stotzas, governed with moderation and guarded Libya in security, setting the army in order, and, if he found anything suspicious in it, sending it to Byzantium and to Belisarius, and enrolling new soldiers in place of those; and removing the surviving Vandals, and not least all their women, out of the whole of Libya. And he surrounded each city with a wall, and, guarding the laws with great strictness, preserved the state as well as possible. 19.4. And Libya became under him strong in revenue of money and otherwise prosperous. 19.5. And when everything had been set in the best order for him, he took the field again against Iaudas and the Moors in Aurasium. 19.6. And first he sent Gontharis, one of his own guardsmen, a man good in matters of war, with an army. 19.7. And he, coming to the river Abigas, encamped near Bagaïs, a desolate city. 19.8. And there, coming to grips with the enemy and being defeated in battle, and withdrawing to the stockade, he was now hard pressed by the blockade of the Moors. 19.9. Then Solomon himself too came up with the whole army, and when he was sixty stades from the camp which Gontharis commanded, making a stockade, he remained there, and, hearing all that had befallen the forces of Gontharis, sent them a part of the army and bade them with good courage fight it out with the enemy. 19.10. But the Moors, having got the upper hand in the encounter, 19.11. as has been said, did as follows. The river Abigas flows from Aurasium, and, coming down into the plain, waters the land in whatever way the men there wish. 19.12. For the natives lead this stream wherever they think it will for the moment be of advantage to them, since in this plain there chance to be many channels, into which the Abigas, dividing and going into all of them, is borne under the earth and again appears above the earth, 19.13. gathering its stream. And this, happening over the greater part of the plain, is set in the power of those who dwell there, by stopping up the channels with a mound, or again by uncovering them, to use the water of this river for whatever they wish. 19.14. At that time, then, the Moors, blocking up all the channels there, let the whole stream be borne about the camp of the Romans. 19.15. From this a deep and impassable marsh came to be and struck them with the utmost dismay and brought them into perplexity. 19.16. Hearing this, Solomon went quickly. But the barbarians, taking fright, withdrew to the foot of Aurasium. And at a place which they call Babosis, encamping, they remained. And Solomon, setting out with the whole army, came there. 19.17. And coming to grips with the enemy and mastering them by far, he turned them to flight. 19.18. And from this the Moors thought it inexpedient for them to fight a pitched battle against the Romans on equal terms; for they did not hope to prevail over them in battle; but in the rough country of Aurasium they had hope that the Romans, giving up through hardship, would in a short time withdraw thence as before. 19.19. So the most of them went off to Mauretania and to the barbarians south of Aurasium, but Iaudas with twenty thousand of the Moors remained there. Now it chanced that he had built a fortress in Aurasium, Zerbule by name. Into this entering with all the Moors, he kept quiet. 19.20. But Solomon by no means wished to spend time in the siege, and, learning that the plains about the city of Tamougadis were full of grain at its prime, led his army against them, and, settling there, ravaged the land. And after burning everything, he returned again to the fortress of Zerbule. 19.21. In the time during which the Romans were ravaging the land, Iaudas, leaving some of the Moors whom he thought most sufficient for the guard of the fortress, himself ascended to the height of Aurasium with the rest of the army, so that, while they were being besieged, provisions might not fail them there. 19.22. And finding a place held up on all sides by cliffs and covered by sheer rocks, 19.23. Toumar by name, there he kept quiet. And the Romans besieged the fortress of Zerbule for three days. And using their bows, since the wall was not high, they struck many of the barbarians on the battlements. 19.24. And by some chance it happened that all the leaders of the Moors, meeting with these missiles, died. 19.25. And when the time of three days had been spent and night came on, the Romans, learning nothing of the death of the leaders among the Moors, were planning to dissolve the blockade. 19.26. For it seemed better to Solomon to go against Iaudas and the multitude of the Moors, thinking that, if he should be able to take them by siege, the barbarians in Zerbule would come over to them more easily and with less toil. 19.27. But the barbarians, no longer thinking they could hold out against the blockade, since all their leaders had now been slain, decided to flee quickly and abandon the fortress. 19.28. Straightway, then, all in silence and giving the enemy no perception, fled, and the Romans at daybreak made ready for the withdrawal. 19.29. And when no one appeared on the wall, although the enemy were withdrawing, they marvelled and were for a long time perplexed with one another. 19.30. And in this helplessness, going round the fortress, they found the postern open, by which the Moors had gone off in flight. 19.31. And entering the fortress, they made everything plunder; yet they by no means planned to pursue the enemy, men lightly equipped and experienced in the regions there. 19.32. And when they had plundered everything, setting guards over the fortress, they all advanced on foot. 20.1. And coming to Toumar, the place where the enemy, having shut themselves up, kept quiet, they encamped somewhere near in a difficult place, where they were destined to have abundance neither of water, except a little, nor of any other necessary. 20.2. And when much time had been spent and the barbarians by no means came out against them, they themselves were no less, if not more, distressed, being hard pressed by the blockade. 20.3. And most of all they were vexed by the scarcity of water, which Solomon himself guarded, and gave out nothing else for the day except indeed a single cup to each man. 20.4. And when he saw them openly impatient and no longer able to bear the present hardships, he planned to make an attempt on the place, although it was hard of access, and, calling all together, exhorted them as follows: 20.5. "Since God has given to the Romans to besiege the Moors in Aurasium — a thing both before greater than hope and now altogether incredible to those who do not see what is being done — it is necessary that we too, serving the help from above, should not betray this favour, but, undertaking the danger with eagerness, should reach out for the good fortune that comes from success. 20.6. For every turn of human affairs comes round to the crisis of the opportune moment; and if anyone, playing the coward, betrays his fortune, he would not justly blame her, having brought the blame upon himself. 20.7. The weakness of the Moors you see surely, and the place where, deprived of all the necessaries, they keep themselves shut up. 20.8. And you must of necessity do one of two things: either, being by no means distressed at the blockade, await the surrender of the enemy, or, making light of this, accept the victory that comes with danger. 20.9. Rather, even to make war upon these barbarians will be free from danger for us, who, I think, fighting as they already are with famine, will never even come to grips with us. Bearing all these things in mind in the present, it is fitting that you should eagerly perform what is commanded." 20.10. After Solomon had thus exhorted them, he considered from what point it would be better for them to make the attempt on the place, and for a long time seemed to be at a loss. 20.11. For the difficulty of the ground seemed to him exceedingly hard to fight against. But while Solomon was pondering these things, fortune provided a way for the matter as follows. 20.12. There was among the soldiers a certain Gezon, an infantryman, the optio of the company in which he himself was enrolled; for thus the Romans call the steward of the pay. 20.13. This Gezon, whether in jest or in anger, or because some divine power moved him, began to ascend alone, as though going against the enemy, and some of his fellow-soldiers followed a little behind him, holding what was being done in great wonder. 20.14. And three of the Moors, who had been stationed to guard the entrance, suspecting that the man was coming against them, met him at a run. 20.15. But inasmuch as in the narrow place they did not advance in order, but each went separately, 20.16. Gezon, striking the first who fell in his way, killed him, and likewise dispatched each of the others too. 20.17. Seeing this, those who were coming behind, with much tumult and confusion, advanced against the enemy. 20.18. And when the whole Roman army heard and saw what was being done, neither awaiting the general to lead them on the way, nor the trumpets to signal the encounter, as was customary, nor indeed keeping their array, but using much din and urging one another on, they ran against the camp of the enemy. 20.19. There Rufinus and Leontius, the sons of Zaunas the son of Pharesmanes, displayed deeds against the enemy worthy of valour. 20.20. And the Moors, dismayed at them, when they learned that their guards too had been slain, straightway turned to flight, each as he could, and most of them, overtaken in the rough country, perished. 20.21. And Iaudas himself, struck in the thigh by a javelin, nevertheless escaped and withdrew to Mauretania. 20.22. And the Romans, having plundered the camp of the enemy, decided no longer to leave Aurasium, but, Solomon building fortresses there, to guard it, so that this mountain might never again be accessible to the Moors. 20.23. Now there is in Aurasium a sheer rock rising up in the midst of cliffs; the natives call it the rock of Geminianus; on it the men of old, making a very small tower, built a refuge strong and impregnable, the nature of the place helping them. 20.24. There it chanced that Iaudas had, a few days before, deposited his money and his women, setting one old Moor as guard of the money. 20.25. For he would never have suspected either that the enemy would come to this place, or that they could ever in all time take the tower by force. 20.26. But the Romans then, searching out the difficult places of Aurasium, came there, and one of them undertook with a laugh to climb up to the tower; and the women jeered, laughing at him as one reaching for the impossible; 20.27. and this the old man too did, peeping down from the tower. But the Roman soldier, when, climbing with hands and feet, he had got somewhere near, quietly drawing his sword, leaped up as fast as he could, and, hitting the old man on the neck, was able to cut him through and through. 20.28. And the head fell to the ground, and the soldiers, now taking courage and holding to one another, climbed up to the tower, and took out thence the women and the money, which was exceedingly great. 20.29. From this Solomon surrounded many of the cities in Libya with walls. 20.30. And when the Moors had withdrawn from Numidia, defeated, as has been said, he added to the Roman dominion, to pay tribute, the country of Zabe, which is beyond Mount Aurasium and is called First Mauretania, having Sitiphis as its metropolis; 20.31. for of the other Mauretania the first city chances to be Caesarea, where Mastigas with his own Moors was settled, holding all the regions there subject and tributary except indeed the city of Caesarea. 20.32. For this Belisarius had previously recovered for the Romans, as has been disclosed by me in the previous narrative; to it the Romans are always sent by ship, but they are not able to go by land, since Moors dwell in this country. 20.33. And from this all the Libyans who were subjects of the Romans, attaining a secure peace and the rule of Solomon, which was prudent and very moderate, and having henceforth nothing hostile in mind, seemed to be the most prosperous of all men. 21.1. But four years later all their good things chanced to turn into the opposite. For when the Emperor Justinian was in the seventeenth year of his reign as autocrat, Cyrus and Sergius, the sons of Bacchus the brother of Solomon, were appointed by the emperor to rule cities in Libya — Cyrus the elder over Pentapolis, 21.2. and Sergius over Tripolis. And the Moors called the Leuathae came with a great army to Leptis Magna to Sergius, noising it abroad that for this reason they had come, that Sergius might give them gifts and the customary tokens and confirm the peace. 21.3. But Sergius, persuaded by Pudentius, a man of Tripolis, whom I have mentioned in the previous narrative as having served the Emperor Justinian against the Vandals at the beginning of the Vandalic war, received into the city eighty of the most notable of the barbarians, promising to fulfil all that was asked, and commanded the rest to remain in the suburb. 21.4. And to these eighty, providing pledges concerning the peace, he thus invited them to a feast. But it is said that these barbarians had come into the city with treacherous intent, so that, having laid an ambush, they might kill Sergius. 21.5. And when they had come to a parley with him, they brought against the Romans, among other charges, that they had ravaged their crops when they ought not. 21.6. And Sergius, making light of this, rose from the seat on which he was sitting and wished to depart. 21.7. And one of the barbarians, laying hold of his shoulder, undertook to hinder him. 21.8. And from this falling into tumult, the others about him now streamed together. 21.9. And one of the guardsmen of Sergius, drawing his sword, dispatched this Moor. 21.10. And from this, a great commotion arising, as was likely, in the chamber, the guardsmen of Sergius killed all the barbarians. 21.11. And one of them, when he saw the others being slain, leaped out of the room where these things were being done, and, escaping the notice of all, came to his fellow-tribesmen and disclosed what had befallen them. 21.12. And they, hearing this, betook themselves at a run to their own camp and with all the rest came in arms against the Romans. 21.13. And when they had come about the city of Leptis Magna, Sergius and Pudentius with all the army met them. 21.14. And the battle being at close quarters, at first the Romans conquered and killed many of the enemy, and, plundering their camp, both got possession of the goods and made slaves of a great number of women and children. 21.15. But afterward Pudentius, given over to inconsiderate daring, perished. And Sergius with the Roman army (for it was now growing dark) marched into Leptis Magna. 21.16. And at a later time the barbarians with greater preparation took the field against the Romans. And Sergius was sent to Solomon his uncle, in order that he too might go with a greater army against the enemy; and there he found his brother Cyrus also. 21.17. And the barbarians, coming to Byzacium, plundered most of the regions there by their incursion; and Antalas (whom I have mentioned in the previous narrative as having remained faithful to the Romans, and for this reason being alone of the Moors a ruler in Byzacium) had now become hostile to Solomon, both because Solomon had taken from him the pay with which the emperor had honoured him, and because he had killed his brother, bringing a charge against him of some disturbance arising among the Byzacenes. 21.18. At that time, then, Antalas saw these barbarians gladly and, making alliance with them, led the way for them against Solomon and Carthage. 21.19. But Solomon, when he heard this, set out with all his army against them, and overtaking them about the city of Theveste, distant six days' journey from Carthage, encamped, both he and the sons of his brother Bacchus, Cyrus and Sergius and Solomon the youngest. 21.20. And fearing the multitude of the barbarians, he sent to the commanders of the Leuathae, blaming them because, being at peace with the Romans, they had then come in arms against them, and demanding that the peace be confirmed between them, and he promised to swear the most terrible oaths that in truth he would use amnesty for what had been done against them. 21.21. But the barbarians, mocking what was said, declared that he should by all means swear by the oracles of the Christians, which they are accustomed to call gospels. 21.22. Since, then, Sergius, after swearing by these, had then killed those who trusted them, they wished, going into battle, to make trial of these oracles, what power they have against perjurers, so that, trusting them most firmly, they might thus enter upon the agreements. Hearing this, Solomon made ready for the encounter. 21.23. On the following day, falling in with a part of the enemy who were carrying off the greatest possible booty, and conquering them in battle, he took away all the booty and kept it. 21.24. And to the soldiers, who were impatient and made it a grievance that he did not give them the spoils, he said that he was waiting for the end of the war, so that they might then distribute everything, as might appear to fall to each according to his worth. 21.25. But when the barbarians again with their whole army set out for the encounter, then some of the Romans were left behind, and the others went into the array without eagerness. 21.26. At first, then, the battle was evenly balanced, but afterward, the Moors far surpassing them in multitude, the most of the Romans fled, while Solomon and some about him for a time held out under the missiles, but afterward, the enemy overpowering them, they fled in haste and came to a ravine made by a brook flowing there. 21.27. There, his horse stumbling, Solomon fell to the ground, and his guardsmen, quickly lifting him in their hands, set him upon his horse. 21.28. But being in great pain and no longer able to hold the rein, he was overtaken by the barbarians, who killed both him and many of his guardsmen. Such was the end of life for Solomon. 22.1. After the death of Solomon, Sergius his nephew, as has been said, by the gift of the emperor took over the rule of Libya. 22.2. He became most of all responsible for great destruction to the Libyan race, and all were distressed at his rule — the commanders, because, being utterly without understanding and young both in character and in years, he became the most arrogant of all men, and outraged them for no reason at all and despised them, ever using to this end the power of his wealth and the authority of his office; the soldiers, because he was altogether unmanly and soft; and the Libyans, for these reasons and because he became a strange lover of other men's women and money. 22.3. But most of all John the son of Sisiniolus was grieved at the power of Sergius. For, being good in matters of war and exceedingly well reputed, he met with simple ingratitude from the man. 22.4. Wherefore neither he himself nor any other of all the men was willing to take up arms against the enemy. 22.5. And almost all the Moors followed Antalas, and Stotzas came at his summons from Mauretania. 22.6. And since no one of the enemy went out against them, they plundered and carried off everything fearlessly. Then Antalas wrote a letter to the Emperor Justinian. 22.7. And the writing disclosed this: "That I am a slave of your majesty I would not myself deny; but the Moors, having suffered unholy deeds at the hands of Solomon while at peace, have been forced most utterly to take up arms, not raising them against you, but defending themselves against their enemy, and I especially. 22.8. For not only did he decide to deprive me of the pay which Belisarius long ago appointed for me and you granted, but he also killed my brother, having no wrong to charge against him. 22.9. The penalty, then, we have taken from him who wronged us. But if it is your wish that the Moors should be slaves to your majesty and serve in all things as they are accustomed, command Sergius the nephew of Solomon, departing hence, to return to you, and send another general to Libya. 22.10. For you will not lack men of understanding and in every way worthier than Sergius; for so long as he commands your army, it is impossible for peace to be established between Romans and Moors." Such things Antalas wrote. But the emperor, 22.11. having read these things and learned the common hatred of all toward Sergius, even so was not willing to remove him from the command, out of respect for Solomon's other virtue and the close of his life. These things, then, were going on in this way. 22.12. But Solomon, the brother of Sergius, who was supposed to have perished from among men together with his uncle Solomon, was neglected both by the rest and by his brother; for no one knew that he was alive. 22.13. Now it chanced that the Moors had taken him alive, inasmuch as he was very young, 22.14. and inquired of him who he might be. And he said that he was a Vandal by race and a slave of Solomon; he said, however, that he had a friend, one of the physicians, Pegasius by name, in the city of Laribus, which was near by, who would purchase him by paying the ransom. 22.15. So the Moors, coming very near the circuit-wall of the city, called Pegasius and showed him Solomon, and asked whether it was his pleasure to purchase him. 22.16. And when he agreed to purchase him, they sold Solomon to him for fifty gold pieces. 22.17. But when he was inside the wall, Solomon mocked the Moors as having been deceived by a mere boy; for he said that he himself was Solomon, the son of Bacchus 22.18. and the nephew of Solomon. And the Moors, grieved at what had befallen and making it a great matter that, having had a strong pledge of Sergius and the Romans, they had then so carelessly let him go, came to Laribus and set about the siege of it, in order to take Solomon together with the city. 22.19. But those who were besieged, dreading the blockade of the barbarians, since they had not chanced to bring in provisions, came to a parley with the Moors, on condition that, paying over much money, they should straightway dissolve the blockade. 22.20. And they, not supposing they could take the city by force, since the Moors are by no means practised in storming walls, and by no means knowing that the besieged were short of provisions, accepted the proposal, and, having received three thousand gold pieces, dissolved the siege, and all the Leuathae withdrew homeward. 23.1. But Antalas and the army of the Moors gathered again in Byzacium, and with them was Stotzas, having some few soldiers and Vandals. 23.2. And John the son of Sisiniolus, the Libyans much beseeching him, gathered an army and came against them. 23.3. Now it chanced that Himerius the Thracian was commander of the detachments in Byzacium; him then John commanded, bringing with him all the detachments there with their several leaders, to come to a place called Menephesse, which is in Byzacium, 23.4. and join them. But afterward, hearing that the enemy were encamping there, John wrote to Himerius, disclosing what had befallen and bidding them join him elsewhere, so that not separately but in common all might meet the enemy. 23.5. But by some chance those who had this letter, using another road, were by no means able to find Himerius, but he, falling with his army into the camp of his opponents, came under their hands. 23.6. Now there was in this Roman army a young man, Severianus, son of Asiaticus, a Phoenician, of Emesa by race, commander of a cavalry detachment. 23.7. He alone, with the soldiers about him, fifty in number, came to grips with the enemy. 23.8. And for some time they held out, but then, overpowered by the great multitude, they ran up to a hill that was there, where also there was a fortress not secure. 23.9. Wherefore by agreement they surrendered themselves to their opponents, who had come up against them. 23.10. And they killed neither him nor any of the soldiers, but, taking them all alive, kept Himerius under guard and delivered the soldiers to Stotzas, who agreed with great eagerness to take the field against the Romans; Himerius, however, they threatened to kill, if he should not do what was enjoined. 23.11. And they enjoined him to deliver to them by some device the seacoast city of Adramytus. And when he maintained that this was his wish, they went with him against Adramytus. 23.12. And when they came near the city, they sent Himerius a little in advance with some of the soldiers who followed Stotzas, dragging along Moors bound, forsooth, while they themselves followed behind. 23.13. And they enjoined Himerius to say to those set over the gates of the city that the emperor's army had won a decisive victory and that John would come straightway, leading a multitude of Moorish captives beyond number; and thus, when the gates were opened to them, to get inside the circuit-wall with those going with him. 23.14. And he did accordingly. And the people of Adramytus, thus deceived (for they could not disbelieve the commander of all the soldiers in Byzacium), opening wide the gates, received the enemy. 23.15. Then those who entered with Himerius, drawing their swords, no longer permitted the guards there to set the gates in place, but straightway admitted the whole army of the Moors into the city. 23.16. And the barbarians, having plundered it and set a few guards, departed. 23.17. And of the Romans who had been taken alive, some, escaping, came to Carthage, among whom were Severianus and Himerius. For from the Moors it was not difficult for those who wished to flee. And many also remained with Stotzas, by no means against their will. 23.18. And not long afterward one of the priests, Paul by name, who had charge of the care of the sick, taking counsel with some of the notable men, said: "I myself 23.19. will be sent to Carthage, and I have hope of returning quickly with an army; and it will be your care to receive the emperor's army into the city." So they, fastening him to some ropes, let him down by night from the wall, and he, coming to the shore of the sea, and chancing upon a fishing-boat that was there, persuaded its owners with much money and sailed to Carthage. 23.20. There, having put in and come into the presence of Sergius, he told the whole story and asked him to give him an army worth mentioning, to recover Adramytus. 23.21. And when this by no means pleased Sergius, inasmuch as the army in Carthage was not large, he asked him to give him some few soldiers, and, taking men not more than eighty, devised the following. 23.22. Making a gathering of ships and many small boats, he embarked many sailors there and other Libyans, clothed in the garments which the soldiers of the Romans are accustomed to wear. 23.23. And setting out with the whole fleet, he sailed in haste straight for Adramytus. And when he had come very near it, he sent some men secretly and signified to the notable men of the city that Germanus, the nephew of the emperor, having lately come to Carthage, had sent to the people of Adramytus an army worth mentioning. 23.24. And he bade them take courage and open one postern for them that night. 23.25. And they did what was enjoined. And thus Paul, with those who followed him, getting inside the circuit-wall, killed all the enemy and recovered Adramytus for the emperor; and the report concerning Germanus, beginning there, advanced as far as Carthage. 23.26. But the Moors and Stotzas with those who followed him, hearing this, at first were dismayed and went off in flight to the extremities of Libya, but afterward, learning the true story, made it a dreadful matter that they, having spared all the people of Adramytus, had suffered such things at their hands. 23.27. Wherefore, falling upon them everywhere, they wrought unholy deeds upon the Libyans, sparing no age, and at that time the country became empty of men over a very great extent. 23.28. For of the Libyans who were left, some fled to the cities, others to Sicily and the other islands. 23.29. But almost all the notable men came to Byzantium, among whom was Paul too, who had recovered Adramytus for the emperor. 23.30. And the Moors more fearlessly, since no one went out against them, plundered and carried off everything, and with them was Stotzas, now in power. 23.31. For many Roman soldiers followed him, some having come as deserters, others having at first been made captives, 23.32. but remaining with him of their own will. And John, who had some reputation among the Moors, having quarrelled exceedingly with Sergius, kept quiet. 24.1. Meanwhile the emperor sent another general to Libya, Areobindus, with some few soldiers, a man of senatorial rank and well born, 24.2. but by no means experienced in deeds of war. And with him he sent Athanasius, a prefect lately come from Italy, and a few Armenians, of whom Artabanes and John were leaders, the sons of John, Arsacids by race, who had lately abandoned the Persian army and come over again to the Romans as deserters with the other Armenians. 24.3. And there were with Areobindus his sister and Praeiecta his wife, the daughter of Vigilantia, the sister of the Emperor Justinian. 24.4. He did not, however, summon Sergius, but commanded both him and Areobindus to be generals of Libya, dividing between them the country and the detachments of the soldiers. 24.5. And he assigned to Sergius the carrying on of the war against the barbarians in Numidia, and to Areobindus to fight continually with the Moors in Byzacium. 24.6. And when this fleet had sailed into Carthage, Sergius went off with his own army to Numidia, while Areobindus, learning that Antalas and Stotzas were encamping about the city of Siccaveneria, distant three days' journey from Carthage, commanded John the son of Sisiniolus to go against them, picking out whatever was best of the army; 24.7. and he wrote to Sergius to join the forces of John, in order that in common all might advance against the enemy. 24.8. Sergius, then, decided to make light of both the letter and this action, while John with a small army, beyond telling, was compelled to come to grips with a multitude of the enemy. 24.9. Now there was always great enmity between him and Stotzas, and each of them prayed to become the slayer of the other and thus to perish from among men. 24.10. At that time, then, as soon as the battle was about to be at hand, both, riding out from the camps, came against one another. 24.11. And John, drawing his bow, while Stotzas was still approaching, hit him, chancing upon his right groin, and he, smitten by a mortal wound, fell there, not yet dead, but destined to survive this wound for some short time. 24.12. And straightway all came up, both those who followed him and the army of the Moors, and placed Stotzas, faint, against a certain tree, while they themselves, advancing with much fury against the enemy, since they far surpassed them in multitude, turned John and all the Romans to flight with no trouble. 24.13. Then it is said that John said he died a sweet death, since the matter of his prayer concerning Stotzas had come to fulfilment. Now there was a steep place there, where his horse, stumbling, threw him off. 24.14. And as he tried to leap upon it again, the enemy, overtaking him, killed him, a man who had become great in reputation and in valour. And Stotzas, learning this, died, saying only this much, that now he died most sweetly. 24.15. In this battle John the Armenian also, the brother of Artabanes, perished, after displaying deeds against the enemy worthy of valour. 24.16. And the emperor, hearing this, and being exceedingly grieved at the valour of John, and thinking it inexpedient that two generals should administer the rule, summoned Sergius at once and sent him to Italy with an army, and handed over to Areobindus the whole power of Libya. 25.1. But Gontharis, two months after Sergius had departed thence, attempted a tyranny in the following manner. It chanced that he himself was commander of the detachments in Numidia and for this reason had his abode there, and he was secretly contriving with the Moors that they should advance against Carthage. 25.2. Straightway, then, an army of the enemy, gathered together from Numidia and Byzacium, went with much haste against Carthage. And the leaders of the Numidians were Cutzinas and Iaudas, of the Byzacenes Antalas. 25.3. And with him was also John the tyrant with his followers, whom the mutineers, after the death of Stotzas, had set up as commander over themselves. 25.4. And Areobindus, learning of the attack, summoned the other commanders with their followers to Carthage, and Gontharis. And there came to him also Artabanes with the Armenians. 25.5. So Areobindus commanded Gontharis to lead all the army against the enemy. 25.6. And he, promising eagerly to serve him in matters of war, did as follows. One of his servants, a Moor by race and a cook by trade, he commanded to go to the camp of the enemy, and to give to the others the appearance that he had run away from his master, but secretly to say to Antalas that Gontharis wished to share with him the rule of Libya. 25.7. So the cook did accordingly, and Antalas heard the proposal gladly, but answered only this much, that noble deeds are not wont to come to men through cooks. 25.8. When Gontharis heard this, he sent at once to Antalas one of his guardsmen, Ulitheus by name, whom he used as most faithful, inviting him to come as near as possible to Carthage. 25.9. For thus he promised to do away with Areobindus. 25.10. So Ulitheus, secretly from the other barbarians, made an agreement with Antalas, on condition that Antalas should rule Byzacium, holding the half of the money of Areobindus and bringing with him fifteen hundred Roman soldiers, while Gontharis should take the imperial dignity, holding the power of Carthage and the rest of Libya. 25.11. And having accomplished these things, he returned to the Roman camp, which they had made entirely before the circuit-wall, dividing among themselves the guard-posts of each gate. 25.12. And the barbarians not long afterward went with much haste straight for Carthage, and, encamping at the place called Decimum, remained there.
