And setting out thence on the following day, they advanced. 25.13. And some of the Roman army, meeting them, came to grips with them unexpectedly and killed not a few of the Moors. 25.14. These Gontharis straightway recalled, abusing them as men who showed daring without consideration and wished to throw the affairs of the Romans into manifest danger. 25.15. Meanwhile Areobindus, sending secretly to Cutzinas, was contriving concerning treachery. And Cutzinas agreed with him that, when they should be in the action, he would turn against Antalas and the Moors in Byzacium. 25.16. For the Moors keep faith neither with any other men nor with one another. These things Areobindus disclosed to Gontharis. 25.17. And he, wishing to deceive and to put off the matter, advised Areobindus by no means to have faith in Cutzinas, unless he should receive his children from him as hostages. 25.18. So Areobindus and Cutzinas, sending continually to one another secretly, were occupied with the plot against Antalas. 25.19. But Gontharis, again sending Ulitheus, made known to Antalas what was being done. 25.20. And he decided neither to make any charge against Cutzinas, nor to make manifest to him that he had learned of the plot, nor indeed did he disclose anything of what had been agreed between him and Gontharis. 25.21. But both, being enemies to one another and hostile in their purposes, ranged themselves together with evil intent, each going to take the field on behalf of his own friend against the other. 25.22. With such a purpose Cutzinas and Antalas led the army of the Moors against Carthage. And Gontharis planned to kill Areobindus, but, in order not to seem to be aiming at tyranny, he wished to do this secretly in the array, so that the plot against the general might seem to have been made by others, while he himself should be compelled by the Roman army to take up the rule of Libya. 25.23. By a trick, then, encompassing Areobindus, he persuaded him to go out against the enemy and engage them, now that they had come very near Carthage. 25.24. It was decided, then, that on the following day he should lead out the whole army against the enemy at sunrise. 25.25. But Areobindus, being very inexperienced in this matter and timid, used delay for no good reason. 25.26. For, practising how he should put on the equipment of arms and making his other preparations for the sortie, he spent the greater part of the day. 25.27. Wherefore, putting off the array to the next day, he remained quiet. 25.28. But Gontharis, suspecting that he had made the delay on purpose, as perceiving what was being done, decided openly to accomplish both the murder of the general and the attempt at tyranny. 26.1. On the following day he did as follows. Throwing open the gates where he himself kept guard, he placed enormous stones underneath, so that no one could easily set them in place, and stationed many men armoured and holding bows in their hands about the battlements, and he himself, putting on his corselet, stood in the midst of the gates. 26.2. He devised this not for the sake of the Moors, that he might receive them into the city (for the Moors, being altogether unstable, are suspicious toward all men. 26.3. And this happens to them not without reason; for whoever is by nature faithless to his neighbours is unable himself to trust anyone whatever, but is compelled to be suspicious toward all men, judging the character of his neighbour from his own mind). 26.4. Wherefore Gontharis did not even hope that the Moors, trusting him, would come inside the circuit-wall, but did this so that Areobindus, falling into great fear, might straightway be set in motion to flight and, quickly leaving Carthage, be conveyed to Byzantium. 26.5. And he did indeed hit upon the true thought, had not a storm coming on meanwhile prevented it. 26.6. And Areobindus, learning what was being done, summoned Athanasius and some of the notable men. 26.7. And there came to him also Artabanes from the camp, himself the third, and advised Areobindus neither to lose heart nor to yield to the daring of Gontharis, but at once to go against him together with all who followed him and set about the work, before any further evil should come to pass. 26.8. At first, then, Areobindus, sending to Gontharis one of his intimates, Phredas by name, commanded him to make trial of his purpose. 26.9. But when Phredas, returning, reported that Gontharis by no means denied the tyranny, he now planned to go against him as to battle. 26.10. Meanwhile Gontharis slandered Areobindus to the soldiers, saying that he was unmanly and, at once held fast by fear of the enemy and unwilling to give them their pay, was planning flight with Athanasius and was about straightway to sail off from Mandracium, so that the soldiers, fighting with famine and the Moors, might perish; and he inquired whether it was their wish to seize both and keep them under guard. 26.11. For thus he hoped that Areobindus, either perceiving the commotion, would take to flight, or, being caught by the soldiers, would be destroyed without any account. 26.12. He agreed, however, to give the soldiers from his own resources as much money as the public treasury owed them. 26.13. And they praised his words and were held by much fury against Areobindus, but meanwhile Areobindus with Artabanes and his followers arrived there. 26.14. And a battle took place both on the battlements and below about the gates where Gontharis stood, in which neither side had the worse. 26.15. And those who were loyal to the emperor, gathering from the camps, were about to take the mutineers by force. For Gontharis had not yet deceived all, but the most still remained pure in their purposes. 26.16. But Areobindus, then for the first time seeing men being slain (for he did not yet chance to be accustomed to this sight), was dismayed and, playing the coward and unable to endure what he beheld, fled. 26.17. Now there is within the circuit-wall of Carthage a sanctuary by the shore of the sea, where dwell men to whom the things pertaining to the divine have been strictly practised; we have always been accustomed to call these men monks; this sanctuary Solomon had built not long before and, surrounding it with a wall, had made it a most secure fortress. 26.18. There Areobindus, fleeing, leaped in, where he had chanced to send his wife and his sister. 26.19. Then Artabanes too went off, and all the rest withdrew thence, each as he could. 26.20. But Gontharis, having conquered by force, held the Palatium with the mutineers, and now kept most constant guard over the gates and the harbour. 26.21. First, then, he summoned Athanasius, and he, without any delay, came to him, 26.22. and, using much flattery, gave the appearance that the action pleased him exceedingly. 26.23. Then, sending the priest of the city, he commanded Areobindus to receive pledges and come to the Palatium, threatening to besiege him if he disobeyed and to give him no further pledges for his safety, but by every device to take him out and kill him. 26.24. So the priest Reparatus maintained that, by the consent of Gontharis, he would swear to Areobindus that nothing unpleasant would befall him at his hands, telling also what threats the man had made if he should not obey. 26.25. And Areobindus, taking fright, agreed straightway to follow the priest, if he, after performing the divine bath, as is customary, should then, on his behalf, swear to him pledges concerning his safety. 26.26. So the priest did accordingly. And Areobindus, without any delay, followed him, wearing a garment fit neither for a general nor for any other military man, but altogether becoming a slave or a private person; the Romans call it a casula in the Latin tongue. 26.27. And when they had come near the Palatium, taking the sacred oracles in his hands from the priest, he came into the sight of Gontharis. 26.28. And falling prone, he lay there a long time, holding out to him the suppliant's branch and the sacred oracles and the child which had been deemed worthy of the divine bath, on whom the priest, as I have said, had given him the pledge. 26.29. And when Gontharis with difficulty raised him up, he inquired of Gontharis, by all things holy, whether his safety was in security. 26.30. And he bade him be of very good courage now; for he should suffer nothing unpleasant at his hands, but on the following day should depart from Carthage with his wife and his money. 26.31. Then, dismissing the priest Reparatus, he bade Areobindus and Athanasius dine with him in the Palatium. 26.32. And he honoured Areobindus as he dined; for he made him recline first upon the couch; but when he had dined he did not let him go, but compelled him to sleep alone in a chamber, whither he sent Ulitheus with certain others against him. 26.33. And these, while he wailed and used many lamentations and uttered many things moving to pity toward them, killed him. Athanasius, however, they spared, despising, I think, the old age of the man. 27.1. On the following day Gontharis sent the head of Areobindus to Antalas, but decided to deprive him of the money and the soldiers. 27.2. Antalas, then, both because Gontharis fulfilled none of their agreements, and considering the oaths sworn and the deeds done by Gontharis against Areobindus, was indignant. 27.3. For it seemed to him that one who had so wronged such oaths would never be faithful either to himself or to anyone else whatever. 27.4. So, reckoning much within himself, he wished to come over to the Emperor Justinian; wherefore he marched back. 27.5. And learning that Marcentius, who commanded the detachments in Byzacium, had fled to one of the islands lying off the coast, he sent to him, told him the whole story, and, giving pledges, won the man over. 27.6. And Marcentius remained with Antalas in the camp, while the soldiers who had their station in Byzacium, being loyal to the emperor, guarded the city of Adramytus. 27.7. But the soldiers of Stotzas, no fewer than a thousand, perceiving what was being done, with John leading them, went at a run to Gontharis; 27.8. and he received them gladly into the city. And there were of them five hundred Romans, about eighty Huns, and all the rest Vandals. 27.9. And Artabanes, taking pledges, went up to the Palatium with the Armenians and agreed to serve the tyrant in whatever he commanded. 27.10. But secretly he was planning to kill Gontharis, having communicated this plan to Gregorius his nephew and Artasires his guardsman. 27.11. And Gregorius, urging him on to the deed, spoke as follows: "Artabanes, now it is in your power alone to win the glory of Belisarius, nay rather even to surpass it by far. 27.12. For he, taking a most notable army and great sums of money from the emperor, came here, having commanders who followed him and many counsellors, and a fleet of ships such as we have never known by hearsay, and much cavalry and arms and, in a word, simply everything prepared for him worthily of the Roman empire. 27.13. And thus with much toil he recovered Libya for the Romans. 27.14. But all this has so perished that, even if it had never been at all, the present state would be the same; except indeed that it has fallen to the Romans now, as a result of the victory of Belisarius, to be damaged in both bodies and money, and besides to have become unable even to guard the good things. 27.15. But the recovering of all this now for the emperor lies in your soul alone and your judgment and your right hand. 27.16. Reckon, then, that you are an Arsacid by descent from of old, and consider that for the well-born to play the man is fitting always and everywhere. 27.17. Many wonderful deeds, indeed, have been done by you on behalf of liberty. For while still a young man you killed Acacius, the ruler of the Armenians, and Sittas, the general of the Romans, and from this, having become known to the king Chosroes, you took the field with him against the Romans. 27.18. But since you are now so great that it belongs to you not to overlook the Roman dominion lying under a drunken dog, show now that by your nobility and valour of soul you have wrought, good sir, those former deeds; and I and Artasires here will serve you with all our power in whatever you command." 27.19. Gregorius said this much; and he set the mind of Artabanes still more eagerly upon the tyrant. 27.20. But Gontharis, leading the wife and sister of Areobindus out of the fortress, compelled them to remain in a certain house, neither outraging them in word or deed, nor having them in want of the necessaries beyond their need, nor forcing them to say or do anything else, except indeed that Praeiecta was compelled to write to her uncle that Gontharis honoured them exceedingly and was altogether pure of the murder of her husband, but that the evil had been wrought by Ulitheus, Gontharis by no means approving. 27.21. And Gontharis did this, persuaded by Pasiphilus, a man who had become first among the mutineers in Byzacium and had especially assisted him in the attempt at tyranny. 27.22. For Pasiphilus maintained that, if he did this, the emperor would give him the girl in marriage and bestow as dowry, by reason of the kinship, great sums of money. 27.23. And he commanded Artabanes to lead the army against Antalas and the Moors in Byzacium. 27.24. For Cutzinas, having quarrelled with Antalas, had revolted from him openly and come over to Gontharis, to whom he gave his son and his mother as hostages. 27.25. So the army, with Artabanes leading, advanced straightway against Antalas. And with him was also John, the commander of the mutineers of Stotzas, and Ulitheus the guardsman; and the Moors followed too, 27.26. of whom Cutzinas was leader. And passing by the city of Adramytus, they came upon their opponents who were somewhere there, and encamping a little apart from the enemy, they bivouacked. 27.27. On the following day John and Ulitheus, holding a part of the army, remained there, while Artabanes and Cutzinas led the army against their opponents. 27.28. And the Moors with Antalas, not withstanding them, turned to flight. 27.29. But Artabanes, playing the coward on purpose, suddenly turned his standard back and marched off. 27.30. Wherefore Ulitheus planned to kill him when he came to the camp. 27.31. But Artabanes, excusing himself, said he feared lest Marcentius, coming to the aid of his opponents from the city of Adramytus, where he chanced to be, should work irreparable deeds upon them; 27.32. and that Gontharis ought to go with the whole army against the enemy. 27.33. And at first he planned, going to Adramytus, to join the emperor's army. 27.34. But after much reckoning it seemed better to him, having made away with Gontharis from among men, to free the emperor and Libya from their troublesome affairs. 27.35. Returning, then, to Carthage, he reported to the tyrant that he would need a larger army against the enemy. 27.36. And he, having communicated with Pasiphilus, wished to arm the whole army, while he himself, after setting a guard in Carthage, should lead the army against the enemy. 27.37. He put to death, then, each day many, against whom he used some suspicion that had no reason. 27.38. And he enjoined upon Pasiphilus, whom he was about to set over the guard of Carthage, to kill all the Greeks, taking no account of any. 28.1. Having managed everything else as seemed to him best, he decided to entertain his intimates, intending on the following day to make the sortie. 28.2. And in a chamber where three couches had been made ready from of old, he held the banquet. 28.3. He himself, then, reclined upon the first couch, as was natural, where also were Athanasius and Artabanes, and some of the acquaintances of Gontharis, and Peter, a Thracian by race, who had formerly been a guardsman of Solomon. 28.4. And on both the other couches were the first and best of the Vandals. 28.5. John, however, who commanded the mutineers of Stotzas, Pasiphilus entertained apart, and each of the rest, wherever it seemed dear to each of the intimates of Gontharis. 28.6. Artabanes, then, when he was invited to this banquet, thinking this time suitable for him for the murder of the tyrant, planned to accomplish his purpose. 28.7. Disclosing the matter, then, to Gregorius and Artasires and three other guardsmen, he commanded the guardsmen to come inside with their swords (for it is the custom, when commanders are feasting, for the guardsmen to stand behind), and, when they were inside, to set to work suddenly, whenever the moment should seem to them most suitable, and that Artasires should first set to work. 28.8. And he enjoined Gregorius, picking out the most stout-hearted of the Armenians, to bring them to the Palatium, carrying their swords only in their hands (for with nothing else is it lawful for those who follow commanders in the city to be armed), and, leaving these in the portico, to go inside with the guardsmen, and to disclose the plan to no one of them, but to say only this much, that he was suspicious toward Gontharis, that with evil intent he had invited Artabanes to the banquet; 28.9. and that he wished them to stand by the guards of Gontharis who were stationed there on guard, and, giving the appearance of playing, to lay hold of the very shields which those men carried, and, brandishing them and otherwise moving them up and down, to keep turning them about continually; and when tumult or shouting arose inside, taking up the shields themselves, to come to the rescue at a run. 28.10. Artabanes, then, gave these orders, and Gregorius carried them out. And Artasires devised the following. Dividing some of his arrows in two, he set them upon the wrist of his left hand, along the divisions, up to the elbow. And binding them tight with thongs, he threw over them the part of his tunic there. 28.11. And he did this so that, if anyone, raising his sword against him, should undertake to strike him, he might suffer nothing dreadful, his left arm being held before him, since the iron, broken off in its rush against the wood, would be unable in any way to touch the body. With such a purpose Artasires did this, as I have said. 28.12. And to Artabanes he said as follows: "I shall undertake the deed with no hesitation, and I have hope of touching the body of Gontharis with this sword, but what comes after that I cannot say — whether God, being angry with the tyrant, will help me to accomplish this daring deed, or whether, exacting penalty for some sin of mine, He will here meet me and be a hindrance. 28.13. If, then, you see the tyrant struck not in a mortal spot, do you with my sword, without any delay, kill me, so that I may not, being maltreated by him, and saying under torture that the deed was undertaken by your judgment, both myself perish most shamefully and be compelled, against my will, to destroy you besides." 28.14. When Artasires had said this much, going with Gregorius and one of the guardsmen to the couches, he stood behind Artabanes. And the rest, remaining by the guards, did what had been enjoined upon them. 28.15. So Artasires, when the banquet had somehow begun, planned to set to work, and already was laying hold of the hilt of his sword. 28.16. But Gregorius prevented him, saying in the Armenian tongue that Gontharis was still wholly in possession of himself, not yet having drunk much of the wine. 28.17. Then Artasires, groaning, said: "O man, how good a spirit have you needlessly checked for the present!" 28.18. And as the drinking went on, Gontharis, now drenched, gave the guardsmen of the food, using a certain liberality. 28.19. And they, taking these portions, were about now to eat outside the room, only three guardsmen being left behind by Gontharis, of whom Ulitheus chanced to be one. 28.20. And Artasires too was going out, as if to taste of the food with the others. 28.21. There a thought came to him, lest, when he wished to draw the dagger, something should be a hindrance. 28.22. So, getting outside, he secretly threw away the sheath of his sword, and, taking it naked under his armpit, hidden by his cloak, he leaped in upon Gontharis, as though to say something secretly from the rest. 28.23. Seeing this, Artabanes, boiling with passion and falling, by the excess of his agony, into deep anxiety, began to move his head and to change the colours of his face many times, and seemed altogether to have become inspired by the greatness of the deed. 28.24. Peter, seeing this, understood what was being done, but did not disclose it to any of the others, since, being loyal to the emperor, what was being done exceedingly pleased him. 28.25. And as Artasires came very near the tyrant, one of the servants pushed him, and as he drew back a little, perceived the naked sword and cried out, saying, "What is this, most excellent man?" 28.26. And Gontharis, putting his hand to his right ear and turning his face, looked at him. 28.27. And Artasires struck him meanwhile with his sword and cut off a part of the forehead together with the fingers. 28.28. And Peter, crying out, urged Artasires on to kill the most unholy of all men. 28.29. And Artabanes, seeing Gontharis leaping up (for he was reclining near), drawing his two-edged dagger, which hung beside his thigh, a great one, thrust it into the left side of the tyrant up to the very hilt and there left it. 28.30. And he, none the less, undertook to leap up, but, having received a mortal wound, fell there. 28.31. Ulitheus, then, brought down his sword upon Artasires, as if to cleave his head; but he, putting his left hand before his head, enjoyed in his utmost need the fruit of his own forethought. 28.32. For the edge of the sword, being checked in the cuttings of the arrows on his arm, he himself, having become unharmed, killed Ulitheus with no trouble. 28.33. And Peter and Artabanes, the one seizing the sword of Gontharis, the other that of the fallen Ulitheus, killed the remaining guardsmen there. 28.34. There arose, then, as was likely, a great clamour and tumult. And when those of the Armenians who stood by the guards of the tyrant perceived this, straightway taking up the shields according to their agreement, they advanced at a run to the couches, and killed all the Vandals and the intimates of Gontharis, no one withstanding them. 28.35. Then Artabanes adjured Athanasius to take charge of the money in the Palatium; for all that had been left to Areobindus was there. 28.36. And when the guards learned the death of Gontharis, many ranged themselves at once with the Armenians; for the most were of the household of Areobindus. Coming to an understanding, then, they shouted the name of Justinian as triumphant. 28.37. And the cry, going forth from a multitude of men and being prodigiously loud, had power to reach the greater part of the city. 28.38. Thence those who were loyal to the emperor, leaping into the houses of the mutineers, killed straightway some who were taking sleep, some food, and some seized with fear and held by dire helplessness. 28.39. Among these was Pasiphilus too. For John with some of the Vandals fled to the sanctuary. 28.40. To these Artabanes, providing pledges, and raising them up thence, sent them to Byzantium, and, having recovered the city for the emperor, guarded it. 28.41. And the murder of the tyrant took place on the thirty-sixth day from the tyranny, in the nineteenth year of the reign of the Emperor Justinian as autocrat. 28.42. And Artabanes from this deed won great glory among all men. 28.43. And Praeiecta, the wife of Areobindus, straightway presented him with great sums of money, and the emperor appointed him general of all Libya. 28.44. But not long afterward Artabanes begged the emperor to summon him to Byzantium, 28.45. and the emperor fulfilled his request. And summoning Artabanes, he appointed John the brother of Pappus sole general of Libya. 28.46. This John, as soon as he came to Libya, coming to grips with Antalas and the Moors in Byzacium and conquering them in battle, killed many of the enemy, and, taking away from these barbarians all the standards of Solomon, sent them to the emperor, which they themselves had taken when Solomon was destroyed from among men. And the rest he drove very far from the Roman dominion. 28.47. But at a later time the Leuathae again, coming with a great army from the regions about Tripolis to Byzacium, joined the forces of Antalas. 28.48. Meeting them, John was defeated in the encounter, and, losing many of those who followed him, fled to Laribus. 28.49. And then indeed the enemy, overrunning everything as far as Carthage, wrought irreparable deeds upon the Libyans who fell in their way. 28.50. But not long afterward John, gathering the survivors among the soldiers, and bringing in as allies the Moors, among others those about Cutzinas, came to grips with the enemy and unexpectedly turned them to flight. 28.51. And the Romans, following them as they fled in no order, killed a great part of them, while the rest escaped to the extremities of Libya. 28.52. And thus to the survivors among the Libyans, few in number and exceedingly poor, there came at last and with difficulty some measure of quiet.

The affairs of the Romans in Libya, then, proceeded in this way. I shall now go on to the Gothic war, telling first what befell the Goths and the Italians before this war. 1.2. While Zeno was reigning in Byzantium, Augustus held the dominion of the West, whom the Romans called by the diminutive Augustulus, because, being still a boy, he had taken over the kingship, which his father Orestes, a man of the utmost sagacity, administered for him. 1.3. Now it chanced that the Romans a little before had brought in as allies the Sciri and the Alani and certain other Gothic nations; and from this it came about that they suffered at the hands of Alaric and Attila the things which I have told in the earlier narrative. 1.4. And in proportion as the strength of the barbarians among them flourished, in like proportion the prestige of the Roman soldiers was already declining; and, under the fair-sounding name of alliance, being tyrannized over by these newcomers, they were oppressed; so that the newcomers compelled them, with no restraint, to do many other things against their will, and finally demanded that they should divide among themselves all the lands of Italy. 1.5. And they commanded Orestes to give them the third part of these, and when he by no means agreed to do this, they straightway killed him. 1.6. Now there was among them a man named Odoacer, one of the bodyguards of the emperor; and he agreed to do for them at that time what they demanded, if they should set him in the position of power. 1.7. And having thus taken over the rule, he did the emperor no further harm, but allowed him to live thenceforth as a private person. 1.8. And by giving the third part of the lands to the barbarians, and in this way binding them most firmly to himself, he made the tyranny secure for ten years. 1.9. About the same time the Goths also, who dwelt in Thrace by permission of the emperor, took up arms against the Romans, under the leadership of Theoderic, a man of patrician rank who had attained the consular chair in Byzantium. 1.10. But the Emperor Zeno, who knew how to settle to his advantage the matters at hand, advised Theoderic to proceed to Italy, and, coming to grips with Odoacer, to win for himself and the Goths the dominion of the West. 1.11. For it was better for him, he said, especially as he had attained the senatorial dignity, to force out a tyrant and rule over all the Romans and Italians than to come into so great danger by contending with the emperor. 1.12. And Theoderic, pleased with the suggestion, went to Italy, and the people of the Goths followed him, placing their children and women and such of their goods as they could carry in the wagons. 1.13. And when they had come close to the Ionian Gulf, they were by no means able to cross it, since no ships were at hand; but going around the circuit of the gulf, they advanced through the land of the Taulantii and the nations there. 1.14. These the forces of Odoacer met, but, being defeated in many battles, shut themselves up with their leader in Ravenna and in the strongest of the other places. 1.15. And the Goths, settling down to a siege, took all the other places in whatever way it chanced for each, but Caesena, the fortress which is distant three hundred stades from Ravenna, and Ravenna itself, where Odoacer chanced to be, they were unable to take either by agreement or by force. 1.16. For this Ravenna lies in a level plain at the extremity of the Ionian Gulf, separated by the measure of two stades from being on the sea, and it appears to be easy of approach neither for ships nor for an army of foot-soldiers. 1.17. For ships are by no means able to put in to the shore there, since the sea itself is a hindrance, forming a shallow no less than thirty stades wide; and for this reason this shore, although it appears very near to those who sail, is in fact very far off by reason of the extent of the shallow. 1.18. And it is by no means accessible to an army of foot-soldiers; for the river Po, which they also call the Eridanus, flowing past from the borders of the Celts, and other navigable rivers, together with certain lagoons, surround the city on every side and make it encompassed by water. 1.19. There a wonderful thing happens every day. In the morning the sea, taking the form of a river, comes up over the land for a journey of one day for an unencumbered man, and renders itself navigable in the midst of the mainland; and then, dissolving the channel again, it turns back about late afternoon and gathers the stream upon itself. 1.20. All those, then, who have occasion to bring provisions into the city, or to carry them out for trade or for any other reason, place their cargoes in the boats, and, having drawn them down at the place where the channel is wont to be formed, await the inflow. 1.21. And when this comes, the boats, lifted little by little from the land, float, and the sailors about them, setting to work, now sail. 1.22. And this happens not there only, but along the whole of that shore continually, as far as the city of Aquileia. 1.23. It does not, however, happen in the same way at all times, but when the light of the moon is faint, the advance of the sea also is not strong, but after the first quarter until the second the inflow is wont to become stronger. So these things are thus. 1.24. But when the third year had now been spent by the Goths and Theoderic in besieging Ravenna, and the Goths were distressed at the blockade and the forces of Odoacer were oppressed by the scarcity of necessaries, they came to a parley with one another through the mediation of the priest of Ravenna, on condition that Theoderic and Odoacer should dwell in Ravenna on terms of equality and likeness. 1.25. And for some time they kept the agreement, but afterward Theoderic, having caught Odoacer, as they say, plotting against him, invited him to a banquet with treacherous intent and killed him; and from this, having won over by persuasion such of the hostile barbarians as chanced to survive, he himself held the power over both Goths and Italians. 1.26. And he did not see fit to assume either the dress or the name of emperor of the Romans, but continued to be called rex to the end of his life (for thus the barbarians are accustomed to call their leaders); yet he presided over his subjects, investing himself with all the qualities which are fitting for one who is by nature king. 1.27. For he took the most extraordinary care of justice and preserved the laws securely; he guarded the land safely from the barbarians dwelling round about, and attained the highest degree of wisdom and manliness. 1.28. And he himself committed scarcely a single act of injustice against his subjects, nor did he permit any other who attempted such things, except indeed that the Goths divided among themselves the portion of the lands which Odoacer had given to his partisans. 1.29. And Theoderic was in name a tyrant, but in deed a true king, inferior to none of those who had distinguished themselves in this office from the beginning; and love for him among both Goths and Italians flourished greatly, and this contrary to the manner of mankind. 1.30. For since in states men of different parties always choose different things, it comes about that the government in power pleases for the moment those to whom its deeds are pleasing, but offends those whose judgment runs counter to it. 1.31. But after a reign of thirty-seven years he died, having become terrible to all his enemies, but having left great longing for himself among his subjects. And he died in the following manner. 1.32. Symmachus and Boethius, his son-in-law, were patricians by descent from of old, and both had been first in the Roman senate and consuls. 1.33. But having cultivated philosophy and given heed to justice no less than any others, and having remedied the want of many of the citizens and of strangers with their money, and having advanced greatly in reputation, they brought the most wicked men into envy of them. 1.34. And Theoderic, persuaded by these slanderers, killed these two men on the charge that they were attempting a revolution, and confiscated their property to the public treasury. 1.35. And a few days later, while he was dining, the servants set before him the head of a great fish. This head seemed to Theoderic to be that of Symmachus newly slain. 1.36. And with the teeth fixed in the lower lip, and the eyes looking at him with a grim and mad gaze, it seemed exceedingly like one threatening him. 1.37. And being terror-stricken at the strangeness of the portent and shivering exceedingly, he withdrew at a run to his own chamber, and, bidding them lay many coverlets upon him, kept quiet. 1.38. But afterward, disclosing all that had befallen to Elpidius the physician, he wept for the wrong he had done to Symmachus and Boethius. 1.39. And after he had wept and grieved deeply over the calamity, he died not long afterward, having done this first and last act of injustice against his subjects, namely, that he had passed judgment concerning the two men without searching out the matter, as had been his custom. 2.1. After his death the kingship was taken over by Atalaric, the grandson of Theoderic by his daughter, being eight years old and reared under his mother Amalasuntha. 2.2. For his father had already departed from among men. And not long afterward Justinian took over the kingship in Byzantium. 2.3. And Amalasuntha, being guardian of her child, administered the government, having attained the highest degree of wisdom and justice, but displaying to a marked degree a masculine quality of nature. 2.4. And during the whole time that she presided over the state she punished none of all the Romans in his person, nor confiscated their money. 2.5. Nor indeed did she yield to the Goths in their desire to do them wrong, but she even restored to the children of Symmachus and Boethius their property. 2.6. Now Amalasuntha wished to make her child resemble the Roman princes in his manner of life, and was already compelling him to attend a school of letters. 2.7. And she chose out three of the old men among the Goths whom she knew to be most prudent and reasonable of all, and bade them associate with Atalaric. 2.8. But this was by no means pleasing to the Goths. For, through their desire to wrong their subjects, they wished to be ruled by him in a more barbarian fashion. 2.9. And once the mother, finding the child doing some wrong in his chamber, struck him; and he, in tears, went off thence to the men's apartment. 2.10. And the Goths, meeting him, made a great matter of it, and, abusing Amalasuntha, maintained that she wished to put the child out of the way as quickly as possible, so that she herself, coming to the bed of another husband, might rule the Goths and Italians along with him. 2.11. And all who were notable among them gathered together and came to Amalasuntha and found fault that the king was not being educated rightly nor in a way to his advantage. 2.12. For letters, they said, are far removed from manliness, and the teaching of old men for the most part results in a cowardly and submissive spirit. 2.13. Therefore the man who is to be bold in any action and great in reputation must be set free from the fear that comes from teachers and must practise the exercises of arms. 2.14. And they said that not even Theoderic would ever allow any of the Goths to send their children to a school of letters; 2.15. for he used to say to them all that, if the fear of the strap once came over them, they would never have the spirit to despise sword or spear. 2.16. And they thought it right that she should reflect that her father Theoderic, before he died, had become master of so great a territory and had invested himself with a kingship in no way belonging to him, although he had no acquaintance even by hearsay with letters. 2.17. "Therefore, O mistress," they said, "bid these tutors now begone, and do you give to Atalaric some companions of his own age to share his life, who, growing up to manhood along with him, will urge him on to valour after the barbarian fashion." 2.18. When Amalasuntha heard this, she did not approve, but, fearing the plot of these men, she gave the appearance that their words were pleasing to her, and conceded all that the barbarians demanded of her. 2.19. And when the old men had left Atalaric, certain boys associated with him to share his life, not yet come to manhood, but a little older in years, who, as soon as he came to manhood, by urging him to drunkenness and intercourse with women, made him exceedingly base in character and, through their folly, more disobedient to his mother. 2.20. So that he by no means thought it right to give heed to her at all, although the barbarians were already openly uniting against her, who indeed bade the woman without restraint withdraw from the palace. 2.21. But Amalasuntha neither was dismayed at the plot of the Goths nor weakened as a woman might, but, still displaying her royal dignity, she chose out three of the most notable among the barbarians who were most responsible for the sedition against her, and commanded them to go to the extremities of Italy — not, however, together, but as far as possible from one another; and in name they were sent to guard the country against the inroad of the enemy. 2.22. But none the less these men, through their friends and kinsmen (for they still came together with them, even though making a long journey), were preparing the plot against Amalasuntha. And being no longer able to bear this, the woman devised the following plan. 2.23. She sent to Byzantium and inquired of the Emperor Justinian whether it was his wish that Amalasuntha the daughter of Theoderic should come to him; for she wished to depart from Italy as quickly as possible. 2.24. And the emperor, pleased at the word, bade the woman come, and gave orders that the finest of the houses in Epidamnus should be made ready, so that, when Amalasuntha should come there, she might lodge there and, after spending as much time as she wished, might thus be conveyed to Byzantium. 2.25. When Amalasuntha learned this, she chose out Gothic men, energetic and most devoted to her, and sent them to kill the three whom I have just mentioned, since they had been most responsible for the sedition against her. 2.26. And she herself, placing in a single ship other money and four hundred centenaria of gold, and embarking on it some of those most faithful to her, bade them sail to Epidamnus, and, when they arrived, to anchor in its harbour, but of the cargo, until she herself should send word, 2.27. to carry nothing whatever out of the ship. And she did this in order that, if she should learn that the three were dead, she might remain where she was and send for the ship, having no longer any fear from her enemies; but if it should chance that one of them survived, then, with no good hope left to her, she might sail in haste and find safety in the emperor's land together with the money. 2.28. With such a purpose Amalasuntha sent the ship to Epidamnus, and when it arrived at the harbour of the Epidamnians, those who had the money did what had been enjoined upon them. 2.29. And a little later Amalasuntha, the murders having been accomplished for her as she wished, sent for the ship and, remaining in Ravenna, made her rule as secure as possible. 3.1. Now there was among the Goths one Theodahad by name, son of Amalafrida the sister of Theoderic, a man already advanced in years, who had partaken of Latin letters and the doctrines of Plato, but was altogether without practice in war and far removed from any energy, though devoted to the love of money in a marvellous degree. 3.2. This Theodahad had become master of most of the lands in Tuscany, and was eager to take from their owners the rest by force as well; for to have a neighbour seemed to Theodahad a kind of misfortune. 3.3. Amalasuntha was eager to check this eagerness of his, and on this account he was always vexed with her and ill-disposed toward her. 3.4. He planned, therefore, to give over Tuscany to the Emperor Justinian, on condition that, receiving much money and the dignity of senator from him, he should spend the rest of his life in Byzantium. 3.5. While Theodahad was planning this, envoys came from Byzantium to the bishop of Rome — Hypatius, the priest of Ephesus, and Demetrius from Philippi in Macedonia — on account of a doctrine over which the Christians dispute among themselves, being in doubt. 3.6. The points in dispute I shall by no means mention, though I know them well; for I consider it a kind of insane folly to investigate the nature of God, of what sort it is. 3.7. For I think that even human things are not accurately comprehended by man, much less the things that pertain to the nature of God. So let these matters be passed over by me in safety, with the sole purpose that things held in honour be not disbelieved. 3.8. For I, for my part, would say nothing whatever about God except that He is altogether good and holds all things in His power. 3.9. But let each speak concerning these matters as he thinks he knows, both priest and layman. But Theodahad, meeting secretly with these envoys, enjoined them to report to the Emperor Justinian what he had planned, telling them all that I have just disclosed. 3.10. Meanwhile Atalaric, having fallen into a debauchery that knew no bounds, was seized by a wasting disease. 3.11. Wherefore Amalasuntha was at a loss; for she had no confidence in the judgment of her child, who had come to such a state of degeneracy, and, if Atalaric himself should depart from among men, she did not think her own life would be in safety thereafter, since she had offended the most notable of the Goths. 3.12. For this reason she wished to give over the power of the Goths and Italians to the Emperor Justinian, in order that she herself might be saved. 3.13. Now it chanced that Alexander, a man of senatorial rank, had come there with Demetrius and Hypatius. 3.14. For when the emperor heard that the ship of Amalasuntha was anchored in the harbour of Epidamnus, but that she still delayed, although much time had been spent, he sent Alexander to spy out everything concerning Amalasuntha and report it. 3.15. And in name the emperor sent Alexander as an envoy, being disturbed about the affairs of Lilybaeum (which I have disclosed in the previous narrative), and because ten Huns from the army in Libya, taking to flight, had come to Campania, and Uliaris, who guarded Naples, had received them, not without the consent of Amalasuntha; and because the Goths, in their war with the Gepaedes about Sirmium, had treated the city of Gratiana, which lies on the borders of Illyricum, as hostile. 3.16. Bringing these charges against Amalasuntha, and writing a letter, he sent Alexander. And he, when he came to Rome, left the priests there transacting the business for which they had come, while he himself, conveyed to Ravenna and coming into the presence of Amalasuntha, reported the emperor's words secretly and handed over the letter openly. 3.17. And the writing disclosed this: "The fortress in Lilybaeum, which is ours, you hold, having taken it by force, and barbarians who have become runaways from me you have received and have not even now decided to give back, but you have also wrought irreparable injury upon my Gratiana, 3.18. though it in no way belongs to you. Wherefore it is time for you to reckon what the end of these things will be." 3.19. When the woman had read this letter, she answered as follows: "A great emperor, and one who lays claim to virtue, ought reasonably to assist an orphan child who by no means perceives what is being done, rather than to be at variance with him for no cause whatever. 3.20. For a contest, unless it be set up between equals, does not bring even victory in a seemly form. 3.21. But you brandish Lilybaeum against Atalaric, and ten runaways, and a wrong committed by soldiers going against their own enemies, which fell upon a friendly city through some ignorance. 3.22. Do not so, O emperor, do not so; but reflect that, when you were taking the field against the Vandals, not only did we set ourselves as no hindrance to you, but we also gave you with great eagerness a road against the enemy and a market of the most necessary things, and among other things so great a multitude of horses, from which most of all your victory over the enemy came about. 3.23. And yet he would justly be called an ally and a friend, not only who holds out the alliance in word to his neighbours, but who also is seen serving each one in war with whatever he may need. 3.24. And reckon that at that time your fleet was able neither to put in to land anywhere from the sea except Sicily, nor to go to Libya without the things purchased there. 3.25. So that the chief part of the victory comes to you from us; for he who provides the solution to those in difficulty has a just claim to the success that follows. 3.26. And what would be sweeter to a man, O emperor, than mastery over his enemies? And indeed it falls to us to be wronged in no moderate degree, since, contrary to the law of war, we do not divide the portion of the spoils. 3.27. But now you think it right to take from us even the Sicilian Lilybaeum, which belonged to the Goths from of old — a single rock, O emperor, not worth even a piece of silver, which it would have been fitting for you to render in turn to Atalaric, who assisted you in your direst need, even if it had chanced from of old 3.28. to belong to your empire." This Amalasuntha wrote openly to the emperor; but secretly she agreed to put the whole of Italy into his hands. 3.29. And the envoys, returning to Byzantium, reported everything to the Emperor Justinian — Alexander what was the purpose of Amalasuntha, and Demetrius and Hypatius all that they had heard Theodahad say, and that Theodahad, wielding great power in Tuscany and having become master of much of the land there, would be able with no trouble to accomplish what had been agreed. 3.30. Overjoyed at this, the emperor straightway sent to Italy Peter, an Illyrian by race, coming from Thessalonica, one of the orators in Byzantium, and otherwise sagacious and gentle and well fitted by nature for persuasion. 4.1. While these things were happening thus, many of the Tuscans denounced Theodahad to Amalasuntha for doing violence to all the people there and taking away their lands for no reason — all the rest, and not least the royal house itself, which the Romans are accustomed to call the patrimonium. 4.2. Wherefore the woman, calling Theodahad to account and convicting him outright by his accusers, compelled him to pay back everything which he had wrongfully taken, and so dismissed him. 4.3. And from this, having offended the man exceedingly, she became at variance with him thenceforth, since he was grieved to the utmost by his love of money, because he was unable to do wrong and to use violence. 4.4. About this time Atalaric, wasted away by his disease, died, having survived for eight years in his rule. And Amalasuntha (for it was fated that evil should befall her), making no account of the nature of Theodahad and of what he had lately done to her, supposed that she would suffer nothing unpleasant at his hands if she did the man some greater good. 4.5. Summoning him, therefore, when he came, she said, taming him with soft words, that she had long known that her child would die before long; for she had heard that all the physicians agreed in their opinion, and she herself had perceived that the body of Atalaric was ever wasting away. 4.6. And since she saw that both Goths and Italians held no good opinion concerning Theodahad himself, to whom the family of Theoderic had come round, she was eager to purge him of this shameful name, so that nothing might be a hindrance to him when he should be called to the kingship. 4.7. And at the same time the matter of justice troubled her, lest, if it should come about that those who already accused him of having wronged them should have no one to whom to report what had befallen them, they should have as master the one who was hostile to them. 4.8. For these reasons, then, she said, she was calling him, now thus purified, to the kingship; but he must be bound by the most terrible oaths that the name of the rule should belong to Theodahad, while she herself in deed should have the power no less than before. 4.9. When Theodahad heard this, having sworn all that Amalasuntha wished, he agreed to it with treacherous intent, keeping in mind all that she had previously done to him. 4.10. Thus Amalasuntha, deceived both by her own judgment and by the oaths of Theodahad, established him in the rule. 4.11. And sending Gothic men as envoys to Byzantium, she disclosed this to the Emperor Justinian. 4.12. But Theodahad, having taken over the leadership, did everything contrary to what she had hoped and what he himself had promised. 4.13. And, having won over the kinsmen of those Goths whom she had killed, who were many and exceedingly notable among the Goths, he suddenly killed some of the relatives of Amalasuntha and kept her under guard, the envoys not having yet arrived at Byzantium. 4.14. Now there is a certain lake in Tuscany, called Bolsena, within which an island rises up, exceedingly small, but having a strong fortress. 4.15. There Theodahad shut up Amalasuntha and kept her under guard. But fearing — which indeed came to pass — that he had thereby offended the emperor, he sent men of the Roman senate, Liberius and Opilio with certain others, and enjoined them to excuse him with all their power before the emperor, maintaining that nothing unpleasant had befallen Amalasuntha at his hands, although she had previously wrought irreparable dreadful deeds against him. 4.16. And to this effect he himself wrote to the emperor, and compelled Amalasuntha, against her will, to write. 4.17. These things, then, were going on in this way. But Peter was already being sent on the embassy, having been directed beforehand by the emperor to meet Theodahad secretly from all the rest, and, when he gave pledges by oath that none of what was being done should become known, thus to settle the matter of Tuscany securely with him, 4.18. and, meeting Amalasuntha secretly, to arrange about the whole of Italy in whatever way was likely to be of advantage to each. 4.19. But openly he was going to act as envoy concerning Lilybaeum and the other matters which I have just mentioned. For the emperor had not yet heard anything concerning the death of Atalaric, or the rule of Theodahad, or what had befallen Amalasuntha. 4.20. And Peter, journeying on the way, first met the envoys of Amalasuntha and learned about the rule of Theodahad; 4.21. and coming a little later to the city of Aulon, which lies on the Ionian Gulf, and there meeting the forces of Liberius and Opilio, he learned of all that had befallen, and, reporting this to the emperor, remained there. 4.22. And when the Emperor Justinian heard this, planning to throw the Goths and Theodahad into confusion, he wrote a letter to Amalasuntha, disclosing that he was eager to take her part as much as possible; and he enjoined Peter by no means to conceal these things, but to make them manifest both to Theodahad himself and to all the Goths. 4.23. And of the envoys from Italy the others, when they were conveyed to Byzantium, reported the whole matter to the emperor, and Liberius most of all; 4.24. for the man was exceedingly fair and good, and knew how to give heed to the truth; 4.25. but Opilio alone maintained most persistently that Theodahad had done no wrong to Amalasuntha. And when Peter arrived in Italy, it befell Amalasuntha to be removed from among men. 4.26. For the kinsmen of the Goths whom she had killed, coming to Theodahad, maintained that neither his life nor theirs was in safety unless Amalasuntha should be put out of the way as quickly as possible. 4.27. And when he gave them leave, they went to the island and straightway killed Amalasuntha. 4.28. This grieved exceedingly all the Italians and the other Goths. 4.29. For the woman had the strongest care for all virtue, 4.30. as I have said a little before. So Peter protested outright to Theodahad and the other Goths that, this dreadful deed having been wrought by them, there would be a truceless war between the emperor and them. 4.31. But Theodahad, in his folly, holding the murderers of Amalasuntha in honour and esteem, wished to persuade Peter and the emperor that this defilement had been wrought by the Goths with his disapproval and most against his will. 5.1. Meanwhile it chanced that Belisarius had won renown against Gelimer and the Vandals. And the emperor, learning what had befallen Amalasuntha, straightway entered upon the war, being in the ninth year of his reign. 5.2. And he commanded Mundus, the general of Illyricum, to go to Dalmatia, which was subject to the Goths, and to make an attempt on Salones (now Mundus was a barbarian by race, but exceedingly loyal to the emperor's cause and good in matters of war); and he sent Belisarius by sea, having four thousand soldiers from the regular forces and the foederati, and about three thousand Isaurians. 5.3. And the commanders of note were Constantinus and Bessas, from the regions of Thrace, and Peranius from Iberia which is near the Medes, who was sprung from the royal line of the Iberians, but had previously come over to the Romans as a deserter through hatred of the Persians; and of the cavalry detachments Valentinus and Magnus and Innocentius, and of the infantry Herodian and Paulus and Demetrius and Ursicinus, and the leader of the Isaurians, Ennes. 5.4. And there followed also two hundred Huns as allies and three hundred Moors. And the general with supreme command over all was Belisarius, who had many notable guardsmen and spearmen. 5.5. And there followed him also Photius, the son of his wife Antonina by a former marriage, still a young man and just growing his first beard, but exceedingly sagacious and displaying strength of nature beyond his years. 5.6. And the emperor enjoined upon Belisarius to set sail in name for Carthage, but, when they should come to Sicily, to disembark there as if on some need and make an attempt on the island. 5.7. And if it should be possible to make it subject with no trouble, to hold it and let go of it no more; but if any hindrance should meet them, to sail in haste to Libya, giving no one any perception of his purpose. 5.8. He sent also to the leaders of the Franks and wrote as follows: "The Goths, having taken our Italy by force, have not only by no means decided to give it back, but have also wronged us in ways neither bearable nor moderate. 5.9. Therefore we have been compelled to take the field against them, and it is reasonable that you should carry through this war along with us, which both right belief, which casts off the opinion of the Arians, and your common hatred toward the Goths make a common one for us." 5.10. So much the emperor wrote; and presenting them with money, he agreed to give more when they should be in the action. And they promised to fight as his allies with great eagerness. 5.11. Mundus, then, and the army with him, having come to Dalmatia and come to grips with the Goths there who met them, and having conquered in the encounter, took Salones. 5.12. And Belisarius, sailing to Sicily, took Catana. And setting out thence, he won over Syracuse by agreement and the other cities with no trouble; except indeed that the Goths who held the garrison in Panormus, trusting in the circuit-wall (for the place was strong), by no means wished to come over to Belisarius, and bade him lead his army away thence in haste. 5.13. But Belisarius, reckoning that it was impossible to take the place from the mainland, commanded the fleet to sail into the harbour, which extended up to the wall. 5.14. For it was outside the circuit-wall and altogether empty of men. There, when the ships had anchored, it came about that the masts were higher than the battlements. 5.15. Straightway, then, filling all the small boats of the ships with bowmen, he hung them from the tops of the masts. 5.16. Whence the enemy, being shot at from above, came into an irresistible fear and straightway surrendered Panormus to Belisarius by agreement. 5.17. And from this the emperor held the whole of Sicily subject, to pay tribute. And at that time it befell Belisarius to have good fortune beyond words. 5.18. For having received the dignity of the consulship for having conquered the Vandals, and still holding it, when he had won over the whole of Sicily, on the last day of his consulship he rode into Syracuse, applauded most heartily by the army and the Sicilians, and throwing gold coin to all. 5.19. This, however, was not done by him on purpose, but a certain fortune befell the man, that, having recovered the whole island for the Romans, on that very day he rode into Syracuse, and laid down the office of consul there, not, as had been the custom, in the senate-house of Byzantium, but there, ceasing to be consul. So it befell Belisarius thus to prosper. 6.1. When Peter learned this, he pressed Theodahad much more strongly and ceased not to frighten him. 6.2. And he, playing the coward and falling into speechlessness no less than if he himself had been a captive together with Gelimer, came to a parley with Peter secretly from all the rest, and came to an agreement with him, on condition that Theodahad should give up to the Emperor Justinian the whole of Sicily, and should send him a golden crown each year weighing three hundred pounds, and three thousand Gothic warriors whenever he should wish; and that Theodahad himself should by no means have authority to put to death any of the priests or senators, or to confiscate his property to the public treasury except by the emperor's consent; 6.3. and if Theodahad should wish to advance any of his subjects to the patrician or other senatorial dignity, that he should not himself give it, but should ask the emperor to give it; 6.4. and that the people of the Romans, in their acclamations, should always shout the name of the emperor first, and then Theodahad, in theatres and hippodromes and wherever else it should be necessary for such a thing to be done. 6.5. And a statue of bronze or of any other material should never be set up for Theodahad alone, but should always be made for both, and should stand thus: on the right that of the emperor, on the other side that of Theodahad. On these terms Theodahad wrote the agreement and dismissed the envoy. 6.6. But a little later a trembling of soul came over the man and led him to fears that knew no bounds and turned his mind, terrifying him with the name of war, and saying that, if the agreement made between him and Peter should by no means please the emperor, war would straightway be at hand. 6.7. Sending again, therefore, for Peter, who was already among the Albani, as if to take counsel secretly with the man, he inquired whether he thought the agreement would be pleasing to the emperor. 6.8. And he said that he so suspected. "But if these things should by no means please the man, what will come of it thereafter?" 6.9. he said. Peter answered: "You will have to make war thereafter, most noble sir." "And is this just, dearest envoy?" he said. And he straightway said in reply: "And how is it not just, good sir, that the practices proper to each man's soul should be preserved?" "What is this?" Theodahad asked. 6.10. "Because for you there is great zeal to be a philosopher," he said, "but for the Emperor Justinian to be a noble Roman emperor. And there is this difference, that for one who has practised philosophy to bring death to men, especially in so great a multitude, would never be seemly, and that too as a partaker of the teaching of Plato, of which surely it is unholy for you, having shared in it, not to be free of all murder; but for him to lay claim to a land that from of old 6.11. belongs to the empire which is his is in no way unreasonable." Persuaded by this suggestion, Theodahad agreed to give up the leadership to the Emperor Justinian. 6.12. And to this effect both he and his wife swore; and he bound Peter by oaths not to make these things known until he should see that the emperor would not accept the former agreement. 6.13. And he sent with him Rusticus, one of the priests and especially intimate with him, a Roman man, on this agreement. To them too he gave a letter. 6.14. So Peter and Rusticus, coming to Byzantium, reported the things which had previously seemed good to the emperor, as Theodahad had enjoined upon them. And when the emperor by no means wished to accept these proposals, 6.15. they showed him the things written afterward. And the writing disclosed this: "I have not become a newcomer to the royal court, for it has chanced that I was born in the family of a king and reared worthily of my race; but of wars and the tumults attending them I am altogether without experience. 6.16. For having from of old had a passionate love for hearing about discourses, and having always made my pursuit of this, it comes about that I am very far from the tumult of battles. 6.17. So that it is by no means reasonable for me, coveting the honours that come from kingship, to pursue a life amid dangers, when it is possible for me to stand apart from both. 6.18. For neither of these is pleasing to me: the one, because it is honoured to the point of satiety — for there is a surfeit of all pleasant things — the other, because the not being accustomed to it leads to confusion. 6.19. But I, if I should be given lands yielding a yearly revenue of no less than twelve centenaria, would account the kingship of less value than these, and would straightway put into your hands the power over Goths and Italians. 6.20. For I would more gladly be a farmer with freedom from cares than live amid royal anxieties, which pass on dangers from dangers. 6.21. But send a man as quickly as possible to whom it is fitting for me to hand over Italy and the affairs of the kingdom." 6.22. So much the writing of Theodahad disclosed. And the emperor, overjoyed, answered as follows: "Long ago I held it by hearsay that you were sagacious, but now I know it also by experience, in that you have decided not to await the issue of war. 6.23. Some, having already suffered this, have stumbled in the greatest matters. And you will never repent of having made us friends instead of enemies. 6.24. But you shall have these things which you ask of us, and besides there shall be added to you that you be enrolled in the first honours of the Romans. 6.25. Now, then, I have sent Athanasius and Peter, in order that there may be security to each through some agreement. And Belisarius too will come to you almost at once, to put an end to all matters 6.26. which are agreed between us." Having written this, the emperor sent Athanasius the brother of Alexander, who had previously gone, as has been said, on an embassy to Atalaric, and again Peter the orator, whom I have mentioned before, enjoining them to assign to Theodahad the lands of the emperor's house which they call the patrimonium, and, making letters and oaths a security for the agreements, thus to summon Belisarius from Sicily, in order that, taking over the palace and the whole of Italy, he might hold it under guard. 6.27. And to Belisarius he sent word to come to them quickly when they should summon him. 7.1. While the emperor was doing this and these envoys were being sent to Italy, meanwhile the Goths, under the leadership of Asinarius and Gripas among others, came to Dalmatia with a great army. 7.2. And when they had come close to Salones, Mauricius the son of Mundus met them with a few men, not for battle, but having come for reconnaissance. 7.3. And a fierce encounter taking place, the first and best of the Goths fell, but of the Romans almost all, and Mauricius the general. 7.4. When Mundus heard this, becoming exceedingly grieved at the calamity and now held by great fury, he straightway went against the enemy in no order. 7.5. And a fierce battle taking place, it befell the Romans to win a Cadmean victory. For the most of the enemy fell there and the rout was brilliant, but Mundus, killing and following wherever he chanced, and by no means able to control his mind by reason of the calamity of his child, was struck by one of the fugitives and fell; and the pursuit ended in this way and both armies were dissolved. 7.6. Then the Romans remembered the verse of the Sibyl, which, sung in former time, had seemed to them a portent. For that oracle said that, when Africa should be held, the world together with its offspring would perish. 7.7. The oracle, however, did not mean this, but, having hinted that Libya would again be under the Romans, it added this also, that then Mundus together with his child would perish. For it runs thus: Africa capta mundus cum nato peribit. 7.8. And since 'world' in the Latin tongue means 'Mundus,' they thought the oracle concerned the world. So these things were thus. And no one entered Salones. 7.9. For the Romans withdrew homeward, since they were left altogether without a leader, and the Goths, no one of their best being left to them, falling into fear, held the fortresses there; 7.10. for they did not even trust the circuit-wall of Salones, especially as the Romans who dwelt there were not very well disposed toward them. 7.11. When Theodahad heard this, he made no account of the envoys who had now come to him. For he was sufficiently inclined by nature to faithlessness, and his mind was by no means firm, but the present fortune always led him, unreasonably and not worthily of the circumstances, into terror that knew no measure, and then again set him into unspeakable boldness. 7.12. And so at that time, hearing of the death of Mundus and Mauricius, he was exceedingly elated and not in proportion to what had been done, and he thought fit to mock the envoys who had now come to him. 7.13. And when Peter at one time abused him for having overstepped what had been agreed with the emperor, Theodahad, calling them both publicly, spoke as follows: 7.14. "The institution of envoys is august and otherwise held in honour among all men, but envoys preserve this privilege among themselves to this extent, that they guard the dignity of the embassy by their own moderation. 7.15. For men have held it just to kill an envoy when he is seen either to have insulted a king, or to have come to the bed 7.16. of a woman living with another man." This Theodahad flung at Peter, not because he had approached a woman, but in order to maintain that there are charges which lead, as is likely, to the death of an envoy. But the envoys answered as follows: 7.17. "Neither are these things, O leader of the Goths, as you have said, nor could you, by unsound pretexts, charge envoys with unholy deeds against men. 7.18. For an envoy cannot become an adulterer even if he wishes, since it is not easy for him even to partake of water except by the will of those guarding him. 7.19. And as for the words which he speaks, having heard them from him who sent him, he would not reasonably bear the blame therefrom, even if they should chance not to be good, but he who commanded would justly bear this charge, while to the envoy belongs only the fulfilment of the service. 7.20. So that we shall say everything which we were sent to say, having heard it from the emperor, but do you hear it calmly; for if you are disturbed, there will be left to you the wronging of envoys. 7.21. Therefore it is time for you of your own will to fulfil all that you agreed with the emperor. For it is for this very thing that we have come. And the letter which he wrote you you already have received, but the writing which he sent to the first men of the Goths we shall give to none other than 7.22. to them." When the envoys had said this, the commanders of the barbarians who were present heard it and enjoined them to put into the hands of Theodahad what was written for them. 7.23. And it ran thus: "It has been our care to take you into our state, at which it is reasonable that you should rejoice. For it is not for your diminishing, but in order that you may be more honoured, that you will come to us. 7.24. And besides, we call the Goths not to strange or unfamiliar customs, but to those with which you became familiar and from which it chanced afterward, on occasion, that you stood apart. For these reasons Athanasius and Peter have now been sent there, 7.25. with whom you must cooperate in all things." So much the writing disclosed. But Theodahad, having read everything, decided neither to fulfil in deed any of what he had promised the emperor and kept the envoys under no moderate guard. 7.26. But when the Emperor Justinian heard this and what had befallen in Dalmatia, he sent Constantianus, who commanded the imperial grooms, to Illyricum, enjoining him to gather an army thence and make an attempt on Salones in whatever way might be possible for him; and he commanded Belisarius to go quickly to Italy and treat the Goths as enemies. 7.27. Constantianus, then, came to Epidamnus and, spending some time there, gathered an army. Meanwhile the Goths, under the leadership of Gripas, coming to Dalmatia with another army, held Salones; 7.28. and Constantianus, when his preparation was in the best state, setting out from Epidamnus with his whole fleet, anchored at Epidaurus, which is on the right as one sails into the Ionian Gulf; and there chanced to be men whom Gripas had sent for reconnaissance. 7.29. And to them, as they observed the ships and the camp of Constantianus, the sea and the whole land seemed to be full of soldiers, and, returning to Gripas, they maintained that Constantianus was bringing no few tens of thousands of men. 7.30. And he, falling into great fear, thought it inexpedient to meet the assailants, and by no means wished to be besieged by the emperor's army, which thus had command of the sea; 7.31. and most of all the circuit-wall of Salones disturbed him, since most of it had now fallen down, and the exceedingly suspicious attitude of those dwelling there toward the Goths. 7.32. And for this reason, departing thence with his whole army as quickly as possible, he encamped in the plain which is between Salones and the city of Scardona. And Constantianus, sailing with all his ships from Epidaurus, put in at Lysina, which lies in the gulf. 7.33. And thence he sent some of his followers, in order that, searching out how the affairs of Gripas stood, they might report it. And learning the whole matter from them, he sailed in haste straight for Salones. 7.34. And when he had come close to it, disembarking the army onto the mainland, he himself remained quiet there, but, picking out five hundred of the army and setting over them as commander Sifilas, one of his own guardsmen, he bade them seize the narrow place which he had learned was in the suburb of the city. And Sifilas did accordingly. 7.35. And Constantianus and the whole army, riding into Salones on the following day, anchored both the infantry and the ships. 7.36. Constantianus, then, took care of the circuit-wall of Salones, rebuilding in haste all that had fallen down; but Gripas and the army of the Goths, when the Romans had taken Salones, on the seventh day setting out thence, were conveyed to Ravenna; and thus Constantianus held Dalmatia and all of Liburnia, winning over all the Goths who were settled there. 7.37. The affairs of Dalmatia, then, were in this state. And the winter was coming to an end, and the first year of this war which Procopius wrote was being completed. 8.1. But Belisarius, leaving garrisons in Syracuse and Panormus, crossed with the rest of the army from Messina to Rhegium (where indeed the poets make Scylla and Charybdis to have been), and the people there came over to him every day. 8.2. For their places being unwalled from of old, they had no garrison of them at all, and they were exceedingly distressed at the present government through hatred of the Goths, as was likely. 8.3. And there came as a deserter to Belisarius from the Goths Ebrimous with all his followers, the son-in-law of Theodahad, who was married to his daughter Theodenantha. And being straightway sent to the emperor, he met with other honours and attained the patrician dignity. 8.4. And the army went on foot from Rhegium through the Bruttii and Lucanians, and the fleet of ships followed close along the mainland. 8.5. And when they came to Campania, they met a city on the sea, Naples by name, strong in the nature of its site and having a garrison of many Goths. 8.6. And Belisarius bade the ships anchor in the harbour, which was out of range of missiles, while he himself, making a camp near the city, first took by agreement the fortress in the suburb, and then permitted those in the city who wished to send some of their notable men to the camp, in order that they might say all that they wished and, having heard his words, might report them to the whole people. 8.7. Straightway, then, the Neapolitans sent Stephanus. And he, when he came to Belisarius, spoke as follows: "You do not do what is just, O general, in taking the field against Roman men who do no wrong, who dwell in a small city and have a garrison of barbarian masters, so that it is not even in our power to act against it 8.8. if we should wish. But it has befallen these guards too, leaving their children and wives and most precious things in the hands of Theodahad, to come for our guarding. 8.9. Therefore, if they do anything toward you, they will plainly be betraying not the city, but their own selves. 8.10. And if I must speak the truth, hiding nothing, you have come against us without even planning what is to your own advantage. For if you take Rome, Naples too will be subject to you with no trouble, but if, as is likely, you are repulsed from there, you will not hold this city either in safety. 8.11. So that the time will be spent by you to no purpose in this blockade." So much Stephanus said. And Belisarius answered as follows: 8.12. "Whether we have come here having planned well or otherwise, we shall not give the Neapolitans to consider. But what is worthy of your deliberation, we wish you to consider, and so to do whatever is likely to be of advantage to your own selves. 8.13. Receive, then, into the city the emperor's army, which has come for the freedom of you and the other Italians, and do not choose for yourselves the most grievous of all things. 8.14. For all who, escaping slavery or some other shameful thing, go to war, these, if they prosper in the struggle, have a double good fortune, having won, along with victory, freedom from evils; and if they are defeated, they bear off for themselves some consolation, in that they did not willingly follow the worse fortune. 8.15. But those for whom it is possible to be free without a fight, but who enter a struggle in order that they may have slavery made secure, these, even though they conquer, if it so chance, have stumbled in the most necessary things, and, having come off from the battle worse than they wished, will have, along with their other misfortune, the calamity that comes from defeat. So much let be said by us to the Neapolitans. 8.16. But to these Goths who are present we give the choice, either henceforth to be ranged with us under the great emperor, or to go home altogether free from harm. 8.17. For if both they and you, neglecting all this, dare to raise arms against us, it will be necessary for us too, if God wills, to treat whoever falls in our way as an enemy. 8.18. If, however, it should be the will of the Neapolitans to choose the emperor's cause and so to be freed from such grievous slavery, I undertake, giving the pledges, that you shall receive from us those things which the Sicilians lately, hoping for, were unable to call us false-swearers in." 8.19. This Belisarius bade Stephanus report to the people. And privately he promised that great good things would come to him, if he should urge the Neapolitans to loyalty toward the emperor. 8.20. And Stephanus, coming to the city, reported the words of Belisarius and himself declared the opinion that it was inexpedient to fight against the emperor. 8.21. And there cooperated with him Antiochus, a Syrian man, who had long dwelt in Naples engaged in maritime trade and had a great reputation there for sagacity and justice. 8.22. But Pastor and Asclepiodotus were orators and exceedingly notable among the Neapolitans, but friends of the Goths to the utmost, and by no means wishing for the present state to be changed. 8.23. These two men, planning how what was being done might be hindered, urged the multitude to put forward many great demands and to bind Belisarius by oaths that they would obtain these from him at once. 8.24. And writing in a little document all that they supposed Belisarius would not accept, they gave it to Stephanus. 8.25. And he, when he came again to the emperor's camp, showing the document to the general, inquired whether it was his wish to fulfil everything that the Neapolitans put forward and to swear concerning these things. And he, promising that everything would be fulfilled for them, dismissed him. 8.26. When the Neapolitans heard this, they now accepted the words and quickly bade the city receive the emperor's army. 8.27. For he maintained that nothing unpleasant would befall them, if anyone could judge from the Sicilians, to whom it had lately fallen, having exchanged barbarian tyrants for the rule of Justinian, to be free and unharmed by all grievous things. 8.28. And held by much tumult, they went to the gates to open them. But to the Goths what was being done was not pleasing; yet being unable to prevent it, they stood aside. 8.29. But Pastor and Asclepiodotus, calling the people and all the Goths together into one place, spoke as follows: "That a city's multitude should throw away itself and its own salvation is in no way strange, especially if, communicating with none of the notable men, it then makes an independent decision about the whole matter. 8.30. But we must, along with you, who are about to perish almost at once, render this exhortation as a last contribution to our fatherland. 8.31.
