We see you, then, citizens, eager to betray to Belisarius both your own selves and the city, when he promises to do you many good things and to swear the most terrible oaths concerning these. 8.32. If, then, he is able to guarantee to you this also, that the mastery of the war will come to him, no one would gainsay that these things are of advantage to you. 8.33. For to grant everything to him who is to become master is great folly. But if this lies in uncertainty, and no man is competent to guarantee the decision of fortune, consider over what calamities your zeal is. 8.34. For if the Goths prevail in the war over their enemies, they will punish you as enemies who have wrought against them the most dreadful things. 8.35. For it is not under the compulsion of necessity, but of your own deliberate will, that you set yourselves to betrayal. So that to Belisarius too, if he masters the enemy, we shall perhaps appear faithless and betrayers of our leaders, and, having become runaways, we shall, as is likely, have a garrison from the emperor for all time. 8.36. For he who has met with a traitor rejoices for the moment, having conquered through the favour, but afterward, by reason of the suspicion that comes from what has been done, he hates and fears his benefactor, having upon himself the tokens of faithlessness. 8.37. If, however, we are faithful to the Goths in the present, nobly undertaking the danger, both they themselves, if they master the enemy, will do us great good, and Belisarius, if he conquers us, 8.38. if it so chance, will be forgiving. For goodwill that has failed is punished by no man except a fool. 8.39. And what has happened to you that you have come to dread the blockade of the enemy, you who, lacking none of your provisions and shut off from none of the necessaries, sit at home, having confidence in the circuit-wall and these guards? And we think that Belisarius would not even have come to this agreement with us, if he had any hope of taking the city by force. 8.40. And yet, if he wished to do what is just and to our advantage, he ought not to frighten the Neapolitans nor to confirm his own power by the wrong done by us to the Goths, but to come to grips with Theodahad and the Goths, so that, without danger and treachery on our part, the city might come to the power of the victors." 8.41. When Pastor and Asclepiodotus had said this, they brought forward the Jews, who maintained that the city would lack none of the necessaries, and the Goths maintained that they would guard the circuit-wall safely. 8.42. Led by these, the Neapolitans bade Belisarius depart thence as quickly as possible. 8.43. But he set about the siege. And many times making an attempt on the circuit-wall, he was repulsed, losing many of his soldiers, and especially those who chanced to lay some claim to valour. 8.44. For the wall of Naples was inaccessible, partly by the sea, partly by certain difficult places, and by no means to be entered by those plotting against it, both for other reasons and because of the steepness. 8.45. And though Belisarius cut the aqueduct which conducted the water into the city, he did not greatly disturb the Neapolitans, since wells within the circuit-wall, supplying their need, did not give them much perception of this. 9.1. The besieged, then, escaping the notice of the enemy, sent to Rome to Theodahad, begging him to come to their aid quickly. But Theodahad made no preparation for war whatever, being by nature unmanly, as I have said before. 9.2. And they say that something else also befell him, which most of all dismayed him and led him to greater terror — though to me they tell what is not credible; 9.3. but even so it shall be told. Theodahad even before had not been without practice in making inquiries of those who professed to foretell anything, and at that time, being at a loss about the present (which most of all is wont to urge men to divinations), he inquired of one of the Hebrews, who had a great reputation for this, what would be the end of this war. 9.4. And he enjoined upon him to shut up thirty swine in three pens, and, having given a name to each group of ten — of Goths and Romans and the emperor's soldiers — to wait quietly for a stated number of days. 9.5. And Theodahad did accordingly. And when the appointed day came, both of them, coming to the pens, observed the swine, and found that of those to whom the name of the Goths belonged all were dead except two; and almost all were living to whom the name of the emperor's soldiers had come; but as for those that were called Romans, it befell them that the hair fell off all of them, and about half survived. 9.6. When Theodahad had observed this and conjectured the issue of the war, they say that great fear came over him, knowing well that it would surely befall the Romans to die in half and to be deprived of their money, and the Goths, being defeated, to be reduced in race to a few, and that to the emperor, with the loss of a few of his soldiers, 9.7. the mastery of the war would come. And on this account they say that no impulse fell upon Theodahad to enter into a struggle with Belisarius. Concerning these things, then, let each speak according to his disposition toward belief or disbelief. 9.8. But Belisarius, besieging the Neapolitans by land and sea, was distressed. For he did not think they would ever come over to him, nor did he hope to take the city, since he had the difficulty of the place opposing him to the utmost. 9.9. And the time spent there vexed him, as he reckoned how he might not be compelled to go against Theodahad and Rome in the winter season. 9.10. And he had already enjoined the army to pack up, intending to depart thence as quickly as possible. And to him, being at the utmost loss, it befell to have the following good fortune. 9.11. A desire seized one of the Isaurians to behold the construction of the aqueduct, and in what manner it supplied the city's need of water. 9.12. And entering it at a distance from the city, where Belisarius had broken it, he walked with no trouble, since the water had failed in it, inasmuch as it was broken. 9.13. And when he came close to the circuit-wall, he met a great rock, set there not by the hands of men, but by the nature of the place. 9.14. To this rock those who built the aqueduct of old, joining their masonry, made a tunnel from there, not, however, sufficient for the passage of a man, 9.15. but only to provide a way for the water. And for this reason it came about that the aqueduct was not of the same width everywhere, but a narrow place met one in that rock, impassable for a man, especially one armoured or carrying a shield. 9.16. When the Isaurian had observed this, it seemed to him not impossible for the army to go into the city, if they should make the tunnel there a little wider in measure. 9.17. But since he was himself an obscure person and had never come to speech with any of the commanders, he brought the matter to Paucaris, an Isaurian man, of repute among the guardsmen of Belisarius. And Paucaris straightway reported the whole matter to the general. 9.18. And Belisarius, breathing again at the pleasure of the word, and promising to present the man with great sums of money, set the matter in motion, and bade him, having taken some of the Isaurians as companions, make the cutting of the rock as quickly as possible, guarding lest they give anyone perception of the work. 9.19. And Paucaris, picking out Isaurians altogether fit for the work, got secretly within the aqueduct with them. 9.20. And coming to the place where the rock made the narrow space, they set to work, cutting the rock not with axes or hatchets, lest they make what was being done evident to the enemy by the noise, but scraping it most constantly with certain sharp iron tools. 9.21. And in a short time it was wrought out so that it was possible for a man, wearing a corselet and carrying a shield, to go through. 9.22. And when everything was now in the best state, the thought came to Belisarius that, if the army should enter Naples by war, it would befall the people to perish and all the other things to happen that are wont to occur to a city taken by enemies. 9.23. And straightway sending for Stephanus, he spoke as follows: "Many times have I seen cities taken, and I am experienced in what then happens. 9.24. For they slay all the men, of every age, and the women, begging to die, they do not see fit to kill, but, being led off to outrage, they suffer things irreparable and worthy of much pity. 9.25. And the children, who have shared neither in food nor in education in this way, must become slaves, and that too to those most hostile, in whose hands they have beheld the blood of their fathers. 9.26. For I forbear, dear Stephanus, to speak of the fire, by which both the other property and the beauty of the city is destroyed. Seeing this Naples suffering, as in a mirror, like the cities taken before, I come to pity both it and you. 9.27. For engines have now been made by me against it, by which it cannot but be taken. But that an ancient city, having inhabitants Christian and Roman from of old, should come to such a fortune, I would not pray, especially when I am the general of the Romans, most of all since I have many barbarians in my army, who have lost brothers or kinsmen before this wall; whose fury, if they take the city by war, I should not be able to restrain. 9.28. Therefore, while it is still in your power to choose and to do what is to your advantage, deliberate the better course and flee calamity; which, when it befalls you, as is likely, you will blame, not fortune justly, but your own judgment." 9.29. Having said this, Belisarius dismissed Stephanus. And he came to the people of the Neapolitans in tears and reported with lamentation all that he had heard Belisarius say. 9.30. But they (for it was not fated that the Neapolitans should become subjects of the emperor without paying a penalty) neither feared anything nor decided to come over to Belisarius. 10.1. Then indeed Belisarius himself made his arrangements for the entry as follows. Picking out about four hundred men at lamp-lighting time and setting over them as commanders Magnus, who led a cavalry detachment, and Ennes the leader of the Isaurians, he bade them all put on their corselets and, taking up their shields and swords, keep quiet until he himself should give the signal. 10.2. And sending for Bessas, he enjoined him to remain there; for he wished to take some counsel with him concerning the army; 10.3. and when the night was far advanced, telling Magnus and Ennes the situation and showing them the place where he had previously broken the aqueduct, he bade the four hundred lead the way into the city, 10.4. taking up lights. And he sent with them two men who knew how to use the trumpets, in order that, when they should get within the circuit-wall, they might be able both to throw the city into confusion and to signal to them what was being done. 10.5. And he himself had ready as many ladders as possible, made beforehand. So the men, slipping into the aqueduct, walked toward the city, while he with Bessas and Photius remained there and did everything with them. 10.6. And sending to the camp, he enjoined them to keep awake and have their arms in their hands. And he had many about himself whom he thought most stout-hearted. But of those who were going into the city, more than half, dreading the danger, were conveyed back. 10.7. And when Magnus, though he exhorted them much, could not persuade them to follow him, he returned with them to the general. 10.8. These Belisarius reviled, and, picking out two hundred of those about himself, bade them go with Magnus. And Photius too, wishing to lead them, leaped into the tunnel; but Belisarius prevented him. 10.9. And being ashamed before the general and Photius and the reviling, even those who were fleeing the danger, daring again to undertake it, followed him. 10.10. But Belisarius, fearing lest perception of what was being done should come to some of the enemy who held the guard in the tower which chanced to be near the aqueduct, came there and bade Bessas converse in the Gothic tongue with the barbarians there, so that no noise of arms might be audible to them. 10.11. And Bessas, shouting loudly to them, urged them to come over to Belisarius, promising that many good things would come to them. 10.12. But they jeered, insulting Belisarius and the emperor much. So these things were done by Belisarius and Bessas in this way. 10.13. Now the aqueduct of Naples is not covered only as far as the wall, but extends thus over a great part of the city, having a high vaulting of baked brick, so that the forces of Magnus and Ennes, when they had got within the circuit-wall, were unable even to conjecture where on earth they were. 10.14. Nor indeed could they get out from there, until the first of them came to a place where the aqueduct chanced to be roofless and there was a quite neglected building. 10.15. There within dwelt a certain woman, alone and living in great poverty, and an olive tree had grown above the aqueduct. 10.16. When these men saw the sky and perceived that they were in the midst of the city, they planned to get out, but they had no means at all, especially with their arms, of departing from the aqueduct. For the building there chanced to be high and had no means of ascent. 10.17. And when the soldiers were at the utmost loss and were crowding into a narrow space (for already a great throng of those coming behind was streaming together), it occurred to one of them to make an attempt at the ascent. 10.18. Laying down his arms straightway, therefore, and forcing the ascent with his hands and feet, he came into the woman's dwelling. 10.19. And seeing her there, he threatened to kill her if she should not keep silence. And she, struck with dismay, remained voiceless. And he, fastening a strong thong to the trunk of the olive, threw the other end of the thong into the aqueduct. And each of the soldiers, laying hold of it, climbed up with difficulty. 10.20. And when all had climbed up and a quarter of the night still remained, they advanced to the wall; and they killed the guards of two towers, who perceived nothing of the evil, about the northern part of the circuit-wall, where Belisarius with Bessas and Photius was standing, awaiting what was being done. 10.21. And these men called the army to the wall with the trumpets, and Belisarius, setting the ladders against the circuit-wall, bade the soldiers climb up there. 10.22. But it came about that none of the ladders reached up to the battlements. For inasmuch as the artificers had not made them in the open, they failed to reach the proper measure. 10.23. Wherefore, binding two together and climbing up on both, the soldiers thus got above the battlements. So these things were done by Belisarius in this way. 10.24. But on the part of the circuit-wall toward the sea, where not the barbarians but the Jews held the guard, the soldiers could neither use the ladders nor climb up to the wall. 10.25. For the Jews, having already offended the enemy, and having been a hindrance to their taking the city without a fight, and for this reason having no hope if they should come under them, fought stubbornly, although the city was already taken, and held out against the assault of their opponents beyond expectation. 10.26. But when day came and some of those who had climbed up went against them, then indeed they too, being struck from behind, fled, and Naples was taken by force. And the gates being now thrown open, the whole Roman army entered. 10.27. But those who had been stationed about the gates that face the rising sun, since no ladders chanced to be at hand, burned these gates, which were altogether unguarded. 10.28. For the wall there was empty of men, the guards having taken to flight. 10.29. And there was much slaughter there. For all, held by fury, and especially those whose brother or kinsman had chanced to die in fighting at the wall, kept killing whoever was in their way, sparing no age, and, breaking into the houses, they made slaves of the children and women and plundered the goods; and most of all the Massagetae, who, not even abstaining from the sanctuaries, killed many of those who had fled into them, until Belisarius, going about everywhere, prevented it, and, calling all together, spoke as follows: 10.30. "Since God has given us to conquer and to attain the highest reputation, having made subject to us a city before invincible, it is necessary for us too not to be unworthy of the favour, but, by humanity toward the vanquished, to display that we have justly mastered them. 10.31. Do not, then, hate the Neapolitans without end, nor make your hatred toward them extend beyond the war. For no one of the victors any longer hates the vanquished. 10.32. And by killing them you will not free yourselves from enemies for the future, but you will be punished by the death of your subjects. Do not, then, work these men any further evil, nor grant everything to your anger. 10.33. For it is shameful to master the enemy but appear weaker than your own passion. Let the rest of the property, then, be your prizes of valour, but let the women, with the children, be given back to the men. And let the vanquished learn by experience how great friends they have lost through their folly." 10.34. Having said this, Belisarius gave back to the Neapolitans all the women and children and the other slaves, who had not come to any experience of outrage, and reconciled the soldiers to them. 10.35. And so it befell the Neapolitans on that day both to become captives and to recover their freedom and to win back the most precious of their goods. 10.36. For those of them who chanced to have gold or any other precious thing had previously buried it in the ground and hidden it, and thereby they were able to escape the notice of the enemy and got back their houses with their goods. And the siege, having extended to about twenty days, ended thus. 10.37. And the Goths who were taken there, being no fewer than eight hundred, Belisarius preserved altogether free from harm and held in honour no less than his own soldiers. 10.38. But Pastor, who, as I have disclosed before, had urged the people to madness, when he saw the city being taken, fell into an apoplexy and suddenly died, neither having been sick before nor having suffered anything unpleasant at anyone's hands. 10.39. And Asclepiodotus, who had done these things along with him, came to Belisarius with the survivors of the notable men. 10.40. And Stephanus reviled him, mocking, as follows: "See, O most wicked of all men, what evils you have wrought upon your fatherland, having sold the salvation of your fellow-citizens for goodwill toward the Goths. 10.41. And then, if the affairs of the barbarians had gone well, you would have thought it right to be yourself in their pay and to lead each one of us who had planned the better course into the charge of betrayal of the Romans. 10.42. But since the emperor has taken the city, and we have been saved by the valour of this man, then you have dared thus inconsiderately to come into the general's presence, as though you had wrought no dreadful thing against either the Neapolitans or the emperor's army — you shall pay a worthy penalty." 10.43. So Stephanus, being in pain at the calamity, flung this at Asclepiodotus. And he answered him as follows: "You do not perceive, noble sir, that you are praising us, in that you reproach us with goodwill toward the Goths. 10.44. For one would never be loyal to masters in danger except from a firmness of judgment. The rulers, then, will have me as such a guardian of the state as they lately found an enemy, since he who has fidelity by nature does not change his judgment along with fortune. 10.45. But you, when affairs do not go in like manner with them, would readily accept the words of the assailants. For he who is sick in the inconstancy of his mind both straightway feared and renounced his fidelity to his dearest." 10.46. So much Asclepiodotus also said. But the people of the Neapolitans, when they saw him withdrawing thence, gathering in a body, charged him with all their present misfortunes. And they did not desist until they had killed him and torn his body to pieces. 10.47. And then, going to the house of Pastor, they sought the man. And when his servants maintained that Pastor was dead, they refused to believe it, until they were shown the man's corpse. And the Neapolitans impaled him in the suburb. 10.48. And thus they begged off Belisarius for what they had done, held by just anger, and, finding him forgiving, were reconciled. So the Neapolitans came off thus. 11.1. But the Goths, who chanced to be about Rome and the regions there, even before holding the inaction of Theodahad in great wonder, in that, being neighbours to the enemy, he did not wish to go to battle, and using among themselves much suspicion toward him, that he was willingly betraying the affairs of the Goths to the Emperor Justinian, and had no other care than that he himself might live quietly, surrounding himself with as much money as possible, when they heard that Naples was taken, now openly charging him with all this, gathered together at a place distant from Rome two hundred and eighty stades, which the Romans call Regata. There it seemed best to them to encamp; for there are many plains there, fit for the pasturing of horses. 11.2. And a river also flows there, which the natives call Decennovium in the Latin tongue, because, going round nineteen markers, which amount to one hundred and thirteen stades, it thus empties into the sea near the city of Tarracina, close to which is Mount Circaeum, where they say Odysseus consorted with Circe — though to me they tell what is not credible, since Homer maintains that the dwelling of Circe was on an island. 11.3. This, however, I am able to say, that this Circaeum, extending far into the sea, resembles an island, and to those who sail near and to those who walk to the shore there it seems to be very much an island. And when one comes upon it, then indeed one unlearns and finds one's former opinion deceived. 11.4. And for this reason perhaps Homer called the place an island. But I shall return to the previous account. 11.5. The Goths, when they had gathered at Regata, chose as king over themselves and the Italians Witigis, a man of no distinguished family, but who had previously won great repute in the battles about Sirmium, when Theoderic was carrying on the war against the Gepaedes. 11.6. Theodahad, then, hearing this, set out in flight and was driving along the road to Ravenna. But Witigis quickly sent Optaris, a Gothic man, enjoining him to bring Theodahad either alive or dead. 11.7. Now this Optaris chanced to be ill-disposed toward Theodahad for the following reason. Optaris was wooing a certain maiden who was both an heiress and fair of face. 11.8. This girl Theodahad took from this suitor and, persuaded by money, betrothed to another. Wherefore, both by his anger and to gratify Witigis, he pursued Theodahad with great zeal and eagerness, slackening neither night nor day. 11.9. And he overtook him while still journeying on the road, and, laying him on his back on the ground, slaughtered him like a sacrificial victim. This was the end of life and of leadership for Theodahad, which had lasted into its third year. 11.10. And Witigis with the Goths who were present rode into Rome. And learning what had befallen Theodahad, he was glad and put his son Theodegisclus under guard. 11.11. And since the affairs of the Goths seemed to him by no means in a state of preparation, he thought it better first to go to Ravenna, and there, having arranged everything in the best way, thus to set about the war. Calling all together, therefore, he spoke as follows: 11.12. "The greatest deeds, fellow-soldiers, are wont to be set right not by sharpness of opportunity, but by good counsel. 11.13. For often delay, coming at the right moment, has profited more, and zeal displayed not when it ought has checked for many the hope of success. 11.14. For most men more easily, when unprepared but fighting on equal terms of strength, are defeated, than those who, with the lesser strength but having prepared in the best way, have entered the struggle. 11.15. Let us not, then, lifted up by the love of immediate glory, work irreparable harm to ourselves; for it is better, being ashamed for a short time, to preserve our good fame without end, than, fleeing the immediate disgrace, to be covered, as is likely, with shame for all time. 11.16. And indeed you surely know that the multitude of the Goths and almost all the equipment of arms chance to be in Gaul and Venetia and the regions farthest off. 11.17. And moreover, against the nations of the Franks we are carrying on a war no less than this, which it is great folly to abandon ill-settled and to go against another. For those who place themselves in an ambiguous position and do not look toward a single enemy are likely to be defeated by their opponents. 11.18. But I say that we must now go straight from here to Ravenna, and, dissolving the war against the Franks and having arranged everything else in the best way, then fight it out with Belisarius with the whole army of the Goths. 11.19. And let no one of you shrink from this withdrawal of ours, nor hesitate to name it a flight. 11.20. For the appellation of cowardice, applied opportunely, has set many right, but the name of courage, born in some men not at the proper time, has then ended in defeat. 11.21. For it is right to follow not the names of things, but the advantage of deeds. For deeds reveal a man's valour not at the beginning, but at the end. 11.22. And those flee the enemy, not who go against them at once with greater preparation, but who, wishing to preserve their own bodies for ever, stand aside. And let no fear come to any of you about the capture of this city. 11.23. For if the Romans are well disposed toward us, they will guard the city securely for the Goths and will have no experience of compulsion, 11.24. since we shall return to them in a short time. And if they have any suspicion toward us, they will harm us less by receiving the enemy; for it is better to fight against foes openly. 11.25. But that no such thing may come to pass, I shall provide. For we shall leave many men and a most sagacious commander, who will be sufficient to guard Rome, so that both these things will lie well for us and no harm would come to us from this withdrawal." 11.26. Witigis said this much. And all the Goths, approving, made ready for the journey. And afterward Witigis, after much exhortation to Silverius the bishop of the city and to the Romans, both those of the senate and the people, and reminding them of the rule of Theoderic, urged all to be well disposed toward the nation of the Goths, binding them by the most terrible oaths concerning these things; and picking out men no fewer than four thousand, and setting over them as commander Leuderis, a man advanced in years and having a great reputation for sagacity, in order that they might guard Rome for them, he thus went to Ravenna with the rest of the army, having most of the senators with him as hostages. 11.27. And when he came there, he took Matasuntha, the daughter of Amalasuntha, a maiden now ripe for marriage, as his wedded wife, against her will, in order that he might hold the rule more securely by his connexion with the family of Theoderic. 11.28. Then, gathering all the Goths from every quarter, he arranged and ordered them, distributing arms and horses to each according to his rank; only the Goths who held the guard in Gaul he was unable to summon, through fear of the Franks. 11.29. Now these Franks were anciently called Germans. But in what manner from the beginning, and where dwelling, they invaded Gaul and became at variance with the Goths, I shall now tell. 12.1. To one sailing the sea from the Ocean and Gadira, the land on the left, as has been said in the previous narrative, is called Europe, and that opposite it has been called Libya, which, as one goes on, they call Asia. 12.2. Now of the parts of Libya beyond I am not able to speak accurately; for it is for the most part desert of men, and on this account the first source of the Nile is by no means known, which they say is borne thence to Egypt. 12.3. But Europe, at its very beginning, is most exactly like the Peloponnesus and lies with sea on either side. And the first country, about the Ocean and the setting sun, is called Spain, as far as the Alps which are in the Pyrenees mountains. 12.4. For the people there are accustomed to call the passage in the narrow place the Alps. And from there to the borders of Liguria it is called Gaul. There too other Alps separate the Gauls and the Ligurians. 12.5. Gaul, however, is much wider than Spain, as is likely, since Europe, beginning narrow, advances proportionately to an unspeakable width as one goes on. 12.6. And each of these countries is surrounded on the north by the Ocean, and on the south has the sea called the Tyrrhenian. 12.7. In Gaul flow other rivers, and the Rhone and the Rhine. These two, going in opposite directions to one another, the one empties into the Tyrrhenian Sea, while the Rhine makes its outlet into the Ocean. 12.8. And there are many lagoons there, where the Germans dwelt of old, a barbarian nation, not worth much account at the beginning, who are now called Franks. 12.9. Next to these dwelt the Arborychi, who, together with all the rest of Gaul and indeed Spain, were subjects of the Romans from of old. 12.10. And beyond them toward the rising sun the Thuringian barbarians settled, the first emperor Augustus having given them the land. 12.11. And the Burgundians dwelt not far from them, turned toward the south wind, and the Suevi above the Thuringians, and the Alamani, powerful nations. These were all independent and settled there from the beginning. 12.12. As time went on, the Visigoths, forcing the dominion of the Romans, held all Spain and the parts of Gaul beyond the Rhone river, having made them subject to themselves to pay tribute. 12.13. Now the Arborychi at that time chanced to have become soldiers of the Romans. And the Germans, wishing to make them subject to themselves, inasmuch as they were neighbours and had changed the polity which they had of old, plundered them and, with the whole people eager for war, went against them. 12.14. But the Arborychi, displaying valour and goodwill toward the Romans, proved themselves good men in this war, and since the Germans were unable to force them, they thought fit to make them comrades and to become connected with one another by marriage. 12.15. And this the Arborychi accepted not unwillingly; for both chanced to be Christians, and thus, coming together into one people, they advanced to great power. 12.16. And other Roman soldiers also had been stationed at the extremities of Gaul for the sake of guard. 12.17. And these, having no means of returning to Rome, and at the same time unwilling to come over to the enemy who were Arians, gave themselves over with their standards and the land which they had long guarded for the Romans to the Arborychi and the Germans; and handing down to their descendants all the customs of their fathers, they preserved them, which, revering, they think fit to keep even down to my time. 12.18. For even to this day they are clearly distinguished by the detachments in which they were stationed of old when they served, and they go into battle carrying their own standards, and use the laws of their fathers continually. 12.19. And they preserve the dress of the Romans in all other respects, and especially in their footwear. 12.20. As long, then, as the Roman polity remained the same, the emperor held the parts of Gaul within the Rhone river; but when Odoacer changed it into a tyranny, then indeed, the tyrant having given way to them, the Visigoths held the whole of Gaul as far as the Alps which separate the borders of the Gauls and the Ligurians. 12.21. But when Odoacer had fallen, the Thuringians and the Visigoths, fearing the now growing power of the Germans (for it had become exceedingly populous and forced openly those who from time to time were in their way), were eager to win over the alliance of the Goths and Theoderic. And Theoderic, wishing to make them his comrades, did not refuse to become connected with them by marriage. 12.22. To Alaric the younger, then, who at that time was leader of the Visigoths, he betrothed his own daughter Theudichusa, a maiden, and to Hermenefris the ruler of the Thuringians Amalaberga, the daughter of his sister Amalafrida. 12.23. And from this the Franks abstained from violence against them through fear of Theoderic, 12.24. but went to war against the Burgundians. But later there came to be alliances and agreements between the Franks and the Goths for the harm of the Burgundians, on condition that each should send an army against them; 12.25. and if, when one was absent, the others, taking the field, should subdue the race of the Burgundians and bring under their hand the land which they held, the victors should receive from those who had not taken the field a stated sum of gold as a penalty, and the captured land should thus be common to both. 12.26. So the Germans came with a great army against the Burgundians according to what had been agreed between them and the Goths, but Theoderic made preparation, forsooth, in word, yet on purpose always put off the going out of his army to the next day, awaiting what should come to pass. 12.27. And with difficulty he sent and enjoined the commanders of the army to make the journey more slowly, and, if they should hear that the Franks had conquered, then to go quickly, but if they should learn that any reverse had befallen them, to journey no further, but to remain where they were. 12.28. And they did what Theoderic enjoined upon them, while the Germans alone came to grips with the Burgundians. 12.29. And a fierce battle taking place, there was great slaughter on both sides; for the encounter was evenly balanced for the most part; 12.30. then the Franks, having routed the enemy, drove them to the extremities of the land which they then inhabited, where they had many strongholds, 12.31. and themselves held all the rest. And the Goths, hearing this, quickly came. And being reviled by their allies, they pleaded the difficulty of the country, and, paying the penalty, divided the land with the victors, as had been agreed. 12.32. And thus the foresight of Theoderic became still more known, in that, having lost none of his subjects, with a little gold he won half the land of the enemy. So at the beginning the Goths and the Germans held a portion of Gaul. 12.33. But afterward the Germans, their power having advanced, making light of Theoderic and the fear that came from him, took the field against Alaric and the Visigoths. 12.34. And Alaric, learning this, sent for Theoderic as quickly as possible. And he went to the rescue with a great army. 12.35. Meanwhile the Visigoths, when they learned that the Germans were encamping about the city of Carcassiana, met them and, making a camp, kept quiet. 12.36. And when much time had been spent by them in this blockade, they were distressed, and, since the land was being plundered by the enemy, made a great matter of it. 12.37. And finally they insulted Alaric much, both reviling him for his fear of the enemy and reproaching the delay of his father-in-law. 12.38. For they maintained that they themselves were a match for the foe and would more easily prevail over the Germans in war by themselves alone. 12.39. Wherefore, the Goths not yet being present with them, Alaric was compelled to go to battle with the enemy. 12.40. And the Germans, having got the upper hand in this encounter, killed most of the Visigoths and Alaric their commander. 12.41. And taking possession of most of Gaul, they held it, and besieged Carcassiana with great zeal, since they had learned that the royal treasure was there, which the elder Alaric had plundered when he took Rome in former times. 12.42. Among these treasures were also the precious things of Solomon the king of the Hebrews, exceedingly worth seeing. For an emerald stone for the most part adorned them, which the Romans had taken of old from Jerusalem. 12.43. But the survivors of the Visigoths proclaimed as their commander Gisalic, a bastard son of Alaric, since Amalaric, the son of Theoderic's daughter, was still quite young. 12.44. Then, when Theoderic came with the army of the Goths, the Germans, taking fright, broke up the siege. 12.45. And withdrawing thence, they held the parts of Gaul beyond the Rhone river turned toward the Ocean. And Theoderic, being unable to drive them out from there, conceded these parts to them, while he himself recovered the rest of Gaul. 12.46. And when Gisalic had been put out of the way, he transferred the rule of the Visigoths to his grandson Amalaric, over whom he himself was guardian, since he was still a child. 12.47. And taking all the money that lay in the city of Carcassiana, he marched off in haste to Ravenna, and, continually sending commanders and an army to Gaul and Spain, he himself held in deed the power of rule, and, providing how he might hold it secure for ever, appointed the rulers there to render him tribute. 12.48. And receiving this each year, in order not to seem grasping after money, he sent an annual gift to the army of the Goths and Visigoths. 12.49. And from this the Goths and Visigoths, as time went on, inasmuch as they were ruled by one man and held the same land, betrothing their children to one another, became connected by kinship. 12.50. Afterward Theudis, a Gothic man, whom Theoderic had sent as commander of the army, took a wedded wife from Spain, not, however, of the race of the Visigoths, but from the house of one of the prosperous natives, who was endowed with great wealth and was mistress of much land in Spain. 12.51. Whence, gathering soldiers about two thousand, and surrounding himself with a force of guardsmen, he ruled the Goths in name by Theoderic's appointment, but in deed was a not undistinguished tyrant. 12.52. And Theoderic, fearing — since he had attained the height of sagacity and experience — lest the Franks should meet him, as was likely, while he was carrying on the war against his own slave, or lest the Visigoths should do some revolutionary thing against him, neither deposed Theudis from his office, but even bade him always lead the army when it went to war. 12.53. He enjoined, however, the first men of the Goths to write to him that he would be doing what is just and worthy of his sagacity, if, coming to Ravenna, he should greet Theoderic. 12.54. But Theudis fulfilled all that Theoderic commanded, and never ceased to render the annual tribute, but neither wished to go to Ravenna nor promised it to those who wrote. 13.1. But when Theoderic had departed from among men, the Franks, no one any longer withstanding them, took the field against the Thuringians, and killed Hermenefris their ruler, and, making all of them subject, held them. 13.2. But the wife of Hermenefris with her children, escaping notice, came to her brother Theodahad, who at that time was ruler of the Goths. 13.3. Afterward the Germans came to grips with the survivors of the Burgundians and, conquering them in battle, shut up their ruler in one of the fortresses there and kept him under guard, and, making the rest subject, compelled them thenceforth to take the field with them against the enemy as captives; and they acquired all the land which the Burgundians previously inhabited, subject to the payment of tribute. 13.4. And Amalaric, who ruled the Visigoths, when he came to man's estate, dreading the power of the Germans, took the sister of Theudibert the ruler of the Germans as his wedded wife, and divided Gaul with the Goths and his cousin Atalaric. 13.5. For the parts within the Rhone river fell to the Goths, while those beyond it came round to the dominion of the Visigoths. 13.6. And it was agreed that the tribute which Theoderic had imposed should no longer be brought to the Goths, and the money which he had taken from the city of Carcassiana Atalaric rightly and justly gave back to Amalaric. 13.7. And since both these nations chanced to have come into the connexion of marriage with one another, they gave the choice to each man who had made his betrothal into the other nation, whether he wished to follow his wife or to bring her into his own race. 13.8. And there were many both who led their wives wherever they wished and who were led by their wives. 13.9. Later Amalaric, having offended his wife's brother, met with a great misfortune. 13.10. For though his wife was of the orthodox faith, he himself holding the Arian heresy, he would not allow her to use the accustomed rites nor to perform her devotions to the divine according to the customs of her fathers, but held her in great dishonour, since she was unwilling to come over to his own customs. And since the woman was unable to bear this, she disclosed everything to her brother. 13.11. Wherefore the Germans and the Visigoths came to war with one another. And the battle was exceedingly fierce for a long time, but at last Amalaric, being defeated, lost many of his own and himself died. 13.12. And Theudibert took his sister with all the money, and as much of Gaul as the Visigoths held by lot. 13.13. And the survivors of the defeated, rising up from Gaul with their wives and children, came to Theudis in Spain, who was now openly playing the tyrant. So the Goths and the Germans held Gaul. 13.14. At a later time Theodahad, the leader of the Goths, when he learned that Belisarius had come to Sicily, made an agreement with the Germans, on condition that they should hold the portion of Gaul which fell to the Goths and, receiving twenty centenaria of gold, should join in this war with them. 13.15. But before he had fulfilled the agreements in deed, he fulfilled his destiny. Wherefore many of the best of the Goths there, of whom Marcias was leader, 13.16. held the guard. These Witigis was unable to remove thence, nor did he think they would be sufficient to array themselves against the Franks, who would, as was likely, overrun Gaul and Italy, if he himself should march with the whole army against Rome. 13.17. Calling together, therefore, whatever was sound among the Goths, he spoke as follows: "Wishing to make to you, kinsmen, an exhortation not pleasant, but necessary, I have gathered you here at the present; but hear it calmly and deliberate worthily of our present circumstances. 13.18. For those whose deeds do not go according to their mind, it is inexpedient not to yield to necessity or fortune and so to manage the present. The other things, then, are in the best state of preparation for the war. 13.19. But the Franks stand in our way, with whom, being enemies of old, expending both our bodies and our money, we have nevertheless been able to hold out until now, since nothing else met us as an enemy. 13.20. But now that we are compelled to go against others, we shall have to dissolve the war against them, first because, if they remain hostile to us, they will surely be ranged with Belisarius against us. 13.21. For the nature of things teaches those who have the same enemy to join with one another in goodwill and alliance. 13.22. Then, even if we carry on the war separately against each army, it will be left to us to be defeated by both. 13.23. It is better, therefore, being diminished a little, to preserve most of our rule, than, coveting to have everything, to perish at the hands of the enemy together with all the power of our leadership. 13.24. I think, then, that if we give to the Germans the parts of Gaul bordering on them, and the money which Theodahad agreed to give them along with this land, they will not only turn away their hatred toward us, but will also join us in this war. 13.25. But that hereafter, when our affairs go well, we may recover Gaul, let no one of you reckon. For an old saying comes into my mind, bidding us settle the present well." 13.26. When the notable men of the Goths heard this, thinking it of advantage, they wished it to be accomplished. Envoys, then, are straightway sent to the nation of the Germans, on condition that they should give them Gaul together with the gold and should make an alliance. 13.27. Now the leaders of the Franks at that time were Ildibert and Theudibert and Cloadarius, who, receiving Gaul and the money, divided them according to the rule of each, and agreed to be exceedingly friendly to the Goths and to send them secretly auxiliaries, not, however, Franks, 13.28. but from the nations subject to them. For they were unable to make an alliance with them openly for the harm of the Romans, since a little before they had agreed to assist the emperor in this war. 13.29. The envoys, then, having accomplished the things for which they were sent, returned to Ravenna. And then Witigis also sent for Marcias with his followers. 14.1. While Witigis was doing this, meanwhile Belisarius was preparing to go to Rome. Picking out, then, three hundred men from an infantry detachment and setting Herodian over them as commander, he established them as the garrison of Naples. 14.2. And he sent guards also to Cumae, as many as he thought would be sufficient for the garrison of the fortress there. For there was no other stronghold in Campania except those in Cumae and Naples. 14.3. In this Cumae the natives show the cave of the Sibyl, where they say her oracle was. And Cumae is on the sea, distant one hundred and twenty-eight stades from Naples. 14.4. Belisarius, then, was arranging the army, and the Romans, fearing lest there should befall them what had befallen the Neapolitans, reckoning, decided that it was better to receive the emperor's army into the city. And Silverius, the bishop of the city, most of all urged them to this. 14.5. And sending Fidelius, a man coming from Mediolanum, which lies in Liguria, who had previously assisted Atalaric (the Romans call this office quaestor), they invited Belisarius to Rome, promising to hand over the city without a fight. 14.6. And he led the army by the Latin Way, leaving the Appian Way on the left, which Appius, the consul of the Romans, made nine hundred years before and gave his name to. Now the Appian Way is a journey of five days for an unencumbered man; for it extends from Rome to Capua. 14.7. And the width of this road is such that two wagons going in opposite directions may pass one another, and it is worth seeing above all things. 14.8. For all the stone, being millstone and hard by nature, Appius cut from another country far off and brought there; 14.9. for in this land it nowhere grows naturally. And having made the stones smooth and even, and fashioned them angular in the cutting, he bound them to one another, having put neither gravel within nor anything else. 14.10. And they are so securely bound to one another and have so coalesced that they give to those who see them the impression that they are not joined together but have grown together; 14.11. and though much time has passed and they are traversed each day by many wagons and all manner of animals, they have neither been separated at all in their joining nor has it befallen any of them to be destroyed or to become smaller, nor indeed have they lost any of their brightness. Such, then, is the Appian Way. 14.12. But the Goths who held the guard in Rome, when they learned that the enemy was somewhere near and perceived the purpose of the Romans, were distressed at being unable then to go to battle for the city and against the assailants, and were perplexed; 14.13. then, the Romans giving way, all departed thence and went to Ravenna, except indeed Leuderis, who commanded them, who, ashamed, I think, at the present fortune, remained there. 14.14. And it befell on that day, at the same time, that Belisarius and the emperor's army entered Rome through the gate which they call Asinaria, while the Goths departed thence through another gate which is called Flaminia; and Rome again, sixty years afterward, came under the Romans, on the ninth day of the last month, called by the Romans December, in the eleventh year of the reign of the Emperor Justinian as autocrat. 14.15. So Belisarius sent Leuderis the commander of the Goths and the keys of the gates to the emperor, while he himself took care of the circuit-wall, which had broken down in many places; and he made each battlement angular, placing another piece of masonry at an angle on the left side, so that those fighting there against the assailants might not be struck by those storming the wall on their left; and he dug about the wall a moat deep and worth much account. 14.16. And the Romans praised the foresight of the general and especially the experience displayed in the matter of the battlements, but, holding it in great wonder, were distressed if, having any thought that the city would be besieged, he supposed that it was possible to enter Rome, which can neither bear a siege through the scarcity of provisions, since it is not on the sea, and is encompassed by so great a circuit-wall, and, lying moreover in an exceedingly level plain, 14.17. is easy of approach for assailants, as is likely. But he, hearing this, none the less made ready everything for a siege, and the grain which he had brought from Sicily in the ships, placing it in public storehouses, he guarded, and compelled all the Romans, though they made a great matter of it, to bring in all the provisions for themselves from the fields. 15.1. Then indeed Pitzas too, a Gothic man, coming from Samnium, put into the hands of Belisarius both himself and the Goths who dwelt there with him, and half of maritime Samnium as far as the river which is borne through the middle of the country. 15.2. For the Goths who were settled on the other side of the river were unwilling either to follow Pitzas or to be subject to the emperor. And Belisarius gave him not many soldiers, in order that they might help him guard the regions there. 15.3. And before this the Calabrians and Apulians, the Goths not being present in their land, had come over to Belisarius of their own free will, both those on the coast and those holding the interior. 15.4. Among these is Beneventum, which the Romans of old named Maleventum, but now call Beneventum, avoiding the ill-omen from the former name; for ventus means wind in the Latin tongue. 15.5. For in Dalmatia, which lies opposite this, on the mainland across the way, a wind is wont to blow hard and prodigiously fierce, which, when it begins to blow, there is no means of finding a man still going on the road there, but all shut themselves up at home and wait. 15.6. For such is the force of this wind that it seizes a horseman together with his horse and bears him aloft, and, having carried him round over a great extent of the air, then, casting him down wherever it may chance, kills him. 15.7. And Beneventum, since it lies opposite Dalmatia, as I have said, and is situated on a high place, it befalls to bear some portion of the difficulty of this wind. 15.8. This city Diomedes the son of Tydeus once built, having been driven from Argos after the capture of Ilium. And as a token he left to the city the tusks of the Calydonian boar, which his uncle Meleager chanced to have received as prizes of the hunt, which are there even down to my time, a sight worth much account to see, having a circumference not less than three spans in a crescent shape. 15.9. There too they say that Diomedes met Aeneas the son of Anchises, coming from Ilium, and, according to the oracle, gave him the image of Athena which he chanced to have stolen along with Odysseus, when the two of them went as spies into Ilium before it became capturable by the Greeks. 15.10. For they say that when he was sick later and inquired about his sickness, the oracle gave him response that there would never be a release from the evil for him unless he should give this image to a Trojan man. 15.11. And the Romans say they do not know where on earth it is, but they show an image of it carved on a certain stone even down to my time, in the temple of Fortune, where it lies before the bronze statue of Athena, which is set up in the open air toward the east of the temple. 15.12. And this image on the stone resembles one fighting and raising her spear as for battle; but even so she has her chiton reaching to the feet. 15.13. And the face does not resemble the Greek statues of Athena, but is altogether such as the Egyptians of old used to make. 15.14. And the Byzantines say that the Emperor Constantine buried this image in the forum which is named after him and set it there. So these things are thus. 15.15. So Belisarius won over all Italy which is within the Ionian Gulf, as far as Rome and Samnium, while the parts outside the gulf as far as Liburnia Constantianus, as has been said, 15.16. held. But in what manner the people there inhabit Italy I shall now tell. The Adriatic Sea, casting out a certain outlet far into the mainland, makes the Ionian Gulf, in no way like the other regions where the rising of the sea onto the mainland, coming to an end, makes an isthmus. 15.17. For the gulf called Crisaean, ending at Lechaeum, where the city of the Corinthians is, in the measure of about forty stades makes the isthmus there; 15.18. and the gulf from the Hellespont, which they call Melas, makes the isthmus in the Chersonese not more, but according to this same measure. 15.19. But from the city of Ravenna, where the Ionian Gulf ends, to the Tyrrhenian Sea is a journey of no less than eight days for an unencumbered man. 15.20. And the reason is that, going on, the rising of the sea is always borne to the right for a great distance. Within this gulf, the first town inhabited is Dryus, which is now called Hydrus. 15.21. On the right of this are the Calabrians and Apulians and Samnites, and next to them the Picentines are settled, as far as the city of Ravenna. 15.22. On the other side is the remaining portion of the Calabrians, and the Bruttii and Lucanians, after whom the Campanians dwell as far as the city of Tarracina, whom the borders of Rome receive. 15.23. These nations hold the shore of each sea and all the interior regions there. And this is what was formerly called Great Greece. For among the Bruttii are the Epizephyrian Locrians and the Crotoniates and the Thurians. 15.24. But outside the gulf the first are Greeks, called Epirotes, as far as the city of Epidamnus, which is inhabited on the sea. 15.25. And next to this is the country of Precalis, after which comes that called Dalmatia, and it is reckoned to the dominion of the West. And from there are Liburnia and Istria and the country of the Venetians, extending as far as the city of Ravenna. 15.26. These dwell on the sea there. But above them the Siscii and Suevi (not the subjects of the Franks, but others beyond these) hold the interior country. 15.27. And above these the Carnii and Norici are settled. And on the right of these dwell the Dacians and Pannonians, who hold other places and Singidunum and Sirmium, extending as far as the river Ister. 15.28. Of these nations, then, the Goths ruled those outside the Ionian Gulf at the beginning of this war, while above the city of Ravenna, on the left of the river Po, dwell the Ligurians. 15.29. And on the north of these the Albani dwell in an exceedingly good land called Langouvilla, and above these are the nations subject to the Franks; while toward the west the Gauls hold the land, and after them the Spaniards. 15.30. And on the right of the Po is Aemilia and the nations of the Tuscans, extending even to the borders of Rome. So these things are thus. 16.1. But Belisarius, having taken all the borders of Rome round about as far as the river Tiber, made them secure. And when everything was in the best state for him, he gave to Constantinus many of his own guardsmen with other spearmen, both Zarter and Chorsamantis and Aeschmanes the Massagetae, and another army, and bade him go to Tuscany, in order that he might win over the regions there. 16.2. And he enjoined Bessas to seize Narnia, a city exceedingly strong, in Tuscany. Now this Bessas was a Goth by race, of those who had dwelt in Thrace from of old and had not followed Theoderic when he led the people of the Goths thence to Italy, but he was energetic and good in matters of war. 16.3. For he was both an excellent general and a skilful worker with his own hands. And Bessas held Narnia, the inhabitants not being unwilling, and Constantinus won over Spolitium and Perusia and certain other towns with no trouble. 16.4. For the Tuscans received him into their cities of their own free will. Setting a garrison in Spolitium, therefore, he himself with the rest of the army kept quiet in Perusia, the first city of the Tuscans. 16.5. But Witigis, hearing this, sent an army and the commanders Unilas and Pissas against them. 16.6. These Constantinus met in the suburb of Perusia and came to grips. And though the barbarians far surpassed them in multitude, at first the battle was evenly balanced, but afterward the Romans, having got the upper hand by their valour, routed the enemy and killed almost all of them in no order as they fled; 16.7. and taking alive the commanders of the enemy, they sent them to Belisarius. When Witigis heard this, he no longer wished to remain quiet in Ravenna, where indeed Marcias and those with him, not yet come from Gaul, were a hindrance to him. 16.8. To Dalmatia, then, he sent a large army and the commanders Asinarius and Uligisalus, in order that they might recover Dalmatia for the dominion of the Goths. 16.9. And he enjoined them, having gathered an army from the regions about Suavia of the barbarians there, thus to go straight for Dalmatia and Salones. 16.10. And he sent with them also many warships, so that they might be able to besiege Salones by land and by sea. 16.11. And he himself was eager to go with his whole army against Belisarius and Rome, bringing horsemen and foot-soldiers no fewer than fifteen tens of thousands, and most of them were armoured together with their horses. 16.12. Asinarius, then, going about Suavia, gathered the army of the barbarians, while Uligisalus alone led the Goths to Liburnia. 16.13. And when the Romans came to grips with them at a place called Scardon, they were defeated in the battle and withdrew to the city of Burnus; and there Uligisalus awaited his colleague. 16.14. But Constantianus, when he heard of the preparation of Asinarius, fearing for Salones, sent for the soldiers who held all the fortresses there. 16.15. And he dug a moat about the whole circuit-wall round about and made all his other preparations for the siege in the best way. And Asinarius, having gathered a very great army of barbarians, came to the city of Burnus. 16.16. There, joining Uligisalus and the army of the Goths, he came to Salones. And they made a stockade about the circuit-wall, and, filling the ships with soldiers, guarded the seaward part of the circuit-wall; and thus they besieged Salones by land and by sea. 16.17. But the Romans, falling suddenly upon the ships of the enemy, turned them to flight, and sank many of them with their men, and took many empty of men. 16.18. The Goths, however, did not break up the blockade, but rather shut up the Romans in the city, besieging them by force. So the armies of the Romans and Goths were faring thus in Dalmatia. 16.19. But Witigis, when he heard from the natives who came from Rome that the army with Belisarius was very small, repented of having withdrawn from Rome and was no longer able to remain in his present position, but, now held by fury, went against them. 16.20. And on this journey one of the priests, coming from Rome, met him. Of him, they say, Witigis inquired with much tumult whether Belisarius was still in Rome, fearing lest he should be unable to overtake him, but he should get the start by running away thence. And the man said that he need by no means be anxious about this; 16.21. for he himself guaranteed that Belisarius would never take to flight, but would remain there. And he hastened still more than before, having prayed openly to behold the wall of Rome before Belisarius should run away thence. 17.1. But Belisarius, when he heard that the Goths were taking the field against him with their whole people, was at a loss. For he neither wished to leave behind the forces of Constantinus and Bessas, especially as his army was altogether small, and to abandon the strongholds in Tuscany seemed to him inexpedient, lest the Goths should have these as fortified positions against the Romans. 17.2. Reckoning, then, he enjoined Constantinus and Bessas to leave a garrison in the most necessary of the places there, as much as would be sufficient to guard them, but to go themselves with the rest of the army quickly to Rome. 17.3. And Constantinus did accordingly. For setting a garrison in Perusia and Spolitium, he marched off to Rome with all the rest. 17.4. But while Bessas was more slowly settling matters in Narnia, it befell that, as the enemy made their passage there, the plains in the suburb were full of Goths. 17.5. These were forerunners in advance of the rest of the army; and Bessas, coming to grips with them, routed those opposed to him beyond expectation, and, after killing many, since he was pressed by the multitude, withdrew to Narnia. 17.6. And there, leaving guards, as Belisarius had enjoined upon him, he went quickly to Rome and reported that the enemy would be present almost at once. For Narnia is distant from Rome three hundred and fifty stades. 17.7. But Witigis by no means undertook to make an attempt on Perusia and Spolitium; for the places are exceedingly strong, and he by no means wished his time to be spent there; 17.8. for his sole desire was to find Belisarius in Rome before he had run away. But even learning that Narnia was held by the enemy, he wished to disturb nothing there, knowing that the place was hard of access and otherwise steep; for it lies on a high mountain. 17.9. And the river Narnus flows past the foot of the mountain, which also gave its name to the city. And two roads lead up there, the one toward the rising sun, the other toward the setting. 17.10. Of these one had a certain difficult narrow place of sheer rocks, but to the other there is no way except through the bridge which, spanning the river, makes a crossing there. 17.11. This bridge Caesar Augustus made in former times, a sight worth much account; for of all arches which we know it is the highest. 17.12. Witigis, then, not awaiting his time to be spent there, departing thence quickly, went with his whole army against Rome, making the journey through the Sabines. 17.13. And when he came near Rome and was distant from it not more than fourteen stades, he met a bridge over the river Tiber. 17.14. There Belisarius, a little before, had built a tower and, putting gates upon it, established a garrison of soldiers, not because the Tiber was crossable for the enemy there only (for there are ships and bridges in many parts of the river), but because he wished the time of the enemy in their journey to be spent more, awaiting another army from the emperor, and in order that the Romans might bring in their provisions still more. 17.15. For if the barbarians, repulsed from there, should undertake to cross by another bridge somewhere, he reckoned that no fewer than twenty days would be expended by them, and that, if they wished to draw down so great a multitude of boats into the Tiber, more time still, 17.16. as was likely, would be wasted. Having this in mind, he established the garrison there; where the Goths bivouacked on that day, being at a loss and supposing they would have to fight against the tower on the following day; 17.17. but there came to them twenty-two deserters, barbarians by race, but Roman soldiers, from a cavalry detachment of which Innocentius was commander. 17.18. And the thought then came to Belisarius to encamp by the river Tiber, so that he might be still more a hindrance to the crossing of the enemy and might make some display of his own courage to his opponents. 17.19. But the soldiers who held the garrison, as has been said, on the bridge, dismayed at the throng of the Goths and dreading the greatness of the danger, abandoning by night the tower which they were guarding, set out in flight. 17.20. And not supposing that they could enter Rome, they went secretly to Campania, either fearing the punishment from the general, or blushing before their comrades. 18.1. On the following day the Goths, destroying the gates of the tower with no trouble, made the crossing, no one standing in their way. 18.2. But Belisarius, not yet having learned anything of what had befallen the garrison, taking a thousand horsemen, went to the bridge over the river, to spy out the place where it would be better for them to encamp. 18.3. And when they had come nearer, they met the enemy already across the river, and came to grips with some of them against their will. And the encounter was of horsemen on both sides. 18.4. Then Belisarius, though previously cautious, no longer kept the place of the general, but fought among the first like a soldier; 18.5. and from this it befell the affairs of the Romans to fall into great danger, since the whole issue of the war rested upon him. 18.6. And he chanced at that time to be mounted on a horse exceedingly experienced in war and knowing how to save its rider, which was grey in its whole body, but its forehead was very white from the head to the nostrils. This horse the Greeks call phalios, the barbarians balan. And it befell that the most of the Goths cast at him and at Belisarius their javelins and other missiles for the following reason. 18.7. The deserters who on the previous day had come to the Goths, when they saw Belisarius fighting among the first, knowing that, if he should fall, the affairs of the Romans would straightway be ruined, raised a shout, 18.8. urging them to strike at the horse balan. And from this the report, passing round, came to the whole army of the Goths, but they did not search out who it was, inasmuch as they were in great tumult, nor did they clearly know that it referred to Belisarius. 18.9. But conjecturing not without reason that the report which was current pointed to all, abandoning all the rest, most of them cast at Belisarius. 18.10. And those of them who laid some claim to valour, now held also by great ambition, coming as close as possible, tried to lay hold of him, and, held by great fury, smote at him with their spears and swords. 18.11. But Belisarius himself, turning this way and that, killed those who from time to time met him, and most of all in this danger enjoyed the goodwill of his own guardsmen and spearmen toward him. 18.12. For gathering about him, all displayed such valour as I do not think has been shown by any men down to this day; 18.13. for holding their shields before the general and his horse, they received all the missiles and beat off, by thrusting, those who from time to time came on. And thus the whole encounter was decided about the body of a single man. 18.14. In this action there fell of the Goths no fewer than a thousand, and these men who fought among the first; and there died of the household of Belisarius many of the best, and Maxentius the guardsman, having displayed great deeds against the enemy. 18.15. But it befell Belisarius to have some fortune that day, that he was neither wounded nor struck, although the battle was about him alone. 18.16. At last by their own valour the Romans routed the enemy, and a very great throng of barbarians fled, until they came to their own camp. For there the Gothic foot-soldiers, being unwearied, withstood the enemy and beat them off with no trouble. 18.17. And when other horsemen came to the rescue, the Romans fled with all their might, until, going up onto a certain hillock, they stood. And when barbarian horsemen overtook them, again a cavalry battle took place. 18.18. There Valentinus, the groom of Photius the son of Antonina, made a most notable display of valour. For, leaping alone into the throng of the enemy, he became a hindrance to the onset of the Goths and saved those with him. 18.19. And thus, having escaped, they came to the circuit-wall of Rome, and the barbarians, pursuing them as far as the wall, pressed hard about the gate which is named Salaria. 18.20. And the Romans, fearing lest the enemy, bursting in with the fugitives, should get within the circuit-wall, by no means wished to open the gates, although Belisarius exhorted them much and shouted with threats. 18.21. For neither were those peeping out from the tower able to recognize the man, since his face and whole head were covered with gore and dust, and at the same time no one could see clearly; for it was about sunset. 18.22. Nor indeed did the Romans think the general was alive; for all who had come fleeing in the previous rout reported that Belisarius had died fighting among the first. 18.23. The throng of the enemy, then, having streamed up in great numbers and held by great fury, planned both to cross the moat at once and to fall upon the fugitives there, 18.24. while the Romans, gathered about the wall within the moat, crowding closely together, were drawn into a small space. 18.25. But those within the circuit-wall, being altogether without a general and altogether unprepared, and afraid both for their own selves and for the city, were by no means able to defend their own people, though they had come into such great danger. 18.26. Then a thought and a daring deed came to Belisarius, which unexpectedly saved the affairs of the Romans. For, exhorting all those with him, he fell suddenly upon his opponents. 18.27. And they, even before in much disorder, inasmuch as they were in darkness and pursuit, when they saw the fugitives coming against them beyond expectation, suspecting that another army too had come to the rescue from the city, and from this falling into great fear, now all fled with all their might. 18.28. But Belisarius, by no means rushing into the pursuit, straightway returned to the wall. And thus the Romans, taking courage, received him and all those with him into the city. 18.29. So great was the danger into which Belisarius and the affairs of the emperor came; and the battle, having begun in the morning, ended at night. And in this battle the most distinguished were, of the Romans Belisarius, of the Goths Visandus Vandalarius, who, when the battle was about Belisarius, since he fell upon him among the first, did not draw back until, having received thirteen wounds in his body, he fell. 18.30. And being supposed straightway to be dead, he was neglected by his comrades, although they were victorious, and lay there with the dead. 18.31. But on the third day, when the barbarians, having encamped close to the circuit-wall of Rome, sent some men to bury their own dead and perform the customary rites for their burial, those who searched the bodies of the fallen found Visandus Vandalarius still breathing, and one of his comrades begged him to utter some word to him. 18.32. But he (for he was unable, since his inner parts were exceedingly parched by famine and the dryness from his other suffering) signed to them to put water into his mouth. And when he had drunk and come to himself, they lifted him up and carried him to the camp. 18.33. And Visandus Vandalarius won a great name from this deed among the Goths, and, being held in the highest repute, survived for a very long time. So these things befell on the third day from the battle. 18.34. Then Belisarius, when he was in safety with his followers, gathering almost all the soldiers and the people of the Romans to the wall, bade them light many fires and keep awake the whole night. And going about the circuit-wall in a circle, he arranged other things and set one of the commanders over each gate. 18.35. And Bessas, who held the guard in the gate called Praenestine, sending a messenger to Belisarius, bade him say that the city was held by the enemy, who had burst in through another gate which is over the river Tiber, named after Pancratius a holy man. 18.36. When those about Belisarius heard this, they advised him to save himself as quickly as possible through another gate. He, however, neither was dismayed, nor maintained that the report was sound. 18.37. And he sent some of the horsemen over the river Tiber in haste, who, having observed the things there, reported that no hostile thing had befallen the city there. 18.38. Straightway, then, sending to each gate, he enjoined the commanders everywhere that, when they should hear that the enemy had burst into some other part of the circuit-wall, they should neither go to the rescue nor abandon their own guard, but remain quiet; for he himself would take care of these things. 18.39. And he did this so that they might not again be thrown into confusion by an untrue report. But Witigis, while the Romans were still in great tumult, sent to the Salarian gate one of the commanders, Vacis by name, a not obscure man. 18.40. He, coming there and reviling the Romans for their faithlessness toward the Goths, reproached them with the betrayal which he said they had committed against their fatherland and themselves, in that they had exchanged the power of the Goths for Greeks who were unable to defend them, from whom in former times they had seen no one come to Italy except tragic actors and mimes and thieving sailors. 18.41. This and many such things Vacis said, but since no one answered him, 18.42. he withdrew to the Goths and Witigis. But Belisarius incurred much laughter from the Romans, since, having scarcely escaped the enemy, he now bade them take courage and despise the barbarians; for he knew well, he said, that he would conquer them by force. But how he came to know and decide this will be told in the later narrative. 18.43. And when the night was far advanced, his wife and those of his intimates who were present scarcely compelled Belisarius, who was still without food, to taste a little bread. So both sides passed that night in this way. 19.1. On the following day the Goths, thinking that they would take Rome by siege with no trouble through the size of the city, and the Romans, defending it, arrayed themselves as follows. The circuit-wall of the city has twice seven gates and certain posterns. 19.2. But the Goths, being unable to surround the whole wall in a circle with their whole army, made six stockades and harassed the space of five gates, from the Flaminian as far as the so-called Praenestine; and all these stockades they had made within the river Tiber. 19.3. Fearing, then, lest the enemy, destroying the bridge which is named after Milvius, should make impassable for them all the parts beyond the river extending as far as the sea, and from this they should have no perception of the evils of those under siege, the barbarians built a seventh stockade outside the Tiber in the plains of Nero, so that the bridge might be between their camps. 19.4. Wherefore it came about that two other gates of the city were harassed by the enemy, the Aurelian (which is now named after Peter, the chief of the apostles of Christ, since he lies somewhere near) and the one over the river Tiber. 19.5. And thus the Goths with their army encircled about half the portion of the wall, but, being in no way at all hindered by the river, they went to war against the whole circuit-wall round about whenever they wished. 19.6. But in what manner the Romans built the wall of the city on either side of the river, I shall now tell. Of old the Tiber, flowing past, was borne for a great part along the circuit-wall there. 19.7. And this region, on which the circuit-wall rises along the stream of the river, is level and exceedingly easy of approach. 19.8. And opposite this region, outside the Tiber, there chances to be a great hill, where all the mills of the city have been made from of old, since much water is there conducted by an aqueduct to the top of the hill, and going down thence with great force. 19.9. Wherefore the Romans of old decided to surround both the hill and the bank of the river by it with a wall, so that it might never be possible for the enemy to destroy the mills and, crossing the river, easily to plot against the circuit-wall of the city. 19.10. Bridging the river there, then, they decided to join the wall, and, building many houses in the place opposite, they made the stream of the Tiber flow through the middle of the city. So these things are thus. 19.11. But the Goths dug deep moats about all the stockades, and, heaping the earth which they took out of them above the inner wall, and making it as high as possible, and fixing a great number of sharp stakes on top, they made all their camps in no way inferior to the strongholds in fortresses. 19.12. And of the stockade in the plain of Nero Marcias was commander (for he had now come from Gaul with his followers, with whom he encamped there), and of the rest Witigis was leader, himself the sixth; for there was one commander to each stockade. 19.13. The Goths, then, having arrayed themselves thus, cut all the aqueducts, so that no water should come into the city from there. Now the aqueducts of Rome are fourteen in number, made by the men of old of baked brick, extending to such a width and depth that it is possible for a man riding a horse to ride within them. 19.14. But Belisarius arranged the guarding of the city as follows. The postern called Pincian and the gate on the right of it 19.15. (which is named Salaria) he himself held. For at these the circuit-wall was assailable, and it chanced to be possible for the Romans to go out against the enemy there. The Praenestine he gave to Bessas. 19.16. And over the Flaminian, which is on the other side of the Pincian, he set Constantinus, having first put the gates in place and blocked them within most thoroughly with a masonry of great stones, so that it might not be possible to open them for anyone. 19.17. For since one of the stockades was very close by, he feared lest some ambush against the city should be there from the enemy. 19.18. And the remaining gates he bade the commanders of the infantry detachments guard. And he closed up each of the aqueducts most securely with masonry for the greatest part, lest anyone from outside should go there to do mischief. 19.19. But when, the aqueducts being cut, as I have said, the water no longer worked the mills, and they were unable to work them by any animals, being in want of all food, inasmuch as they were in a siege (for they could scarcely take care of the horses necessary to them), Belisarius devised the following. 19.20. In front of the bridge which I just now mentioned as being near the circuit-wall, he fastened ropes most tightly stretched from each bank of the river, and to these he bound two boats beside one another, two feet apart, just where the inflow of the water, coming with full force from the arch of the bridge, came down; and, placing two mills in each boat, he hung between them the mechanism which is wont to turn the mills. 19.21. And beyond these he bound other boats, each one to those behind in order, and he placed the mechanisms in like manner for a great distance. 19.22.
