So, as the force of the water advanced, all the mechanisms in succession, revolving upon themselves, worked the mills connected with them and ground enough for the city. When the enemy learned this from the deserters, they destroyed the mechanisms in the following way. 19.23. Gathering great trees and bodies of Romans newly slain, they cast them into the river. 19.24. And most of these, borne with the stream into the midst of the boats, broke off the mechanism. But Belisarius, observing what was being done, contrived the following in addition. 19.25. He hung long iron chains in front of the bridge, reaching across the whole Tiber. Against these everything that the river bore came and was held, and went no further forward. 19.26. And those to whom this work was assigned, always drawing these things up, carried them to the land. And Belisarius did this not so much for the sake of the mills as because from this he came into fear and the thought lest the enemy, with many boats, should secretly get within the bridge and into the midst of the city. 19.27. And thus the barbarians abstained from the attempt, since nothing succeeded for them in this way. And thereafter the Romans used these mills, but were altogether shut off from the baths through the scarcity of water. 19.28. They had, however, enough water to drink, since even those who dwelt farthest from the river could draw water from wells. 19.29. And as for the sewers, which carry out of the city whatever is not clean, he was compelled to devise no security for them, since they all have their outlets into the river Tiber, and for this reason no plot against the city could come from there from the enemy. 20.1. The arrangements for the siege, then, Belisarius managed thus. But many sons of the Samnites, pasturing sheep in their own country, picking out two of themselves who were well grown of body, and calling one of them by the name of Belisarius and naming the other Witigis, 20.2. bade them wrestle. And as they entered the struggle most vigorously, it befell that Witigis, forsooth, fell. And the throng of boys, in play, hung him on a tree. 20.3. And when by some chance a wolf appeared there, the boys all fled, but Witigis, hanging on the tree, the time having been spent in this punishment, died. 20.4. And when this became known to the Samnites, they neither imposed any punishment on these children and, conjecturing what had happened, maintained that Belisarius would conquer Witigis by force. So these things happened thus. 20.5. But the people of the Romans, being altogether unaccustomed to the evils of war and siege, when they were oppressed by the lack of bathing and by the want of necessaries, and were compelled to guard the circuit-wall sleepless, and suspected that the city would be taken before long, and at the same time saw the enemy plundering the fields and everything else, were distressed and made a great matter of it, that they, having done no wrong, should be besieged and come into so great a magnitude of danger. 20.6. And uniting among themselves, they openly reviled Belisarius, in that he, having received an insufficient force from the emperor, had dared to take the field against the Goths. 20.7. This too those of the senate which they call the synkletos reproached Belisarius with in secret. And Witigis, hearing this from the deserters, and wishing to make them clash still more, and thinking that the affairs of the Romans would in this way fall into great confusion, sent as envoys to Belisarius certain men and Albis. 20.8. These, when they came into the presence of Belisarius, with the Romans of the senate present and all who were commanders of the army, spoke as follows: "Long ago, O general, names have been well and fairly distinguished by men for things; among which is this one, that rashness is distinguished from courage. 20.9. For the one of these, to whomsoever it is added, leads with dishonour into danger, but the other bears sufficiently the reputation of valour. 20.10. One of these two has brought you toward us, but which, you will straightway disclose. For if, trusting in courage, you took the field against the Goths — for you surely see from the wall the camp of the enemy, and it is amply in your power, noble sir, to play the man; but if, held by rashness, you set out against us, surely you also repent of what was done at random. 20.11. For the judgments of the reckless, when they come into the struggles, are wont to repent. Now, then, neither prolong further the wretchedness for these Romans, whom Theoderic reared in a life luxurious and otherwise free, nor stand in the way of the master of Goths and Italians. 20.12. For how is it not strange that you, thus shut up and cowering before the enemy, should sit in Rome, while the king of this city, abiding in a stockade, should work the evils of war upon his own subjects? 20.13. But we will grant to you and your followers to make your departure now at your discretion, keeping all your own possessions. For to trample upon those who have relearned moderation we consider neither holy nor worthy of the manner of mankind. 20.14. And we would gladly ask these Romans too, what ever charge they had to bring against the Goths that they betrayed both us and themselves, who enjoyed our kindness until now, and now are experiencing the help you give." 20.15. So much the envoys said. But Belisarius answered as follows: "The time of counsel will not rest with you. For men are by no means wont to make war according to the judgment of the enemy, but it is the custom for each to manage his own affairs in whatever way may seem to him best. 20.16. And I say to you that there will come a time when you will wish to hide your heads under the brambles but will by no means be able to. 20.17. Rome, however, having taken, we hold nothing belonging to others, but you, having previously usurped this city, which in no way belonged to you, have now against your will given it back to those who possessed it of old. 20.18. And whoever of you has hope of setting foot in Rome without a fight errs in judgment. For while Belisarius lives it is impossible for him to give it up." So much Belisarius said. 20.19. But the Romans, in great fear, sat quietly, and dared not gainsay the envoys at all, although reviled by them much for their betrayal to the Goths, except indeed that Fidelius decided to mock them. 20.20. He, at that time, chanced to have been established as prefect of the court by Belisarius, and from this seemed most of all to be well disposed toward the emperor. 21.1. So the envoys were conveyed to their own camp. And when Witigis inquired of them what manner of man Belisarius was and what was his purpose concerning the withdrawal from there, they answered that the Goths were hoping for what was unlikely, if they supposed that they would frighten Belisarius in any way. 21.2. Hearing this, Witigis planned to storm the wall with great zeal and made ready his preparations for the assault on the circuit-wall as follows. 21.3. He made wooden towers equal to the wall of the enemy, and he chanced to have hit upon the true measure by repeatedly measuring it by the courses of the stones. 21.4. And under the base of these towers wheels were placed, set under each corner, which, rolling, were destined to move them most easily wherever those storming the wall should wish, and oxen yoked together drew the towers. 21.5. Then he made ready also many ladders, reaching up to the battlements, and four engines which are called rams. 21.6. Now the engine is of this kind. Four upright wooden columns stand opposite and equal to one another. Into these columns they fit eight cross-beams, four above and four near the bases. 21.7. And making the form of a four-sided little house, they cover it round about with hides instead of walls and a wall, so that the engine may be light for those drawing it and those within may be in safety, struck as little as possible by their opponents. 21.8. And within it they hang another beam from above, crosswise, by loose chains, holding it about the middle of the engine. And making its end sharp, they cover it with much iron like the point of a missile, or they make the iron four-sided, like an anvil. 21.9. And the engine is raised on four wheels, set one under each column, and men no fewer than fifty move it from within. 21.10. And when they have set it against the circuit-wall, they draw back the beam which I just mentioned by some mechanism, turning it, and then let it go against the wall with great force. 21.11. And it, struck repeatedly, is able to shake down and most easily break apart whatever it falls upon, and from this the engine has this name, since the projecting end of this beam is wont to strike whatever it chances upon, like the males of the flocks. 21.12. Of those storming the wall, then, the rams are such. 21.13. And the Goths had ready a very great quantity of faggots made of wood and reeds, so that, casting them into the moat, they might make the place level and the engines might by no means be hindered in crossing there. Thus, then, the Goths, having made their preparation, set out to storm the wall. 21.14. But Belisarius placed engines on the towers which they call ballistrae. These engines have the form of a bow, and below it a kind of hollow wooden horn projects, itself loosely hung, lying upon a straight iron piece. 21.15. When, then, men wish to shoot at the enemy from there, they make the pieces of wood which form the ends of the bow lean toward one another by the insertion of a short cord, and they place the shaft in the hollow horn, half the length, about, of the other missiles which they shoot from bows, but four times the width. 21.16. It is held, however, not by the usual feathers, but, inserting thin pieces of wood in the place of the feathers, they imitate the whole form of the arrow, putting in a point exceedingly large and proportionate to the thickness. 21.17. And men on either side draw it tight with great strength by certain mechanisms, and then the hollow horn, advancing, springs forward, and the missile flies out with such force that it reaches no less than twice the distance of a bow-shot, and, meeting a tree or a stone, easily cuts it through. 21.18. Such is the engine, called by this name because it shoots most vigorously. And they fixed other engines on the battlements of the circuit-wall, fit for casting stones. 21.19. These resemble a sling and are called wild-asses. And at the gates they set up wolves on the outside, which they make in the following way. 21.20. They set up two beams from the ground reaching up to the battlements, and, placing worked pieces of wood one upon another, they fit some upright, some crosswise, so that the openings between the joinings appear as holes to one another. 21.21. And from each joining a projection juts out, very like a thick goad. And fitting the cross-pieces of wood into each beam, reaching from above to the half measure, they lean the beams back over the gates. 21.22. And when the enemy come nearer to them, those above, laying hold of the ends of the beams, push, and these, falling suddenly upon the assailants, by the projecting goads easily kill all whom they may catch. Belisarius, then, did this. 22.1. The Goths, on the eighteenth day from the beginning of the blockade, under the leadership of Witigis, about sunrise, went against the circuit-wall to storm it, and the sight of the towers and rams, coming on and being altogether unfamiliar, dismayed all the Romans. 22.2. But Belisarius, seeing the line of the enemy advancing with the engines, laughed and bade the soldiers remain quiet and by no means begin the action until he himself should give the signal. And why he was laughing he did not for the moment disclose, but it was learned later. 22.3. The Romans, however, suspecting that he was dissembling, reviled him and called him shameless, and, because he did not check the enemy as they advanced, made a great matter of it. 22.4. But when the Goths came nearer the moat, first the general, drawing his bow, struck one of the armoured men who led the army, hitting him in the neck. 22.5. And he, smitten by a mortal wound, fell on his back, and the whole people of the Romans raised a prodigious shout, louder than the ear could bear, thinking that the best omen had befallen them. 22.6. And when Belisarius let fly the missile a second time, this same thing happened again, and a greater shout was raised from the circuit-wall, and the Romans now thought that the enemy were defeated. 22.7. And then Belisarius signaled to the whole army to set all their arrows in motion, but those about himself he bade shoot at the oxen only. 22.8. And when all the oxen straightway fell, the enemy were neither able to move the towers further forward nor, being at a loss, to contrive anything in the very midst of the action. 22.9. And thus the foresight of Belisarius became known, in that he did not try to check the enemy while they were far off, and that he was laughing at the simplicity of the barbarians, who had hoped, so inconsiderately, to bring oxen up to the wall of the enemy. These things happened about the Salarian gate. 22.10. But Witigis, repulsed there, left a large army of Goths in that place, and, making a deep phalanx of them and enjoining the commanders to make no assault on the circuit-wall, but, remaining in array, to shoot constantly at the battlements and give Belisarius as little opportunity as possible to go to the rescue elsewhere on the wall where he himself should intend to assault with a larger army, thus went with a great army to the Praenestine gate, to a part of the circuit-wall which the Romans call Vivarium, and where the wall was most assailable; 22.11. and there chanced to be there already other engines of towers and rams and many ladders. 22.12. Meanwhile another assault of the Goths was made on the Aurelian gate in the following way. The tomb of Hadrian the Roman emperor is outside the Aurelian gate, distant from the circuit-wall about a stone's throw, a sight worth much account. 22.13. For it is made of Parian marble, and the stones cohere with one another, having nothing else within. And it has four sides equal to one another, each one having a width of about a stone's throw, but a height greater than the wall of the city; 22.14. and there are wonderful statues above of men and horses, of the same marble. This tomb the men of old (for it seemed to be a fortified position against the city) surrounded with two walls reaching to it from the circuit-wall, and made it a part of the wall. 22.15. It resembles, then, a high tower set before the gate there. So the stronghold there was most sufficient. And Belisarius chanced to have set Constantinus in charge of its garrison. 22.16. He enjoined him also to take care of the guard of the adjoining wall, which had a poor and not noteworthy garrison. For since the circuit-wall was least assailable there, the river flowing past, supposing that no assault would be made there, he had established no noteworthy garrison there, but, his soldiers being few, he had assigned the multitude to the most necessary of the places. 22.17. For the emperor's army that gathered in Rome at the beginning of this siege was about five thousand. 22.18. But Constantinus (for it was reported to him that the enemy were attempting the crossing of the Tiber), fearing for that wall, himself went quickly there with a few men to the rescue, and enjoined the greater part to take care of the garrison at the gate and the tomb. 22.19. Meanwhile the Goths assaulted the Aurelian gate and the tomb of Hadrian, having no engine, but bringing a very great quantity of ladders and thinking that by the multitude of arrows they would more easily bring the enemy into difficulty and master the garrison there through the fewness of men with no trouble. 22.20. And they advanced holding shields before them, in no way inferior to the bucklers of the Persians, and they escaped the notice of their opponents in coming very close to them. 22.21. For hidden under the colonnade which extends to the temple of the apostle Peter, they came, and, appearing suddenly thence, set to work, so that the guards were neither able to use the so-called ballistra (for these engines do not shoot except straight ahead) nor to defend themselves against the assailants with their arrows, the matter being against them by reason of the shields. 22.22. But when the Goths pressed on vigorously, shooting constantly at the battlements, and were now about to set the ladders against the wall, having almost surrounded those defending from the tomb (for they kept getting behind them on the flanks as they advanced), for a short time there was dismay among the Romans, who had no means by which, defending themselves, they might be saved; but afterward, taking counsel, they broke up most of the statues, which were exceedingly large, and, lifting up huge stones thence with both hands, hurled them down upon the heads of the enemy, and they, being struck, gave way. 22.23. And as they withdrew little by little, the Romans, now having the advantage, took courage and with a louder shout defended themselves against those storming the wall with bows and casts of stones. 22.24. And, laying hold of the engines, they brought their opponents into great fear, and the assault of them came to an end in a short time. 22.25. And Constantinus too was now present, having frightened those who were attempting the river and easily thrust them back, since they had found the wall there not altogether unguarded, as they supposed. And thus the matters about the Aurelian gate became safe. 23.1. But to the gate over the river Tiber, which is called Pancratian, a force of the enemy came but did anything worth account by reason of the strength of the place; for the circuit-wall of the city there is steep and not easy of approach. 23.2. Paulus held the guard there with an infantry detachment of which he himself was commander. Nor indeed did they make an attempt on the Flaminian gate, since, lying in a precipitous place, it is not very easy of approach. 23.3. The Reges, an infantry corps, guarded there, and Ursicinus, who commanded them. Now between this gate and the postern next on the right, which is named Pincian, a certain part of the circuit-wall, anciently broken apart of itself into two, not, however, from its foundation, but only as to half its length, neither fell nor was otherwise destroyed, but leaned over so to either side that part of it appeared outside the rest of the wall and part inside. 23.4. And from this the Romans in their own tongue call the place the Broken Wall from of old. 23.5. And when Belisarius at the beginning undertook to pull down and rebuild this part, the Romans prevented him, maintaining that the apostle Peter had promised them that he himself would take care of the guard there. And this apostle the Romans revere and hold in awe above all others. 23.6. And everything in this place turned out for them as they planned and expected. For neither on that day, nor indeed during the whole time that the Goths besieged Rome, did any force of the enemy come there, nor did any disturbance chance to take place. 23.7. And we marveled that this part of the circuit-wall never came either to our memory or to that of the enemy during the whole time, neither when they were storming the wall nor when by night they were plotting against the wall, as they often attempted. 23.8. Wherefore no one afterward even dared to rebuild it, but down to this day the wall there is thus divided. So these things are thus. 23.9. At the Salarian gate a Gothic man, tall of stature and good in matters of war, wearing a corselet and having a helmet on his head, and being not obscure in the nation of the Goths, did not remain in array with the rest, but, standing on a tree, shot constantly at the battlements. 23.10. This man an engine, which was on a tower at the left part, struck by some chance. 23.11. And passing through both his corselet and his body, the missile sank more than half into the tree, and, binding the man fast by its insertion, hung him there a corpse. 23.12. When the Goths saw this, falling into dismay and getting out of range of missiles, they remained still in array, but no longer harassed those on the wall. 23.13. But Bessas and Peranius, since Witigis was pressing them most strongly at the Vivarium, sent for Belisarius. And he, fearing for the wall there (for it was most assailable there, as has been said), went quickly to the rescue himself, leaving one of his intimates at the Salarian gate. 23.14. And finding the soldiers in the Vivarium afraid of the assault of their opponents, which was great and full of men, he bade them despise the enemy and set them toward courage. 23.15. Now the place there was quite level and from this exposed to the approaches of those coming on. And by some chance the wall there had broken apart for a great distance, so that the joining of the bricks did not hold together very well. 23.16. And the Romans of old had surrounded it on the outside with another small wall, not for the sake of any security (for it neither had the strength of towers, nor were any battlements made there, nor anything else from which it would be possible to beat off the plot of the enemy against the circuit-wall), but for a kind of unseemly luxury, in order that, shutting up lions and the other beasts there, they might keep them. 23.17. Wherefore it is named Vivarium; for thus the Romans call the place where the untamed animals are wont to be reared. Witigis, then, prepared other engines in different parts of the wall and bade the Goths dig through the outer wall, thinking that, if they should get within it, they would master the wall with no trouble, since he knew that it was by no means strong. 23.18. But Belisarius, seeing the enemy digging through the Vivarium and assaulting the circuit-wall in many places, allowed the soldiers neither to defend themselves nor to remain at the battlements, except a very few, although he had with him whatever was notable in the army. 23.19. But below, about the gates, he kept all in readiness, armoured and carrying swords only in their hands. And when the Goths, having broken through the wall, got inside the Vivarium, sending Cyprian with certain others quickly against them, he bade him set to work. 23.20. And they killed all who had burst in, who neither defended themselves and were destroyed by one another in the narrow space at the exit. 23.21. And the enemy being dismayed by the unexpected and not arrayed in order, but each going one way, Belisarius, suddenly throwing open the gates of the circuit-wall, sent out the whole army against his opponents. 23.22. And the Goths by no means looked toward defence, but set out in flight, each where he chanced; and the Romans, pursuing, most easily killed those in their way, and the pursuit became great, since the Goths were storming the wall there far from their own stockades. 23.23. And Belisarius bade them burn the engines of the enemy, and the flame, rising up to a great height, made the dismay greater, as was likely, for the fugitives. 23.24. Meanwhile it befell that the like fortune occurred also at the Salarian gate. For they suddenly opened the gates and fell unexpectedly upon the barbarians, and killed these men, who did not defend themselves but turned their backs, 23.25. and burned the engines opposite them. And the flame rose to a great height in many parts of the wall, and the withdrawal of the Goths now took place by force from the whole circuit-wall, and the shout on both sides was prodigious, those on the wall urging on the pursuers, those in the stockades bewailing the excess of their suffering. 23.26. And there died of the Goths on that day thirty thousand, as their commanders maintained, and the wounded were more; for inasmuch as they were in a great multitude, both those from the battlements for the most part chanced to be shooting at them, and those who made the sallies destroyed a very great number of men dismayed and fleeing. 23.27. And the storming of the wall, having begun in the morning, ended in late afternoon. And both sides bivouacked that night, the Romans on the circuit-wall singing paeans and extolling Belisarius and holding the spoils of the dead, the Goths tending their wounded and bewailing the dead. 24.1. And Belisarius wrote a letter to the emperor; and the writing disclosed this: "We have come to Italy, as you commanded, and have won over much of its land and taken Rome, having thrust out the barbarians there, whose commander Leuderis I lately sent to you. 24.2. But it has befallen us, having established a multitude of the soldiers in Sicily and Italy for the guard of the strongholds which we have been able to master, that our army has been left to about five thousand. 24.3. And the enemy have come against us gathered to the number of fifteen tens of thousands. And first, when we had gone for reconnaissance of the men by the river Tiber, and were compelled against our judgment to come to grips with them, it befell us almost to be buried under the multitude of spears. 24.4. Then the barbarians, storming the wall with their whole army and assaulting with engines all parts of the wall, came within a little of taking both us and the city at the first shout, had not some fortune snatched us up. 24.5. For events that surpass nature would not reasonably be attributed to the valour of men, but to the higher power. 24.6. The things, then, that have been done by us up to now, whether by some fortune or by valour, are in the best state; but for what comes hereafter I would wish things to be better for your affairs. 24.7. What it is fitting for me to say and you to do, I shall never conceal, knowing that human affairs go on in whatever way may be God's will, but that those in charge of all works bear forever the blame or the praise from what has been done by themselves. 24.8. Let arms, then, and soldiers be sent to us in such number that we may thenceforth join battle with the enemy on equal terms of power in this war. 24.9. For we must not trust everything to fortune, since it is not wont to be borne in the same way for all time. But let this come to you, O emperor, that if now the barbarians prevail over us, we shall both be cast out of your Italy and lose the army besides, and there will be added to us this so great shame for what has been done. 24.10. For I forbear to say that we should seem to have destroyed the Romans too, who have made their own safety of less account than their fidelity to your sovereignty. 24.11. So that it will befall us that the good fortune which has come to us up to now will have ended in a foundation of calamities. 24.12. For if we had chanced to be repulsed from Rome and Campania and, much earlier, from Sicily, the lightest of all the evils would gnaw us, that we had not been able to grow rich on the goods of others. 24.13. And indeed this too is worth your reckoning, that it has never been possible to guard Rome for any long time even with many tens of thousands, since it is surrounded by much land and, by not being on the sea, is shut off from all the necessaries. 24.14. And the Romans are now well disposed toward us, but when their evils are prolonged, as is likely, they will not delay to choose the better course for themselves. 24.15. For those who have come to goodwill toward some at short notice are wont to preserve their fidelity to them, not when they fare ill, but when they fare well. 24.16. And besides, the Romans will be compelled by famine to do many things which they would not wish. 24.17. I know, then, that I owe death to your sovereignty, and for this reason no one could drive me out from here while I live; but consider what reputation such an end of Belisarius will bring you." 24.18. So much Belisarius wrote. And the emperor, exceedingly disturbed, hastily gathered an army and ships and enjoined the forces of Valerianus and Martinus to go quickly. 24.19. For these, having been sent with another army about the winter solstice, chanced to be on the point of sailing to Italy. 24.20. But they, having sailed to Greece (for they were unable to force the voyage further), were wintering in the regions of Aetolia and Acarnania. 24.21. Having disclosed this to Belisarius, the Emperor Justinian strengthened still more both him and all the Romans in their eagerness. 24.22. Meanwhile it befell the following to happen in Naples. There chanced to be in the marketplace an image of Theoderic the ruler of the Goths, composed of certain mosaic cubes, exceedingly small, and dyed in almost all colours. 24.23. The head of this image chanced to break apart while Theoderic was alive, the setting of the cubes being disturbed of itself, and it befell Theoderic to end his life almost at once. 24.24. And eight years later the cubes that formed the belly of the image suddenly fell apart, and Atalaric the grandson of Theoderic straightway died. 24.25. And a little time having passed, the cubes about the private parts fell to the ground, and Amalasuntha the child of Theoderic was removed from among men. So these things happened. 24.26. And when the Goths set about the siege of Rome, it befell that the parts of the image from the thighs to the extremities of the feet were destroyed, 24.27. and thereby the whole image disappeared from the wall; and the Romans, conjecturing this matter, maintained that the emperor's army would prevail in the war, thinking that the feet of Theoderic were nothing else than the people of the Goths whom he ruled, and from this they became still more of good hope. 24.28. In Rome, however, some of the patricians brought forward the oracles of the Sibyl, maintaining that the danger to the city had come about only as far as the month of July. 24.29. For at that time, they said, an emperor must be established over the Romans, from whom Rome would thenceforth fear nothing Getic; 24.30. for they say the Goths are a Getic nation. And the oracle ran thus: Quintili mense rege nihil Geticum iam. 24.31. And they maintained that July was the fifth month — some because the siege had begun at the beginning of March, from which it follows that July is the fifth; others because they reckoned March the first month before the reign of Numa, when the time of the year amounted to ten months for the Romans, and July was from this called Quintilis. But none of this was sound. 24.32. For neither was an emperor established over the Romans at that time, and the siege was to be broken up a year later, and again, under Totila the ruler of the Goths, Rome was to come into similar dangers, as will be told by me in the later narrative. 24.33. For it seems to me that the oracle does not disclose this inroad of the barbarians, but some other, either already past or to come at some later time. 24.34. For to discover the meaning of the oracles of the Sibyl before the event is, I think, impossible for a man. 24.35. And the reason I shall now disclose, having gathered all that. The Sibyl does not speak all the events in order nor making any connexion of the discourse, but, having uttered some verse about the evils of Libya, she straightway leaps to the affairs of the Persians, 24.36. and thence, coming to the memory of the Romans, transfers her discourse to the Assyrians. And again, prophesying about the Romans, she foretells the sufferings of the Britons. 24.37. And thus it is impossible for any man whatever to understand the oracles of the Sibyl before the event, unless time itself, the matter having already come to pass and the saying having been put to the test, should become an accurate interpreter of the verse. But let each reckon these things as is dear to him. And I shall return to the point from which I digressed. 25.1. When the Goths were repulsed from storming the wall, both sides bivouacked that night as has been said. 25.2. On the following day Belisarius bade all the Romans convey their children and wives away to Naples, and such of their servants as they thought would not be necessary for the guarding of the wall, so that they might not come into want of provisions. 25.3. And this same thing he enjoined upon the soldiers also, if any one of them had a manservant or maidservant. For he said he was no longer able to provide their rations during the siege in the customary way, but it was necessary for them to receive half each day in the provisions themselves, and the rest in money. 25.4. And they did accordingly. And a great multitude straightway went to Campania. And some were conveyed by chancing upon ships which were anchored in the harbour of Rome, while others went on foot by the road called the Appian. 25.5. And no danger or fear from the besiegers fell either upon those who journeyed there or upon those who went to the harbour. 25.6. For the enemy were neither able to surround the whole of Rome with their stockades through the size of the city, nor did they dare in small numbers to be left far from their camps, fearing the sallies of their opponents. 25.7. And on this account there was for the besieged for some time much freedom both to depart from the city and to bring provisions into it from outside. 25.8. And most of all by night the barbarians always came into great fear, and, making guards, kept quiet in their camps. 25.9. For from the city others and many Moors, going out, wherever they might find the enemy either sleeping or going along the road in small numbers (such things being wont to happen frequently in a great army, both for other necessary needs and for the pasturing of horses and mules and animals fit for food), killed them and, having quickly despoiled them, if more of the enemy chanced to fall upon them, withdrew at a run, being men swift of foot by nature and lightly equipped and getting the start by their flight. 25.10. Thus the great multitude were able to withdraw from Rome, and some went to Campania, some to Sicily, and others wherever it was thought easier and better for them. 25.11. But Belisarius, seeing that the number of the soldiers by no means reached around the circuit of the wall (for they were few, as I have said before), and that the same men were not able always to keep guard sleepless, but some, as was likely, chose sleep while others were stationed for the guard, and that the greatest part of the people, oppressed by poverty and lacking the necessaries (for inasmuch as they were laborers having everything from day to day and compelled to be idle through the siege, no means of livelihood came to them), he mingled soldiers and private men and assigned them to each guard-post, appointing a stated wage to a private man each day. 25.12. From these were formed companies sufficient for the guard, and the guard of the circuit-wall fell upon each company by a fixed night, and they all guarded by turns. And in this way Belisarius solved the difficulty of both. 25.13. And when suspicion arose against Silverius the bishop of the city, that he was practising betrayal to the Goths, he sent him straightway to Greece, and a little later established another bishop, Vigilius by name. 25.14. And he drove out some of the senators also on the same charge, and, when the enemy had broken up the siege and withdrawn, brought them back again to their own homes. 25.15. Among these was Maximus too, whose ancestor Maximus had wrought the calamity against the Emperor Valentinian. And fearing lest some plot arise from the guards at the gates, and lest someone from outside should go to corrupt them with money, twice each month he removed all the keys and renewed them always into another form, and he set the guards at another guard-post far off from the former, and over those who held the guard on the circuit-wall he set others each night. 25.16. Upon these it was incumbent, going round a measure of the wall by turns, to record the names of the guards, and if any one of them was absent there, to set up another in his place at the moment, and to report on the following day to him whoever the absent one might be, so that the fitting punishment might come upon him. 25.17. And he bade the musicians use their instruments on the circuit-wall by night, and he sent out some of the soldiers, and not least of the Moors, who were always to pass the night about the moat, and with them he let loose dogs, so that no one going to the circuit-wall even from afar might escape notice. 25.18. At that time too some of the Romans, forcing the doors of the temple of Janus, secretly tried to open them. 25.19. Now this Janus was the first of the ancient gods whom the Romans in their own tongue called Penates. And he has his temple in the marketplace before the senate-house, a little beyond the Tria Fata; 25.20. for thus the Romans are accustomed to call the Fates. And the whole temple stands of bronze in a four-sided form, of such size, however, as only to cover the statue of Janus. 25.21. And this statue is of bronze, no less than five cubits, like a man in all other respects, but having a head with two faces, and one of the faces is turned toward the rising, the other toward the setting sun. 25.22. And there are bronze doors at each face, which in peace and good circumstances the Romans of old were accustomed to keep closed, but, when they were at war, opened. 25.23. But when the Romans honoured the doctrine of the Christians, if any did, they no longer opened these doors even when at war. 25.24. But in this siege certain men, having in mind, I think, the old belief, undertook to open them secretly, yet were not altogether able, except that the doors no longer closed against one another, as before. 25.25. And those who had undertaken to do this escaped notice; and no search for the deed was made, inasmuch as there was great tumult, since it was not learned by the commanders, nor came to the multitude, except to a very few. 26.1. But Witigis, at first held by fury and at a loss, sent some of his guardsmen to Ravenna and bade them kill all the Romans of the senate whom he had brought there at the beginning of this war. 26.2. And some of them, learning beforehand, were able to flee, among whom were Vergentinus and Reparatus, the brother of Vigilius the bishop of Rome, both of whom, conveyed to Liguria, remained there; but all the rest were destroyed. 26.3. Afterward Witigis, seeing that the enemy had much freedom both to carry out anything they wished from the city and to bring in provisions by land and sea, decided to seize the harbour which the Romans call Portus. 26.4. This is distant from the city one hundred and twenty-six stades; for by so great a measure Rome is shut off from being on the sea. 26.5. And it is where the river Tiber has its outlets, which, borne from Rome, when it comes nearer the sea by about fifteen stades, splitting into two, makes there the so-called Sacred Island. 26.6. And as the river advances the island becomes wider, so that the measure of its width is proportionate to its length; for each stream has between them fifteen stades. 26.7. And the Tiber remains navigable on both sides. The part on the right of the river makes its outlets into the harbour, outside which the Romans of old built a city by the bank, surrounded by a circuit-wall most strong, and they call it Portus, with the same name as the harbour. 26.8. And on the left, by the other outlet of the Tiber into the sea, lies the city of Ostia, outside the bank of the river, of much account in former times, but now altogether unwalled. 26.9. The road, then, which leads to Rome from Portus, the Romans made from the beginning level and having no obstacle. 26.10. And many barges always lie on purpose in the harbour, and not a few oxen stand ready close by. 26.11. So whenever the merchants come with their ships into the harbour, taking the cargoes thence and placing them in the barges, they sail through the Tiber to Rome, using neither sails nor oars (since neither can the boats be driven by any wind there, the river winding much and not going in a straight course, nor can the oars do anything, the force of the water being borne always against them), 26.12. but, fastening ropes from the barges to the necks of the oxen, they draw them like wagons up to Rome. 26.13. But on the other side of the river, going from the city of Ostia to Rome, the road is wooded and otherwise neglected and not even near the bank of the Tiber, since the towing of the barges does not take place there. 26.14. Finding, then, the city by the harbour unguarded, the Goths took it at the first shout and killed many of the Romans who dwelt there, 26.15. and held the harbour together with it. And, establishing a thousand of themselves there as guards, the rest withdrew to the camps. 26.16. And from this it was impossible for the besieged to bring in things from the sea, except through Ostia, with toil, as was likely, and great danger. 26.17. For neither could the ships of the Romans put in there any longer, but they anchored at Antium, distant a day's journey from Ostia. 26.18. And taking the cargoes up thence, they conveyed them with difficulty; and the cause was the fewness of men. For Belisarius, fearing for the circuit-wall of Rome, was unable to secure the harbour with any garrison. 26.19. For I think that, if even three hundred had guarded there, the barbarians would never have made an attempt on the place, since it was exceedingly strong. 27.1. These things, then, the Goths did on the third day after they had been repulsed in storming the wall. And twenty days after Portus and the city and harbour were taken, Martinus and Valerianus came, bringing sixteen hundred horsemen. 27.2. And most of these were Huns and Sclaveni and Antae, who are settled above the river Ister not far from its bank there. 27.3. And Belisarius was glad at their presence and thought they should henceforth make war upon the enemy. 27.4. On the following day, then, he bade one of his own guardsmen, high-spirited and energetic, Traianus by name, taking two hundred of the spearmen who were horsemen, go straight against the barbarians, and, when they came nearer the stockades, to go up onto a high hill and remain quiet, showing him a certain place. 27.5. And if the enemy should go against them, not to let the battle become hand-to-hand, nor to lay hold of sword or any spear, but to use arrows only, and whenever he should see his quiver empty, to flee with all his might, ashamed at nothing, and withdraw to the circuit-wall at a run. 27.6. Having enjoined this, he kept ready the engines for shooting and the artificers about them. And Traianus with the two hundred went out by the Salarian gate against the camp of the enemy. 27.7. And they, dismayed at the suddenness, came to the rescue from the stockades, as each one chanced to be equipped from the available means. 27.8. But the forces of Traianus, going up onto the hill which Belisarius had shown them, from there defended themselves against the barbarians by shooting. 27.9. And it befell that their shafts, falling into a great throng, hit for the most part a man or a horse. But when all their missiles had now failed them, these men marched off behind in haste, and the Goths, pursuing, pressed on. 27.10. But when they came nearer the circuit-wall, the artificers worked the missiles from the engines, and the barbarians, dreading them, abstained from the pursuit. 27.11. And it is said that no fewer than a thousand of the Goths died in this action. A few days later Belisarius, sending Mundilas, another of his own guardsmen, and Diogenes, exceedingly good in matters of war, with three hundred spearmen, bade them do the same as the former. And they did accordingly. 27.12. And when the enemy met them, it befell no fewer of them, if not more, to perish than in the former action in the same way. 27.13. And sending also a third time, with three hundred horsemen, Oilas the guardsman, in order that they might do the like to the enemy, he wrought the same. 27.14. And by making three sallies, as I have said, he destroyed about four thousand of his opponents. 27.15. But Witigis (for the difference in the armies in armament and practice for the deeds of war did not occur to him) himself supposed that he would most easily work irreparable harm upon the enemy, if he should make his inroad against them with a small army. 27.16. He sent, then, five hundred horsemen, bidding them go very close to the circuit-wall, and what they had often suffered at the hands of a few of the enemy, this to display against their whole army. 27.17. And these, getting onto a high place not far from the city, but just out of range, stood. 27.18. But Belisarius, picking out a thousand men and setting over them as commander Bessas, enjoined them to advance against the enemy. 27.19. And they, surrounding the barbarians and shooting always from behind, killed many and forced the rest, by violence, to come down into the plain. 27.20. There, the battle being hand-to-hand, not on equal terms of strength, the most of the Goths were destroyed, and a few, scarcely escaping, withdrew to their own camp. 27.21. These Witigis reviled as having been defeated by cowardice, and, promising to retrieve the disaster before long with certain others, kept quiet for the present, but three days later, picking out five hundred men from all the stockades, he bade them display against the enemy deeds worthy of valour. 27.22. And when Belisarius saw them coming nearer, he sent against them fifteen hundred men and the commanders Martinus and Valerianus. 27.23. And a cavalry battle taking place at once, the Romans, far surpassing the enemy in multitude, routed them with no trouble and destroyed almost all of them. 27.24. And to the enemy it seemed altogether dreadful and a stroke of adverse fortune, that, being many, they were defeated by a few of the enemy coming against them, and that, going again against them in small numbers, they were destroyed. 27.25. But the Romans publicly praised the sagacity of Belisarius, holding it, as was likely, in great wonder, while privately his intimates asked him from what evidence, on that day on which he had thus escaped from the enemy, having been defeated, he had become of good hope to prevail over them by force in the war. 27.26. And he himself said that, having at the beginning come to grips with them with a few men, he had observed what was the difference in each army, so that, if he should make the encounters proportionate to the strength, the multitude of the enemy could in no way injure his own fewness of men. 27.27. And the difference was that the Romans, almost all of them, and the allied Huns are good mounted archers, but for the Goths this art was practised by none; rather their horsemen are wont to use only spears and swords, and their archers, being on foot and protected by the heavy-armed, go into battle. 27.28. So the horsemen, unless the encounter be hand-to-hand, having no means of defending themselves against opponents using bows, are easily shot and destroyed, and the foot-soldiers could never be sufficient to make sallies against horsemen. 27.29. For these reasons Belisarius maintained that the barbarians in these encounters were being defeated by the Romans. And the Goths, having in mind the strangeness of what had befallen them, neither went thereafter against the circuit-wall of Rome in small numbers nor pursued the enemy when they harassed them, except only so far as to thrust them back from the stockades. 28.1. Afterward all the Romans, elated by their previous successes, were eager to go to battle with the whole army of the Goths and thought they should make war openly. 28.2. But Belisarius, thinking that the difference between the two armies was still very great, shrank always from risking everything with his whole army, and was the more zealous for the sallies and devised plans against the enemy. 28.3. But when, being reviled by the army and the other Romans, he gave up, he wished to fight with his whole army, but to make the encounter none the less by a sally. 28.4. And many times he was repulsed when he set out for this, and was compelled to put off the inroad to the next day, since he found the enemy prepared beyond expectation, having learned beforehand what would happen from the deserters. 28.5. Wherefore he wished thenceforth to fight it out openly, and the barbarians gladly entered the battle. And when the preparations for the encounter had been made in the best way by both sides, Belisarius, gathering the whole army, exhorted them as follows: 28.6. "It was not from condemning any softness in you, fellow-soldiers, nor from dreading the power of the enemy, that I shrank from the encounter with them, but, since our affairs stood well when we carried on the war by sallies, I thought I ought to preserve forever the cause of our good success. 28.7. For those whose present affairs go according to their mind, I think it inexpedient to change to another course. Seeing, however, that you are eager for this danger, I am of good hope and shall never stand in the way of your impulse. 28.8. For I know that the greatest part of the issue in wars is always allotted to the judgment of the combatants, and that things are for the most part set right by their eagerness. 28.9. That few men arrayed with valour are able to prevail over a multitude of their opponents, each one of you knows well, not having taken it by hearsay, but having come to the experience of the daily struggle. 28.10. But that you may not disgrace either the former reputation of my generalship or the hope that comes from this eagerness of yours, it will rest with you. 28.11. For everything that has chanced to be done by us in this war must of necessity be judged by the outcome of the present day. 28.12. And I see that the present moment also assists us, which, the spirit of the enemy having been enslaved by their previous reverses, will, as is likely, easily place their conquest in our hands. 28.13. For the judgments of those who have often been unfortunate are by no means wont to play the man. And let no one of you spare his horse or bow or any other weapon. 28.14. For I will straightway render to you in return others for all that is destroyed in the battle." 28.15. Having thus exhorted them, Belisarius led out the army through the Pincian postern and the Salarian gate, and bade a few go through the Aurelian gate into the plain of Nero. 28.16. Over these he set Valentinus, commander of a cavalry detachment, and enjoined him to begin no battle, nor to go nearer the camp of the enemy, but always to give the appearance of being about to assault at once, so that none of the enemy there, crossing the bridge there, might be able to come to the aid of those from the other stockades. 28.17. For since the barbarians encamping in the plain of Nero were many, as I have disclosed before, it seemed sufficient to him that all these should be cut off from the rest of the army by not taking part in the encounter. 28.18. And when some of the people of the Romans of their own will took up arms and followed, he did not allow them to be arrayed with them for the encounter, fearing lest, having come into the struggle, they should dread the danger and throw the whole army into confusion, being laborers and altogether without practice in war. 28.19. But he bade them, outside the Pancratian gates, which are over the river Tiber, making a phalanx, remain quiet until he himself should give the signal, reckoning, which indeed came to pass, that, if the enemy in the plain of Nero should see both them and the forces of Valentinus, they would never take courage to leave their own stockade and go into battle against them with the rest of the army. 28.20. And it was a piece of luck and worth much account that so great a multitude of the enemy's army should be cut off. 28.21. Thus, then, he wished to make only a cavalry battle on that day, and the most of the other foot-soldiers, by now not thinking it right to remain in their present condition, having plundered horses of the enemy and become not without practice in riding, 28.22. were horsemen. But the foot-soldiers, being few and neither able to make a phalanx worth account nor having yet taken courage to come to grips with the barbarians, but always setting out in flight at the first onset, he thought it not safe to array far from the circuit-wall, but bade them remain in array close by the moat, so that, if it should befall their horsemen to be routed, they might be able to receive the fugitives and, being unwearied, defend themselves against their opponents along with them. 28.23. But a certain Principius, one of his guardsmen, a notable man, a Pisidian by race, and Tarmutus an Isaurian, the brother of Ennes the leader of the Isaurians, coming into the presence of Belisarius, spoke as follows: 28.24. "Best of generals, do not see fit to cut off from your army, which is small and is to fight against many tens of thousands of barbarians, the phalanx of foot-soldiers, nor think it right that the Roman infantry should be insulted, through which we hear that the rule of the Romans of old advanced to this magnitude. 28.25. For if it chances that nothing worth account has been wrought by them in this war, this is no proof of the cowardice of the soldiers, but the commanders of the foot are justly to bear the blame, who alone are mounted on horses in the array, but do not think fit to share the fortune of war in common, but each one of them by himself for the most part uses flight even before the struggle. 28.26. But do you, having all the commanders of the foot — for you see that they have become horsemen and are by no means willing to be arrayed with their own subjects — with the rest of the cavalry army enter into this encounter, and grant us to lead the foot-soldiers into the array. 28.27. For being foot-soldiers ourselves, we shall bear with them the multitude of the barbarians, having hope to do to the enemy whatever God may grant." 28.28. Hearing this, Belisarius at first did not consent; for he loved these two exceedingly warlike men beyond measure and was unwilling to risk a few foot-soldiers. 28.29. But at last, forced by the eagerness of the men, he left some few at the gates and up at the battlements with the people of the Romans about the engines, and, setting Principius and Tarmutus over the rest, he bade them stand behind in array, so that they themselves might not, dreading the danger, throw the rest of the army into confusion, and, if ever any portion of the horsemen should be routed, they might not go off as far as possible, but, taking refuge with the foot-soldiers, might be able with them to defend themselves against the pursuers. 29.1. The Romans, then, made their preparations for the encounter thus. But Witigis armed all the Goths, leaving no one in the stockades except those unfit for battle. 29.2. And he bade the forces of Marcias remain in the plain of Nero and take care of the guard at the bridge, so that the enemy might not go against them from there; while he himself, gathering the rest of the army, spoke as follows: 29.3. "Perhaps I might seem to some of you to be afraid for my rule, and on this account to be showing you my other kindness and now to be uttering words enticing to courage. 29.4. And this they reckon not according to the manner of mankind. For ignorant men are wont to treat with gentleness those whom they need, even though they chance to be much their inferiors, but to be hard of approach toward those whose service they do not require. 29.5. To me, however, neither the end of life nor the loss of rule is a concern. For I would pray even to strip off this purple today, if a Gothic man should be about to put it on. 29.6. And I have considered the end of Theodahad to have been among the most blessed, in that it befell him to give up both his rule and his life at the hands of his own kinsmen. 29.7. For a calamity falling upon one privately, when one's race is not destroyed along with him, is for those who are not foolish not without consolation. 29.8. But when I consider the calamity of the Vandals and the end of Gelimer, nothing moderate comes upon me, but I seem to see the Goths with their children enslaved, and your women serving the most hateful of men in the most shameful of all things, and myself led, together with the daughter of Theoderic's child, wherever the present enemy please; these things I would wish that you too, fearing lest they befall, should enter into this battle. 29.9. For thus you would account the end of your life in the place of the encounter of more value than safety after defeat. For noble men consider that they are unfortunate in one thing only, in being worsted by the enemy. 29.10. And death, especially when it comes swiftly, always makes blessed those who before were not faring well. 29.11. And it is plain that, if you carry through this encounter with these reckonings, you will most easily conquer your opponents, who are few and Greeks, and you will punish them almost at once for the injustice and insolence which they began against us. 29.12. For we boast that we surpass them in valour and in multitude and in all other things, but they are emboldened against us, lifted up by our misfortunes, and having as their sole provision our negligence. For the prosperity beyond their desert feeds their boldness." 29.13. Having thus exhorted them, Witigis too arranged his army for battle, setting the foot-soldiers in the middle, and the horsemen on both wings. 29.14. He arrayed the phalanx, however, not far from the stockades, but close by, so that, as soon as the rout should come, the enemy might easily be overtaken and destroyed, the pursuit of them taking place over much ground. 29.15. For he hoped that, if the battle should be hand-to-hand in the plain, they would not hold out even a short time, judging from the great strangeness of it that the army of the enemy was not a match for his own. 29.16. The soldiers, then, beginning early, set to work on both sides; and Witigis and Belisarius, exhorting from behind, urged both to good courage. 29.17. And at first the affairs of the Romans were uppermost, and many of the barbarians fell by the arrows; yet no pursuit of them took place. 29.18. For inasmuch as the Goths were stationed in a great multitude, others most easily stood in the place of those who were destroyed, and gave no perception of those perishing among them. And to the Romans, being exceedingly few, it seemed sufficient that the struggle should be confined to this for them. 29.19. And having carried the battle even to the camps of their opponents by midday, and having now destroyed many of the enemy, they wished to return to the city, if any pretext should arise for them. 29.20. In this action three Roman men proved the best of all — Athenodorus, an Isaurian man, of repute among the guardsmen of Belisarius, and Theodoriscus and Georgius, 29.21. guardsmen of Martinus, Cappadocians by race. For always going out from the front of the phalanx, they dispatched with their spears many of the barbarians. These things happened thus. 29.22. But in the plain of Nero each side sat opposite the other for a long time, and the Moors, always making sallies and hurling their javelins, distressed the Goths. 29.23. For they by no means wished to go out against them, fearing those of the people of the Romans who were not far off, whom they supposed to be soldiers and to be remaining quiet, making some ambush against them, so that, getting behind them and putting them between two fires, they might destroy them. 29.24. But when the day was now half spent, the army of the Romans rushed suddenly upon the enemy, and the Goths, dismayed by the unexpected, were routed beyond expectation. 29.25. And they were not even able to flee into the stockade, but, going up onto the hills there, kept quiet. Now the Romans were many, but not all soldiers, 29.26. but the most were an unarmed throng. For inasmuch as the general was elsewhere, many in the camp of the Romans, sailors and servants eager to share in the war, mingled with the army there. 29.27. And by their multitude, having dismayed the barbarians, as has been said, they routed them, but by their disorder they overthrew the affairs of the Romans. 29.28. For by mingling with them the soldiers fell into great confusion, and, although Valentinus exhorted them much, they by no means gave heed to the commands. 29.29. Wherefore, neither pursuing the fugitives, did they kill any, but permitted them, remaining quiet on the hills, to behold without fear what was being done. 29.30. Nor did they take thought to break up the bridge there, so that the city might not thereafter be besieged on both sides, the barbarians being no longer able to encamp over the river Tiber. 29.31. Nor indeed, by crossing the bridge, did they get behind the enemy who were fighting against the forces of Belisarius there. Which, had it come about, the Goths, I think, would no longer have looked toward defence, but would have set out in flight at once, as each one could. 29.32. But as it was, having taken the stockade of the enemy, they turned to plundering the goods, and carried off much silver plate and much other property thence. 29.33. But the barbarians, for some time beholding what was being done, kept quiet and remained where they were, but at last, taking counsel, and held by great fury and shouting, advanced against their opponents. 29.34. And finding men plundering their goods in no order, they killed many of them and quickly drove out the rest. For those of them who, being caught, were not destroyed, throwing the goods from their shoulders, fled gladly. 29.35. While these things were happening in the plain of Nero, meanwhile the rest of the army of the barbarians, fencing themselves with shields close by their own camps, defended themselves vigorously against their opponents, and destroyed many men, but many more horses. 29.36. And when of the Romans some had become wounded, and others, their horses being destroyed, left the array, in an army already small the fewness of men became still more apparent, and the difference of the throng of the Goths appeared great. 29.37. Having this in mind, the horsemen of the barbarians from the right wing went at a run against the enemy opposed to them. And the Romans there, not enduring their spears, set out in flight and came to the phalanx of the foot-soldiers. 29.38. But neither did the foot-soldiers withstand the assailants, but the most of them fled along with the horsemen. And straightway the rest of the Roman army also withdrew, the enemy pressing upon them, and the rout took place by force. 29.39. But Principius and Tarmutus, with a few of the foot-soldiers about them, displayed deeds worthy of valour against them. 29.40. For the most of the Goths, fighting and by no means thinking fit to be routed along with the others, the most of the Goths stood, holding this in great wonder. And from this both the other foot-soldiers and the most of the horsemen were saved with less fear. 29.41. Principius, then, his whole body cut to pieces, fell there, and about him forty-two foot-soldiers. 29.42. But Tarmutus, having two Isaurian javelins in both his hands, and always thrusting, turning this way and that, against those coming on, when, being cut about the body, he gave out — his brother Ennes having come to the rescue with some horsemen — recovered his breath and at a swift run, full of gore and wounds, went to the circuit-wall, having thrown away neither of his javelins. 29.43. And being swift of foot by nature, he was able to escape, although in such a state of body, and, coming to the very Pincian gates, fell. And, being supposed to be dead, he was lifted upon a shield and carried by some of his comrades. 29.44. And surviving two days, he died, having left a great name for himself among the Isaurians and the rest of the army. 29.45. And the Romans, now in fear, took care of the guard on the wall, and, putting the gates in place with much tumult, did not receive the fugitives into the city, fearing lest the enemy should burst in with them. 29.46. And those of them who had not arrived inside the circuit-wall in time, crossing the moat and setting their backs against the wall, trembled and stood having forgotten all defence, and were by no means able to defend themselves against the barbarians, although they pressed on and were about to cross the moat against them. 29.47. And the reason was that the spears of most had been broken in the encounter and the flight, and they were unable to work their bows by reason of the narrowness of their position with one another. 29.48. As long, then, as not many were seen at the battlements, the Goths pressed on, having hope to destroy all those shut out and to overpower those within the circuit-wall. 29.49. But when they saw a great number of soldiers and of the people of the Romans defending themselves at the battlements, straightway despairing, they marched off behind, reviling their opponents much. 29.50. And the battle, having begun in the stockades of the barbarians, ended in the moat and the wall of the city.

After this the Romans no longer dared to risk a battle with their whole army; but by making cavalry engagements in the manner of sudden raids, as before, they were for the most part victorious over the barbarians. 1.2. Foot-soldiers also went out from both sides, not drawn up in a phalanx, 1.3. but following the horsemen. And once Bessas, in the first charge, leaping in among the enemy with his spear, slew three of their best horsemen and put the rest to flight. 1.4. On another occasion Constantinus, bringing up the Huns into the Plain of Nero about late afternoon, when he saw that his opponents were overpowering them by their numbers, 1.5. did as follows. There is there a great stadium from of old, where in former times the gladiators of the city used to contend; and the men of old built many other structures about this stadium, so that, as is natural, there are narrow lanes everywhere in that quarter. 1.6. So then Constantinus, since he could neither prevail over the throng of the Goths nor flee without great danger, dismounted all the Huns from their horses and on foot, together with them, took his stand in one of the narrow lanes there. 1.7. And from there, shooting from a safe position, they killed many of the enemy. And for some time the Goths, though shot at, held their ground; 1.8. for they hoped that, as soon as the arrows of the Huns should fail in their quivers, they would surround them with no trouble, and binding them would lead them off to their own camp. 1.9. But when the Massagetae, who were good bowmen and were shooting into a large throng, were hitting an enemy with almost every arrow, the Goths perceived that they had lost more than half their number, and since the sun was already going down to its setting and they did not know what to do, they rushed into flight. 1.10. Thereupon many of them fell; for the Massagetae, pressing close upon them, since they understand the art of shooting most skilfully even while riding at full speed, kept shooting them in the back and killing them none the less. Thus Constantinus came back into Rome with the Huns at nightfall. 1.11. And not many days later, when Peranius led some of the Romans against the enemy through the Salarian Gate, the Goths fled with all their might; but when a sudden counter-pursuit took place about sunset, one of the Romans, a foot-soldier, falling into great confusion, tumbled into a certain deep pit, such as many were made there in former times by the men of old 1.12. for the storing of grain, I suppose. And since he dared not raise a cry, inasmuch as the enemy were encamped somewhere near, and was not able to get out of the hole by any means whatever, since it offered no place to climb up, he was forced to pass the night there. 1.13. And on the following day, when there was again a rout of the barbarians, one of the Goths fell into the same pit. 1.14. Then indeed the two came together in friendliness and goodwill toward each other, since necessity drew them together, and they gave pledges, in very truth, that each would be earnest for the other's safety; and then both of them shouted out loud and clear. 1.15. The Goths accordingly, following the sound and peering down over the pit, inquired who in the world it was that was shouting. 1.16. And since it had been thus decided between the two men, the Roman kept silence, while the other declared in his native tongue that he had just now fallen in during the rout that had taken place, and begged them to let down a noose so that he might climb up. 1.17. And they, as quickly as possible, throwing down the ends of the ropes, thought to be drawing up the Goth; but the Roman, seizing the nooses, was hauled up, saying this, that if he himself climbed up first, the Goths would never neglect his comrade, but if they should learn that the enemy alone was there, they would take no account of him. 1.18. Having said this, he climbed up. And when the Goths saw him, they were amazed and seized with great perplexity; and hearing the whole story from him, they drew up the comrade second, who told them of the agreements between them and the pledges given by both. 1.19. And he went off with his comrades, while they let the Roman go unharmed into the city. 1.20. After this the horsemen on either side, not many at a time, often armed themselves as if for battle, but the contests always ended for them in single combat, and in all of them the Romans were victorious. Such, then, was the course of these events. 1.21. A little later, when an engagement took place in the Plain of Nero and pursuits were being made here and there by small bodies of horsemen, Chorsamantis, a man of repute among the guards of Belisarius, a Massagete by birth, was pursuing seventy of the enemy together with some others. 1.22. And when he had got far out into the plain, the other Romans rode back, but Chorsamantis alone still kept up the pursuit. And the Goths, observing this, turned their horses and came at him. 1.23. And he, charging into their midst and killing one of the best with his spear, went on against the rest; but they again turned and rushed into flight. 1.24. But being ashamed before those in the camp (for they suspected that they were already being observed by them too), they wished to go at him once more. 1.25. And meeting the same fate as before, and losing one of their best, they were turned to flight none the less, until Chorsamantis, having carried the pursuit up to their stockade, returned alone. 1.26. A little later, when he had been hit in the left shin in another battle, it was thought that the missile had grazed the surface of the bone. 1.27. And being kept out of the fighting for some days by this wound, as a barbarian man he did not bear it calmly, but threatened to avenge himself most speedily on the Goths for the outrage to his leg. 1.28. So when he had recovered not long afterward and was flushed with wine at his luncheon, as was his custom, he resolved to go alone against the enemy and to avenge himself for the outrage to his foot; and coming to the Pincian postern, he said that he was being sent by Belisarius to the camp of the enemy. 1.29. And the guards there (for they could not distrust a man who was the best of the guards of Belisarius) opened the gates and let him go wherever he wished. 1.30. And when the enemy caught sight of him, at first they supposed that some deserter was coming over to them; but when, on coming near, he laid hold of his bow, not knowing who in the world he was, twenty of them advanced against him. 1.31. And driving them off easily, he rode away at a walk, and when more Goths came against him he did not flee. 1.32. And when, as a great multitude poured against him, he saw fit to defend himself, the Romans, watching from the towers, suspected that the man was mad, but they did not yet know that it was Chorsamantis. 1.33. And after displaying deeds great and worthy of much account, and falling into the encirclement of the enemy's army, 1.34. he paid the penalty of his irrational rashness. And when Belisarius and the Roman army learned of this, falling into great grief, since the hope which all had placed in the man had been destroyed, they lamented him.

Thus Belisarius, while affairs were still in suspense, came to Byzantium bringing with him Wittigis and the notable Goths and the children of Ildibadus and all the goods, and there followed him Ildiger and Valerianus and Martinus with Herodian, these alone. 1.2. And the emperor Justinian saw Wittigis with his wife gladly, and marvelled at the throng of the barbarians for the beauty and stature of their bodies. 1.3. And receiving the wealth of Theoderic, which was a thing worth seeing, he set it out in the Palatium as a spectacle for those of the senate in private, taking pride in the magnitude of what had been done; but he neither displayed it to the populace nor granted the triumph to Belisarius, as he had done when he came after conquering Gelimer and the Vandals. 1.4. Yet in all men's tales Belisarius was the theme, having won two victories such as it had never before befallen any man to achieve, and having led two kings captive to Byzantium, and having made the race and the wealth of both Gizeric and Theoderic spoil for the Romans, contrary to expectation—men than whom none more illustrious had ever arisen among the barbarians—and having brought back the wealth from the enemy again into the state, and having recovered for the empire in a short time nearly half the portion of land and sea. 1.5. And it was a delight to the people of Byzantium to see Belisarius going forth from his house into the forum each day, or returning to it, and no one was ever sated with this sight. 1.6. For his going forth resembled a most crowded procession, since a multitude of Vandals and Goths and Moors always followed him. And he was also handsome in body and tall and most comely of countenance of all men. 1.7. And he showed himself so gentle and so easy of approach to those who met him that he resembled a man both very poor and of no repute. 1.8. And the love of his rule that was invincible among the soldiers and the country folk arose because he had become the most generous of all men toward the soldiers; for those who had been unfortunate in an engagement he consoled for their former wounds with great sums of money, and to those who had distinguished themselves he gave as prizes armlets and necklaces to wear; and if a soldier's horse or bow or any other thing whatever had been lost in battle, another was straightway provided in its place by Belisarius. And toward the country folk he used such sparingness and forethought that, while Belisarius was general, it never befell that they suffered any violence, but it came about, contrary to expectation, that all on whom a multitude of his army was quartered grew rich. 1.9. For all their goods were sold to them at their own price. And whenever the crops were at their height, he guarded strictly lest his horse, passing through, should do harm to anyone. 1.10. And of the ripe fruits on the trees no one whatever was at all permitted to touch any. 1.11. And indeed he laid claim to chastity in a prodigious degree; for he touched no woman whatever except his own wedded wife. 1.12. So that, although he had taken captive from among the Vandals and Goths so great a number of women, and women of such beauty of countenance as no one anywhere of men ever saw, he permitted no one of them either to come into his sight or to meet him in any other way. 1.13. And he was, besides all his other qualities, exceedingly quick-witted and most capable of devising the best course in difficulties. 1.14. In the dangers of war he was both stout-hearted with safety and most daring with calculation, and was keen and slow in the attack on the enemy by turns, 1.15. as each was needful. And apart from these things, in terrors he kept his mind hopeful and superior to confusion, while in success he was neither lifted up nor wanton; indeed, no one ever saw Belisarius drunk. 1.16. Now during all the time that he commanded the Roman army both in Libya and in Italy, he continued to conquer and always to win what lay before him. 1.17. But when he came, summoned, to Byzantium, his valour became known to the greatest degree even more than before. 1.18. For being himself pre-eminent in all valour, and surpassing all the generals who had ever been both in the abundance of his wealth and in the power of his shield-bearers and guards, he became, as was natural, terrible to all commanders and soldiers. 1.19. For no one, I think, dared to oppose his command, and they never refused to carry out fully whatever he ordered, both out of respect for his valour and out of fear of his power. 1.20. For he provided seven thousand horsemen from his own household, of whom not one had ever proved a failure, but each one of them claimed to stand first in the line of battle and to challenge the best of the enemy. 1.21. And the elders of the Romans, when, being besieged by the Goths, they watched what was being done in the engagements of the war, marvelled greatly and cried out that a single household was undoing the power of Theoderic. 1.22. So Belisarius, having become powerful both in dignity and in judgement, as has been said, deliberated what would be advantageous to the emperor's affairs and always carried out what had been decided by his own independent judgement. 1.23. But the other commanders, being rather equal among themselves and having in mind to accomplish nothing except their own private gains, began both to plunder the Romans and to give over the subjects to the soldiers, and they neither themselves any longer thought what was needful nor kept the soldiers obedient to their orders. 1.24. Wherefore many errors were committed by them, and the affairs of the Romans were all ruined in a short time. By what manner this came about I now proceed to tell. 1.25. When Ildibadus learned that Belisarius had set out from Ravenna and was going on his journey, he gathered about himself all the barbarians and as many of the Roman soldiers as a revolution pleased. 1.26. And he attended most carefully to his rule, and was eager to recover for the race of the Goths the mastery over the Italians. 1.27. At the beginning, then, not more than a thousand followed him, and they held a single city, Ticinum; but little by little there came over to him all who were in Liguria and Venetia. 1.28. Now there was a certain Alexander in Byzantium set over the public accounts; this office the Romans, using Greek, call logothete. 1.29. This man always charged against the soldiers the loss to the public treasury. And bringing them under such accusations, he himself quickly became of repute from being obscure, and from being poor simply rich, and indeed he exacted great sums of money for the emperor, if anyone ever did; but he became, of all men, most responsible for the soldiers being few and poor and slow toward dangers. 1.30. And the people of Byzantium called him also by the surname Psalidios, because it was easy for him, by cutting off the gold coin in a circle, to make it less by as much as he wished, and yet to preserve the round shape which it had before. 1.31. For psalidion they call the instrument with which one does such things. This Alexander the emperor, when he had summoned Belisarius, 1.32. sent into Italy. And he, when he had come to Ravenna, set forth accounts that had no reason.
