For the Italians, who had neither touched the emperor's money nor done anything improper toward the treasury, he called to account, bringing against them the charge of their injustice toward Theoderic and the other rulers of the Goths, and compelling them to pay back if they had gained anything by deceiving those men, as he himself alleged. 1.33. And the wounds and dangers of the soldiers he requited, contrary to their expectation, with the pettiness of his accounts. Wherefore the Italians became ill-disposed to the emperor Justinian, and none of the soldiers any longer wished to set himself in the danger of war, but, playing the coward on purpose, they always made the affairs of the enemy advance greatly. 1.34. So the other commanders for these reasons remained quiet, but Vitalius alone (for he happened to have in Venetia both another multitude of an army and a large throng of Erulian barbarians) dared to come to battle with Ildibadus, fearing, as happened, lest, when at a later time he had come to a great measure of power, they should no longer be able to hold him back. 1.35. And when a fierce battle had taken place about the city of Tarbesion, Vitalius, defeated by far, fled, saving some few, but losing the most of his men there. In this battle many of the Eruli fell, and Visandus the leader of the Eruli was killed. 1.36. And Theudimundus the son of Mauricius the son of Mundus, being still a youth, came into danger of death, yet escaped with Vitalius. And the name of Ildibadus from this exploit came both to the emperor and to all men. 1.37. Afterward it befell that Uraïas gave offence to Ildibadus from the following cause. There was to Uraïas a wife who bore off the first prize for wealth and beauty of body among these barbarians, above all. 1.38. She once went down to the bath, clothed in a great quantity of finery and bringing with her an attendance worthy of much account. 1.39. And seeing the wife of Ildibadus there in plain garments, she neither did obeisance to her as one dwelling with a king, but otherwise despised and insulted her. For Ildibadus was still in poverty, since he had by no means come upon the royal wealth. 1.40. And the wife of Ildibadus, being grievously distressed at the strangeness of the insult, came to her husband in tears and saw fit that he should avenge her, who had suffered irreparable things at the hands of the wife of Uraïas. 1.41. Wherefore Ildibadus at first slandered Uraïas to the barbarians, alleging that he was about to desert to the enemy, and a little later killed him by treachery, and from this he fell into the hatred of the Goths. 1.42. For it was by no means their wish that Uraïas should thus, without consideration, be removed from among men. And many now, gathering among themselves, reviled Ildibadus as one who had wrought unholy deeds. None, however, was willing to avenge this murder upon him. 1.43. Now there was among them a certain Velas, a Gepid by race, who had come to the dignity of being one of the king's guards. 1.44. This man, having become betrothed to a woman fair of face, fell into a prodigious love; but while he had been sent against the enemy, in order that he might make with certain others an assault upon them, Ildibadus, whether led by ignorance or by something else, gave the betrothed woman in marriage to another of the barbarians. 1.45. And when Velas, returning from the camp, heard this, being passionate by nature, he did not bear the insult arising from the deed, but resolved straightway to kill Ildibadus, 1.46. thinking that he would thereby gratify all the Goths. And watching him once feasting the best of the Goths, he set about the plot. 1.47. For it is the custom that, while the king is feasting, many others and the guards stand around. So while Ildibadus, putting his hand to the food, was lying prone on the couch, Velas suddenly struck him on the neck with his sword, 1.48. so that, while the food was still held in the man's fingers, the head, falling forward onto the table, struck all present with consternation and brought them into great amazement. 1.49. This vengeance came upon Ildibadus for the murder of Uraïas. And the winter was ending, and the sixth year of this war which Procopius has written was coming to a close.

And all of them struck at him at once with their spears. But since his corselet withstood them, the other blows did not hurt him much, but one of the Goths, coming upon him from behind above the right armpit, where the body was unprotected, close to the shoulder, struck the young man—not a fatal blow, however, nor one bringing him into danger of death. 2.23. And in front another, piercing his left thigh, cut the muscle there, not with a straight blow, but with a slanting one. 2.24. But Valerianus and Martinus saw what was happening, and their reinforcements as quickly as possible both routed the enemy, and the two of them, laying hold of the bridle of the horse of Bochas, came into the city. And night came on, and Euthalius arrived with the money. 2.25. When all had got into the city, they attended to their wounds. The physicians, wishing to draw the missile out of the face of Arzes, were perplexed for some time, not so much on account of the eye, which they supposed could never be saved, but lest, by the puncturing of membranes and tendons, of which there are many there, they should destroy the best man of the household of Belisarius. 2.26. Then one of the physicians, Theoctistus by name, pressing against the back of the neck, asked the man if he felt much pain. 2.27. And when he said that he did feel pain, “Then you yourself will be saved,” he said, “and your sight will not be harmed.” This he affirmed, judging that the point of the missile had penetrated not far from the skin. 2.28. So cutting off as much of the shaft as showed outside and throwing it away, and dividing the skin at the back of the head where the man felt most pain, he drew out the point from there with no trouble, bringing with it the three barbs that projected backward and the remaining portion of the missile. 2.29. Thus Arzes remained altogether unharmed, and not even a trace of the wound was left on his face. 2.30. But Cutilas, when the little spear had been pulled out of his head with some violence (for it had been driven very deep), fell into a swoon. 2.31. And the Goths, perceiving this, no longer wished to risk a battle with the enemy, but kept watch that nothing might be brought in to them for the future. 3.3. Now there are two aqueducts between the Latin and the Appian Way, exceedingly high and raised up for the most part on arches. 3.4. These two aqueducts, at a place fifty stades distant from Rome, meet each other and for a little while change their courses to the opposite direction. 3.5. For the one which before had its place on the right then goes along bearing to the left. 3.6. Then again coming together and resuming their former position, they are separated for the rest of the way, and from this it comes about that the space between is enclosed by a fortification formed by the aqueducts. 3.7. The lower arches of these the barbarians blocked up with stones and clay and made into the form of a fort, and there, encamping with no fewer than seven thousand men, they kept guard that the enemy might no longer bring anything of the necessities into the city. 3.8. Then indeed every hope of good had failed the Romans, and every form of evil encompassed them. So long as the grain was at its height, the most daring of the soldiers, urged on by their desire for money, mounting their horses and dragging others along, would get into the standing crops by night, not far from the city. 3.9. And cutting the ears of grain and placing them on the horses which they themselves led along, they would carry them into the city unobserved by the enemy and sell them for much money to the wealthy among the Romans. 3.10. The rest, however, lived on certain herbs, such as grow in abundance both in the suburbs and inside the wall. For herbage never fails the land of the Romans, neither in the winter season nor at any other time, but it always blossoms and flourishes at all seasons. 3.11. For which reason it has happened that those besieged there even pastured their horses. And some, making sausages of the mules that died in Rome, sold them secretly. 3.12. And when the crops no longer had grain, and all the Romans had come into great evil, they crowded around Belisarius and tried to compel him to settle matters with the enemy in a single battle, promising that none of the Romans would be left out of the engagement. And as he was at a loss before the present situation and was greatly distressed, some of the men of the people spoke to him as follows: 3.13. “The present fortune has overtaken us, O general, when we did not expect it, but in everything our hopes have turned out to the contrary. 3.14. For having obtained what we formerly desired, we have now come to our present calamity, and the opinion which we held before, that it was a noble thing to seek the emperor's protection, has now turned about and proved to be folly and the cause of the greatest evils. 3.15. From this we have come to such a pass of necessity that even now we are constrained, and have dared to take up arms against the barbarians. 3.16. And forgiveness if we speak boldly to Belisarius—for the belly, when it lacks the necessities, does not know how to be ashamed; 3.17. but let fortune make our defence for our rashness. For with good reason life, prolonged for those who fare not well, is held to be the most grievous of all things. The misfortunes that have befallen us you see, doubtless. 3.18. These fields and the whole countryside have fallen under the hands of the enemy; and this city has been shut off from all good things—we know not for how long a time. 3.19. Of the Romans, some already lie dead, having drawn the lot of not even being hidden by the earth, while we who survive—to speak in a word of all our terrors—pray to be ranged among those who lie thus. 3.20. For famine shows all evils bearable to those it meets, and wherever it appears, it comes attended by forgetfulness of all else, and makes all forms of death pleasant to men, except that which comes from itself. 3.21. While, therefore, the evil has not yet conquered us, grant us to take up the contest on our own behalf, from which it will come about for us either to prevail over the enemy or to be released from our hardships. 3.22. For those to whom delay brings a hope of safety would be very foolish to thrust themselves prematurely into a danger involving everything; but for those to whom the contest becomes more difficult by slowness, even to put it off for a short time is more blameworthy than immediate rashness.” 3.23. Thus much the Romans said. And Belisarius answered as follows: “But for me all that has come from you has happened quite as I expected, and nothing has fallen out contrary to my opinion. 3.24. For I have long known that a populace is a most ill-counselled thing, and that it is by nature able neither to bear the present nor to take forethought for the future, but only knows how to undertake the impossible easily and to perish unconsidered. 3.25. I, however, would never of my own free will, on account of your faintheartedness, either destroy you or ruin the emperor's affairs along with you. 3.26. For war is not wont to be brought to a successful issue by unreasoning haste, but by good counsel and forethought, always weighing the turn of opportunities. 3.27. You, then, thinking that you are playing at dice, wish to cast the single throw for everything; but it is not my custom to choose the quick way before the advantageous. 3.28. Then, too, you propose to go against the enemy through battle along with us—when have you practised the exercises of war? Or what man who has learned such things by arms does not know that battle does not proceed to the trial? Nor does the enemy himself give one a chance to practise in the contests. 3.29. For the present I admire your zeal, and I forgive this disturbance; 3.30. but that these things have come upon you at no opportune time, and that we are using a prudent delay, I shall make plain. The emperor, having gathered from every land an army superior in number, has sent it, and a fleet such as never before was assembled by the Romans now covers the shore of Campania and most of the Ionian Gulf. 3.31. And within a few days they will come to us with all the necessities, both to put an end to our want and to overwhelm the camps of the barbarians with a multitude of missiles. 3.32. I have reckoned, therefore, that it is better to put off the time of engagement until their arrival, and to win the mastery of the war in safety, rather than, growing bold with unreasoning haste, to throw away the safety of all. But that they shall come at once and delay no longer, I shall see to.”

Now a certain rock rises exceedingly high before the wall, from which it is possible to observe everything being done in Verona and to count the people there, and indeed to see the plain for the most part. 3.15. And the Roman army, having come within forty stades of the city, went no farther forward, since the generals were disputing with one another about the goods in the city. 3.16. And while they were still contending about this booty, the day had now become clearly bright, and the Goths, from the summit, observing exactly both the enemy in the city and how far off the rest of the army stood from Verona, advanced at a run to the city through the very gates from which they had departed before; for those who had entered were not able to hold them. 3.17. The Romans, then, taking counsel together, took refuge about the battlements of the wall, and as the barbarians in great numbers came to close quarters with them, both the others and Artabazes above all, displaying marvellous deeds, most stoutly defended themselves against the assailants. 3.18. And then the commanders of the Roman army, having settled with one another about the goods in Verona, resolved to advance against the city with the whole rest of the army. 3.19. Wherefore Artabazes and his men, overpowered by the multitude of the enemy and despairing of the help from their own people, all leaped down outside from the wall. 3.21. Now those who chanced to fall on level ground were brought unharmed to the Roman camp, among whom was also Artabazes; but all who fell into difficult places perished there. 3.22. And he instructed him to load as many ships as possible with grain, and to gather all the soldiers who happened at the moment to have come from Byzantium, or had been left there for the guarding of horses or for any other purpose whatever—of whom he had heard that many had gone to the regions in Campania—and to take some also of the garrisons there, and to come bringing the grain to Ostia, where is the port of the Romans. 4.3. And he, with Mundilas the spearman and a few horsemen, passed by night through the gate which is named after Paul the Apostle, escaping the notice of the enemy's camp which kept guard close to the Appian Way. 4.4. And when Mundilas and his men, returning to Rome, reported that Procopius had already reached Campania without meeting any of the barbarians—for the enemy never went outside their camp by night—all became hopeful, and Belisarius, now taking courage, devised the following. 4.5. He sent many of the horsemen to the strongholds near by, instructing them, if any of the enemy should come that way to bring provisions into the camps, to make sorties and ambushes against them everywhere in those regions and never to permit it, but to keep them off with all their might, in order that the city might be less hard pressed by want than before, and that the barbarians might seem to be besieged rather than to be besieging the Romans. 4.6. So he ordered Martinus and Trajan with a thousand men to go to Tarracina. And with them he sent also his wife Antonina, instructing her to set out for Naples with some few men and to await in safety the fortune that should befall them. 4.7. And Magnus and Sinthues the spearman he sent, taking with them about five hundred men, to the fortress of Tibur, which is one hundred and forty stades distant from Rome. 4.8. But to the town of Alba, which is the same distance away but lies on the Appian Way, he had previously sent Gontharis with some of the Eruli, whom the Goths drove out from there by force not long afterward. 4.9. There is a certain church of Paul the Apostle, fourteen stades distant from the wall of Rome, and the river Tiber flows past it. In that place there is no fortification whatever, but a colonnade extending from the city as far as the church, and many other buildings about it, make the place not easy to attack. 4.10. And there is a certain reverence among the Goths toward these sacred places. In neither of the churches of the two apostles, indeed, during the whole period of the war, was any unpleasant thing done by them, but all the rites were duly performed there by the priests, as was their custom. 4.11. In this place he ordered Valerianus, taking off all the Huns, to make a stockade by the bank of the Tiber, in order that their horses might be fed with less fear and that the Goths might be still more held back from going at will as far as possible from their camps. 4.12. And he did accordingly. And when the Huns had encamped there where the general directed, Belisarius rode back into the city. 4.13. Having accomplished these things, Belisarius kept quiet, not beginning battle, but eager to defend himself from the wall, if anyone should come from outside to do mischief to it. 4.14. And he provided grain for some of the populace of the Romans. And Martinus and Trajan, having passed by night through the camps of the enemy, when they reached Tarracina, sent Antonina with a few men into Campania, while they themselves, occupying the strongholds there and making sudden sorties from them, held back the Goths who went about the regions there. 4.15. And Magnus and Sinthues rebuilt in a short time as much of the fortress as had fallen down, and when they were in safety, they now harried the enemy still more, since their fort was not far off, both by constant raids and by always striking with terror, through the unexpectedness, those of the barbarians who escorted provisions, until Sinthues, struck by a spear in some battle in his right hand, with the tendons cut, became unfit for fighting for the rest of the time. 4.16. And the Huns, having made their camp in the neighbourhood, as I have said, did the Goths no less harm, so that they too were now hard pressed by famine, since there was no longer security for them to bring in provisions as before. 4.17. And a pestilence, falling upon them, destroyed many, and especially in the camp which was their last toward the Appian Way, 4.18. as has been shown by me before. And the few of them who were not destroyed withdrew from there to the other stockades. And the Huns, suffering this same thing, came into Rome. 4.19. These things, then, happened thus. And Procopius, when he had come into Campania, gathered there no fewer than five hundred soldiers, and filling a great number of ships with grain, kept them in readiness. 4.20. And Antonina also was present with him not long afterward, and together with him took charge of the fleet. 4.21. At that time too the mountain Vesuvius rumbled, but did not erupt, although there was a strong expectation arising from it that it would erupt. For which reason it came about that the inhabitants fell into great fear. 4.22. This mountain is seventy stades distant from Naples, turned toward the north wind from it, and it is altogether precipitous, being thickly wooded in a circle at the lower parts, but at the upper parts craggy and terribly inaccessible. 4.23. And on the summit of Vesuvius, about the middle, a cave appears, very deep, so that one may guess it extends to the very bottom of the mountain. 4.24. And there fire may be seen, if one dares to bend over it; and at other times the flame turns upon itself, giving trouble to none of the people there, but whenever the mountain sends forth a noise resembling a bellowing, it throws up not long afterward a great quantity of ashes from far below. 4.25. And if it catch anyone walking on the road, there is no means by which that man can live, and if it fall upon any houses, these too fall, weighed down by the quantity of the ashes. 4.26. And if a hard wind happen to come, it comes about that the ashes are carried up to a great height, so as no longer to be visible to a man, and they are borne wherever the wind blows them and fall to earth wherever it chances to be very far off. 4.27. And once, they say, the ashes fell upon Byzantium and so terrified the people there that from that time even to this day they have determined to propitiate God with yearly prayers in a public manner; and at another time they fell upon Tripolis in Libya. 4.28. And formerly they say this rumbling happened at intervals of a hundred years or even more, but later it came to pass much more quickly. 4.29. This, however, they affirm strongly, that whenever it falls to Vesuvius to erupt these ashes, of necessity that land flourishes with crops of all kinds. 4.30. And the air on this mountain is very thin and naturally most conducive to health of all places. Indeed, physicians send there from the most ancient times those who are seized with consumption. Such, then, is the situation regarding Vesuvius.

And Totila, learning what had happened in Verona, summoned many of the Goths from Verona, and when they were present, with the whole army, which was five thousand, he went against his opponents. And when the commanders of the Roman army learned this, they deliberated about their present situation. 4.2. And Artabazes coming forward spoke as follows: “Let none of you, men in command, see fit to despise the enemy because we are now inferior in numbers, nor, because we contend against those who have been enslaved by Belisarius, let him go against them with a slack reckoning. 4.3. For many, deceived by an untrue opinion, have brought themselves to ruin, and contempt, arising at the wrong time, has had the power to undo the existing strength of some, since besides their previous misfortune calls these men to good fortune. 4.4. For fortune, coming to the despair of good hopes, turns about to an excess of daring. 4.5. And I have said this among you now not led by suspicion, but from those things by which, having risked myself against them lately, I have learned the daring of these men. 4.6. And let none suppose that, because I was defeated with a few men, I marvel at the power of the enemy. For the valour of men is made manifest both to those who surpass in numbers and to those who are inferior in this, to those at least who will fight against them. 4.7. I think, then, it will be more advantageous for us, watching the crossing of the river by the barbarians, to come to close quarters when they are crossing midway, than when they have already all come together in a mass. 4.8. And let such a victory be deemed inglorious by none. For the issue of affairs is wont to give the name of glory or inglory, and men are accustomed to praise the victors, not searching into the manner of 4.9. the victory.” Artabazes said so much. But the commanders, opposing his opinion, did nothing of what was needful, but remaining where they were, wasted the opportunity. 4.10. And now the army of the Goths had come close, and when they were about to cross the river, Totila, calling all together, exhorted them as follows: “All other battles, men of my kindred, for the most part announcing a battle of a similar kind to the armies, urge them to the contest; but we set ourselves to this contest against the enemy using not an equal fortune, but with much that differs. 4.11. For if they should be defeated, as may chance, they will not long afterward be able to renew the fight against us. For in the forts of all Italy a multitude of soldiers has been left them, and it is in no way unlikely that another army from Byzantium will immediately come to their aid. But if we suffer this same thing, it will be left for the name of the Goths to perish together with the hope. 4.12. For from two hundred thousand it has befallen us to be reduced to five thousand. Having said so much, I think it not out of place to remind you of this also, that when you resolved with Ildibadus to take up arms against the emperor, the multitude that lived with you was no more than a thousand, and the whole country surrounded you up to the city of Ticinum. 4.13. But when you became superior in the engagement, the affairs both of your army and of the country went forward for you. So that if you are now willing to play the man, I have hope, as the war advances, as is likely, of altogether prevailing over our opponents. 4.14. For it always befalls the victors to have become both more numerous and more powerful. Let each of you, then, be eager to come to close quarters with the enemy with all his might, knowing well that for us, who have not now distinguished ourselves, it is impossible to renew the fight against our opponents. 4.15. And it is worth while for us to come to close quarters with the enemy with good hope, being bold in the injustice of these men. 4.16. For their life toward their subjects has been such that the Italians now need no other punishment for the treachery they ventured against the Goths, which they ought not. So that, to put it in a word, all evils have befallen them at the hands of those whom they received. 4.17. And what could be more easily taken than enemies whose dealings with God are evidently not sound? And indeed it would befit us to become hopeful for the contest from the fear that there is of us toward them. 4.18. For we go against no other men than those who lately, having come into the very midst of Verona, gave it up for no reason, although none whatever was pursuing them, and thus shamefully rushed into flight.” 4.19. Having exhorted them thus, Totila ordered three hundred of his followers, crossing the river about twenty stades off, to get behind the camp of the enemy, and when the battle should be at close quarters, going against their rear, to shoot at them and harass them with all their might, in order that those men, being thrown into confusion, might be mindful of no resistance. 4.20. And he himself with the whole rest of the army immediately crossed the river and went straight against his opponents; 4.21. and the Romans straightway came to meet them. And when both, advancing on their way, came nearer one another, a Goth, Valaris by name, great in body and exceedingly terrible in appearance, yet energetic and good in matters of war, riding his horse out ahead of the rest of the army, took his stand in the space between, corselet-clad and having a helmet on his head, and challenged all the Romans, if anyone wished to come to close quarters with him. 4.22. The rest, then, dismayed, remained quiet, but Artabazes set himself to the contest with him alone. 4.23. So both, driving their horses against each other, when they came close, thrust their spears; and Artabazes, anticipating, struck Valaris first in the right side. 4.24. And the barbarian, struck a mortal blow, was about to fall backward to the earth, but his spear, propped behind on the ground against a certain rock, by no means allowed him to fall. 4.25. And Artabazes pressed on still more, thrusting his spear into the man's vitals. For he did not yet suspect that he had been caught by a mortal blow. 4.26. And so it befell that the iron point of Valaris' spear, having become nearly upright, touched the corselet of Artabazes, and advancing little by little passed through the whole corselet, but slipping off the skin about the neck of Artabazes, grazed it. 4.27. And by some chance the iron, going forward, cut an artery which was somewhere there, and there was straightway a flow of much blood. 4.28. But the man had no sensation of pain, but he himself rode his horse back to the Roman army, 4.29. while Valaris fell there dead. And Artabazes too, the blood not ceasing, on the third day afterward was removed from among men, and shook all the hope of the Romans, since then too, having become unfit for fighting in this engagement, he brought their affairs to ruin in no small matters. 4.30. But the barbarians straightway began to despair of the war and to deliberate how they might withdraw from there, being destroyed by both the pestilence and the enemy, and having been reduced now from many tens of thousands to a few; and they were especially hard pressed by famine, in word besieging, but in deed besieged by their opponents and shut off from all the necessities. 6.2. And when they learned that another army was coming to the enemy by both land and sea from Byzantium—not so great as it actually was, but as great as the unbounded power of rumour was able to make it—being dismayed at the danger, they deliberated about their withdrawal. 6.3. They sent, therefore, envoys to Rome—a Roman man of repute among the Goths, with two others—who, coming to Belisarius, spoke as follows: 6.4. “That the war has turned out to the advantage of neither of us, each of us knows well, having come to the very experience of the hardships hereof. 6.5. For what would either of the two armies deny, when it has fallen to neither of them to lie in ignorance? 6.6. And that it is the part of senseless men to be willing to suffer endless toil for the sake of immediate contentiousness, and to find no release from their troubles, no one, I think, who is not foolish would gainsay. 6.7. And when these things are so, it behoves the leaders of both sides not to sacrifice the safety of their subjects to their own reputation, but to choose what is both just and advantageous not for themselves alone but also for their opponents, and thus to make a settlement of the present hardships. 6.8. For aiming at moderation gives a way through all difficulties, but to contentiousness it is natural that nothing of what is needful be accomplished. 6.9. We, then, having deliberated about the ending of this war, and offering what is advantageous to both, in which we think we are giving up something of justice as well, have come to you. 6.10. And may you too, not using any contentiousness toward us, resolve to choose what will profit yourselves rather than to be destroyed together with us. 6.11. And it is fitting that both make their speeches not in continuous discourse, but interrupting on the instant, 6.12. if anything seem to have been said unsuitably. For thus it will come about for both to have stated briefly all that is in their mind and to have done what is needful.” Belisarius answered: 6.13. “Thus, as you say, nothing shall hinder the dialogue from proceeding, provided what is said by you be peaceful and just.” 6.14. Again, then, the envoys of the Goths said: “You have wronged us, men of Rome, in taking up arms, as you ought not, against those who were friends and allies. And we shall say what we think each of you also knows along with us. 6.15. For the Goths did not acquire the land of Italy by taking it from the Romans by force, but Odoacer at one time, having deposed the emperor and changed the government here into a tyranny, held it. 6.16. And Zeno, then ruling the East and wishing both to avenge his fellow-emperor and to free this land from the tyrant, but being unable to overthrow the power of Odoacer, persuaded Theoderic our ruler, although he was about to besiege both him and Byzantium, to lay aside his enmity toward him, remembering the honour which he had already received from him—for he had become a patrician and consul of the Romans—and to take vengeance on Odoacer for his injustice toward Augustulus, and thereafter that he himself and the Goths should hold the land rightly and justly. 6.17. Thus, then, having taken over the rule of Italy, we have preserved both the laws and the government as well as any who have ever reigned, and of Theoderic or of anyone else who succeeded to the rule of the Goths there is no law at all, either written or unwritten. 6.18. And the matters of piety and faith toward God we have so exactly guarded for the Romans that not one of the Italians, willingly or unwillingly, has changed his belief to this day, and of the Goths who changed there has been no recall whatever. 6.19. And indeed the sacred places of the Romans have received from us the highest honour; for no one who fled for refuge to any of these has ever been violated by any man, but all the magistracies of the state the Romans themselves have continued to hold, 6.20. and no Goth has had a share in them. Or let someone come forward and refute us, if he thinks we have not spoken with truth. And one might add that the Goths conceded to the Romans even the dignity of the consulship, to receive it each year from the emperor of the East. 6.21. But you, these things being so, did not lay claim to Italy when it was being maltreated by the barbarians of Odoacer, although he wrought these terrible deeds not for a short time but for ten years; and now you do violence to those who possess it justly, though it in no way belongs to you. 6.22. Therefore stand out of our way from here, keeping what is your own and all that you have happened to plunder.” And Belisarius said: “Your promise foretold that what was said would be brief and moderate, but your speech has become long and not far from boastfulness for you. 6.23. For the emperor Zeno sent Theoderic to make war on Odoacer, not on condition that he himself should hold the rule of Italy; for why would it matter to the emperor to exchange one tyrant for another? But on condition that it should be free and subject to the emperor. 6.24. But he, after settling matters with regard to the tyrant well, in other respects used a thanklessness that was not within moderate bounds; for he never resolved to give back the land to its master. 6.25. And I, for my part, hold that both he who uses force and he who does not willingly give back his neighbour's property are equal. I, then, would never give over the emperor's land to anyone else. 6.26. But if you wish to obtain anything else, I give you leave to speak.” 6.27. And the barbarians said: “That all has been spoken truly by us has escaped none of you. But we, in order that we may seem least of all to be contentious, give up to you even Sicily, which is so great in size and so rich, without which it is not possible for you to hold Libya in safety.” 6.28. And Belisarius said: “And we, in turn, concede to the Goths the possession of all Britain, which is much greater than Sicily and was subject to the Romans from of old. 6.29. For it is right to requite with equal favours those who have begun some benefaction or kindness.” 6.30. The barbarians: “Then if we should say something to you about Campania too, or about Naples itself, would you not accept it?” 6.31. Belisarius: “For we are not authorized to administer the emperor's affairs otherwise than as is his will.” The barbarians: “Not even if we should appoint ourselves to bring fixed sums of money to the emperor each year?” 6.32. Belisarius: “No indeed. For we have authority over nothing else than to guard the land for its owner.” 6.33. The barbarians: “Come then, we must needs send to the emperor and make the agreements concerning everything with him. And it is necessary also to fix a definite time within which the armies should come to a truce.” 6.34. Belisarius: “So be it; let these things be done. For I shall never stand in your way when you deliberate for peace.” 6.35. Having said thus much, both parties broke off from the discussion, and the envoys of the Goths withdrew to their own camp. 6.36. And in the following days, going frequently to and fro to each other, they arranged matters concerning the truce, and how, in regard to it, each side should furnish to the other some of their notable men in the position of hostages.

But Belisarius dismissed them with laughter, saying that this complaint was a mere pretext, and that no one was ignorant of why the Goths had abandoned these places. 7.25. And for the rest they treated each other with a certain suspicion. After this Belisarius, when he saw Rome flourishing with a multitude of soldiers, sent some horsemen to regions far distant from Rome, and ordered John, the nephew of Vitalian, with the horsemen following him, eight hundred in number, to winter about the city of Alba, lying in Picenum; 7.26. and he sent with him four hundred of those following Valerianus, whom Damianus the nephew of Valerianus commanded, and eight hundred men of his own guards, exceedingly good in matters of war. 7.27. And over them he set two spearmen, Suntas and Adegis, and he ordered them to follow John wherever he should lead; and to John he gave instruction that, as long as he saw the enemy keeping the agreements made with them, he should stay quietly; but when it should come about that the truce was broken for them, he should do as follows: 7.28. with his whole army suddenly and by a sudden raid he should overrun the land of Picenum, going about all the regions there in order and arriving in person ahead of the report. 7.29. For of almost all that country no men at all had been left, since all, as it appears, had marched against Rome, but the children and wives of the enemy and their goods were everywhere. 7.30. He was therefore to enslave and to plunder everything in his path, taking care never to harm any of the Romans dwelling there. 7.31. And if anywhere he should come upon a place having men and a fortification, as is likely, he should make trial of it with all his might. 7.32. And if he should be able to take it, he should go on; but if the matter, as might chance, withstood him, he should ride back or stay where he was. 7.33. For if he went forward and left this fortification behind him, there would be great danger for a long time, since they would never be able to defend themselves easily, if they should be troubled by their opponents. And he was to guard all the booty, in order that the army might distribute it rightly and justly. 7.34. Then with a laugh he added this also: “For it is not just that the drones be destroyed with great toil by some, while others enjoy the honey with no hardship.” Having given so many instructions, Belisarius sent John with the army. 7.35. And about the same time both Datius, the bishop of Mediolanum, and notable men of the citizens, coming to Rome, begged Belisarius to send a few guards with them. 7.36. This city is situated in Liguria, lying about midway between the city of Ravenna and the Alps which are on the borders of the Gauls; 7.38. for from either side it is a journey of eight days to it for an unencumbered man; and it was the first of the cities of the West, after Rome at least, in size and in population and in the rest of its prosperity. And Belisarius, promising to fulfil their request, kept them there during the winter season.

But he, having wasted all the opportunity in this dread, when he both feared the emperor's threats and, being reproached by the others, gave way, himself none the less remained there, but sent the whole army with Herodian and Demetrius and Phazas to Naples, the winter season now pressing most strongly. 7.4. And when the Roman fleet came near Naples, a hard wind came down, stirring up a prodigious storm. 7.5. And the darkness gave way everywhere, and the surge did not allow the sailors to draw up the oars or to do anything else. So the barbarians, boarding the vessels of their opponents at their will, killed and sank them, no one withstanding them. And they took alive many others and Demetrius the general. 7.7. And Totila, fastening a cord about the neck of Demetrius, dragged him to the wall of Naples and ordered him to exhort the besieged no longer to perish trusting in useless hopes, but to be released from great evils by handing over the city to the Goths as quickly as possible. 7.9. For it was impossible for the emperor to send them any further help, but on this fleet all their power and hope had perished. Demetrius said so much as Totila ordered. 7.10. And the besieged, now prodigiously hard pressed by famine and the rest of their want, when they saw the suffering of Demetrius and heard all his words, despairing of all hope, fell into wailings and helplessness, and the city was full of much tumult and lamentation. 7.11. After this Totila, calling them together to the battlements, spoke as follows: “Having no charge or complaint against you, men of Naples, we have now set ourselves to this siege, but in order that, having freed you from most hateful masters, we may be able to repay you the thanks for those things on account of which you suffered the most grievous things from the enemy in this war. 7.12. For it has befallen you alone of all the Italians to have displayed the greatest goodwill toward the nation of the Goths and to have come most unwillingly under your opponents. 7.13. So that even now, being compelled to besiege you along with them, we are ashamed, as is natural, of your good faith, although we make this siege not for the harm of the Neapolitans. 7.14. Do not, then, being distressed at the terrors of the siege, think you ought to hold the Goths in anger. For those eager to benefit their friends are worthy to bear no charge from them, even if they are not compelled to accomplish their kindness toward them through what is pleasant. 7.15. And let no fear of the enemy enter into you, nor, led by what has happened before, think that they will prevail over us; for the strange events of life, which come contrary to expectation by some chance, are wont in time to fall again. 7.16. And we are so well-disposed to you that we grant Conon and all the soldiers to go unharmed wherever they wish, if you give over the city to us and depart from there, keeping all their own goods; and nothing will hinder us from swearing concerning these things and the safety of the Neapolitans.” 7.17. Totila said so much, and both the Neapolitans and all the soldiers with Conon approved. For great necessity of famine oppressed them. 7.18. Keeping their good faith toward the emperor, however, and still waiting for some help to come to them, they agreed to give over the city within thirty days. 7.19. But Totila, wishing to drive away from them all hope from the emperor, fixed a period of three months, on condition that after this they should do what had been agreed. But the envy of fortune was already swelling against the Romans, when she saw their affairs going forward well and fairly, and wishing to mingle these with some evil, she devised a quarrel from no cause worthy of mention between Belisarius and Constantinus, the manner of whose origin and the issue in which it ended I now proceed to tell. 8.2. There was a certain Presidius, a Roman man, dwelling at Ravenna, and not obscure. This Presidius, because he had given offence to the Goths, at the time when Wittigis was about to march against Rome, fled with a few of his servants, setting out ostensibly for a hunt, neither communicating his plan to anyone nor having any of his goods with him, except indeed that he himself carried two daggers, the sheaths of which happened to be adorned with much gold and precious stones. And when he came to Spolitium, he lodged in a certain church outside the wall. 8.3. And Constantinus, hearing of this (for he happened to be still staying there), sent one of his guards, Maxentiolus, and took away both the daggers with no right. 8.4. And the man, being grievously distressed at what had befallen him, set out for Rome to Belisarius as quickly as possible; and there not long afterward Constantinus too arrived, for the army of the Goths was now reported to be not far off. 8.5. So long, then, as the affairs of the Romans stood in confusion and danger, Presidius remained silent; but when he saw the affairs of the Romans superior and the envoys of the Goths sent to the emperor, as I have said before, going frequently to Belisarius, he reported the wrong and begged that justice be done him. 8.6. And Belisarius, blaming Constantinus much both himself and through others, exhorted him to free himself from an unjust deed and shameful repute. 8.7. But Constantinus (for it was fated that evil should come to him) always thrust aside his words with mockery and jeered at the man who had been wronged. 8.8. And once when Belisarius was riding on horseback in the forum, Presidius met him and laid hold of the bridle of the horse, and crying out loudly asked whether the laws of the emperor said this, that whenever anyone, fleeing the barbarians, should come as a suppliant to them, these men should take away by force whatever he happened to have in his hands. 8.9. And when many people stood around and ordered him with threats to let go the bridle, he did not let go before Belisarius promised that he would give him the daggers. 8.10. So on the next day Belisarius, calling Constantinus and many of the commanders together into a certain small room in the Palatium, reminded them of what had happened the day before and exhorted Constantinus, late though it was, to give back the daggers. 8.11. But he said he would not give them; for he would more gladly throw them into the water of the Tiber than give them to Presidius. 8.12. And Belisarius, now seized with anger, asked whether Constantinus did not think he was under his command. And he agreed that in all other respects he would obey him in everything, for this was the emperor's will; this, however, which he was now ordering, he would never do. 8.13. So Belisarius ordered the guards to come in, and Constantinus said, “In order, of course, that they may kill me.” “By no means,” Belisarius said, “but in order that they may compel your guard Maxentiolus, who brought you the daggers by force, to give back to the man what he 8.14. took from him by violence.” But Constantinus, thinking he would be killed at once, wished to do some great thing before he himself should suffer anything. 8.15. Wherefore he drew the dagger which hung at his thigh and suddenly thrust it at the belly of Belisarius. But he, struck with consternation, started back and, throwing his arms around Bessas, who was standing somewhere near, managed to escape. 8.16. So Constantinus, still seething with anger, kept coming on, but Ildiger and Valerianus, observing what was being done, the one laying hold of his right hand and the other of his other hand, drew him back. 8.17. And in the meantime the guards came in whom Belisarius had called a little before, and seized the dagger from the hand of Constantinus with much force, and laying hold of him with great tumult, did him no harm at the moment, out of respect for the commanders present, I suppose, but leading him off to another room, at the order of Belisarius, 8.18. they killed him some time later. This is the only deed wrought by Belisarius that was unholy and in no way worthy of his character; for he used great fairness toward all others. But it was fated, as has been said, that evil should come to Constantinus.

For consider: at the beginning of this war we had a multitude of soldiers brilliant in repute and in experience of dangers, and money, to speak briefly, greater than could be numbered, and a prodigious abundance of horses and arms, and all the forts there are among the Italians. But when, being ranged under Theudatus, a man who set justice below his desire to be rich, we by no means rendered God propitious to us by our lawlessness in conduct, you know, doubtless, whither our fortune has gone, by what and by how many men we have been defeated. 8.22. But now God, having sufficiently taken the penalty from us for the things in which we erred, again orders our life according to our wish, and, to put it altogether, leads our affairs better for us than according to our hope, since it has befallen us to have conquered the enemy beyond our existing power. 8.23. To maintain, then, the pretext of victory by doing what is just will be more profitable than, going contrary to it, to seem to have become envious against ourselves. 8.24. So Wittigis, going with the remaining army toward Ravenna, strengthened the fortifications of the places with a multitude of garrisons, leaving in Clusium, the city of the Tuscans, a thousand men and Gibimer as commander, and in Urbiventus the same number, over whom he set as commander Albilas, a Goth; and Uligisalus he left in Tudera with four hundred. 11.2. And in the land of Picenum he left four hundred in the fort of Petra, who had also dwelt there before, and in Auximus, which is the greatest of all the cities there, he left four thousand Goths gathered for their valour, and as commander an exceedingly energetic man, Visandus by name, and with Moras two thousand in the city of Urbinus. 11.3. There are also two other forts, Caesena and Monteferetra, in each of which he established a garrison of no fewer than five hundred men. And he himself went with the rest of the army straight to Ariminum to besiege it. 11.4. Now it happened that Belisarius, as soon as the Goths broke off the siege, had sent Ildiger and Martinus with a thousand horsemen, in order that, going more quickly by another road, they might forestall the enemy in reaching Ariminum, and he instructed them to remove John and all his men from there as quickly as possible, and in their place to establish many men most sufficient for the guarding of the city, taking them from a fort which is by the Ionian Gulf, Ancon by name, 11.5. two days' journey distant from Ariminum. For he had not long before occupied it, sending Conon with an army of Isaurians and Thracians, not a small one. 11.6. For he hoped that, if foot-soldiers alone, with no commanders of note present, held Ariminum, the Goths would never bring their power to the siege of it, but would disregard it and go straight to Ravenna; and if they should wish to besiege Ariminum, the provisions would suffice the foot-soldiers for a longer time; 11.7. and that two thousand horsemen, going outside with the rest of the army, would, as is likely, work much harm to the enemy and would more easily force them to the breaking off of the siege. 11.8. With such a purpose Belisarius gave these instructions to Martinus and Ildiger. And they, journeying by the Flaminian Way, went far ahead of the barbarians. 11.9. For inasmuch as the Goths were in a great throng, they journeyed more slowly, and were compelled to make certain long circuits both because of the want of necessities and because they were least willing to go close to the fortifications on the Flaminian Way, since the enemy, as has been shown by me before, held Narnia and Spolitium and Perusia. 11.10. And the Roman army, when they came upon Petra, making it a side-task of the road, made trial of the fort there. Now this fortification men did not build, but the nature of the place discovered it; for the road is exceedingly precipitous. 11.11. On the right of this road a certain river, impassable for anyone because of the swiftness of its current, comes down, and on the left, not far off, a rock rises, sheer and reaching to such a height that men who, as may chance, stand on the summit appear to those below to be like the smallest birds in size. 11.12. And to one going forward there was anciently no passage. For the rock, ending, reaches to the very current of the river, offering no crossing to those who go that way. 11.13. So the men of old, working a passage there, made a postern for the place at this point. 11.14. And blocking up most of the other entrance, except indeed that a postern was left there too, they made a self-grown fort and called it Petra, with a fitting name. 11.15. So Martinus and Ildiger and their men first fought at one of the posterns and shot many missiles but accomplished nothing, although the barbarians there scarcely defended themselves; then, forcing their way up the ascent behind through the precipitous part, they cast stones down from the height upon the Goths. 11.16. And these, entering their houses at a run and with much tumult, kept quiet. And then the Romans, since they could not hit any of the enemy with their casts of stones, devised the following. 11.17. Making great fragments out of the cliff, and many of them pushing them together, they hurled them, aiming, upon the houses. 11.18. And these, wherever they touched the structure, even slightly, in falling shook everything sufficiently and brought the barbarians into great fear. 11.19. Wherefore the Goths held out their hands to those who were still at the postern and surrendered themselves together with the fort by agreement, on condition that they should remain unharmed, being slaves of the emperor and subjects of Belisarius. 11.20. And of them Ildiger and Martinus took up the most and led them along with themselves on equal and like terms, but some few they left there with their children and wives. And they left also a Roman garrison. 11.21. And going from there to Ancon and taking many of the foot-soldiers there, they reached Ariminum on the third day and announced the decision of Belisarius. 11.22. But John was not willing to follow himself, and kept Damianus with the four hundred. And the others, leaving their foot-soldiers there, withdrew quickly from there with the guards and shield-bearers of Belisarius.

So matters about Tibur it befell to happen thus. And Belisarius, coming with the whole fleet to Ravenna, gathered together the Goths present and the Roman soldiers and spoke as follows: “Not now for the first time, men, has it befallen that the works of valour have been melted away by baseness. 11.2. For from above this is simply implanted in human affairs, that the wickedness of the basest has had the power both to check and to destroy the many deeds of good men. This same thing has now too brought to ruin the affairs of the emperor. 11.3. To whom it is so much a care to set right the errors that, setting the mastery over the Persians below these things, he has resolved to send me now to you, in order that I may set right and heal if anything has been wrought wrongly by the commanders either toward his own soldiers or toward the Goths. 11.4. Now that nothing be done amiss by anyone is neither human nor outside the nature of affairs, but to set right the errors befits an emperor abundantly and is worthy of consolation enough to those who are loved. 11.5. For not only will it befall you to be freed from your difficulties, but it will at once be added that you both know and enjoy the goodwill of the emperor toward you; than which what could be more worthy to a man of all possessions? 11.6. Since, then, I am present with you for this very purpose, it behoves each of you to use all his power, 11.7. in order that you may have the benefit of the help arising from this. And whoever of you has kinsmen or friends with Totila the tyrant, let him summon them as quickly as possible, making plain the emperor's purpose. 11.8. For thus there would come to you the good things both from peace and from the great emperor. As for myself, I have come here neither desiring to make war on anyone, nor would I ever willingly be an enemy to the emperor's subjects. 11.9. But if, even now, holding it a trifling matter to choose what is better for themselves, these men go against us, it is of necessity that we too use them, most unwillingly, as enemies.” 11.10. Belisarius said so much. But none of his opponents came over to him, neither Goth nor Roman. And thus Thurimuth came to Belisarius at Ravenna. 11.19. Then Belisarius sent three of his guards, Thurimuth and Ricilas and Sabinianus, with a thousand soldiers to the city of Auximus, to help Magnus and the Romans besieged there. 11.20. And they, escaping the notice of Totila and the camp of the enemy, came by night to Auximus and purposed to make certain sorties against their opponents. 11.21. And on the following day, learning about midday that some of the enemy were somewhere close, they went out to meet them, but resolved to send scouts against them first to observe their power, in order that they might not go against them unconsidered. 11.22. But Ricilas the guard of Belisarius (for he happened at that time to be flushed with wine) would not let others go on the scouting, but he himself alone, riding his horse out, went quickly. 11.23. And falling in with three Goths in a precipitous place, at first he took his stand as if to array himself against them; for he had come to the height of courage. But seeing many pouring against him from all sides, he rushed into flight. 11.24. And as his horse stumbled in the difficult ground, a great shout arose from the enemy, and all hurled their javelins at him. When the Romans perceived this, they came to the aid at a run. 11.25. And Ricilas, covered with many spears, died; but Thurimuth and his men, routing their opponents and taking up the corpse, conveyed it to the city of Auximus—the man having drawn a lot for the close of his life not worthy of his valour. 11.26. After this Sabinianus and Thurimuth, taking counsel with Magnus, found it inexpedient for them to make any further stay there, reckoning that they would never be a match for the enemy, who were many, and that, consuming the provisions of the besieged, they would make the city even more quickly capturable for their opponents. 11.27. And when this had been resolved, they themselves and the thousand prepared for the departure, intending to begin the retreat by night; but immediately one of the soldiers, deserting secretly to the camp of the enemy, made known what was being done. 11.28. Totila, then, selecting two thousand men for their valour, when night came on, guarded the roads thirty stades from Auximus, giving perception to no one. 11.29. And when these saw the enemy passing about midnight, drawing their swords they set to work. 11.30. And they killed two hundred of them, while Sabinianus and Thurimuth with the rest, since it was in the dark, were able both to escape notice and to flee to Ariminum. 11.31. The Goths, however, mastered all the beasts of burden, which carried the soldiers' service-baggage and arms and clothing. 11.32. Now there are two towns by the shore of the Ionian Gulf, Pisaurus and Fanus, lying between the cities of Auximus and Ariminum. The houses of these Wittigis had burnt at the beginning of this war, and had razed the walls to about half, in order that the Romans, occupying them, might not give trouble to the Goths. 11.33. One of these, Pisaurus, Belisarius resolved to occupy; for it seemed to him that the place lay suitably for pastures of horses. So sending some of his friends by night, he secretly measured out exactly the breadth and length of each gate. 11.34. And constructing the gates and binding them about with iron, and then putting them into certain skiffs, he sent them, ordering Sabinianus and Thurimuth quickly to fit them to the walls and remain inside the wall, and, when they were in safety, to rebuild, in whatever way, all that had fallen of the wall, throwing in stones and clay and anything else. They, then, did so. 11.35. But Totila, learning what was being done, came against them with a great army. 11.36. And making trial and spending some time there, when he was not able to take it, he withdrew without accomplishing anything to the camp at Auximus. 11.37. And none of the Romans any longer sallied out against the enemy, but each remained inside the walls. And Belisarius, sending two of his guards to Rome, Artasires a Persian and Barbation a Thracian, to guard the city with Bessas, who happened to be there, instructed them by no means to sally out against the enemy. 11.38. Who in the world the Eruli are, and whence they came into alliance with the Romans, I now proceed to tell. They dwelt of old beyond the Ister river, holding the belief in a great throng of gods, whom they thought it holy to propitiate even with sacrifices of human beings. 14.2. And they used many customs not in accordance with those of other men. For it was not permitted them to live when they grew old or fell sick, but whenever one of them was seized either by age or by sickness, it became necessary for him to ask his kinsmen to remove him from among men as quickly as possible. 14.3. And they, heaping up much wood to a great height and seating the man on top of the wood, would send to him one of the Eruli, but a stranger, with a dagger; 14.4. for it was not lawful for the slayer to be a kinsman of his. And when the slayer of their kinsman returned, they straightway burned all the wood, beginning from the edges. 14.5. And when the flame had ceased for them, gathering the bones, they immediately hid them in the earth. 14.6. And when an Erulian man died, it was necessary for his wife, if she laid claim to virtue and wished to leave a good name for herself, to die not long afterward by fastening a noose beside the tomb of her husband. 14.7. And if she did not do this, it remained for her for the future to be without repute and to have given offence to the kinsmen of her husband. Such, then, were the customs the Eruli used of old. 14.8. But as time went on, having become superior in power and in numbers to all the barbarians around them, and attacking, as was natural, 14.9. they conquered each in turn and by force plundered them. And at last they made the Lombards, who were Christians, and certain other nations subject to themselves in the payment of tribute—a thing not customary to the barbarians there, but they had been led to it by love of money and by arrogance. 14.10. When, however, Anastasius took over the empire of the Romans, the Eruli, having no men left against whom they could go, laid down their arms and remained quiet, and a period of three years was spent by them in this peace. 14.11. And they, being exceedingly distressed, reviled their ruler Rodulphus without restraint, and going constantly to him, called him soft and womanish, and abused him in no orderly fashion with certain other names, taunting him. 14.12. And Rodulphus, bearing the insult by no means well, marched against the Lombards who were doing no wrong, neither bringing any charge of fault against them nor pretending any breaking of the agreements, 14.13. but bringing a war that had no cause. And when the Lombards learned of this by report, sending to Rodulphus, they inquired and saw fit to ask the reason for which the Eruli were going in arms against them, agreeing that, if they had withheld anything of the tribute, they would pay it at once with much added; but if they complained that the tribute set for them was moderate, the Lombards would never be slow to make it greater. 14.14. These things the envoys offered, but Rodulphus dismissed them with a threat and drove forward. And they again, sending other envoys to him, entreated and besought much concerning the same things. 14.15. When these second envoys too had been sent away, a third embassy coming to him forbade the Eruli to bring upon them a war without pretext. 14.16. For if those men should go against them with such a purpose, they too, not willingly but as being most compelled, would array themselves against the attackers, calling God to witness, of whose inclination even the very slightest weight at all would be set against all the power of men; and it was likely that he, being moved by the causes of the war, would adjudge for both the issue of the battle. 14.17. These things they said, thinking thereby to frighten the attackers, but the Eruli, holding back nothing of all, resolved to come to close quarters with the Lombards. 14.18. And when both armies had come close to each other, it came about that the air above the Lombards was covered by a black and exceedingly thick cloud, while above the Eruli there was prodigious clear sky. 14.19. From which, judging by signs, one would have guessed that the Eruli were going to the engagement to their own harm; for there can be no more bitter portent for barbarians setting themselves to battle than this. 14.20. The Eruli, however, did not even pay attention to this, but altogether disregarding it, with much contempt advanced against the enemy, measuring the issue of the war by the multitude of their throng. 14.21. But when the battle was at close quarters, many of the Eruli were killed, and Rodulphus himself was killed, and all the rest fled with all their might, mindful of no resistance. 14.22. And as the enemy pressed close upon them, most of them fell there, but some few were saved. 14.23. Wherefore they could no longer remain in their ancestral abodes, but removing from there as quickly as possible, they kept going forward, traversing the whole land which is beyond the Ister river, together with their children and wives. 14.24. And when they came to a region where the Rogi anciently dwelt, who, having mingled with the army of the Goths, had gone into Italy, there they settled. 14.25. But when they were oppressed by famine, since the land was deserted, removing from there not long afterward, they came close to the country of the Gepaedes. 14.26. And the Gepaedes at first, when they had become suppliants, permitted them to settle and be neighbours to them. 14.27. Then they began, from no cause, to display unholy deeds toward them. For they did violence to their women and seized their oxen and other goods, and they left out no act of injustice at all, and finally began to lay unjust hands upon them. 14.28. And the Eruli, no longer able to bear these things, crossed the Ister river and resolved to dwell near the Romans there, Anastasius holding the imperial power, who received them with much friendliness and permitted them to settle there. 14.29. But not long afterward these barbarians gave offence to him, having wrought unholy deeds against the Romans there; wherefore he sent an army against them. 14.30. And the Romans, conquering them in battle, killed most of them, and had it in their power to destroy them all. 14.31. But the survivors of them, having become suppliants of the generals, begged both to be preserved and to be henceforth allies and servants of the emperor. 14.32. And when Anastasius learned this it pleased him, and from this it came about that some of the Eruli were left, though they neither became allies of the Romans nor did them any good. 14.33. But when Justinian took over the empire, presenting them with good land and other goods, he was able to make them altogether his friends and persuaded them all to become Christians. 14.34. Wherefore, changing their mode of life to the more gentle, they resolved to go over for the most part to the laws of the Christians, and in alliance for the most part they array themselves with the Romans against the enemy. 14.35. They are, however, still faithless toward them and, being gripped by greed, are eager to do violence to their neighbours, 14.36. the deed bringing them no shame. And they perform unholy unions, both with men and with asses, and they are the basest of all men and, being evil, are destined to perish evilly. 14.37. Afterward a few of them remained in treaty with the Romans, as shall be written by me in the subsequent narrative; but all the rest revolted from the following cause. 14.38. The Eruli, displaying the beastlike and frenzied quality of their character against their king (this man was Ochus by name), suddenly killed the man from no cause, bringing no other charge than that they wished for the future to be without a king. 14.39. And yet even before this the king had the name among them, but carried off almost nothing more than any private man whatever. 14.40. But all saw fit both to sit together with him and to be his messmates, and without restraint anyone who wished insulted him; 14.41. for there are no men more faithless or more unstable than the Eruli. And when the evil had been wrought by them, they now repented. 14.42. For they said they were not able to live without a ruler or without a general; so after much deliberation it seemed altogether better to them to summon one of the royal line from the island of Thule. And what this is I shall presently make plain.

There was a certain Chilbudius, of the household of the emperor Justinian, exceedingly energetic in matters of war, and so superior to money that in place of the greatest possession in his property he held the possessing of nothing; 14.2. this Chilbudius the emperor, when he had held the imperial power for four years, proclaiming general of Thrace, established over the guard of the river Ister, ordering him to keep watch that the river should no longer be crossable by the barbarians there, since the Huns and Antae and Sclaveni, having often made the crossing of it, had wrought irreparable deeds against the Romans. 14.3. And Chilbudius became so terrible to the barbarians that for a period of three years, all the time that he was staying there with this office, not only was no one able to cross the Ister against the Romans, but the Romans, often going to the opposite mainland with Chilbudius, both killed and enslaved the barbarians there. 14.4. But three years later Chilbudius crossed the river where he was wont with a small army, and the Sclaveni met him in full force. 14.5. And when a fierce battle had taken place, many of the Romans fell and Chilbudius the general. 14.6. And for the future the river became crossable at all times for the barbarians at their will, and the affairs of the Romans became easy to assail, and the whole Roman empire was by no means able in this matter to become a counterpoise to the valour of one man. 14.7. And some time later the Antae and Sclaveni, having become at variance with one another, came to close quarters, where it befell the Antae to be defeated by their opponents. 14.8. In this battle a Sclavenian man took prisoner one of the enemy, Chilbudius by name, just growing his first beard, and taking him went home. 14.9. This Chilbudius, as time went on, became most well-disposed to his master and energetic against the enemy. 14.10. And often having risked himself ahead of his master, he distinguished himself exceedingly and was able to gird himself with great fame from this. 14.11. About this time the Antae, falling upon the regions of Thrace, plundered and enslaved many of the Romans there. Leading them off, they were conveyed back to their native abodes. 14.12. And fortune brought one of these captives to a kindly and gentle master. But this man was very mischievous and such as to circumvent those he met by deceit. 14.13. And since, wishing to return to the land of the Romans, he was by no means able, he devised the following. Coming into the sight of his master, he praised his kindness and affirmed that on account of this many good things would come to him from God, and that he himself would in no way appear thankless to a most kindly master, but that, if he should be willing to listen to him as he set forth the best advice, he would make him master of great wealth not long hence. 14.14. For there was in the nation of the Sclaveni Chilbudius, the man who had been general of the Romans, in the position of a slave, escaping the notice of all the barbarians as to who he was. 14.15. If, then, it should be his wish to put forth the price of Chilbudius and to convey the man to the land of the Romans, it was not unlikely that he would gird himself with good repute and a very great quantity of wealth from the emperor. 14.16. The Roman, saying this, straightway persuaded his master, and with him came into the midst of the Sclaveni; for these barbarians now treated with one another and mingled fearlessly. Putting forth, then, much money to the master of Chilbudius, they bought the man and went off with him immediately. 14.17. And when they were in their own abodes, the purchaser inquired of the man whether he were Chilbudius himself, the general of the Romans. 14.18. And he did not refuse to tell what was, with the true account, in order, that he himself was an Ante by race, and fighting with his kinsmen against the Sclaveni, who were then enemies to them, had been taken by one of his opponents; but now, since he had come to his native abodes, he would for the future be free himself too, according to the law. 14.19. So he who had put forth the gold for him, falling into speechlessness, was distressed, having failed of a not moderate hope. 14.20. But the Roman, wishing to console the man and to thrust aside the truth, in order that nothing might be difficult for him about his return home, affirmed that this very man was indeed that Chilbudius, but that, being afraid because he was in the midst of barbarians, he was by no means willing to reveal the whole account; if, however, he should come to the land of the Romans, he would not only not hide the true account, but would even, as is natural, pride himself on this name. At first, then, these things were done secretly from the other barbarians. 14.21. But when the report, going about, came to all, nearly all the Antae gathered for this, and saw fit that the matter should be common, thinking that great good would come to them, since they had now become masters of Chilbudius the general of the Romans. 14.22. For these nations, the Sclaveni and the Antae, are not ruled by one man, but live in a democracy from of old, and for this reason both the advantageous and the difficult matters of affairs are always brought to common counsel among them. And in like manner, to speak generally, all other things too are and have been customary among these barbarians from above. 14.23. For they hold that one god, the maker of lightning, is alone lord of all, and they sacrifice to him oxen and all victims; but fate they neither know nor in any other way admit that it has any power among men, but whenever death is already at their feet, either being seized by sickness or setting themselves to war, they promise that, if they escape, they will straightway make a sacrifice to the god in return for their life, and having escaped they sacrifice what they promised, and they think that their safety has been bought by this sacrifice. 14.24. They worship, however, both rivers and nymphs and certain other divinities, and sacrifice to all of these, and make their divinations in these sacrifices. They dwell in wretched huts, scattered far from one another, and each for the most part changes the place of his habitation. 14.25. When they set themselves to battle, the most go against the enemy on foot, holding small shields and javelins in their hands, but they put on no corselet. 14.26. And some have neither tunic nor cloak, but, fitting on only their trousers up to the privy parts, thus set themselves to engagement with their opponents. And there is for both one tongue, altogether barbarous. 14.27. Nor indeed do they differ at all from one another in appearance. For they are all both tall and exceedingly strong, and as to their bodies and hair they are neither very white or fair, nor are they at all turned wholly to the dark, but they are all ruddy. 14.28. And they have a hard and neglected mode of life, like the Massagetae, and like them they are most continually full of filth; yet they are by no means wicked or mischievous, but even in their simplicity they preserve the Hunnic character. 14.29. And indeed there was one name for both the Sclaveni and the Antae from above; for both were anciently called Spori, because, I think, they dwell in the land scattered (sporaden), in scattered tents. 14.30. Wherefore they hold a large land; for they occupy the most of the other bank of the Ister. So much, then, for this people. 14.31.
