There with all the commanders of the army they deliberated whither it would be more advantageous for them to go first against the enemy. 16.3. For if they should go against those besieging Ariminum, they suspected that those in Auximus, coming behind them, would, as is likely, do irreparable harm both to themselves and to the Romans dwelling there; and they feared for the besieged, lest they should suffer something terrible from the want of necessities. 16.4. Now the most of them, being angry at John, made their speeches. For they reproached him because, by unreasoning rashness and by love of much money, he had come to such danger, and did not allow the operations of the war to be carried on in order or as Belisarius directed. 16.5. But Narses (for John was the dearest of all men to him), fearing lest Belisarius, yielding to what had been said by the commanders, should put the affairs at Ariminum in second place, spoke as follows: 16.6. “You are deliberating, men in command, not about the usual matters, nor do you hold counsel about things concerning which one might reasonably be in doubt, but about matters in which it is possible even for those who have come to no experience of war to choose offhand the better course. 16.7. For if the danger seemed to be equal and the harm to those who failed equal on either side, it would be worth while to deliberate sufficiently and, going to the greatest length of calculation, thus to make the decision concerning the present situation. 16.8. But we, if we should wish to put off the assault on Auximus to some other time, shall in no way suffer loss in essential matters; for what difference would there be in the interval? But at Ariminum, if, as is likely, we fail—not to put it too bitterly—we shall undo the strength of the Romans. 16.9. So if John has insulted your instructions, most excellent Belisarius, you have taken a great penalty from him, since it is in your power both to save the man who has erred and to give him over to the enemy. 16.10. But beware lest you take from the emperor and from us the penalties for the things in which John, through ignorance, has erred. For if the Goths now take Ariminum, it will come about that an energetic Roman general and a whole army and a city subject to the emperor have been made captive. 16.11. And the danger will not stop at this, but they will be able to overturn the whole fortune of the war. For reckon thus concerning the enemy, that in multitude of soldiers they still even now far surpass us, but they have fallen into a cowardice from the disasters in which they have often failed. And with reason; for the opposition of fortune has taken from them all their boldness. 16.12. If, then, they prosper at the present time, they will not long afterward recover their spirit, and for the rest will carry on this war not only with daring equal to ours, but with much greater. 16.13. For those who escape from difficulties are wont always to have better hopes than those who have not yet met with misfortune.” Narses said so much. 16.14. And a certain soldier, escaping the guard of the barbarians from Ariminum, came to the camp and showed Belisarius a letter which John had written to him. 16.15. And the writing made plain the following: “Know that all the provisions have long since failed us, and that for the future we are not able either to hold out against the populace or to defend ourselves against the assailants, but within seven days we shall, unwillingly, hand over both ourselves and this city to the enemy; 16.16. for to force the present necessity further we are by no means able—a necessity which to make our defence on our behalf, if we should do anything not seemly, 16.17. I think sufficient.” Thus John wrote. And Belisarius was at a loss and fell into great perplexity. For he both feared for the besieged and suspected that the enemy in Auximus would ravage all the regions there more boldly, going about them, and would lie in ambush for his camp from behind, especially whenever they should come to grips with their opponents, and would, as is likely, work much irreparable harm. 16.18. After this, however, he did as follows. He left Aratius there with a thousand men, on condition that they should make a camp by the sea, two hundred stades distant from the city of Auximus. 16.19. And he ordered them neither to remove from there and go elsewhere nor to fight with the enemy, except in so far as they defended themselves from their camp, if those men should ever go against them. 16.20. For in this way he hoped that the barbarians especially, since the Romans were encamped somewhere close to Auximus, would remain quiet and would never follow to do them mischief. 16.21. And he sent a most considerable army with ships, of which Herodian and Uliaris and Narses the brother of Aratius were in command. 16.22. And supreme over the fleet was Ildiger, whom Belisarius instructed to sail straight for Ariminum, taking care not to attempt to put in at the shore there while the foot-army was left far behind; for they were to journey not far from the coast. 16.23. And he ordered another army, of which Martinus was in command, to go along by the seacoast keeping pace with these ships, instructing them, whenever they should come near the enemy, to burn many fires, not in proportion to the army, and to give their opponents the impression of a multitude much greater. 16.24. And he himself, with Narses and the rest of the army, went by another road furthest from the coast, through the city of Urbisalia, which in former times Alaric so destroyed that nothing whatever of its former adornment is left to it, except a single gate and a small remnant of the foundations of its ground-plan.

There was a certain man among the priests of Rome, Pelagius by name, a deacon in rank, who, having stayed a long time in Byzantium, had become a most intimate friend of the emperor Justinian, and being girt with great wealth had happened to come to Rome a little before. 16.6. And in this siege, having put forth the most of his money to those in want of the necessities, being of repute even before among all the Italians, he bore off, as is natural, a greater fame for kindness. 16.7. This Pelagius the Romans, when they were suffering helpless things from famine, persuaded both to go to Totila and to arrange for them a truce of some few days, on condition that, if no help should come to them from Byzantium within this truce, they would give over both themselves and the city to the Goths by agreement. 16.8. On this embassy Pelagius came to Totila. And Totila, greeting him with much reverence and friendliness, spoke first as follows: 16.9. “To all barbarians, for the most part, it is a custom to revere the office of envoys, but to me it has been from above an object of eagerness to honour those who lay claim to any of the virtue which you yourself possess, and otherwise too. 16.10. And honour and insult toward an envoy I think are distinguished not by the gentleness of countenance nor by the loftiness of words of those who receive him, but in this, whether one tells him the truth or uses unsound speech to him. 16.11. For it befalls that man to be especially honoured to whom, openly revealing the true account, they thus send the man away, but for him to be especially insulted who, having heard hollow and fabricated words, goes off and departs. 16.12. Except for three things, then, O Pelagius, of all the rest, whatever you may ask, you will never fail to obtain it from us. 16.13. Concerning which it is better that you, guarding yourself, keep silence, in order that, having become most responsible to yourself for accomplishing nothing of what you came for, you may not lay upon us the blame concerning them. 16.14. For from asking unsuitably about present matters, the accomplishing of nothing is for the most part implanted. And I say, in order that you may make your speeches neither for the sake of any of the Sicilians, nor of the walls of Rome, nor of the slaves who have come over to us. 16.15. For it is not possible either that the Goths use sparing toward any of the Sicilians, or that this wall stand, or that the slaves who have campaigned with us be slaves to their former owners. And in order that I may not seem to put these things forward with an unreasoning purpose, I shall dissolve the suspicion by telling at once the reasons. 16.16. The island was prosperous from of old in revenue of money and in abundance of all crops growing there, so that it not only sufficed those who dwelt in it, but you Romans, importing from there each year, had the carrying of provisions sufficiently. 16.17. Wherefore at the beginning the Romans begged Theoderic not to establish a garrison of many Goths there, in order that nothing might be a hindrance to their freedom or their other prosperity. 16.18. These things being so, the army of the enemy sailed down to Sicily, neither in multitude of men nor in any other thing whatever a match for us. 16.19. But the Sicilians, seeing the fleet, did not report these things to the Goths, did not shut themselves up in the forts, did not resolve to give any offence to their opponents, but throwing open the gates of the cities with all eagerness received the army of the enemy with upturned hands, like, I think, the most untrustworthy of slaves, watching from a long time for the chance to escape from the hand of their owners and to find new and unknown masters for themselves. 16.20. And setting out from there as from a bulwark, the enemy held the rest of Italy with no toil and occupied this Rome, bringing in from Sicily such a quantity of grain as to hold out against a siege for a year's length for all the Romans. 16.21. Such, then, is the case of the Sicilians, for whom there will be no means for the Goths to be forgiving, the magnitude of their offences taking from those who have done wrong all pity. 16.22. Now the enemy, having shut themselves up inside these walls, by no means resolved to come down into the plain and array themselves against us, but by stratagems and circumventions always and every day driving the Goths back, they have become masters of our affairs unexpectedly. 16.23. In order, then, that we may not suffer this same thing afterward too, it is worth while to take forethought. For those who, once tripped up by ignorance, have fallen into the same misfortune again, not foreseeing the calamity already become familiar to them by experience—this seems to be not an opposition of fortune, but, as is natural, 16.24. to come round to the folly of those who have failed. And one might add that the razing of the wall of Rome will above all be advantageous to you. For no longer being shut up with others and shut off from all the necessities, you will not be besieged by those who come against you, but both sides will risk themselves in battle against one another, and you will become the prize of the victors without dangers of your own. 16.25. As for the slaves who have come over to us, we shall say so much, that, if we should learn that we are now putting into your hands those who arrayed themselves with us against your opponents and who received from us the agreement that we would never give them over to their former owners, we shall not even keep good faith toward you. 16.26. For it is not possible, it is not, that he who disregards his agreements toward the most pitiable of all should display his purpose firm toward any other, but, as if of another mark of his nature, he is wont always to carry his faithlessness round to all who deal with him.” 16.27. Totila said so much, and Pelagius answered as follows: “You have made me your earnest object above all, O noble man, and, alleging the name of the embassy, have ranged us in the most dishonoured portion. 16.28. For to insult a man who is both a friend and an envoy, I think, is not he who would strike him on the cheek and use other wantonness toward him, but he who would resolve to send away unsuccessful the man who came to him. 16.29. For men are wont to set themselves to the embassy not in order that they may obtain some honour from those who receive them, but in order that, having accomplished some good for those who sent them, they may return to them. 16.30. So that it will be more advantageous to have been reviled and accomplished something of what they came for than, having heard kindlier words, to return having failed of their hope. To beg off, then, I do not know why I should about these things which you yourself have said. 16.31. For why should one trouble him who, before the defence, has refused the agreement? But this I would not keep silent, that it is plain how great kindness you intend to display toward the Romans who have taken up arms against you, who have resolved to bring an irrevocable hatred against the Sicilians, who have in no way met you. 16.32. But I, for my part, leaving aside my entreaty to you, shall transfer my embassy to God, who is wont to be wrathful against those who despise supplications.”

And to Gubazes he wrote thus: "Two things govern the life of men: power and prudence. Here it befell me to see a sight of the following kind. When the army with John came into Picenum, there was, as was natural, much confusion among the people there. 17.2. And of the women, some fled suddenly wherever it had become possible for each, while others, being caught, were carried off in no orderly fashion by those who fell in with them. 17.3. In one of these places a certain woman who had just given birth happened to have left her child lying on the ground in its swaddling-clothes, and whether fleeing or caught by someone, she was no longer able to return there; for it befell her plainly to have vanished either from among men or from Italy. 17.4. So the child, left in this solitude, kept weeping. And a single she-goat, seeing it, took pity on it and, coming near (for she too happened to have just given birth), gave it the teat and guarded the child carefully, 17.5. lest a dog or some wild beast should harm it. And as much time was spent in the confusion, it came about that the child shared in this teat for a long while. 17.6. And when it became known to the people of Picenum afterward that the emperor's army had come there for the harm of the Goths, but that the Romans would suffer nothing unpleasant from it, 17.7. they all returned home straightway. And when in Urbisalia the women had come with the men, all who were Roman by race, when they saw the child surviving in its swaddling-clothes, being unable to account for what had happened, they were in great wonder that it lived. 17.8. And each one offered her teat who happened to be in a suitable condition for this. But the child would no longer take human milk, and the goat was by no means willing to let it go, but bleating most continually about the child, she seemed to the bystanders to be doing dreadful things because the women, coming close to the child, were thus troubling it, and to put it in a word, she laid claim to the infant as her own. 17.9. And from this the women no longer troubled the child, and the goat reared it more fearlessly and, taking care of it otherwise, guarded it. Wherefore the people of the place called this child Aegisthus. 17.10. And when it befell me to be present there, making a display of the marvel, they used to bring me to the child and on purpose, 17.11. in order that it might cry, troubled it. And it, distressed by those who troubled it, wept, and the goat, hearing it (for she was distant from it about a stone's throw), at a run and bleating loudly came to it, and coming and standing over it, took her stand, so that no one might be able to trouble it for the rest of the time. Such, then, are the things about this Aegisthus. 17.12. And Belisarius advanced through the mountains there. For being far surpassed in numbers by his opponents, he was not willing to come to close quarters with them in the open, since he saw too that the barbarians were resolved to die in their encounters; 17.13. and he thought that they, as soon as they should learn that an army of the enemy was advancing against them from all sides, would be mindful of no resistance, but would straightway turn to flight. And he hit upon the true opinion, having suspected nothing far from what was to be. 17.14. For when they had come into the mountains, about a day's journey distant from Ariminum, they fell in with a few Goths who were travelling by the road on some errand. 17.15. And these, falling unexpectedly upon an army of the enemy, were by no means able to turn aside from the road, until, being shot at by those who went in front, some of them fell there, while others, having become wounded, ran up onto some of the cliffs there and escaped notice. 17.16. From there, observing the Roman army pouring into all the difficult places, they supposed them to be far more than the true measure. 17.17. And there, seeing also the standards of Belisarius, they knew that he was leading this army. And night came on, and the Romans bivouacked there, while the wounded among the Goths went secretly to the camp of Wittigis. 17.18. And coming there about midday, they showed their wounds and affirmed that Belisarius with an army greater than could be numbered would presently be at hand. 17.19. And they were preparing as if for battle, turned toward the north wind of the city of Ariminum (for there they supposed the enemy would arrive), and they all kept looking continually toward the heights of the mountain. 17.20. But when, night having come on for them, they laid down their arms and were resting, they saw many fires to the east of the city, about sixty stades off, which the army with Martinus was burning, and they came into helpless fear; 17.21. for they suspected they would be encircled by the enemy at daybreak. So this night they bivouacked in such fear, and on the following day, with the sun rising, they saw a fleet of ships coming against them, prodigious in size; and falling into speechlessness, they rushed into flight. 17.22. And packing up quickly, they were held by so great a tumult and shouting that they neither heard the orders given nor took anything else into their mind than how each one might first get away from the camp and get inside the wall of Ravenna. 17.23. And if there had happened to be any strength or courage left to the besieged, they would have sallied out and killed very many of the enemy there, and the whole war would have ended there. 17.24. But as it was, this was prevented both by the great fear that had come upon them before and by the weakness, befalling many through the want of necessities. So the barbarians, by the excess of their tumult leaving some of their goods there, ran at full speed toward Ravenna.

Having said so much, Pelagius departed. And the Romans, when they saw him returning unsuccessful, fell into much helplessness. And the famine, growing ever more at its height, wrought irreparable things upon them each day. The soldiers, however, had not yet run out of the necessities, but still held out. 17.2. Wherefore the Romans, gathering in a body and coming to the commanders of the emperor's army, Bessas and Conon, in tears and with much wailing spoke as follows: “We see, O generals, that our present fortunes are such that, even if we were able to do you some unholy deed, this charge would bring upon us no blame. 17.3. For the excess of necessity has its defence in itself. But now, being unable to defend ourselves by deed, we have come to you to make plain in word and to bewail our calamity. Hear us gently, not being thrown into confusion by the boldness of our words, but measuring this by the height of our suffering. 17.4. For he who has been compelled to despair of safety is no longer able for the rest to preserve decorum either in deeds or in words. 17.5. Think of us, O generals, neither as Romans nor as kinsmen to you, nor as having become of the same character as the customs of the state, nor as having received the emperor's army into the city of our own will, but as being enemies from the first and having taken up arms against you, then defeated in battle, having become your captive slaves taken in war according to the law of war. 17.6. And furnish to your captives food not sufficient for our need, but having enough to keep us alive, in order that we who survive may in turn serve you in whatever it is fitting for servants to render to their owners. 17.7. But if this is not easy or pleasing to you, but you see fit to release us from your hand, gaining this, that you do not toil over the burials of slaves; and if not even this is left to us, see fit to kill us and do not deprive us of a temperate death nor grudge us the death sweetest of all, but by a single act release the Romans from countless 17.8. difficulties.” When Bessas and his men heard this, they said that to furnish them provisions was impossible, and to kill them unholy, yet that to release them was not without danger. And they affirmed that Belisarius and the army from Byzantium would be present immediately, and consoling them in this way dismissed them. 17.9. But the famine, growing still more at its height and being prolonged, rose to a great measure of evil, suggesting foods strange and beyond the bounds of nature. 17.10. At first, then, Bessas and Conon, who commanded the garrison in Rome (for they happened to have stored within the wall of Rome a great measure of grain), and the soldiers, cutting off from their own need, sold to the wealthy of the Romans for great sums of money; for the price of a measure had become seven gold pieces. 17.11. But those whose household affairs did not go so well as to be able to share in food of such worth, putting down a quarter of the price and filling a measure with bran, ate it, necessity making their food sweetest and most luxurious to them. 17.12. And an ox, which the shield-bearers of Bessas might take in their sorties, they sold for fifty gold pieces. And whoever had a dead horse or anything else of the kind was ranked among the exceedingly fortunate, since he could luxuriate on the flesh of a dead animal. 17.13. But the whole rest of the throng ate only nettles, of which many grow about the wall and everywhere in the ruins of the city. 17.14. And in order that the sharpness of the herb might not bite their lips and the parts about the throat, they boiled them with care and ate them. 17.15. So long, then, as the Romans had gold coin, thus, as has been said, they bought the grain and the bran and got off. But when this had now failed them, those who carried their furniture to the market exchanged all of it for their daily life. 17.16. But at last, when the emperor's soldiers had no grain to sell to the Romans (except indeed that a little was still left to Bessas), and the Romans had nothing to buy with, all looked to the nettles. 17.17. And as this food was not sufficient for them—since they could not even come to fullness of it at all—their flesh for the most part became wasted, and their colour, coming little by little to lividness, made them most like phantoms. 17.18. And many, while still walking and chewing the nettles with their teeth, died suddenly and fell to the ground. 17.19. And now they even ate one another's dung. And many, hard pressed by famine, made away with themselves, since they no longer found dogs or mice or any other dead animal on which to feed. 17.20. There was a certain Roman man there, the father of five children, whom the children, standing around him and laying hold of his garment, asked for food. 17.21. And he, neither wailing nor showing that he was thrown into confusion, but most strongly hiding the whole suffering in his mind, ordered the children to follow him as though to receive food. 17.22. And when he came to the bridge of the Tiber, binding his garment over his face and covering his eyes with it, he leaped from the bridge into the water of the Tiber, the children and all the Romans there watching what was being done. 17.23. And for the rest the commanders of the emperor, taking other money, released the Romans, as many as wished to depart from there. 17.24. And some few being left there, all the others went off, fleeing as each had become able. And the most of them, their strength being already withered away by famine, died as they sailed or went on the road. 17.25. And many, caught by the enemy on the road, perished. To this had fortune gone for the senate and people of Rome.

For I see that you despise the enemy as being altogether defeated. 18.14. And I fear lest you, being deceived by this untrue opinion, work irreparable harm both to yourselves and to the affairs of the Romans. 18.16. For those who seem to have conquered, lifted up by what has been done, are more easily destroyed than those who have failed contrary to expectation, but for the rest are gripped by fear and much anxiety toward their opponents. 18.17. For carelessness has destroyed some of those who were well established, but toil with care has profited many of the unfortunate. 18.18. So that now more than before our affairs stand in danger, since we have fallen into a kind of encirclement by the enemy. 18.21. For I forbear to say that they declare the Franks too are arrayed with them in Liguria, a thing which it is sufficiently worth while for all the Romans to call to mind, not without great fear. 18.22. I say, then, that a part of the army ought to be sent to Liguria and Mediolanum, while the rest for the present should go against Auximus and the enemy there, to accomplish whatever God may grant; and then to manage the other operations of the war in whatever way may seem best and most excellent.” Belisarius said so much. 18.23. And Narses answered as follows: “In other respects, O general, no one would gainsay that all has been spoken by you with truth. 18.24. But to set apart this whole army of the emperor for Mediolanum and Auximus alone I think altogether inexpedient. 18.25. But that you should lead such of the Romans as you wish against these is in no way unfitting; we, however, will win for the emperor the land of Aemilia, which they say the Goths especially lay claim to, and will so throw Ravenna into confusion that you will deal with the enemy near you as you wish, they being shut off from all hope of those who might defend them. 18.26. And Belisarius, fearing lest, the Romans going into many parts, the affairs of the emperor should fall to ruin and be confounded by the disorder thence arising, showed a letter of the emperor Justinian which he had written to the commanders of the army. 18.28. But Narses, laying hold of the very end of the letter, contended on the contrary that Belisarius was now deliberating for the advantage of the state; wherefore it was not necessary for them to follow him.

When the army with John and Isaaces came to Epidamnus and joined Belisarius, John saw fit that all, ferrying across the gulf and going on foot with the whole army, should bear in common what should befall; but to Belisarius this seemed inexpedient, but rather that it would be more advantageous for them to sail to the regions about Rome. 18.2. For going on foot, more time would be wasted for them and perhaps some hindrance would meet them; but John, going through Calabria and the nations there, should drive out the barbarians there (who were quite few) and, making subject the parts within the Ionian Gulf, should join them, coming to the regions about Rome. 18.3. Where Belisarius himself too purposed to put in with the rest of the army. For he thought that, since the Romans were being most bitterly besieged, even, as is natural, the very shortest delay would do irreparable harm to affairs. 18.4. When the Goths perceived this, all who had been ranged for the siege of the fort there, breaking off the siege, were immediately conveyed to the city of Brentesium, distant two days' journey from Dryus, but lying by the shore of the gulf and being unwalled, suspecting that Belisarius would immediately cross the strait there, and reported their situation to Totila. 18.7. And he both made the whole army ready as though to meet him and ordered the Goths in Calabria, wherever it should be possible for them, to keep watch over the passage. 18.8. But when Belisarius, a favourable wind blowing, sailed away from Dryus, the Goths, being careless, kept a not earnest mode of life among the Calabrians, and Totila, remaining quiet, guarded still more the entrances into Rome, in order that nothing of the provisions might be able to be brought in. 18.9. And in the Tiber he devised the following. Observing a place where the river especially comes down in a narrow channel, about ninety stades from the city, he laid there very long beams reaching from one bank to the other into the form of a bridge. 18.10. And building two wooden towers by either bank, he established a watch-station of warlike men, in order that no longer should it be possible for any skiffs or other vessels sailing up from Portus to come into the city. 18.11. In the meantime Belisarius put in at the harbour of the Romans, and the army with John remained. And John ferried across to Calabria, the Goths by no means perceiving it, who were staying, as has been said, about Brentesium. 18.12. And taking two of the enemy going on the road for scouting, he killed one straightway, but the other, laying hold of his knees, begged to be taken alive. 18.13. “For I shall not be useless,” he said, “to you and the Roman army.” And when John asked him what he, not being killed, would ever be of advantage to the Romans and to himself, the man promised to set him over the Goths when they were least expecting it. 18.14. And he said that he would not at all fail of his entreaty, but that he ought first to show him the pastures of the horses. So when the barbarian agreed to this too, he went with him. 18.15. And first, finding the horses of the enemy grazing, all who happened to be on foot mounted upon them; and they were many and excellent. Then they advanced at a run against the camp of their opponents. 18.16. And the barbarians, being unarmed and altogether unprepared, and struck with consternation at the unexpectedness, the most of them perished there, being mindful of no resistance, while some few escaping were conveyed to Totila. 18.17. And John, consoling and winning over all the Calabrians, brought them into goodwill toward the emperor, promising that many good things would come to them both from the emperor and from the Roman army. 18.18. And setting out as fast as he could from Brentesium, he occupied a city named Canusium, which lies about the middle of Apulia and is distant from Brentesium a journey of five days for one going westward and toward Rome. 18.19. Twenty-five stades from this Canusium is Cannae, where they say the great disaster befell the Romans in earlier times, Hannibal commanding the Libyans. 18.20. There a certain Tullianus, the son of Venantius, a Roman man, having great power among the Bruttii and Lucanians, coming into the sight of John, charged the emperor's army with what they had previously wrought against the Italians, but agreed that, if they should henceforth use any fairness toward them, he would put into their hands the Bruttii and Lucanians, who would again be subject to the emperor in the payment of tribute none the less than they were before. 18.21. For they had not come over willingly to barbarians who were Arians, but had done so as being especially forced by their opponents and wronged by the emperor's soldiers. 18.22. And when John affirmed that for the future all good things would come to the Italians from them, Tullianus went with him. 18.23. And from this the soldiers no longer held the Italians in any suspicion, but the most of the parts within the Ionian Gulf became both friendly to them and subject to the emperor. 18.24. When Totila heard this, selecting three hundred Goths, he sent them to Capua. And he instructed them, when they should see the army with John going from there to Rome, to follow them, giving them no perception of it; 18.25. for the rest would be his concern. And John, fearing on account of this lest he should fall into some encirclement of the enemy, no longer went to Belisarius, but advanced into the Bruttii and Lucanians. 18.26. Now there was among the Goths a certain Recimundus, a man of repute, whom Totila had happened to establish over the garrison of the Bruttii, having some of the Goths and Roman soldiers and Moorish deserters, in order that with them he might guard both the strait at Scylla and the shore there, so that none might be able to set out from there to Sicily or to sail down from the island to there too fearlessly. 18.27. Upon this army, between Rhegium and Vebo, John, falling unexpectedly and self-announced, struck them with consternation suddenly as they were mindful of no resistance, and straightway turned them to flight. 18.28. And they fled to the mountain that rises there, which was hard to traverse and otherwise precipitous, but John, pursuing and coming with the enemy to the steep ground, and coming to close quarters with them before they had yet strengthened themselves in the difficult places, killed very many both of the Moors and Roman soldiers, who defended themselves most stoutly, and took Recimundus and the Goths with all the rest by agreement. 18.29. John, then, having accomplished these things, remained there, and Belisarius, always waiting for John, remained quiet. And he found fault that John had not, by risking himself and coming to close quarters with the three hundred guarding at Capua, undertaken to make the passage, although he had with him barbarians gathered for their valour. But John, despairing of the passage, advanced into Apulia, and remained quiet in a place called Cervarium.

It is a law among the Persians that, whenever they are about to make an expedition against any of the enemy, the king sits upon the royal throne, and many baskets are there somewhere, and the general who is reckoned likely to lead the army against the adversaries is present, and this army passes before the king's sight man by man, and each of them throws one missile into the baskets; after which these, sealed with the king's seal, are guarded, and whenever this army returns to the Persians, each of the soldiers takes one missile from the baskets.

Then, counting how many of the missiles have not been taken up by the men, those on whom this office is laid announce to the king the number of soldiers who have not returned, and in this way it becomes manifest how many have died in the war.

Such, then, is the law among the Persians from of old. And Belisarius, when he had taken Urbinus about the winter solstice, thought it inexpedient to go to Auximus immediately; for he suspected that much time would be spent for them in the siege of it. 20.2. For it was impossible to take the place by force because of the strength of its defences, and the barbarians, many and excellent, who held the garrison there, as has been shown by me before, having plundered a large district, had brought in for themselves a great quantity of provisions. 20.3. And he ordered Aratius with a large army to winter in Firmum and to keep watch that for the future the barbarians might not at their will, making sorties from there, more boldly do violence to the regions there; while he himself led the army against Urbiventus. 20.4. For Peranius urged him to this, since he had heard from the deserters that the Goths there were running short of provisions, and he hoped that, if in addition to the want of necessities they should see Belisarius present with the whole army, they would more easily give in; 20.5. which happened. For Belisarius, as soon as he came to Urbiventus, ordered all to encamp in a suitably situated place, while he himself, going about in a circle, looked to see whether somehow it might not be impossible to take it by force. And it seemed to him there was no device for taking the place by force. 20.6. But it seemed to him not altogether impracticable to gain mastery of it secretly through a plot. 20.7. For a certain hill rises alone out of a hollow land, level and flat at the upper parts, but precipitous below. And about the hill rocks of equal height make a kind of encirclement, not being very close, but distant about a stone's throw. 20.8. On this hill the men of old built the city, neither throwing walls around it nor making any other fortification, since the place seemed to them impregnable by nature. 20.9. For there happens to be one entrance to it from the rocks, which, if the inhabitants guard it, they need not fear any assault of the enemy elsewhere. 20.10. For apart from the place where nature has made the entrance to the city, as has been said, a river, always great and impassable, holds the space between the hill and the rocks of which I just made mention. 20.11. Wherefore the ancient Romans made a small building at this entrance. And there is a gate there, which the Goths then guarded. Such, then, is the situation regarding Urbiventus. 20.12. And Belisarius set himself with the whole army to the siege, having the hope either of doing them mischief by means of the river or of reducing the enemy by famine. 20.13. And the barbarians for a while were not altogether in want of the necessities, although they had them in less than sufficient measure; nevertheless they held out against the hardship beyond expectation, by no means coming to fullness of food, but using just so much of victuals each day as not to die of famine. 20.14. But when all the provisions had failed them, they soaked hides and skins in water for a long time and then ate them; for Albilas who commanded them, a man most highly esteemed among the Goths, fed them with empty hopes. 20.15. And when the season, coming round again, brought the summer time, the grain was already at its height in the fields of its own accord, not so much, however, as before, but much less. 20.16. For since it had been hidden in the furrows neither by ploughs nor by the hands of men, but happened to lie on the surface, the earth was able to bring only a small part of it to fruit. 20.17. And as no one reaped it, having come far past its prime it fell again, and nothing thereafter grew from it. And this same thing happened also in Aemilia. 20.18. Wherefore, leaving their homes, the people there went to Picenum, supposing that the regions there, because they were by the sea, would not be altogether oppressed by want. 20.19. And the famine laid hold of the Tuscans too none the less, from the same cause, but all of them who dwelt in the mountains, grinding the acorns of the oaks like grain and making bread from them, ate it. 20.20. And of all kinds of diseases, as was natural, most of them were seized, 20.21. but some, surviving, were saved. In Picenum, however, it is said that no fewer than fifty thousand of the people, Roman farmers, perished of famine, and many more still beyond the Ionian Gulf. 20.22. And of what appearance they became, and in what manner they died, I now proceed to tell, having myself been an eyewitness. 20.23. They became thin and pale, all of them; for the flesh, lacking nourishment, fed, according to the ancient saying, upon itself, and the bile, which now held the mastery over the body by its abundance, gave to these a colour resembling its own. 20.24. And as the evil advanced, all moisture failed them, and the skin, becoming exceedingly dry, was very like leather, giving the appearance of being fixed upon the bones. And changing from livid to black, they resembled torches burnt exceedingly. 20.25. And their faces were always full of amazement, and they always looked terribly somewhat frenzied. And some died from want of food, others even from coming too much to fullness of it. 20.26. For since all the heat which nature kindled within them had been quenched, if anyone fed them to satiety, and not little by little, like infants newly born, these, no longer being able to digest the food, perished much more quickly. 20.27. And some, the famine overpowering them, tasted of one another. And it is said that two women in a certain field above the city of Ariminum ate seventeen men, who happened to be the only ones left in the place. 20.28. For it came about that strangers travelling there lodged in the cottage where these women dwelt; and them, while they slept, the women killed and ate. 20.29. They say, then, that the eighteenth stranger, rising from sleep, just when these women were about to set upon him, leapt up and learned from them the whole story, and killed both of them. 20.30. This, then, they say happened thus. And most, gripped by the necessity of famine, if anywhere any herb chanced to be, would go to it with much eagerness, and kneeling down would try to pull it up from the ground. 20.31. Then (for they were not able, since all strength had failed them) falling over the herb and their hand, they died. 20.32. And no one hid them anywhere in the earth; for there was no one to whom even an account of burial might fall; yet no bird touched them, of which many are wont to feed on dead bodies, 20.33. since they had nothing on which they might rush. For all the flesh, as I have said before, had already happened to be consumed by the famine. Such, then, was the state of things regarding the famine.

For those on whom the guard always lay had much liberty to sleep, since no one was set over them who would make any account of such a thing; nor did any go around the walls in a circle, as was wont, and see fit to search out what the guards were doing; nor indeed could any of the inhabitants help them keep guard. 20.3. And he, agreeing that he would have abundant gratitude toward them if they should accomplish this, and would make them masters of great sums of money, sent two of his followers with them to observe the place from which the men said it was possible for the Goths to come into the city. 20.6. And these, when they came to the wall, taking hold of the ropes, went up onto the battlements, no one there either speaking or perceiving what was being done. 20.7. And when they were there, the Isaurians showed the barbarians everything, that if they wished to come up no obstacle would arise, and that to those who came up there would be much liberty, no one whatever withstanding them; and ordering them to report these things to Totila, they sent them away. 20.8. When Totila heard this, he was somewhat pleased at the message, but, being even so gripped by suspicion against the Isaurians, saw fit not to trust them too much. 20.9. And not many days later the men came to him again, urging him to the deed. And he sent two others with them, in order that they too, searching out everything exactly, might report. 20.10. And they, returning to him, announced everything in like manner to the former men. In the meantime many Roman soldiers, sent out for scouting from the city, fell in with ten Goths going on the road not far off, whom they took and brought straightway to Bessas. 20.11. And he inquired of these barbarians what Totila was purposing, and the Goths said they were in hope that some of the Isaurians would give over the city to them; for the report had now become known to many of the barbarians. 20.12. But Bessas and Conon, hearing even this, held it in much disregard and made no account of it. And a third time the Isaurians, coming into the sight of Totila, urged the man to the deed. 20.13. And he sent others with them and one of his kinsmen, who, returning to him and reporting the whole account, strengthened him for the deed. 20.14. And Totila, as soon as night had come, arming the whole army quietly, led it against the Asinarian gate. And he ordered four of the Goths who were well off in courage and strength to go up to the battlements through the nooses with the Isaurians, at that time of night, of course, at which the guard of the wall there fell to these Isaurians, the others taking their sleep in turn. 20.15. And these, when they were inside the wall, went down to the Asinarian gate, no one withstanding them, and destroyed with axes the wood which, fitted by insertion into each wall, they were wont to use to fasten the gates, and all the irons with which the guards, putting in the keys, were always wont both to lock the gates and to open them as need required. 20.16. And thus, throwing open the gates as they wished, they received into the city Totila and the Gothic army with no trouble. And Totila, gathering them there into one place, by no means allowed them to scatter; for he feared lest some ambush by the enemy should befall them. And when confusion, 20.17. as is natural, and tumult fell upon the city, the most of the Roman soldiers fled with their commanders through another gate, as it became easy for each, but some few took refuge with the rest of the Romans in the churches. 20.18. And of the patricians Decius and Basilius with certain others (for they happened to have horses present) were able to flee with Bessas. 20.19. But Maximus and Olybrius and Orestes and certain others fled to the church of Peter the apostle. Of the people, however, it befell that five hundred men were left in all the city, who took refuge in the churches with difficulty. 20.20. For of all the rest, some had previously gone off to other countries, and some had perished of famine, as has been said by me before. Many, then, announced to Totila by night that Bessas and the enemy were fleeing. And he, saying that they had spoken a pleasant word, would not allow them to pursue. 20.21. For what could be sweeter to a man, he said, than that the enemy should flee? 20.22. And when it was now day and no suspicion of any ambush was any longer left, Totila went to the church of Peter the apostle to pray, while the Goths destroyed those who had fallen in their way. 20.23. And there died in this manner twenty-six of the soldiers and sixty of the people. And when Totila came to the church, Pelagius came into his sight bearing the oracles of the Christians in his hands, and in every way putting forward his supplication, said, “Spare your own, O master.” 20.24. And he, mocking and exulting, said, “Now, O Pelagius, you have come to supplicate me.” “When,” Pelagius answered, “God has made me your slave. 20.25. But for the future, O master, spare your slaves.” Totila, receiving this supplication, forbade the Goths to kill for the future any of all the Romans, but to take out for himself the most precious of the goods, and the rest to plunder for themselves at their will. 20.26. Much, then, he found in the houses of the patricians, but most of all where Bessas lodged. For the unholy prices of the grain, as has been shown, this wretched man was gathering for Totila. 20.27.
