And Calonymus, having sworn and holding what he had sworn of no account, for the moment plundered the money, but not long after paid the penalty in Byzantium.
At first, then, sending some of her intimates to him on an embassy, she inquired for what reason he had outraged her, when she had neither played the harlot nor done any other unkind thing to him.

And from there, sending about everywhere, he gathered the army and established his camp there, and answered the commanders in Hierapolis thus: "If Chosroes is going against other men, but not subjects of the Romans, your counsel is well and most safely taken;
For seized by the disease called apoplexy and going out of his mind and biting off his own tongue, he then died. But these things took place at a later time.
But when she could accomplish nothing by this, taking up the manly garb she went to deeds of war.

for those to whom it is in their power, remaining quietly, to be free of evils, it is great folly to go into some unnecessary danger; but if now this barbarian, having departed thence, shall attack some other country of the Emperor Justinian, and this an exceedingly good one, but having no garrison of soldiers, know well that to perish with valour is altogether better than to be saved without a battle.
Gathering, then, at once four hundred ships and putting into them an army of no fewer than a hundred thousand fighting men, she herself led the way against the Varni with this host.
For this would justly be called not safety, but betrayal. But come as quickly as possible to Europum, where, having gathered the whole army, I have hope, whatever God gives,
And she brought along too one of her own brothers, to help her settle the present affairs, not, however, as holding the kingship, but as still ranking in the position of a private man.
to work upon the enemy." When the commanders saw this brought to them, they took courage and left Justus with a few there to guard Hierapolis, and the rest with the army came to Europum.
And these islanders are the bravest of all the barbarians we know, and they go into the engagements on foot.

For they are not only unpractised in riding, but they do not even know what a horse is, since a horse in this island they do not even behold in a picture; for this creature never appears to have existed in Brittia.

And if ever it befall any of them, on an embassy or for some other reason, to visit the Romans or the Franks or anyone else who has horses, and there it be necessary for them to ride horses, they have no means at all of leaping upon them, but other men, lifting them up, set them upon the horses; and when they wish to dismount from there, again others, raising them up, set them down on the ground.

Nor indeed are the Varni horsemen, but they too are all foot-soldiers. Such, then, are these barbarians. And there was no supernumerary in this fleet, but all were rowers of their own oars. Nor do these islanders happen to have sails, but they always sail by rowing alone.

And when they had put in to the mainland, the maiden who ruled them, having pitched a strong stockade close beside the very outlet of the river Rhine, remained there with a few men, while she ordered her brother to lead all the rest of the army against the enemy.

And the Varni were then encamped not far from the shore of the Ocean and the outlet of the Rhine. There, when the Angiloi quickly came, both sides closed in combat, and the Varni were utterly defeated.

And of them many fell in this struggle, while the rest, with their king, all turned to flight, and the Angiloi, making the pursuit upon them for a little, as is fitting for foot-soldiers, withdrew to the camp.

And the maiden reviled them as they returned to her, and railed at her brother most bitterly, maintaining that nothing worthy of mention had been done by the army, since they had not brought her Radigis alive.
And, picking out the most warlike of them, she at once sent them off, ordering them to bring the man a spear-captive by every device.
And they, fulfilling her command, went about searching accurately all the regions there, until they found Radigis hiding in a dense wood; and, binding him, they brought him to the maiden.

And he stood in her sight, trembling and supposing he would very straightway die by a most pitiable death; but she, contrary to expectation, neither killed him nor did him any other unkind thing, but, reproaching him with the outrage to her, inquired of the man for what reason he, disregarding the agreement, had come to the bed of another woman, and that too when his betrothed had not played the harlot toward him.

And he, defending himself against the charge, put forward his father's injunctions and the eagerness of his subjects, and offered words of supplication and mingled his defence with many entreaties, referring the blame to necessity.
And he agreed to live with her, if it were her wish, and to heal by what should follow the things not justly done by him before.

And when these things pleased the maiden, Radigis was loosed from his bonds and was thought worthy of all other kindness, and he at once sent away the sister of Theudibert and married the Brittian woman. These things went forward thus.
And in this island of Brittia the men of old built a long wall, cutting off a great part of it; and the air and the soil and all else are not alike on the two sides of the wall.
For the parts of the wall toward the rising sun there is a healthfulness of air, changing with the seasons, in summer moderately warm, cold in winter;
and many men dwell there, living in the same way as the rest of mankind, and the trees flourish with fruits ripening in season, and the corn-lands bloom no less than the rest;

and the country, moreover, appears abundantly luxuriant with waters. But toward the setting sun all is the opposite, so that, in fact, it is not possible for a man to live there even half an hour, but vipers and serpents innumerable and all manner of kinds of other wild beasts have been allotted that place.

And, most paradoxical of all, the natives say that if any man, crossing the wall, should go to the other side, he dies straightway, not enduring at all the pestilential nature of the air there, and to the wild beasts going there death at once meets them and receives them.

But, having come to this point in my history, I am bound to mention an account most like a legend, which to me seemed by no means trustworthy at all, although it is forever brought out by countless men who maintained that they themselves had been the doers of the deeds and the hearers of the words; yet it is not to be passed over altogether, lest, in recording the matters of the island Brittia, I should win the reputation of a perpetual ignorance of what happens there.

They say, then, that the souls of men who die are always carried off to this place. But in what manner I shall now make plain, having often heard the men there relating it most earnestly, though I have judged what is bruited abroad to be referred to some power of dreams.

Along the shore of the Ocean opposite Brittia there happen to be very many villages. And men dwell in them who busy themselves with fishing and farming the land and sailing for trade to this island, being for the rest subjects of the Franks, yet never having paid them any tribute, this burden having been remitted to them from of old, on account of some service, as they say, which I shall now relate.

The men there say that the escort of the souls is laid upon them in turn. Those, then, who on the coming night must go to this task by the succession of the service, these, as soon as it grows dark, withdrawing to their own houses, sleep, awaiting the conductor of the matter.
And in the dead of night they perceive their doors being knocked, and they hear a certain unseen voice calling them together to the work.
And they themselves, with no hesitation, rising from their beds, go to the shore, not understanding what necessity leads them to this, but nevertheless compelled.
And there they see boats made ready, altogether empty of men—not their own, however, but certain others—into which, embarking, they lay hold of the oars.

And they perceive that the barges are weighed down with a multitude of passengers, sunk by the surge to the very edges of the planks and to the place of the oar-locks, lacking of the water no more than a single finger; yet they themselves see no one, but, rowing a single hour, they put in to Brittia.

And yet, when they sail in their own boats, not using sails but rowing, they scarcely cross there in a night and a day. But having put in to the island, after discharging the cargo, they depart very straightway, the barges becoming light suddenly and rising up out of the surge and sinking in the water in no other part except as far as the keel itself.

And they themselves see no man, either sailing with them or departing from the ship, but they say they hear a certain voice from there seeming to announce to those who receive them each one of those who have sailed with them, by name, reciting the dignities they formerly enjoyed and calling them by their fathers' names.
And if women too happen to have crossed with them, they recite the names of the men with whom they lived as wives.
These things, then, the men there say happen. But I return to the former account.

Hermogenes then, as soon as the battle by the Euphrates had taken place, coming to Cabades on an embassy, accomplished nothing concerning the peace for which he came, since he found him still swelling against the Romans; therefore he withdrew unsuccessful.

And Chosroes, learning that Belisarius with the whole Roman army was encamped at Europum, no longer resolved to advance, but sent to Belisarius one of the royal secretaries, Abandanes by name, having a great repute for intelligence, to spy out what sort of man the general was, and ostensibly to complain that the Emperor Justinian had by no means sent the envoys to the Persians to dispose the matters of the peace according to the agreement. When Belisarius learned this, he did as follows.
Then Belisarius, since the occasion led to it, bade a breakfast be made for them where Gelimer was wont to feast the leaders of the Vandals.

And Belisarius, when he heard that Uraïas and the barbarians were besieging Mediolanum, sent Martinus and Uliaris with a large army against them. 21.2. And they, coming to the river Padus, which is distant a day's journey from Mediolanum, encamped and remained there. And much time was spent by them there, while they deliberated about the crossing of the river. 21.3. And when Mundilas heard this, he sent to them one of the Romans, Paulus by name. 21.4. And he, escaping the notice of the enemy, came to the bank of the Padus. And finding no boat at the moment, he stripped and, swimming, made the crossing at great risk. 21.5. So being brought to the Roman camp and coming to the commanders, he spoke as follows: “Martinus and Uliaris, you are doing things neither just nor worthy of your own reputation, having come in word for the safety of the emperor's affairs, but in deed increasing the power of the Goths. 21.6. For this Mediolanum, which surpasses by far all the cities in Italy in size and in population and in the rest of its prosperity, and apart from these things, being a bulwark against the Germans and the other barbarians and set, so to speak, before the whole Roman empire, has fallen into great danger together with Mundilas and the emperor's army, being troubled by the enemy and neglected by you. 21.7. How greatly the emperor has been wronged by you at the present time, I forbear to say. For the occasion does not allow me to use many words, since I seek some swift help for the city, while there is still some hope left. 21.8. And I say that you ought immediately to defend the Mediolanenses who are in danger. For if you use any delay toward us at the present time, it will come about that we, having suffered the most bitter of all things, shall perish, and that you will have given over the emperor's power to the enemy. 21.9. For traitors, I think, are justly called not only those who throw open the gates to the enemy, but no less, if not more, those who, when it is in their power to defend their dearest who are besieged, choose the safe shrinking instead of the contest and thus give the mastery to the enemy, as is natural.” 21.10. Paulus said so much, and Martinus and Uliaris, promising to follow him immediately, sent the man away. 21.11. And he, again escaping the notice of the barbarians, entered Mediolanum by night, and lifting up the soldiers and all the Romans with hopes, strengthened them still more in their loyalty to the emperor. 21.12. None the less, Martinus and his men, gripped by shrinking, remained there, and much time was spent in this delay. 21.13. And afterward Martinus, wishing to free himself from blame, wrote to Belisarius as follows: “You sent us here to defend those in Mediolanum who are in danger, and we with much eagerness, just as you ordered, have come as far as the river Padus, which the army fears to cross, since we hear that there is a great force of Goths and a very great multitude of Burgundians with them in Liguria, against whom we think ourselves unable to contend alone. 21.14. But order John and Justinus as quickly as possible (for they are in our neighbourhood in the land of Aemilia), together with their followers, to share this danger with us. 21.15. For going from here in common, we shall both be safe ourselves and be able to do some harm to the 21.16. enemy.” So much Martinus's letter made plain. And Belisarius, when he had read it, ordered John and Justinus to go quickly to Mediolanum with Martinus and his men. But they said they would do nothing unless Narses gave them instructions. 21.17. Wherefore Belisarius wrote also to Narses as follows: “Consider the whole army of the emperor to be one body, which, if it does not display one purpose, like the limbs of a man, but wishes to act apart from one another, it will be left to us to perish, having accomplished none of the things that are needful. 21.18. Therefore let Aemilia alone, which has neither any fortification nor brings to the Romans at the present time any weight of advantage. 21.19. But order John and Justinus immediately to go straight against the enemy in Mediolanum together with Martinus and his men, being near and sufficient for the mastery over the barbarians. 21.20. For I have here no multitude of an army which I might send, and besides, I think it inexpedient for soldiers to go to Mediolanum from here. 21.21. For much time will be wasted, so that they will come to it later than the necessary opportunity, and they will by no means be able to use their horses against the enemy, on account of the length of the road, when they come to them. 21.22. But if these men go to Mediolanum together with Martinus and Uliaris, they will both prevail, as is likely, over the barbarians there, and will recover Aemilia again, with no one any longer withstanding them.” 21.23. When Narses saw this letter brought to him, he instructed John and Justinus to go to Mediolanum with the rest of the army. 21.24. And a little later John was sent to the coast in order to bring boats from there, so that the army might be able to cross the river. But a sickness befalling him prevented the carrying out of the plan. 21.25. While Martinus and his men were using their shrinking from the crossing, and John's men were waiting for the instructions of Narses, in the meantime it befell that a great deal of time was spent in the siege. 21.26. And the besieged, now exceedingly hard pressed by famine and the evil overpowering them, most of them tasted of dogs and mice and of other animals which never came to the food of man. 21.27. So the barbarians, sending envoys to Mundilas, ordered him to give over the city to them, on condition that he himself and the soldiers should remain unharmed. 21.28. And he agreed to do this, if those men should both give pledges on their behalf and that they would do nothing unpleasant to any of the inhabitants. 21.29. But when the enemy gave pledges to Mundilas and the soldiers, while it was clear that, being gripped by much anger against the Ligurians, they would destroy them all, Mundilas, calling together all the soldiers, spoke as follows: 21.30. “If ever any others, when it was in their power to live shamefully, chose rather to die gloriously, exchanging an honourable end of life for immediate safety, such men at the present time I should wish you also to be, and not, through love of life, to pursue a life with shame, and this too, from the teaching of Belisarius, in which, having shared from of old, it is unholy for you not to be noble and exceedingly bold. 21.31. For to all who come into the light one fortune comes forth, to die at the appointed times; but in the manner of death men for the most part differ from one another. 21.32. And the difference is this, that cowards, as is natural, all owing insult and mockery to their enemies first, then none the less fulfil their fate at the times appointed from above, but to noble men it befalls to suffer this together with valour and an abundance of good repute. 21.33. And apart from these things, if it were in our power, while saving these people, to be slaves to the barbarians, this at least would bring some pardon for our shameful safety. 21.34. But if it is necessary to behold so great a multitude of Romans destroyed by the hands of the enemy, what would one call more bitter than this death? 21.35. For we should seem to be doing nothing else than helping the barbarians to accomplish the terrible deed. While, therefore, we are still masters of ourselves, let us adorn necessity with valour, and account the fortune that has fallen upon us a glorious one. 21.36. And I say that we ought, all of us being armed as best we can, to go against the enemy who are not expecting it. 21.37. For one of two things will be ours: either to have wrought through fortune something better than hope, or, having met with a happy end, to be most gloriously released from our present evils.” 21.38. Mundilas said so much, but none of the soldiers was willing to undertake the danger, but on the terms which the enemy proposed they gave over both themselves and the city. 21.39. And the barbarians, doing them no harm, kept them in custody together with Mundilas, but razed the city to the ground, killing all the males, no fewer than three hundred thousand, and making the women into the account of slaves, whom they gave to the Burgundians, repaying them thus for their alliance. 21.40. And finding Reparatus, the prefect of the court, they cut him into small pieces and threw his flesh to the dogs. 21.41. But Cervatinus (for he happened to be inside Mediolanum) was conveyed through Venetia and the nations there, together with his followers, to Dalmatia. And he came from there to the emperor, announcing this great disaster which had befallen the Romans. 21.42. And from this the Goths took the other cities by agreement which happened to have Roman garrisons, and again held the mastery over the whole of Liguria. And Martinus and Uliaris with the army returned to Rome.

On the following day Totila, calling all the Goths together, spoke as follows: “Not to make to you any new or unknown exhortation have I gathered you here, fellow-soldiers, but to say those things which I have often said to you, and which, when you received them, it befell the greatest of goods to come to pass. 21.2. Do not, then, through this use any disregard toward the exhortation now. 21.3. For of words that lead to prosperity it is not natural that there be satiety for a man, even if one should seem to weary him by their length; since it is not right to refuse the benefit arising from them either. 21.4. And I say that lately, when twenty myriads of most warlike soldiers gathered together, using prodigious wealth and displaying a certain abundance, as great as possible, of horses and arms, and a great throng of most intelligent elders—which seems most advantageous to those who set themselves to contests—we were defeated by seven thousand Greeks, and have been deprived of the rule and of all the rest for no reason. 21.5. But now, having been reduced to a few, naked and pitiable and experienced in nothing whatever, it has befallen us to master the enemy, who are more than twenty thousand. 21.6. The things done, then, to speak in a word, are such; but the causes of things befalling thus I shall now make plain to you who know them: that the Goths formerly, setting justice below all other things, wrought unholy deeds both toward one another and toward the Roman subjects, by which, as is natural, God, being led against them, then campaigned with the enemy. 21.7. And on account of these things, although surpassing our opponents by far in numbers and in valour and in the rest of the preparation for war, we were defeated by a certain power unseen and least of all knowable. 21.8. Therefore the guarding of these goods will lie with you, preserving plainly justice. For if you change, the things from God too will immediately be hostile. 21.9. For it is not wont to ally itself either with a race of men or with the nature of nations, but with those by whom the reckoning of justice is more honoured. And there is no toil for it to transfer good things to others. 21.10. For for a man only not to do wrong lies in his purpose, but for God all things naturally lie in his power. 21.11. I say, then, that you ought to keep justice both toward one another and toward your subjects. For it would be the same thing as to say that you preserve your prosperity for ever.” 21.12. Saying so much to the Goths, Totila, calling together those of the Roman senate, reproached and reviled them much, who, having received many good things from Theoderic and Athalaric, and being themselves established for ever over the whole rule and managing the state, and being girt with a great quantity of wealth, then, gripped by much thanklessness toward the Goths their benefactors, had looked to a revolt, which they ought not, to their own harm, and had brought in the Greeks against their country, having suddenly become traitors to themselves. 21.13. And he inquired whether they themselves had ever suffered any evil at the hands of the Goths. 21.14. And he compelled them to say if any good had befallen them from the emperor Justinian, enumerating everything in order: that they had been deprived of nearly all the magistracies, and, being maltreated by the so-called logothetes, had been compelled to render accounts of their dealings in office toward the Goths, and, being worn down by the war, paid the public taxes to the Greeks no less than in time of peace; and many other things he put into his speech, such as it is likely a hostile master should reproach those he has enslaved. 21.15. And, pointing out to them Herodian and the Isaurians who had given over the city to him, “You,” he said, “though brought up with the Goths, did not resolve to give over to us even a deserted place to this day, but these men received us both into Rome itself and into Spolitium. 21.16. Wherefore you have come to be in the position of slaves, while these men, having become, as is natural, friends and kinsmen to the Goths, will for the future hold your 21.17. magistracies.” So the patricians, hearing this, kept silence. But Pelagius did not cease begging off Totila on behalf of men who had failed and been unfortunate, until he dismissed them, making a promise of kindness. 21.18. After this he sent Pelagius and one of the orators in Rome, Theodorus by name, as envoys to the emperor Justinian, binding them with the most dreadful oaths, that they would use goodwill toward him and would be eager to return to Italy as quickly as possible. 21.19. And he instructed them to obtain peace for him from the emperor with all their might, in order that he might not be compelled to raze the whole of Rome to the ground and destroy those of the senate, and to carry the war into Illyricum. And he wrote a letter to the emperor Justinian. 21.20. Now the emperor had already heard what had happened in Italy. And when the envoys came to him, they reported what Totila instructed them and put the letter into his hands. 21.21. And the writing made plain the following: “As to what has befallen to happen in the city of the Romans, since I think you have learned all, I have resolved to keep silent. 21.22. But for what reasons I have sent these envoys you will know at once. We ask that you both receive yourself the good things from peace and concede them to us. 21.23. Of which we have the finest memorials and examples in Anastasius and Theoderic, who reigned not long before, and filled all the time of their reign with peace and good things. 21.24. For if this should ever be your wish, you would justly be called my father, and you would have us 21.25. for the future as allies against whomever you should wish.” When the emperor Justinian saw this brought to him and heard all the words of the envoys, he dismissed them immediately, making them this answer alone, and writing to Totila, that he had made Belisarius supreme commander of the war, and that he therefore had the authority to settle matters with Totila in whatever way he wished.

Thus, then, the matters of the wars in each country happened to come about. And the Gothic war was carried on as follows. The emperor, having summoned Belisarius to Byzantium, as I have said in the earlier books, held him in honour, and, not even when Germanus had died, did he think to send him to Italy, but, though he was general of the East, appointing him commander of the imperial bodyguards, he kept him there.
And Belisarius came to the emperor at Byzantium, summoned, stripped of the office he held, in order that he might make an expedition against the Vandals.

He himself, choosing out six thousand men, tall and very fair in body, set out as though to hunt far off from the camp, and Diogenes the bodyguard and Adolius the son of Acacius, a man Armenian by race, who ever served the emperor in the palace in matters of quiet (the Romans call those on whom this honour lies silentiarii), and then commanded some Armenians, he bade cross the river with a thousand horsemen and go about the bank there, ever giving the enemy an impression that, if they should wish, having crossed the Euphrates, to go by the road to their own land, they would never permit it. And they did accordingly.

The Romans call the place Delphix, not in their own tongue, but hellenizing it according to the old fashion. For in the Palatium in Rome, where it chanced the king's couches were, a tripod stood from of old, on which the king's cup-bearers used to set the cups.
And Belisarius was first in rank of all the Romans, although some of them had earlier been enrolled among the patricians and had ascended to the very chair of the consuls.
And Sittas, this having been resolved by the Emperor Justinian, came there to guard the East.

And Belisarius, when he learned that the envoy was very near, having pitched a tent of certain thick linen cloths, which they have been accustomed to call a pavilion, sat there, as in a desert place, intimating that he had come there with no preparation.

And the tripod the Romans call Delphix, since it first came to be in Delphi, and from this both in Byzantium and wherever the king's couch chances to be they call the building Delphix, since the Romans, hellenizing, call the king's house Palatium too.
But even so all yielded the first place to him, ashamed to use the law against his merit and to gird themselves with the right derived from it.
And the Persians again invaded Mesopotamia with a great army, the chanaranges and Aspebedes and Mermeroes leading them.
And he arranged the soldiers thus. On either side of the tent were Thracians and Illyrians, and after them Goths, and next to these Heruls, after whom were Vandals and Moors.

For Pallas, a Greek man, having dwelt in this place before the capture of Ilium and built a house worthy of account there, they called this building Palatium, and since Augustus, having received the supreme rule, resolved first to lodge there, they call from him the place where the king lodges Palatium.

And these things pleased the emperor exceedingly. But John, the son of Vitalian, was wintering at Salona. And the soldiers of the Roman army, awaiting him in Italy at this time, remained inactive. And the winter was ending, and the sixteenth year was coming to a close in this Gothic war, the history of which Procopius has written.
And since no one dared to come to blows with them, settling down before Martyropolis they besieged it, where Bouzes and Bessas chanced to have been stationed for the guard.

And they extended over a great part of the plain. For they did not stand always in the same place, but, standing apart from one another and making walks, they looked at the envoy of Chosroes carelessly and in no way earnestly.
In the Delphix, then, Belisarius dined, and whatever was notable in the army.
And in the year that followed John was minded to rise up from Salona and lead the army as quickly as possible against Totila and the Goths.

This lies in the country called Sophanene, distant from the city of Amida two hundred and forty stades toward the north wind; and it is by the Nymphius river, which divides the land of the Romans and the Persians.
And none of them had either cloak or any other shoulder-garment, but, clad in linen tunics and trousers, then girded up, they walked about.

And it chanced that the breakfast made on the previous day for Gelimer was in readiness. And we feasted on the very victuals, and the attendants of Gelimer set them before us and poured the wine and served us in the rest.
But the emperor hindered him, and ordered him to remain there until Narses the eunuch should arrive. For he had determined to appoint him commander-in-chief of this war.
The Persians, then, assaulted the wall, and the besieged at first manfully withstood them, but were reckoned likely not to hold out long.
And each had his horse-whip, but the weapon of one was a sword, of another an axe, of another bare bows.
And it was possible to see Fortune adorning herself and making display that all things are hers and nothing becomes the property of man.

But for what reason these things were the emperor's wish became plainly clear to none of all men; for a counsel of the emperor is impossible to learn unless it be of his own free will. But what men, suspecting, said, I shall make plain.

For the wall was very assailable for the most part and easily to be taken by a siege of the Persians, and they themselves did not have provisions sufficiently, nor indeed engines nor anything else adequate with which to defend themselves.
And all gave an impression that, taking no thought of all else, they were eager to hunt.
And it befell Belisarius on that day to win such repute as had never come to any of his time nor to any other of those of old.
A thought came to the emperor Justinian that the other commanders of the Roman army would by no means be willing to obey John, not thinking fit to be in any way inferior to him in rank.
Sittas and the Roman army came to a place Attachas, distant a hundred stades from Martyropolis, but did not dare to go forward; rather, encamping there, they remained.

Abandanes, then, coming into the presence of Belisarius, said that King Chosroes was indignant, because, as had been agreed before, the Caesar (for so the Persians call the Emperor of the Romans) had not sent the envoys to him, and on this account Chosroes had been compelled to come in arms into the land of the Romans.

For though the Roman soldiers were not wont, without tumult, to go into a city subject to them, not even by five hundreds and especially unexpectedly, this general so kept all his subjects orderly that there was neither outrage nor threat,
And from this he feared lest, dissenting in opinion or playing the malingerer through envy, they should throw the operations into confusion.
And Hermogenes was with them, having again come on an embassy from Byzantium. At this point it befell that the following thing happened.

But Belisarius, neither cowering, though so great a multitude of barbarians was encamped very near, nor falling into any disturbance at the word, but with a laughing and relaxed face, replies, saying, "Not in this way which Chosroes has now done is it customary for men to manage their affairs.

nor indeed any hindrance to the business of the city, but in a captured city which had changed its government and exchanged its kingship, not even of those in the market was the house of anyone shut, but the clerks, writing the billets, brought the soldiers into the houses, as was wont, and they, buying their breakfast from the market as each wished, remained quiet.

And they, gathering in companies, pitched their huts here and there about the place; but the Goths, observing them to be at a long distance from one another and not easily able to come to one another's aid, since it was a great plain, suddenly about late afternoon advanced against the enemy, toward the parts to the east of the city, where Belisarius happened to be still making a camp with his guards and shield-bearers. 23.11. And they, taking up their arms from what was at hand, defended themselves against the assailants, and very easily thrusting them back by their valour, routed them, and pursuing the fugitives came to the middle of the hill. 23.12. And many of them, daring to undertake the danger and escaping the notice of the enemy, entered Auximus. And Belisarius, observing that Auximus was most strong in its safe position, and that it was altogether impossible for him to make an assault on the wall, thought he would never take the place by force, but he had hope, by a strict siege, of bringing the enemy into want of necessities and of making them subject in time. 23.17. Not far from the wall the earth, sending up much herbage, brought every day an occasion of engagement to the Romans and the Goths. 23.18. For when the Romans saw their opponents always cutting this for the sake of their horses, going up onto the hill at a run, and coming to close quarters with the enemy, and displaying deeds worthy of valour, they by no means allowed them to carry off the herbage, and always destroyed many of their opponents in this place. 23.19. And the barbarians, being worsted by the valour of the enemy, devised the following. Taking off the wheels of the wagons with the axles alone, they kept them in readiness, and beginning to cut the herbage, when they saw the Romans now coming up into the middle of the hill, they let the wheels go to rush down upon them from the height. 23.20. But by some chance it befell that these wheels came down to the level ground without touching any man. So having failed in this attempt, the barbarians for the moment fled inside the wall, but afterward did as follows. 23.21. Setting an ambush of their notable men in the ravines which are close to the wall, a few of them showed themselves to the enemy about the herbage; and when the battle was at close quarters, those who were hidden, leaping out of the ambushes, both far surpassing their opponents in numbers and dismaying them because they had not perceived it beforehand, killed very many and always turned the rest to flight. 23.22. And those of the Romans who stood in the camps saw the enemy rising from the ambushes, but, calling their comrades with much shouting, accomplished nothing, since the combatants by no means heard their cry, being separated from them by the length of the hill, and the barbarians always on purpose clashing their arms against them. 23.23. And while Belisarius was at a loss before the present situation, Procopius, who wrote this, coming to him, said: “Those who anciently used trumpets in the Roman army, O general, understood two notes, of which the one resembled most a command bidding the soldiers rush to battle, while the other called the combatants back to the camp, whenever this seemed best to the general. 23.24. And in this way the generals always ordered the soldiers what was fitting, and they were able to carry out the deeds enjoined. 23.25. For a shout in engagements is in no way able to signify anything clearly, since a din, as is natural, resounds everywhere, and fear confounds the senses of the combatants. 23.26. But since at the present time, through ignorance, such an art has slipped away, and it is impossible with a single trumpet to make both signals clear, do you henceforth do as follows. 23.27. With the cavalry trumpets command the soldiers to fight the enemy, and with the infantry trumpets call the men back to the retreat. 23.28. For it is impossible for them not to understand each of the two sounds, since the one comes from leather and exceedingly thin wood, the other from some thick bronze.” 23.29. Procopius said so much. And Belisarius was pleased with the suggestion, and calling the whole army together, spoke as follows: “Eagerness for this work I think both advantageous and worthy of much praise, so long as, being moderate, it brings no harm to those who have it. 23.30. For by excess all good things are wont always to turn to the worse. Do you, then, no longer be tripped up by contentiousness; for there is no shame in fleeing one who is doing mischief. 23.31. And since he was not able to rebuild in a short time as much of the wall as Totila had razed, he did as follows. 24.4. Gathering the stones that were somewhere near, he threw them upon one another in no order, having nothing whatever inside, since he had neither lime nor anything else of the kind, but only in order that the face of the building might be preserved, and he set a great quantity of stakes outside. 24.5. And he had previously happened to dig deep trenches about the whole wall, as has been said by me in the previous narrative. 24.6. And as the whole army wrought these things with all eagerness, in twenty-five days all of the wall that had been razed was completed in this manner. 24.7. And those of the Romans who dwelt about the regions there gathered there, both out of desire of dwelling in Rome and because, having for a while been in want of the necessities, they found there an abundance which Belisarius was able to make, filling as many ships as possible with all the necessities and bringing them into Rome through the river. 24.8. When Totila heard this, setting out immediately with the whole army he came against Belisarius and Rome, Belisarius not having yet been able to fit gates to the wall. 24.9. For Totila had happened to destroy all of them, which Belisarius had not had time to make for want of craftsmen. 24.10. And when the army of the barbarians came near, for the moment, encamping, they bivouacked by the river Tiber, and on the following day, with the sun rising, gripped by much anger and tumult, they went against the wall. 24.11. And Belisarius, selecting the most warlike of the soldiers, stationed them in the place of the gates, and ordered the rest to defend themselves against the assailants from above on the walls with all their might. 24.12. There was, then, a fierce battle. For the barbarians at first had hope of taking the city at the first shout, but the matter withstanding them, and the Romans defending themselves most stoutly, using anger they pressed upon the enemy, their rage urging them beyond their power to daring. 24.13. And the Romans held out beyond expectation, the danger, as is natural, leading them to courage. 24.14. There was, then, much slaughter of the barbarians, being shot at from above, and both sides were gripped by much weariness and hardship, and the battle, beginning in the morning, ended at nightfall. 24.15. After this the barbarians, coming into their camps, bivouacked, attending to the wounded among them, while of the Romans the rest held guard within the wall, but those who were well off in courage above all guarded the place of the gates in turn, setting many caltrops in front, so that the enemy might not come against them by a sudden raid. 24.16. The caltrops are of this kind. Fitting together at the back four stakes of equal length, they make their straight lines into the form of a triangle on every side, and they throw them on the ground wherever they chance. 24.17. And in this way three of the stakes always stand most firmly on the ground, and the one remaining, rising alone, always becomes a hindrance to both men and horses. 24.18. And whenever anyone rolls this caltrop, the one which before had drawn the lot of the upright space in the air stands to the ground, and another taking its place is a hindrance above to those wishing to go forward. Such are the caltrops. So both sides bivouacked thus after the battle. 24.19. On the following day Totila resolved to assault the wall again with the whole army, and the Romans defended themselves in the manner described. And having become superior in the engagement, they took courage to sally out against the enemy. 24.20. And as the barbarians withdrew, some of the Romans, pursuing, got somewhere far from the wall. These the barbarians were about to encircle, so that they might not be able to return to the city. But Belisarius (for he observed what was being done), sending many of those about him there, was able to save the men. 24.21. And thus the barbarians, thrust back, withdrew, having lost many of their fighting men and bringing very many wounded to the camp. 24.22. And there they remained quiet, treating their wounds and attending to their arms (for many of them had now been destroyed) and making all the rest in full readiness. And many days later they went against the wall as though to assault it. 24.23. But the Romans, meeting them, came to close quarters. And by some chance he who bore the standard of Totila, being struck a mortal blow, both fell from his horse and threw the standard to the ground. 24.24. And the Romans who fought in the front rushed to seize the standard and the corpse. But the most daring of the barbarians, anticipating, seized the standard and, cutting off the left hand of the corpse, took it with them. 24.25. For he who had fallen happened to be wearing on it a golden bracelet worthy of account, on which they were by no means willing that their opponents should glory, fleeing plainly the shame arising from the deed. 24.26. And the army of the barbarians turned to withdrawal in no order, while the Romans both spoiled the rest of the corpse, and pursuing the enemy for the most part killed many, and came into the city altogether unharmed. 24.27. Then those who were notable among the Goths, coming to Totila, both reviled him and without restraint reproached him for his ill-counsel, that, having taken Rome, he neither razed it all to the ground, so that it might no longer be capturable by the enemy, nor held it himself, but what had been wrought by them with toil and much time, this he himself destroyed for no reason. 24.28. So is it implanted in men always to order their judgement according to the issues of affairs, and to make their mind go along with the current of fortune, and from this to make abrupt changes of opinion. 24.29. Wherefore the Goths, when Totila prospered in his undertakings, regarded him as equal to a god, calling him invincible and unconquerable, when he allowed a portion of the walls of captured cities to be destroyed; but when he failed, as has been said, they did not refuse to revile him, forgetting what they had lately said about him, and going against it with no shrinking. 24.30. The slave Heruls, indeed, go to battle even without a shield, and when they become brave men in war, then their masters allow them shields to hold before them in the engagements. So the affairs of the Heruls stand thus.
And one of them smote Marcellus with his sword, not knowing who he was, and thus John was able to escape with them and came quickly to the city.
And the Romans, not enduring the enemy, all fled at full force, neither remembering valour nor having any shame or other good thing in mind.

And if he had taken courage to go at once to the emperor, I think he would have suffered nothing unpleasant from him; but as it was, having fled to a church, he gave the empress full power to use the plot against him as she pleased.

But the Persians, suspecting that they had not turned to so shameful a flight, but were using some ambushes against them, pursued as far as the difficult ground and then turned back, not daring to fight in the open, few against many.

At that time, then, having become from a prefect a private man, he was removed thence and conveyed to another place, which is situated in the suburb of the city of Cyzicus—the Cyzicenes call the suburb Artace. There, against his will, he was clothed in the garb of a priest, not of a bishop, however, but of one whom they have been accustomed to call presbyter.

The Romans, however, and especially all the generals, thinking that the enemy were ever making a pursuit against them, fled still more, letting slip no opportunity, urging on their running horses with whip and shout, and throwing their corselets and their other arms to the ground with haste and tumult.

But he was by no means willing to perform priestly office, lest it should ever be an obstacle to him in going again to the magistracies; for he by no means wished to let go of his hopes. And his money was at once registered to the treasury.

For they had no courage to take their stand and array against the Persians who were overtaking them, but had the hopes of safety in the feet of their horses alone; and, to say all, the flight became such that scarcely one of their horses survived for them, but when they stopped running, falling at once they perished.
Of which the emperor remitted to him a great part;
And this was a great disaster for the Romans, such as never before befell. For many of them died, and still more came under the enemy.

for he was still held by his sparing toward him. There it was in John's power, having become careless of all dangers, and having got great riches about him—both what he himself had chanced to hide and what by the emperor's will had remained with him—to live luxuriously at his pleasure, and, by prudent reckoning, to count the present circumstances happy.
And their arms and baggage animals the enemy took so great in number that the affairs of the Persians seemed to become richer from this deed.
Therefore all the Romans were simply vexed at the man, in that, having become most wicked of all demons, he held a life happier than before beyond his deserts.

And Adolius, passing through a fortress in this retreat lying in Persarmenia, was struck on the head with a stone by one of the inhabitants there and perished; and those under Justus and Peranius, having invaded the regions of Tarauna and plundered a few things, at once returned.
But God, I think, did not allow the requital for John to be settled at this, but was preparing for him a greater punishment. And it came about as follows.
There was in Cyzicus a bishop, Eusebius by name, harsh to all who came in his way, no less than John; this man the Cyzicenes, slandering to the emperor, called to trial.
But when they accomplished nothing, Eusebius having got round them with much power, certain young men, taking counsel together, killed him in the forum of Cyzicus.
Now John happened to have become most at variance with Eusebius, and from this the suspicion of the plot came to him.

There were sent, then, from the senate men to search out this defilement; who first shut John up in prison, and then, a man who had become so powerful a prefect, and who had been registered among the patricians and had mounted the chair of the consuls—than which there is nothing greater, it seems, at least in the state of the Romans—they set him up naked, like some robber or footpad, and scourging him with many strokes over the back compelled him to tell the things he had done in his life.
And though John was not very clearly convicted as the cause of the murder of Eusebius, yet the justice of God seemed to be exacting from him the penalties of the whole world.

Then, having taken from him all his money, they put him naked into the ship, wearing a single garment, and that an exceedingly coarse one, bought for a few obols, and those who escorted him bade him, wherever the ship should put in, ask bread or obols from those he met.
And thus begging everywhere along the journey, he is conveyed to Antinous in Egypt. And this is the third year they keep him shut up there.

And he, though he had come into such sufferings, did not even let go the hope of the kingship, but resolved to slander certain of the Alexandrians too, as owing gold to the treasury. So this requital for his political deeds overtook John the Cappadocian ten years later.
At that time the emperor again appointed Belisarius General of the East, and sending him to Libya he gained the country, as shall be told in the books to follow.
In the following year Chosroes the son of Cabades for the fourth time invaded the land of the Romans, leading the army against Mesopotamia.

Thus Theudibert, having marched into Italy, made his departure. And Martinus and John returned none the less, in order that the enemy might not make some assault upon those who were besieging. 26.2. But the Goths in Auximus, having learned nothing about the coming of the Franks, and despairing of the hope from Ravenna which was thus delaying, again purposed to call Wittigis to witness, but being unable to escape the guard of the enemy, they mourned. 26.3. After this, seeing one of the Romans, a Bessian by race, Burcentius by name, ranged under Narses the Armenian, alone keeping guard at midday, lest anyone from the city should go out to take the herbage, they came to a parley with him, coming nearer, and giving pledges that they would do him no harm, they bade him join them, promising that great sums of money would come to him from them. 26.4. And when they had come to the same place, the barbarians begged the man to convey a certain letter to Ravenna, fixing for him at once a stated sum of gold, and promising to give more when the letters of Wittigis should come back to them. 26.5. And the soldier, persuaded by the money, agreed to perform this and fulfilled the promise. So taking the sealed letters, he came quickly to Ravenna. And coming into the sight of Wittigis, he put the letter into his hands. 26.6. And it made plain the following: “In what condition our present affairs are you will know clearly by inquiring who in the world is the conveyer of the letter. 26.7. For it is impossible for a Goth to get outside the wall. And the most accessible of our foods is the herbage by the wall, of which we cannot now even touch as much as a little, unless we lose many in the struggle for it. To what end these things will come for us you and the Goths in Ravenna must consider.” 26.8. When Wittigis had read this, he answered as follows: “Let no one think, O dearest of all men, that we have given up, nor that we have come to such a degree of baseness as to throw away the affairs of the Goths through carelessness. 26.9. For lately the preparation for the sally had been made by me as fully as possible, and Uraïas, summoned from Mediolanum with the whole army, had come. 26.10. But the assault of the Franks, falling upon us unexpectedly, has checked all our preparations, for which I would not justly bear the blame. 26.11. For whatever is greater than human power both grants to those who have failed to be free from blame, fortune always drawing to herself the charges arising from what has been done. 26.12. Now, however (for we hear that Theudibert has been removed from our path), we shall be with you not long hence, God willing, with the whole army of the Goths. 26.13. And you ought to bear what befalls you both manfully and in a way suited to the necessity, reckoning your valour, for the sake of which I selected you from all and established you in Auximus, and respecting the reputation in which all the Goths, holding you in regard, have set you forth as a defence both of Ravenna 26.14. and of their own safety.” Having written so much, Wittigis presented the man with much money and sent him away. And he, coming to Auximus, went to his comrades, and pretending that some sickness had befallen him, and that on this account he had been idling at a certain church not far off, he again took his station at the watch where he was wont, and, escaping the notice of all, gave the letters to the enemy; which, being read aloud to the multitude, strengthened all still more, 26.15. although they were hard pressed by famine. Wherefore they were by no means willing to come over to Belisarius, who was constantly trying to win them. And again (for no army was reported to have come out from Ravenna for them, and they were now prodigiously distressed by the want of necessities) they sent Burcentius once more, making plain only this in the letter, that within five days they were no longer able to fight against the famine. And he returned to them again, having a letter of Wittigis that buoyed them up with the same hopes. 26.16. But the Romans, none the less distressed because they had made the siege so long in a deserted land, were at a loss, seeing the barbarians not giving in to them amid so many evils. 26.17. Wherefore Belisarius was eager to take alive one of the notable men among the enemy, in order that he might learn for what reason the barbarians were enduring these terrors, and Valerianus agreed to perform such a thing for him easily. 26.18. For he said there were some among his followers of the nation of the Sclaveni, who are accustomed to hide themselves behind a small stone or any chance bush and snatch up an enemy man. 26.19. And this they always display by the river Ister, where they are settled, both against the Romans and against the other barbarians. Belisarius was pleased with the proposal and ordered him to attend to the matter quickly. 26.20. So Valerianus, selecting one of the Sclaveni who was well off in greatness of body and exceedingly energetic, instructed him to bring an enemy man, affirming that great rewards would be his from Belisarius. 26.21. And he said he would do this easily in the place where the herbage happens to be; for the Goths for a long time, in want of necessities, were feeding there. 26.22. So the Sclavenian, coming at deep dawn close to the wall, hiding himself in a certain bush and drawing his body into a small space, lay concealed about the herbage. 26.23. And at daybreak a Goth came there and quickly began gathering the plants, suspecting nothing unpleasant from the bush, but looking frequently toward the camp of the enemy, lest anyone should come from there against him. 26.24. And the Sclavenian, falling upon him suddenly from behind, snatched him up, gripping the man firmly with both hands around the middle, and carried him into the camp, and bringing him put him into the hands of Valerianus. 26.25. And when he inquired in whom the Goths were trusting and what stronghold they had that they were by no means willing to come over to them, but willingly held out against the most terrible things, the barbarian told the whole story about Burcentius and convicted him to his face when he came into his sight. 26.26. And Burcentius, when he perceived that he had already become known, hid nothing of what had been done. Wherefore Belisarius gave him over to his comrades to deal with as they wished, and they not long afterward burnt him alive, the enemy watching what was being done. Thus Burcentius reaped the fruit of his love of money.

While these things were being done thus, in the meantime to John, besieging the fort of Acherontis and accomplishing nothing, there came a thought and a daring which was able both to save the senate of the Romans and to gird himself with great and prodigious fame among all men. 26.2. For hearing that Totila and the army of the Goths were assaulting the wall of Rome, selecting the most notable of the horsemen, with no warning to anyone, he went, relaxing neither night nor day, to the Campanians (for there Totila had happened to leave them), in order that, falling upon them unexpectedly, he might be able both to snatch up and to save those of the senate, since the regions there were altogether unwalled. 26.3. Now it befell about this time that Totila, fearing, as happened, lest some of the enemy should come to do mischief to the captives, sent an army of horsemen to Campania. 26.4. And when these came to the city of Menturna, it seemed best to them that the most should remain quiet there and attend to the horses (for it befell them to have met with much weariness on this journey), but to send some to observe what was at Capua and the regions there. And the country between happens to be no more than three hundred stades. 26.5. So four hundred, who happened to have fresh horses and bodies, they sent for scouting. 26.6. And by some chance it befell on that day, about the same time, that the army with John and these four hundred barbarians were at Capua, neither having heard anything before of their opponents. 26.7. And a fierce battle suddenly took place; for the moment they saw each other, they came to close quarters; and the Romans conquered by force and straightway killed the most of the enemy. 26.8. And some few of the barbarians were able to flee, and going at a run came to Menturna. When the others saw them, some bathed in blood, others still bearing the missiles in their bodies, others neither uttering anything nor reporting any of what had befallen, but still gripped by their withdrawal and showing the fear in themselves, they straightway leaped onto their horses and fled with them. 26.9. And coming to Totila, they reported that the multitude of the enemy was beyond telling, healing in this way, of course, the shame from their flight. 26.10. Now there happened to be Roman soldiers, no fewer than seventy of those who had previously deserted to the Goths, going to the regions of Campania, 26.11. who resolved to come over to John. And John found there some few men of the senate, but nearly all the women. 26.12. For when Rome was being taken, many men, fleeing and following the soldiers, came to Portus, but it befell all the women to be taken. 26.13. Clementinus, however, a patrician man, taking refuge in one of the churches there, was by no means willing to follow the Roman army, since, having previously given over to Totila and the Goths a fort which is close to Naples, he feared the emperor's anger, as is natural; and Orestes, who had been consul of the Romans, happened to be somewhere close, but for want of horses was by no means willing to go, and remained there. 26.14. So those of the senate, together with the seventy soldiers who had come over, John straightway sent to Sicily. 26.15. And Totila, hearing this, was in great mourning and hastened to avenge himself upon John for this deed. Wherefore he marched against him with the greater part of the army, leaving a portion of his followers there for the sake of a garrison. 26.16. Now John happened to have made his camp with those about him, who were a thousand, among the Lucanians, and to have previously sent scouts, who, searching out all the roads, kept watch lest an army of the enemy should go against them to do mischief. 26.17. And Totila, having such a thing in mind, that it was not possible for John and his men to sit in the camp without scouts, leaving the accustomed roads, drove against them through the mountains, which there rise many, precipitous and exceedingly high—which one could not have suspected, since these mountains are reckoned impassable. 26.18. Now those sent for the scouting by John, perceiving that an army of the enemy had come about the regions there, but learning nothing clear concerning this, but fearing, as happened, drove themselves toward the Roman camp. 26.19. And it befell them to come there together with the barbarians by night. And Totila, now gripped by much anger and not provident judgement, reaped the folly from his rage. 26.20. For having with him an army tenfold that of his opponents, and it being plain that it is advantageous for a superior army to fight in the open, and that he ought rather to come to close quarters with the enemy at dawn, in order that they might not be able to escape notice in the dark, this he by no means guarded; for he would, having netted them all, have straightway taken his opponents; but gratifying his rage, at an unseasonable hour of the night he stood over the army of the enemy. 26.21. And none of them at all looked to resistance, since the most were still sleeping, yet the Goths were not able to kill many, but the most, rising, were able to escape notice in the dark. 26.22. And getting outside the camp, into the mountains which rise many somewhere close, they ran up and were saved. 26.23. Among whom was John himself and Arufus the leader of the Eruli. And there died about a hundred Romans. 26.24. Now there was with John a certain Gilacius by name, an Armenian by race, commander of some few Armenians. This Gilacius knew neither how to speak Greek nor to utter the Latin or Gothic or any other tongue except only Armenian. 26.25. Some Goths, falling in with him, inquired who in the world he was. For they were by no means willing to kill whoever fell in their way, in order that they might not be compelled to destroy one another in the night-battle, as was natural. 26.26. And he was able to answer them nothing else than that he was Gilacius the general. For the dignity, which he had happened to receive from the emperor, he was able to learn by often hearing it. 26.27. So the barbarians, perceiving from this that he was an enemy, for the moment took him alive, but not long afterward put the man to death. 26.28. John, then, and Arufus with their followers fled with all their might and came at a run to Dryus, and the Goths, having plundered the Roman camp, withdrew.
And the emperor, learning what was being done in Croton, sent to Hellas and ordered the guards in Thermopylae to sail to Italy with all speed and to aid the besieged in Croton with all their power.

When this came to Chosroes and the Persians, they were terribly vexed, and they now repented of the peace they had made with the Romans, since they perceived that their power was advancing to greatness.
This inroad of this Chosroes was made not against the Emperor Justinian, nor against any other of men, but only against the God whom the Christians worship.

And they did accordingly; and, setting out with much eagerness and meeting with a favouring wind, they put in unexpectedly at the harbour of the people of Croton. And the barbarians, suddenly seeing the fleet, falling at once into great fear, with much tumult broke up the siege.

And Chosroes, sending envoys to Byzantium, said that he rejoiced with the Emperor Justinian, and asked with a pretended laugh to receive his share of the spoils from Libya, since the emperor would never have been able to prevail in the war against the Vandals,
For when, in the first onset, having failed of Edessa, he withdrew, much dejection had come upon him and the Magi, as having been worsted by the God of the Christians.
And some of them fled with ships to the harbour of the Tarentines, while others, going on foot, withdrew to Mount Scyllaeum. And these events much further enslaved the spirit of the Goths.
had the Persians not made the treaty with him. Then, therefore, Justinian, having gifted Chosroes with money, dismissed the envoys not long after.
Consoling which, Chosroes threatened in his palaces to enslave all the Edessenes to the country of the Persians and to make the city a pasture for sheep.

And from this Ragnaris, a most approved Gothic man, who commanded the garrison among the Tarentines, and Moras, who was set over the guards in Acherontia, came to a conference with Pacurius the son of Peranius, the Roman commander of those in Hydrus, by the counsel of their followers, on condition that, receiving pledges concerning their safety from the emperor Justinian, they should hand over themselves to the Romans with their followers and the strongholds over which they had been set as guards. On this agreement, then, Pacurius was conveyed to Byzantium.

And in the city of Daras the following thing befell. There was a certain John there, enrolled in a regiment of foot. This man, not with all the soldiers in agreement with him, but with a few, setting up a tyranny, seized the city.

With his whole army, then, coming near Edessa, he sent some of the Huns who followed him against the wall of the city which is above the hippodrome, to do no other mischief, but to seize the flocks which the shepherds chanced to have stationed in great number there by the wall, taking courage in the strength of the place, because it was exceedingly steep, and thinking the enemy would never dare to go so near the wall.
And Narses, setting out from Salona, went against Totila and the Goths with the whole Roman army, which was exceedingly great; for he had received fairly great sums from the emperor.
And sitting in the palace as in a citadel, he strengthened his tyranny day by day.
The barbarians, then, were already laying hold of the flocks, but the shepherds most vigorously prevented them.

From which he was both to gather a most considerable army and to meet the other necessities of the war, and to discharge for the soldiers in Italy all the former arrears, in which the emperor had become overdue for them a long time, they not receiving from the treasury, as is the custom, the allowances appointed for them; and moreover, to overcome the minds of those who had deserted to Totila, so that they, having become tractable through this money, might repent of their choice concerning their allegiance.

And had it not chanced that the Persians were then holding to the peace toward the Romans, irreparable evils would have come from this to the Romans. But as it was, the agreement, anticipating, prevented this, as I have said.

And many Persians having come to the aid of the Huns, the barbarians were able to take off some herd from there, but, the Roman soldiers and some of the populace having come out against the enemy, the battle became hand to hand, and the herd returned of its own accord to the shepherds.
For the emperor Justinian, having earlier carried on this war very negligently, made his preparation for it most considerable at the last.

On the fourth day from the tyranny the soldiers, taking counsel together by the purpose of Mamas the priest of the city and Anastasius, one of the notable citizens, went up into the palace at the height of noon, each having hidden a small sword under his cloak.
And one of the Huns, fighting before the rest, troubled the Romans most of all.

For when Narses saw him eager that he should campaign into Italy, he displayed an ambition befitting a general, agreeing to serve the emperor at his command on no other terms than if he were to bring with him forces able to fight.

And first, at the inner door, finding a few of the bodyguards, they at once killed them. Then, going into the men's hall, they laid hands on the tyrant; but some say that the soldiers did not do this first, but that, while they were still hesitating in the inner court and dreading the danger, one of the sausage-sellers who was with them sprang in with his cleaver and, falling unexpectedly upon John, struck him.
And some husbandman, hitting him with a sling on the right knee, struck him, and he fell prone at once from his horse to the ground, which encouraged the Romans still more.
Money, then, and men and arms in this way were procured by the emperor worthily of the Roman empire, and Narses himself, displaying a most unhesitating eagerness, roused a competent army.
And he, not struck with a mortal blow, but fleeing with much tumult, fell suddenly upon these soldiers.
And the battle, having begun in the morning, ended at midday, in which both sides, thinking they had the upper hand, parted.
For from Byzantium he brought a great multitude of Roman soldiers, and from the regions of Thrace and from the Illyrians he gathered many.

And thus they, laying hands on the man, at once set fire to the palace and burned it, that no hope might be left from there to those attempting revolutionary measures, and leading the man off to prison bound him.
And the Romans got within the wall, but the barbarians all encamped, bivouacking seven stades from the city.
And John too came with his own army and with that left to him by Germanus his father-in-law.

And one of them, fearing lest the soldiers, learning that the tyrant survived, should again cause trouble for the city, killed John, and in this way put an end to the disturbance. So the affairs concerning this tyranny turned out thus.
Then Chosroes either saw some vision of a dream or some thought came to him, that, having attempted twice, if he should be unable to take Edessa, it would befall him to take on much shame.

And Audoin, the leader of the Lombards, persuaded by great sums of money and by the compact of the alliance, picking out two thousand five hundred of his followers, men good in matters of war, sent them in alliance to him, whom there followed a retinue of more than three thousand fighting men.
Therefore he resolved to sell the withdrawal to the Edessenes for much money.

And there followed him also more than three thousand of the Herul nation, all horsemen, of whom, among others, Philemuth was leader; and a great multitude of Huns, and Dagisthaeus with his followers, released from prison for this purpose, and Cabades, with many deserting Persians, the son of Zames and grandson of Cabades the king of the Persians, of whom I made mention in the earlier books, in that, by the diligence of the chanaranges, he escaped Chosroes his uncle and came long before to the homes of the Romans; and Asbadus, a certain young man, a Gepid by race, exceptionally energetic, having with him four hundred of his own race, men good in matters of war; and Aruth, a Herul by race, but who from childhood had loved the Roman manner of life and had made the wife of Mauricius the son of Mundus his wedded wife, himself most warlike and having many of the Herul nation as followers, most approved in the dangers of war; and John, surnamed the Glutton, of whom I made mention in the earlier books, bringing a throng of Roman fighting men.
On the following day, then, Paul the interpreter, coming to the wall, said that the Romans ought to send some of the men of repute to Chosroes.

Now Narses was most munificent and exceedingly quick to benefit those in need, and, being clothed with great power from the emperor, he used his judgment more fearlessly in the matters he was eager about.
And they quickly choosing out four of the conspicuous among themselves sent them.
And from this many in earlier times, both commanders and soldiers, found him their benefactor.

When these came to the camp of the Medes, Zabergan, meeting them by the king's purpose and frightening them with many threats, inquired of them which of the two was more to be chosen, the things leading to peace or to war.

When, then, he had been appointed general against Totila and the Goths, each man most gladly wished to campaign under him, some wishing to repay old kindnesses, others awaiting, as is likely, to obtain great benefits from him.
And when they agreed that they would choose peace before dangers, "Then," said Zabergan, "you must buy this for much money."
And the Heruls especially and the other barbarians were favourably disposed toward him, having been exceptionally well treated by the man.
And the envoys said they would give as much as they had given before, when, having taken Antioch, he came against them.
And when they came very close to Venetia, he sent a messenger to the leaders of the Franks who commanded the garrisons there and asked them to grant them passage as being friends.
And Zabergan dismissed them with laughter, that, having deliberated most continually about their safety, they might thus come to them again.

But they said they would by no means grant this to Narses, openly not bringing out the cause, but hiding it as much as possible—that they made the hindrance for the sake of the advantage of the Franks or out of goodwill toward the Goths—and putting forward a pretext that seemed not very specious, that he was bringing along the Lombards, their bitterest enemies.

And a little later Chosroes, sending for them, when they came to him, recounted both how many and in what manner he had enslaved Roman places, and threatened that more dreadful things would befall the Edessenes at the hands of the Persians, unless they gave him all the money they had within the wall; for thus alone would the army depart thence, he said.

Upon this, while Narses was at a loss at the outset, and was inquiring of the Italians present with him about what was to be done, certain ones reported that, even if the Franks should permit them to make this passage, yet they would have no way to be conveyed from there to Ravenna, nor to make this journey except as far as the city of Verona.
The envoys, hearing this, agreed to buy peace from Chosroes, if he should not enjoin upon them the impossible; but the end of the danger, they said, was clear to none of all before the contest.

For Totila, picking out whatever was approved in the Gothic army, and setting over them as general Teias the Goth, a man exceptionally good in matters of war, had sent them to the city of Verona, which was subject to the Goths, in order that he might hinder, so far as possible, the passage of the Roman army. And so it was.
For war for those who wage it is never on the agreed terms. Then, indeed, with anger Chosroes bade the envoys depart as quickly as possible.

And when Teias came to be in the city of Verona, he blocked off all the passage there for the enemy, contriving by hand-wrought necessity that the regions everywhere about the river Po should be without exit and altogether impassable, and in some places making thickets and trenches and ravines, in others guarding most accurately, for the Gothic army, the deepest marshes and certain swampy places, so as to come to close quarters with the Romans, if they should make any attempt at the road from there.

On the eighth day from the siege, wishing to raise an artificial mound against the wall of the city, since he had cut the trees with their very leaves from places somewhere near and set them in a square before the wall, where an arrow from the city could not reach, and heaping a great quantity of earth above the trees, he threw on a great mass of stones, not suited for building, but cut at random, caring only for this, that the mound might rise to a great height as quickly as possible.

And Totila contrived these things, thinking that by the coast of the Ionian gulf it would never be possible for the Romans to make the journey, since very many navigable rivers, having their outlets there, render the regions there altogether impassable; and that they had by no means so great a multitude of ships as to ferry across the Ionian gulf all together with the whole army, while, if they should sail in small numbers, he himself, with the remaining Gothic army, would with no toil check those who at any time disembarked.
And ever throwing in long pieces of wood between the earth and the stones, he made a binding of the work,

With such a purpose, then, Totila gave these orders, and Teias did them. But when Narses was exceedingly at a loss, John the son of Vitalian, being experienced in the regions there, advised him to go with the whole army along the coast, the men there being subject to them, as has been shown before, and to have some of the ships and many boats follow along.

lest, having become high, it be weak. But Peter the Roman general (for he chanced to be there with Martin and Peranius), wishing to check those who were doing this, sent some of the Huns who followed him against them.

For whenever the army should come to the outlets of the rivers, making a bridge from these boats over the surge of the river, they would more easily and with less toil make the crossing. John advised this, and Narses was persuaded, and in this way he was conveyed with the whole army to Ravenna.
And they, coming suddenly, killed many, and most of all one of the bodyguards, Argek by name;
for he alone killed twenty-seven. But the barbarians for the rest keeping exact guard, no one could come out against them any longer.

And when the craftsmen of this work, advancing, came within bowshot, the Romans, now defending themselves most vigorously from the wall, plied both the slings and the bows against them. Therefore the barbarians devised the following.

Coverings of goat's hair, which they call Cilician cloths, having sufficient thickness and length, hanging them from long pieces of wood, they ever set in front of those working the agesta (for so the Romans called what was being done in the Latin tongue).
For there neither fire-bearing arrows nor the other missiles could reach, but, being repelled there upon the coverings, all remained.

And then the Romans, fallen into great fear, sent the envoys to Chosroes with much tumult, and Stephanus with them, learned among the physicians of his time, who, having once cured Cabades the son of Perozes when sick, had become master of great wealth from him.
He, when he came with the others to Chosroes, spoke as follows: "All from of old have held the humanity of a king to be the mark of a good one.
Then, O most mighty King, to you working slaughters and battles and enslavements of cities, it will perhaps be possible to obtain other names, but to seem to be good will never be.
And yet least of all ought anything paltry to befall the city of the Edessenes from you.

For from there I have come, who, foreseeing nothing of what was to be, reared you and became a counsellor to your father, that he should set you up as successor to his rule, and so became most to blame for the kingship of the Persians to you, and for the present evils to my fatherland.
For men for the most part fasten on themselves most of the misfortunes of what shall come.
But if any memory of such a benefit comes upon you, do us no further harm, giving me this recompense, from which, O King, it will befall you not to seem most savage." So much Stephanus said.
But Chosroes agreed that he would not depart thence before the Romans handed over to him both Peter and Peranius, because they, being his ancestral slaves, had dared to oppose him.

And if this were not pleasing for the Romans to do, but they were forced to choose one of two things, either to give him five hundred centenaria of gold, or to receive into the city some of his intimates, who, having searched out all the money, would come to him bringing all the gold and silver that chanced to be there,

but would leave the rest to the owners to have. These things Chosroes hurled out, having hope of taking Edessa with no trouble. And the envoys (for all that he announced seemed impossible to them), perplexed and exceedingly distressed, walked to the city.
And when, getting within the wall, they reported the things from Chosroes, the city became full of tumult and lamentations.
