The construction of the mound, then, both rose to a great height and went forward with much haste. And the Romans, not knowing what to do, again sent the envoys to Chosroes.

And they, when they came to the camp of the enemy, saying they had come to beg about the same things, obtained no speech at all from the Persians, but, driven thence with insult and much tumult, went to the city.

At first, then, the Romans attempted to overtop the wall facing the mound with another building; but when this too the work of the Persians far surpassed already, they stood off from the building, and persuaded Martin to arrange the matters about the agreement in whatever way he wished. And he, coming very near the camp of the enemy, came to a parley with some of the commanders among the Persians.

And they, deceiving Martin, said that their king wished peace, but that he himself was by no means able to persuade the Emperor of the Romans, leaving off his contentiousness against Chosroes, ever to make peace with him;

since even Belisarius—who, that he far surpassed Martin in power and dignity not even he himself would deny—had lately persuaded the King of the Persians, who was indeed in the midst of the Romans, to depart thence to the country of the Persians, promising that envoys would come to him not long after from Byzantium and confirm the peace in security, but had done none of what was agreed, having been unable to force the judgement of the Emperor Justinian.

Meanwhile the Romans did as follows. Having made a trench from the city beneath the mound of the enemy, they bade those digging not let go of this work, until they should get under the middle of the mound. For there they purposed to burn this mound.

And Belisarius, seeing that the barbarians were holding out against the hardship none the less, purposed to set the plot against the water, thinking that in this way he would take the enemy more easily and with less trouble. 27.2. And, since there was a certain spring of Auximus toward the north wind in a precipitous place, distant about a stone's throw from the wall, which let its stream little by little into a certain cistern there from of old, and the cistern, having become full from this small inflow, allowed those in Auximus to draw water with no toil—a thought came to Belisarius that, if the water did not collect there, the barbarians, being shot at by the enemy, would never be able in a long time to fill their jars from the inflow. 27.3. Wishing, then, to destroy the cistern, he devised the following. Arming the whole army, and drawing it up in a circle about the wall as if for battle, he gave his opponents the impression that he was about immediately to assault the wall from all sides. 27.4. Wherefore the Goths, dreading the assault, remained quiet on the battlements, intending to defend themselves from there against the enemy. 27.5. In the meantime Belisarius brought into the cistern five Isaurians experienced in building, with axes and other tools suited for the cutting of stones, hidden by a multitude of shields, and ordered them to destroy and break up the walls with all their might quickly. 27.6. And the barbarians for a while suspected that the men were going against the wall, and kept quiet, in order that, when they should come very close, they might shoot them easily, having no thought of what was being done; but when they saw the Isaurians inside the cistern, they hurled all their stones and arrows at them. 27.7. Then all the rest of the Romans withdrew at a run, but the five Isaurians alone, when they had got into safety, set to work; for a vault had been made over the water for the sake of shade by the men of old there. 27.8. And getting inside this, they took no heed of the enemy, although they shot many missiles. 27.9. Wherefore the Goths no longer endured to remain inside the wall, but opening the postern there, all went against the Isaurians, gripped by much anger and tumult. 27.10. And the Romans, Belisarius urging them on, met them with much eagerness. So a fierce battle took place, having for a long time a shoving and much slaughter on both sides. 27.11. But of the Romans more in number fell. For the barbarians, defending themselves from above, few though they were, overpowered many, and prevailing in the shoving, killed more than they themselves died. 27.12. The Romans, however, were by no means willing to give in, ashamed before Belisarius who was present and urging them on with shouting. 27.13. Then indeed a missile came at the belly of the general with a great rush, from one of the enemy, whether by some chance or by design shot at that point. 27.14. This Belisarius did not at all see. For he was able neither to guard against it nor to turn aside in any way. But a certain guard, Unigastus by name, standing by him, perceived it not far from the belly of Belisarius, and throwing forward his right hand, saved the general from the unexpected, but himself, struck by the arrow, immediately, being in great pain, withdrew. 27.15. And afterward, the tendons being cut, he was no longer able to use the hand. And the battle, having begun in the morning, came to midday. 27.16. And seven Armenian men, ranged under Narses and Aratius, displayed deeds worthy of valour, running about the difficult ground, which was most steep, as if on the level, and killing those of the enemy who always withstood them, until, thrusting back the barbarians there, they routed them. 27.17. And the rest of the Romans, seeing the enemy now giving in, pursued them, and the rout became brilliant, and the barbarians got inside the wall again. 27.18. So the Romans thought that the cistern had been destroyed and that the whole work had been accomplished by the Isaurians, but they had not been able to take away even so much as a pebble from there. 27.19. For the ancient craftsmen, taking the greatest care for valour in their works, had so wrought this structure too that it yielded neither to time nor to the plotting of men. 27.20. So the Isaurians, having accomplished nothing, when they saw the Romans masters of the place, departing from the cistern, withdrew to the camp. 27.21. Wherefore Belisarius ordered the soldiers to throw into the water the dead bodies of animals and herbs of a kind naturally sufficient for the destruction of man, and to throw in there and slake quicklime burnt most thoroughly (which they anciently were accustomed to call titanos, but now asbestos). 27.22. And they did so, but the barbarians during this time used a well inside the wall which had a very small amount of water, in less measure than their need. 27.23. And for the rest Belisarius was eager neither to take the place by force nor to display any plot concerning water or anything else, having the hope of prevailing over the enemy by famine alone. 27.24. And from this he most strongly attended to the guard. And the Goths, still waiting for the army from Ravenna, kept quiet in much want of the necessities. 27.25. And now the besieged in Fisula were most hard pressed by famine, and being unable to bear the evil, and despairing also of the hope from Ravenna, resolved to come over to their opponents. 27.26. So coming to a parley with Cyprianus and Justinus, and taking pledges concerning their lives, they surrendered both themselves and the fort by agreement. And Cyprianus and his men, taking them along with the Roman army, and establishing a sufficient garrison in Fisula, came to Auximus. 27.27. And Belisarius, constantly showing their commanders to the barbarians in Auximus, exhorted them to let go of their madness, shaking off the hope from Ravenna; for there would never be any profit for them either, but, after being most grievously worn down by hardship, they would none the less come to the same fortune as those in Fisula. 27.28. And they, after much deliberation among themselves, since they could no longer hold out against the famine, admitted his words and saw fit to surrender the city, on condition that they themselves should march to Ravenna unharmed with their goods. 27.29. Wherefore Belisarius was at a loss before the present situation, thinking it inexpedient that enemies of such valour and such numbers should mingle with those in Ravenna, but being by no means willing to be too late for the opportunity, and to go against Ravenna and Wittigis while affairs were still in suspense. 27.30. For the Franks disturbed him, being very likely to come immediately to the help of the Goths. Being eager to forestall their coming, he was unable to break off the siege while Auximus was not yet taken. 27.31. And the soldiers would not allow him to concede their goods to the barbarians, displaying the many wounds which they had received there from them, and enumerating all the toils that had befallen them in this siege, of which, they affirmed, the spoils of the conquered were the prizes. 27.32. At last both the Romans, compelled by the sharpness of the opportunity, and the Goths, forced by famine, came to an agreement with one another, on condition that the Romans should distribute half of the goods among themselves, and the Goths, keeping the remainder, should be subjects of the emperor. 27.33. Both, then, gave pledges concerning these things—the commanders of the Romans that the agreements should be binding, and the Goths that they would hide nothing whatever of the goods. 27.34. And thus they distributed all the goods, and the Romans held Auximus, and the barbarians mingled with the emperor's army.

So the armies among the Italians went on thus. And the emperor Justinian resolved to send another army against the Goths and Totila, led by the letters of Belisarius, since he urged him to this, often signifying their present situation. 27.2. First, then, he sent Pacurius the son of Peranius and Sergius the nephew of Solomon with some few men. And these, coming to Italy, immediately joined the rest of the army. 27.3. After this he sent Verus with three hundred Eruli and Varazes an Armenian by race with eight hundred Armenians, and, removing Valerianus the general of the Armenians from there with the guards and shield-bearers following him, who were more than a thousand, ordered him to go to Italy. 27.4. Verus, then, putting in first at Dryus and leaving his ships there, was by no means willing to remain there, where the camp of John was, but riding with those about him went forward. 27.5. For this was a man not in earnest, but for the most part given over to the disease of drunkenness, and from this always gripped by unconsidered boldness. 27.6. And when they came close to the city of Brentesium, encamping there they remained. When Totila learned this, he said, “Verus is one of two things: either he is using a great power, or he is gripped by much folly. 27.7. Let us go against him at once, then, in order that we may either make trial of the man's power or that he may perceive his own 27.8. folly.” Saying this, Totila went against him with a great army, but the Eruli, observing the enemy now present, took refuge in a certain wood that was somewhere near. 27.9. And the enemy, encircling them, destroyed more than two hundred, and were about to seize Verus himself and the rest who were hiding in the thorns, but a certain fortune that befell them saved them unexpectedly. 27.10. For the ships in which Varazes and the Armenians with him were sailing suddenly put in at the shore there. When Totila saw this, suspecting that the army of the enemy was more than it was, setting out immediately he drove away from there, and Verus and his men gladly came at a run to the ships. 27.11. And Varazes resolved to sail no farther forward, but came with them to Taras, where John the nephew of Vitalian arrived with the whole army not long afterward. These things, then, proceeded thus. 27.12. And the emperor wrote to Belisarius that he had sent him a large army, with which he ought, joining the enemy in Calabria, to come to close quarters. 27.13. And now Valerianus too, having come near the Ionian Gulf, thought it inexpedient to ferry across for the present at least. 27.14. For the provisions would by no means suffice for the soldiers and horses at that time of the year, since it was about the winter solstice. 27.15. And sending three hundred of his followers to John, he agreed that, having wintered, he too would come at the beginning of spring. 27.16. Belisarius, then, when he had read the emperor's letter, selecting nine hundred for their valour, seven hundred horse and two hundred foot, and establishing all the rest for the guard of the country there, and setting Conon over them as commander, immediately sailed for Sicily. 27.17. And from there he set out, purposing to put in at the harbour of Taras, having on his left the place called Scylaeum, on which the poets say Scylla came into being—not because the bestial little woman, as those men say, was there, but because a great quantity of pups, which they now call little dogs, happen to be there in the strait from of old even to my time. 27.18. For names, at the beginning, are always fitting to things, but report, carrying them around to some other men, makes there opinions that are not right, through ignorance of the true. 27.19. And time, going on thus, immediately becomes a strong artificer of the myth, and, as is natural, by the license of his art makes the poets witnesses of what did not happen. Thus the people of the place anciently named one promontory of the island of Corcyra which is to the east the Dog's Head, but others wish from this that the people there are dog-headed. 27.20. And indeed they call some of the Pisidians Lycocranitae, not because they have the heads of wolves, but because the mountain that rises there was called Lycu Cranus (Wolf's Skull). But let these things seem and be said in whatever way is pleasing to each. But I return to the point from which I digressed.

And while these things were being done thus, meanwhile the following happened. Ildigisal, a Lombard man, of whom I made mention in the earlier books as being an enemy of Audoin, who ruled these barbarians (for Audoin held by force the rule which belonged to Ildigisal by descent), fled from his ancestral homes and was conveyed to Byzantium.
And the trench advancing about the middle of the mound, a certain noise came to the Persians standing above.

And when he came there, the emperor Justinian thought him exceedingly worthy of kindness, and appointed him commander of one of the companies stationed for the guard of the Palace, which they call the Scholae.
And perceiving what was being done, they themselves, beginning from above on either side of the middle, dug, so that they might catch the Romans doing mischief there.
And there followed him men of the Lombard nation, good in matters of war, no fewer than three hundred, who first had one dwelling-place in Thrace.

When the Romans learned this, they refrained from it, throwing earth on the emptied space, but from the extremity of the mound below, which chanced to be by the wall, carrying out wood and stones and earth, they made as it were the shape of a little house, and threw in there dry stumps of the most easily burning trees, soaked in oil made of cedar and in much sulphur and pitch.

Ildigisal, then, Audoin demanded back from the emperor Justinian, as being a friend and ally of the Romans, exacting from him, as the wage of friendship, the betrayal of his suppliant; but the emperor in no way gave him up.

And they had these things in readiness, but the commanders of the Persians, often meeting Martin, discoursed such things as I have said, giving an impression that they would accept the arguments about peace.

And some time later Ildigisal, complaining that his honour and his maintenance were more scanty than according to his worth and the reputation of the Romans, seemed to be much distressed. This Goar perceived, a Goth, long before a spear-captive in this war from Dalmatia, who had come there when Vittigis the king of the Goths was carrying on the war against the Romans;

But when the mound was now finished for them, and, approaching the wall of the city, rose high overtopping it greatly, they dismissed Martin, expressly refusing the agreement, and were about to set to work for the rest.

and being passionate and exceedingly energetic, he had continued struggling against the fortune present to him. And when the Goths, after the mastery of Vittigis, looked to revolt, taking up arms against the emperor, he was caught openly working mischief against the state. And, punished with exile, he was conveyed to the city of Antinous in Egypt, and much time was spent by him in this penalty.

Therefore the Romans at once burned the stumps of the trees which had been prepared for this. And the fire having burned a part of the mound, but not yet been able to reach through the whole, it chanced that all the wood was consumed. For they ever threw other wood into the trench, letting slip no opportunity.

But afterwards the emperor, pitying him, brought him back to Byzantium. This Goar, seeing Ildigisal vexed, as I have said, most assiduously admonishing him, persuaded him to use flight, agreeing to depart from Byzantium together with him.

And the fire now working through the whole mound, a smoke appeared above everywhere on the mound by night, and the Romans, not yet wishing to give the Persians perception of what was being done, devised the following.

And when this plan pleased them, they fled suddenly with a few men, and, coming to Apros, the Thracian city, mingled with the Lombards there. And, lighting upon the imperial horse-pastures, they brought along from there a great number of horses and went forward.

Filling small vessels with coals and fire, they sent these and fire-bearing arrows thickly everywhere over the mound; which the Persians, who had guard there, going about with all haste, extinguished, and thought that from this the smoke arose.
When the emperor perceived this, sending to all Thrace and Illyria, he gave orders to all the commanders and soldiers to confront these runaways with all their might.
And as the evil advanced, the barbarians came to the rescue in great multitude, but the Romans, shooting at them from the wall, killed many.

And first a few of the Huns called Cutrigurs (who, having risen from their ancestral homes, as I have related a little before, the emperor granting it, settled in Thrace) came to blows with these fugitives.
There Chosroes too came about sunrise, and the greater part of the army followed him, and going up onto the mound he first got perception of the evil.

And, being worsted in battle, some of them fell, while the rest, turning, no longer pursued, but remained there. And thus Ildigisal and Goar with their followers passed through all Thrace, with no one harassing them.
For he declared that the cause of the smoke was below, not from what the enemy were shooting, and bade the whole army come to the rescue quickly.
And, coming to be in Illyria, they found a Roman army gathered with care for their harm.

And the Romans, taking courage, insulted them, while of the barbarians some, throwing on earth, others water, where the smoke showed through, hoped to get the better of the danger, but were able to accomplish nothing at all.
And of this army, among others, Aratius and Rhecithancus and Leonianus and Arimuth were commanders, who happened to have been riding the whole day.

For where the earth was thrown on, there the smoke, as is likely, was checked, but elsewhere not long after it gave out, the fire compelling itself to force its exit where it could; and the water, where it most fell, made the pitch and the sulphur work much more and brought the material in its path to a height, and ever led the fire forward, since within the mound it was by no means able to reach with so much water as to be able to quench the flame by excess.
And coming to a wooded place about lamp-lighting time, they halted, intending to bivouac and pass the night there.
And the smoke toward late afternoon became so great that it was manifest both to the Carrhenes and to certain others dwelling far beyond.
These commanders, then, gave orders to the soldiers, among other things, to take care of their own horses and to refresh themselves beside the river flowing there, soothing the weariness of the road.
And many Persians and Romans having gone up over the mound, and a battle and push having arisen there, the Romans conquered.
And they themselves, each taking three or four bodyguards along, secretly drank of the river; for they were held, as was likely, by grievous thirst.
Then too the flame, brilliantly given out, appeared above the mound, and the Persians refrained from this work.

And those about Goar and Ildigisal, being somewhere near and having sent scouts, learned these things. And, standing over them unexpectedly as they drank, they killed them all, and thenceforth more fearlessly arranged the matters of their journey as they wished.
On the sixth day from this, at deep dawn, with ladders they secretly assaulted a portion of the wall where the fortress is named.
For the soldiers, having become without commanders, were at a loss and, altogether helpless, marched back. Goar, then, and Ildigisal, escaping thus, came to the Gepids.
And the Romans who had guard there sleeping a gentle sleep, since the night was going to its end, they quietly set the ladders against the wall and were already climbing up.

And there happened to be also a certain man of the Gepids, Ustrigotthus by name, who had fled to the Lombards in the following manner. Elemundus, who had been king of the Gepids, had not long before vanished from among men by sickness, and, only this Ustrigotthus, his son, being left, whom Thorisin, having done violence to him (for he was still a stripling), held the rule.
But one of the husbandmen, alone awake among all the Romans, with shouting and much tumult roused them all.
Wherefore the boy, having no way to avenge himself upon the wrongdoer, rising up from his ancestral homes, went off to the Lombards, who were enemies of the Gepids.
And a fierce battle having arisen, the Persians were worsted, and withdrew to the camp, leaving there the ladders, which the Romans drew up at their pleasure.

And there came to be a little later between the Gepids and the emperor Justinian and the nation of the Lombards a reconciliation, and they bound one another by most terrible oaths that they would thenceforth preserve an endless friendship toward one another.
And Chosroes about midday sent a great portion of the army against the so-called great gate as though to storm the wall.

And when the matters of the reconciliation had been most surely accomplished for them, the emperor Justinian and Audoin the leader of the Lombards, sending to Thorisin the ruler of the Gepids, demanded Ildigisal back as a common enemy, asking him to make the betrayal of his own suppliant a first display of his friendship toward them.
Whom the Romans, meeting—not soldiers only, but also husbandmen and some of the populace—and conquering in battle, routed the barbarians by far.
And he, conferring with the men of repute among the Gepids about the present matter, eagerly inquired whether he should do what was asked by the two kings.
And the Persians being still pursued, Paul the interpreter, coming from Chosroes, reported among the Romans that Rhecinarius had come from Byzantium for the peace, and thus both sides parted.
But they outright forbade it, maintaining that it was better for the nation of the Gepids to perish very straightway, women and all offspring, than to become unholy by such an impiety.
Already some days before Rhecinarius had come to the camp of the barbarians.

Hearing this, Thorisin fell into helplessness. For he could neither, his subjects being unwilling, fulfil the deed, nor was he willing to renew war, which had been ended with much toil and time, against the Romans and the Lombards. Afterwards, however, he devised the following.

But the Persians by no means brought this out to the Romans, plainly awaiting the plot against the wall, that, if they should be able to take it, they might seem in no way to transgress against the treaties, but, worsted, which happened, they might make the terms of the agreement, the Romans inviting them to it.
Sending to Audoin, he demanded back the son of Elemundus, Ustrigotthus, urging him to a like sin to his own, and calling for an exchange of the betrayal of the suppliants.

When Rhecinarius got within the gates, the Persians thought fit that those who would dispose the peace should go to Chosroes very soon, but the Romans said that envoys would be sent three days later; for now Martin the general was badly affected in body.
For he had hope that, by their shrinking from the like absurdity, he would check their demand; but Audoin would, with no delay, seize him by lawlessness and by the agreement.

And Chosroes, suspecting that the word was not sound, prepared the matters of battle. And then he threw a very great quantity of bricks onto the mound, and two days later went against the wall of the city with his whole army as though to storm it.

And, these things being decided by them, knowing well that neither the Lombards nor the Gepids were willing to take a share of the pollution among themselves, they did nothing openly, but each by craft killed the other's enemy.
And setting at each gate some of the commanders and a portion of the army, and surrounding the whole wall thus, he brought up ladders and engines against it.

In what manner, however, I forbear to say; for the accounts about them do not agree with one another, but differ greatly, as is the way with the most secret of matters. The matters concerning Ildigisal and Ustrigotthus, then, ended thus.
And behind he arranged all the Saracens with some of the Persians, not that they should assault the wall, but that, the city being taken, they themselves might net and seize the fugitives.
With such a purpose Chosroes thus arranged the army. And the battle, having begun in the morning, at first the affairs of the Persians had the upper hand.
For many fought against very few, since most of the Romans were unaware of what was being done and altogether unprepared.
But as the engagement advanced, the city became full of tumult and disturbance, and all now, with the very women and little children, went up onto the wall.
Those in their prime, then, with the soldiers, defended themselves against the enemy most vigorously, and many of the husbandmen displayed marvellous deeds against the barbarians.
And children and women with the aged gathered stones for the fighters and rendered other service.

And some, filling many cauldrons with oil and heating them everywhere on the wall for a sufficient time and pouring the oil, exceedingly boiling, with certain sprinklers, distressed still more the enemy who approached the wall.
And the Persians now, giving up, threw down their arms, and coming into the king's sight said they were no longer able to hold out against the toil.
But Chosroes, held by much anger and urging all on with threats, drove them against the enemy.
And they with shouting and much tumult brought up the towers and the other engines to the wall and set on the ladders, as though to take the city at the first shout.
But the Romans shooting thickly and defending themselves with all might, the barbarians were routed by force, and the Romans mocked Chosroes as he withdrew, inviting him to storm the wall.
Only Azarethes about the gates called the Soenae fought with his followers, where they call the place Tripyrgia.

And the Romans there not being a match for them, but giving up against the assaults, the barbarians, having now broken through the outer wall, which they call the outwork, in many places, pressed most vigorously on those who defended themselves from the great wall, until Peranius with many soldiers and some of the Edessenes came out against them and, conquering in battle, drove them off.

And the storming of the wall, having begun in the morning, ended toward late afternoon, and both sides remained quietly that night, the Persians fearing for their palisades and for themselves, and the Romans gathering stones onto the battlements and making all other preparation, as though to fight on the morrow with the enemy when they should assault the wall.

On the following day, then, none of the barbarians came to the wall, but on the day after, a portion of the army, Chosroes urging them on, assaulted the gates called Barlaus, but the Romans meeting them, they were worsted by far in the battle and in a short time withdrew to the camp.
And then Paul the Persian interpreter, coming to the wall, called Martin, that he might dispose the matters of the agreement.

And thus, Martin having come to a parley with the commanders of the Persians, they came to terms, and Chosroes, having received five centenaria from the Edessenes, left them in writing the agreement to do the Romans no further harm, and burning all the palisades withdrew home with his whole army.

About this time two generals of the Romans died, Justus the emperor's nephew and Peranius the Iberian, Justus destroyed by disease, but it befell Peranius, having fallen from his horse in a hunt, to be burst.

And when Belisarius had taken Auximus, he was eager to besiege Ravenna and led the whole army there. And sending Magnus with a large multitude beyond Ravenna, he ordered him always to go about the bank of the river Padus and keep guard, in order that for the future the Goths might not bring in provisions from there. 28.2. And Vitalius too, coming to him with an army from Dalmatia, guarded the other bank of the river. There befell them a certain chance, making manifest at once that fortune herself directs the affairs of both sides. 28.3. For the Goths, having before collected many boats in Liguria, had let them down into the Padus, intending, after filling them with grain and the other provisions, to sail to Ravenna. 28.4. But the water of this river at that time so failed that it was altogether impossible to sail upon it, until the Romans, coming up, took the boats with all their cargoes. 28.5. And the river not long afterward, returning to its proper flow, became navigable again for the rest of the time. And we know by report that this never happened to it before. 28.6. And now the barbarians began to be in want of provisions. For they could neither bring anything in through the Ionian Gulf, the enemy holding mastery of the sea everywhere, and they had been shut off from the river. 28.7. And the rulers of the Franks, perceiving what was being done, and wishing to make Italy their own, sent envoys to Wittigis, offering a promise of alliance, 28.8. on condition that they should rule the land together with him. When Belisarius heard this, he too sent envoys to oppose the Germans, among others Theodosius, who was set over his own household. 28.9. So first the envoys of the Germans, coming into the sight of Wittigis, spoke as follows: “The rulers of the Germans have sent us, being distressed because they have heard that you are being besieged by Belisarius, and being eager to help you as quickly as possible according to the alliance. 28.10. Now we think that an army of fighting men no fewer than fifty thousand has already crossed the Alps, with whom we boast that we shall overwhelm the whole Roman army with our axes in the first charge. 28.11. And you it behoves to follow in purpose not those who would enslave you, but those who set themselves to the danger of war out of goodwill toward the Goths. 28.12. And besides, if you take up arms with us, no hope will be left to the Romans of coming to close quarters with both armies, but from the very outset, with no toil, we shall bind on the mastery of the war. 28.13. But if the Goths array themselves with the Romans, not even so will they hold out against the nation of the Franks (for the contest will not be of equal forces), but it will be your lot to be defeated along with the bitterest enemies of all. 28.14. And to go to manifest evil, when it is possible to be saved free from danger, is much folly. And altogether the race of the Romans is faithless to all barbarians, since it is by nature hostile. 28.15. We, then, will rule the whole of Italy together with you, if you wish, and will administer the land in whatever way may seem best. But it is fitting for you and the Goths to choose whatever is going to be advantageous to you.” The Franks said so much. 28.16. And the envoys of Belisarius, coming forward, spoke as follows: “That the multitude of Germans, with which these men see fit to frighten you, will do no harm to the emperor's army, why should one speak at length among you, to whom, through long experience, it has befallen to know thoroughly every turn of war, and that valour is least wont to be inferior to a throng of men? 28.17. For we forbear to say that to the emperor above all it is possible to prevail over the enemy by a multitude of soldiers. And the good faith of these men, which they boast they use toward all barbarians, except indeed the Thuringians and the nation of the Burgundians, has been displayed by them toward you their allies. 28.18. For we would gladly ask the Franks by what god they intend to swear that they affirm they will give the assurance of good faith to you. 28.19. For the god already sworn by them, in what manner they have honoured him, you doubtless know; they who, having received such great sums of money, and all the Gauls, from you for alliance, not only by no means resolved to share the danger with you, but also took up arms so wantonly against you, if any account survives among you of what happened by the Padus. 28.20. And what need is there, by mentioning what is past, to convict the impiety of the Franks? Nothing could be more abominable than their present embassy. 28.21. For, as if having forgotten what they themselves agreed and swore by the treaties, they see fit to share everything in common with you. 28.22. And if they should obtain this too from you, to what end the insatiableness of their love of money will come for them, it is fitting to consider.” 28.23. So much the envoys of Belisarius also said. And Wittigis, after much consultation with the best of the Goths, chose the agreements with the emperor and dismissed the envoys of the Germans without accomplishing anything. And for the rest the Goths and Romans now treated with one another, but Belisarius none the less kept watch that the barbarians might not bring in provisions. 28.24. And he ordered Vitalius, going into Venetia, to bring in as much as possible of the places there, while he himself, sending Ildiger, guarded the Padus on both sides, in order that the barbarians might the more, through want of necessities, give in and make the agreements in the way he wished. 28.25. And when he learned that much grain was still stored in public buildings inside Ravenna, he persuaded with money one of the inhabitants there to set fire secretly to these buildings together with the grain. 28.26. And they say that these things were destroyed by the resolve of Matasuntha, the wife of Wittigis. And when the grain had been suddenly burnt, some suspected that the deed had been done by design, while others suspected that the place had been struck by lightning. 28.27. And reckoning both, the Goths and Wittigis fell into helplessness still more, no longer able to trust even themselves and thinking that they were being warred upon by God. These things, then, were thus done. 28.28. In the Alps which separate the Gauls and the Ligurians, which the Romans call the Cottian Alps, there happen to be many forts. 28.29. There Goths, many and excellent, settled from of old together with their wives and children, held the guard, whom, when Belisarius heard that they wished to come over to him, he sent one of his followers, Thomas by name, with some few men, in order that, giving pledges, they might win over the barbarians there by agreement. 28.30. And when they had come to the Alps, Sisigis, who commanded the watch-stations there, receiving them in one of the forts, both came over himself and induced each of the others to this. 28.31. In the meantime Uraïas, selecting four thousand from the Ligurians and from the forts in the Alps, went quickly to Ravenna to help. 28.32. And these, when they learned what Sisigis had done, fearing for their own families, 28.33. saw fit to go there first. Wherefore Uraïas went with the whole army to the Cottian Alps and besieged Sisigis together with Thomas and his men. And when John, the nephew of Vitalian, and Martinus learned this (for they happened to be very close to the river Padus), they quickly came to the aid with the whole army, and falling by a sudden raid upon some of the forts in the Alps, took them, and enslaved those who dwelt there, among whom it befell that there were many children and wives of those serving under Uraïas. 28.34. For very many of them, setting out from these forts, followed him. 28.35. And these, when they learned that their own families had been taken, deserting the camp of the Goths suddenly, resolved to come over to John and his men, and from this Uraïas was able neither to accomplish anything there nor to help the Goths in danger in Ravenna, but coming with a few men to Liguria without accomplishing anything, remained quiet. And Belisarius at his ease shut up Wittigis and the notable Goths in Ravenna.

Belisarius, then, was eager to go straight to Taras. Now there is a certain crescent-shaped shore there, where, the beach receding, the sea goes up, as it were in a gulf, far into the land. 28.2. And the whole sailing-course of this shore extends to a thousand stades, and on either side, by the outlet of the current, lie two towns: one, Croton, toward the setting sun, and Taras toward the rising. 28.3. And in the middle of the beach the city of Thurii is settled. And as the storm was against him and the wind, with much surge, forced him, and by no means permitted the ships to go farther forward, he put in at the harbour of the people of Croton. 28.4. So Belisarius, since he neither found any fort there nor had any place from which provisions might be brought for the soldiers, himself with his wife and the foot-soldiers remained there, in order that he might be able from there to summon and direct the army with John; 28.5. but he ordered all the horsemen to go forward and encamp by the entrances of the country, setting Phazas the Iberian and Barbation the spearman over them. 28.6. For thus he thought they would most easily provide all the provisions for themselves and their own horses, and would be able, as is natural, to repel the enemy in the narrow place. 28.7. For the mountains of the Lucanians, extending to the Bruttii and coming together in a narrow space, make there only two very narrow entrances, of which one is called Petra Haematos (Rock of Blood) in the Latin tongue, and the other the people of the place are wont to call Lavula. 28.8. There by the shore is Ruscianae, the port of the Thurii, and above it about sixty stades the ancient Romans built a most strong fort. This John had long before happened to occupy and establish a garrison worthy of account. 28.9. So the soldiers of Belisarius, going somewhere there, fell in with an army of the enemy, which Totila had sent to make trial of the fort there. 28.10. And coming immediately to close quarters with them, they routed them by their valour with no toil, although being inferior by far in number, and destroyed more than two hundred. 28.11. And the rest, fleeing, came to Totila and reported all that had befallen; and the Romans, encamping there, remained, and, being without a leader and victorious, used a more fearless mode of life. 28.12. For neither, being gathered, did they remain quiet, nor, sitting close to the narrow place, did they guard the entrances, but, turning to disregard, by night they slept scattered as far as possible from one another, and in the day went about searching for provisions, neither sending out any for scouting nor having deliberated anything else concerning safety. 28.13. Totila, then, when he learned all this, selecting three thousand horsemen from the whole camp, went against the enemy. 28.14. And falling upon them unexpectedly, not drawn up but going about thus as has been said, 28.15. he struck them all with consternation and threw them into confusion. There Phazas (for he happened to be encamped somewhere close), meeting the enemy and displaying deeds worthy of valour, became the cause for some of escaping, but he himself with all those about him died. 28.16. And this was a great disaster for the Romans, since all placed their hope in them as being pre-eminent in matters of war. 28.17. All who were able to flee, however, were saved as it became possible for each. And first Barbation the guard of Belisarius, fleeing with all his might with two others, came to Croton. And reporting the present fortune, he added that he thought the barbarians would be present immediately. 28.18. When Belisarius heard this, he was in great mourning and leaped into the ships. And setting out from there and meeting a wind, on that day they put in at Messana of Sicily, which is distant seven hundred stades from Croton and lies opposite Rhegium.
And to those about Narses, when they came to the city of Ravenna, there were joined Valerian and Justin the generals, and whatever other Roman army had been left there.

Therefore the emperor, setting up others in their place, sent Marcellus, his own nephew just becoming bearded, and Constantianus, who a little before had been sent together with Sergius as envoy to Chosroes.
And when a period of nine days had been spent by them in Ravenna, Usdrilas, a Goth, exceptionally good in matters of war, commander of the garrison in Ariminum, wrote to Valerian thus:
Then the Emperor Justinian sent envoys to Chosroes for the agreement, Constantianus and Sergius.

"Having seized everything with rumours, and having now held all Italy with phantoms, and putting on airs beyond what is human, and having thus, as you suppose, frightened the Goths, you then sit now in Ravenna, in order, I think, to be as little plain as possible to the enemy by hiding yourselves—still keeping up this spirit—but with a motley throng of barbarians wearing out a country that belongs to you from no quarter. But rise up as quickly as possible and lay hold of deeds of war at last, and show yourselves to the Goths, and do not hang us up with longer hopes,
And they overtake him in Assyria, where there are two towns, Seleucia and Ctesiphon, built by the Macedonians who, after Alexander the son of Philip, ruled the Persians and the nations there.

awaiting the spectacle from of old." The letter declared this much. When Narses saw this, brought to him, laughing at the boastfulness of the Goths, he at once set about going out with the whole army, leaving a guard with Justin in Ravenna.
And the Tigris river divides both these; for they have no other country between.
And, coming near the city of Ariminum, they found the passage from there not easy for them, the Goths having destroyed the bridge there not long before.
There the envoys, meeting Chosroes, thought fit that he give back the places of Lazica to the Romans and confirm with them most firmly the matters of the peace.

For the river which flows past Ariminum is scarcely passable for a single unarmed man going on foot over the bridge with toil and much hardship, and that too with no one harassing him or checking the passage; but for a multitude of men, and that too exceptionally armed, especially with enemies withstanding them, to cross there in any way is impossible.

But Chosroes said it was not easy for them to come to terms with one another, unless, having first made some armistice, and thus ever going more fearlessly to one another, they should both dissolve their differences and establish the matters of the peace in security for the rest.
Wherefore Narses, coming to be at the place of the bridge with a few men, at a loss for a long time, considered from where he might find some means for the matter.
And he said that for the perpetual armistice the Emperor of the Romans must both give him money and send a certain physician, Tribunus by name, that he should pass a fixed time with him.

Thither too Usdrilas came, bringing along certain horsemen, lest any of the operations should escape his notice. And one of those who followed Narses, drawing his bow, shot at them, and, hitting one of the horses, straightway killed it.
For this physician chanced to have rid him of a grievous disease before, and from this was his friend and most longed-for.

And those about Usdrilas then, departing quickly from there, came within the circuit-wall, and at once, bringing along others of their most warlike men, rushed against them through another gate, in order to fall upon them unexpectedly and dispatch Narses very straightway.
When the Emperor Justinian heard this, he at once sent Tribunus and the money, amounting to twenty centenaria.

For he had already come to the other side of the river, searching out with the army the crossing. But some of the Heruls, by some chance meeting them there, killed Usdrilas, and, whoever he was, recognized by a Roman man, taking off his head, came to the Roman camp, and, showing it to Narses, encouraged all by their eagerness, who took from what had befallen the proof that the things from God were hostile to the Goths; since they who had laid an ambush for the general of the enemy had themselves, not by plot or any forethought, suddenly been deprived of their commander.
And thus a treaty was made for the Romans and the Persians for five years, in the nineteenth year of the Emperor Justinian holding the supreme rule.

But Narses, although Usdrilas had fallen, who commanded the garrison in Ariminum, pressed the army forward. For he wished to harass neither Ariminum nor any other place held by the enemy, so that no time should be wasted for him, nor the most urgent business be hindered by an incidental matter.
A little later Arethas and Alamoundaras, the rulers of the Saracens, waged war against one another by themselves, neither the Romans nor the Persians helping them.
And the enemy, since their commander had fallen, keeping quiet and no longer setting themselves as an obstacle, Narses, more fearlessly bridging the river, ferried his whole army across with no toil.

And Alamoundaras, taking by a raid one of the sons of Arethas who was pasturing horses, at once sacrificed him to Aphrodite, and from this it was known that Arethas was not betraying the affairs of the Romans to the Persians.

And, leaving the Flaminian road from there, he went on the left. For Petra, the so-called Pertusa, the strength of whose stronghold by the nature of the place I have described in the earlier books, having been seized by the enemy long before, the regions there, at least along the Flaminian road, happened to be impassable for the Romans and altogether without exit. Narses, then, on this account, leaving the shorter road, went by the passable one.

After this both came to battle with their whole army, and those with Arethas conquered by force, and routing the enemy killed many. And Arethas came near to taking two of the sons of Alamoundaras alive, but did not take them. So the affairs of the Saracens stood thus.

But Chosroes, the King of the Persians, became manifest as having made the armistice with the Romans with a treacherous mind, that, taking them slack on account of the peace, he might work some irreparable thing.

For in the third year of the armistice he contrived as follows. There were among the Persians two brothers, Phabrizus and Isdigousnas, invested there with the greatest offices and otherwise the most wicked in reckoning of all the Persians, and having great repute for cleverness and ill-disposition.

Having purposed, then, to take the city of Daras by a raid and to drive all the Colchians out of Lazica, and to settle Persians as inhabitants in their place, he chose these two men to serve in both works;

for it seemed a windfall and worth much account to him, having appropriated the land of Colchis, to hold it in security of possession, reckoning that this would be expedient to the Persian realm in many ways.
For he would have Iberia in safety for the future, the Iberians no longer having any men to whom, having revolted, they might be saved;

for when the most notable of these barbarians together with Gourgenes the king resolved on revolt, as I have said before, the Persians neither conceded that a king should be set up for them for the future, nor were the Iberians of their own will subject to the Persians, but were held by much suspicion and distrust toward one another.
And the Iberians were manifestly most exceedingly indignant and would revolt not long after, if ever they should be able to take hold of some opportunity.

And by the Huns dwelling near Lazica the Persian realm would for ever be unravaged, and they could send them more easily and with less toil against the Roman realm, whenever it should be his wish; for the land of the Lazi is nothing else to the barbarians dwelling in the Caucasus than a bulwark.

And most of all in this he hoped the mastery of Lazica would profit the Persians, that, setting out from it, they would be able, with no trouble, overrunning by foot and by ships the places on the so-called Euxine Sea, to subdue the Cappadocians and the Galatians and Bithynians adjoining them, and to take Byzantium by a raid, no one opposing them.
For these reasons, then, Chosroes wished to appropriate Lazica, but he had no confidence at all toward the Lazi.

For when the Romans withdrew from Lazica, the multitude of the Lazi was tolerably vexed with the Persian realm. For the Persians are, if any others, of a solitary disposition and exceedingly hard in their way of life.

And their laws are difficult of approach for all men, and their commands by no means bearable. But toward the Lazi especially the difference both of disposition and of way of life appears great, since the Lazi are Christians most of all, but with the Persians all things concerning the divine are the opposite of theirs.
And apart from these things, salt is in no way produced in Lazica, nor indeed does grain or wine or any other good thing grow.

But from the Romans of the seacoast all things come in to them by ships, and these not giving gold to those who deal with them, but skins and slaves and whatever else chances to be there in great surplus.
Of which, as is likely, being shut off for the rest, they were distressed. When Chosroes perceived this, he was eager to anticipate in safety, before they should make any revolution against him.

And in his deliberation it seemed most expedient to him, having made away with Gubazes the king of the Lazi as quickly as possible, to remove the Lazi thence with all their people, and thus to settle Persians and certain other nations in this country.

Having resolved these things, Chosroes sends Isdigousnas as though on an embassy ostensibly in word to Byzantium, and sent with him five hundred Persians, chosen for valour, charging them to get into the city of Daras and to lodge in many houses, and to burn all these by night, and, the Romans being occupied about this fire, as is likely, all of them, to open the gates at once and receive into the city the rest of the Persian army.

For it had been said before to the commander of the city of Nisibis to have a multitude of soldiers in readiness, hiding very near. For thus Chosroes thought they would with no trouble both make away with all the Romans and, having seized the city of Daras securely, hold it.

But someone well knowing what was being done, a Roman man, who had a little before come as a deserter to the Persians, tells the whole matter to George, who then had his abode there, whom I have mentioned in the foregoing, as having persuaded the Persians besieged in the fortress of Sisauranon to hand over themselves to the Romans.

George, then, meeting this envoy at the borders of the Romans and Persians, said that what was being done was not according to embassy, and that never should so great a multitude of Persians lodge in a Roman city.
For all the rest must be left in the place Ammodios, and he himself, with a few, might enter the city of Daras.
Isdigousnas, then, was indignant and seemed distressed, as having been needlessly outraged, although sent on an embassy to the Emperor of the Romans.
But George, paying no heed to him in his savagery, saved the city for the Romans. For with twenty men only he received Isdigousnas into the city.

Having failed of this attempt, then, this barbarian came to Byzantium as though on an embassy, bringing with him his wife and two daughters (for this was for him the screen of the throng that had come together), and coming into the emperor's sight he was able to say nothing great or small about any serious matter, although he spent not less than ten months in the land of the Romans.

The gifts, however, from Chosroes, as is customary, and a letter he gave to the emperor, through which Chosroes thought fit that the Emperor Justinian should signify whether his body was in the best state of health.
This Isdigousnas, however, the Emperor Justinian saw with much friendliness, most of all the envoys we know, and held him in sufficient honour;
so that even when he feasted him, Braducius, who followed him as interpreter, he reclined with him on the couch, a thing that had never happened before in all time.
For no one ever saw an interpreter even of any of the lesser rulers, much less one made table-companion to a king.
But also more magnificently than befits an envoy he received and dismissed this man, although he had made the embassy for no purpose,

as I have said. For if one should reckon up the expenses and the gifts which Isdigousnas, departing, took thence, he will find them amounting to more than ten centenaria of gold. So the matter of the plot against the city of Daras came to this for Chosroes.
And to Lazica first he sent a great quantity of wood suitable for the making of ships, telling no one for what purpose he sent it, but in word he sent these to set up engines about the wall of Petra.

And then envoys came from the emperor, Domnicus and Maximinus, both of senatorial rank, in order to make peace on the following terms: 29.2. that Wittigis should carry off half of the royal wealth, and should rule the land which is beyond the river Padus; and that half of the goods should be the emperor's, and that he should make subject in the payment of tribute all that is within the river Padus. 29.3. And the envoys, showing the emperor's letters to Belisarius, were conveyed to Ravenna. And when the Goths and Wittigis had learned for what they had come, they gladly agreed to make the treaty on these terms. 29.4. When Belisarius heard this, he was distressed, regarding it as a great misfortune if anyone should not allow him, when it was possible with no toil, both to win the mastery of the whole war and to lead Wittigis a captive to Byzantium. 29.5. And when the envoys came to him from Ravenna, he was by no means willing to confirm the agreements with letters of his own. 29.6. The Goths, perceiving this, suspected that the Romans were offering them peace with treacherous intent, and used great suspicion toward them, and now declared openly that without the letters and oaths of Belisarius they would never make a treaty with them. 29.7. And Belisarius, hearing that some of the commanders reviled him as plotting against the emperor's affairs and being by no means willing to bring the war to an end, called all together, in the presence of Domnicus and Maximinus, and spoke as follows: 29.8. “That the fortune of war stands least of all in safety, I myself know, and I think that each of you knows the same as I about it. 29.9. For the hope of victory, when it is most expected to come to them, has tripped up many, and to those who seemed to have been unfortunate among their enemies it has befallen, contrary to expectation, to survive. 29.10. Wherefore I say that those who deliberate about peace ought not to put forward the good hope alone, but to keep in mind that the issue will be on either side, and thus to make the choice of their resolve. 29.11. These things being so, it seemed best to me to bring in you my fellow-commanders and these envoys of the emperor, in order that, choosing freely at the present time whatever may seem advantageous to the emperor, you may never afterward make any reproach against me concerning these affairs. 29.12. For it would be most absurd to keep silent while it is possible to choose the better course, but, when looking to the issue of fortune, to make accusations. 29.13. What, then, has been resolved by the emperor and is desired by Wittigis for the ending of the war, you doubtless know. 29.14. But if these things seem advantageous to you too, let each one come forward and say so. If, however, you think you are able to recover the whole of Italy for the Romans and to gain the mastery over the enemy, nothing will hinder you from saying it, holding back nothing.” When Belisarius had said this, 29.15. all openly declared that the emperor's plans were best, and that they would not be able to do the enemy any further harm. 29.16. And Belisarius, pleased with the opinion of the commanders, saw fit that they should make it plain in writing, in order that they might never deny it. And they, writing it in a little book, made plain that they were not able to prevail in the war over their opponents. 29.17. These things were happening in the Roman camp. But the Goths, hard pressed by famine and no longer able to hold out against the hardship, were distressed with the rule of Wittigis, as having been most unfortunate, but shrank from coming over to the emperor, fearing nothing else than lest, having become slaves of the emperor, they should be compelled to remove from Italy and, going to Byzantium, to settle there. 29.18. Deliberating, then, among themselves, whatever was uncorrupt among the Goths, they resolved to proclaim Belisarius emperor of the West. And sending to him secretly, they begged him to set himself in the kingship; for in this way they affirmed they would gladly follow him. 29.19. But Belisarius was by no means willing to set himself in power without the will of the emperor; 29.20. for he was prodigiously distressed at the name of tyrant, and had previously been bound by the most dreadful oaths to the emperor that he would never, while he lived, attempt a revolution. But in order that he might manage the present situation as well as possible, he resolved gladly to admit the words of the barbarians. 29.21. Perceiving this, Wittigis was afraid, and saying that the Goths had deliberated most excellently, he himself too secretly advised Belisarius to go into the kingship; 29.22. for no one would stand in his way. And then Belisarius again, calling together both the envoys of the emperor and all the commanders, asked whether it seemed to them worthy of much account to make all the Goths together with Wittigis captives, and to plunder all the goods, 29.23. and to recover the whole of Italy for the Romans. And they said this would be a lofty and prodigious piece of good fortune for the Romans, and saw fit for him to do whatever he was able as quickly as possible. 29.24. So immediately Belisarius sent some of his friends to Wittigis and the notable Goths, ordering them to fulfil what they had promised. 29.25. For the famine did not allow them to put off the matter to any other time, but, pressing still harder, urged them to this. 29.26. Wherefore they sent envoys to the Roman camp again, to say one thing to the multitude, but secretly to receive pledges from Belisarius that he would do harm to none of them, and that he himself for the future would be emperor over both the Italians and the Goths, and that thus he would come with them and the Roman army to Ravenna. 29.27. And Belisarius swore to all the other things, just as the envoys saw fit, but said that he would swear concerning the kingship to Wittigis himself and to the commanders of the Goths. 29.28. And the envoys, thinking that he would never reject the kingship but desired it above all things, ordered him immediately to go to Ravenna with them. 29.29. And then Belisarius ordered Bessas and John and Narses and Aratius (for these he suspected to be most ill-disposed to him) to go off, each in a different direction, with their followers, to provide themselves with the necessities; for he said it was no longer possible for him to bring provisions into this place for the whole army. 29.30. And they did so, together with Athanasius the prefect of the praetorian guards, who had just come from Byzantium; while he himself with the rest of the army went with the envoys of the Goths to Ravenna. 29.31. And filling a fleet of ships with grain and the other provisions, he ordered them to sail quickly into the harbour of Classes; for so the Romans call the suburb of Ravenna where the harbour is. 29.32. And to me at that time, as I observed the entrance of the Roman army into Ravenna, a thought came that affairs are accomplished by no means through the wisdom of men or any other excellence, but that there is a certain divine power which always turns their minds and leads them there, where there will be no hindrance to the things being accomplished. 29.33. For the Goths, far surpassing their opponents in numbers and power, and neither settled by battle, since they were in Ravenna, nor enslaved in spirit by anything else whatever, became captives of those inferior to them and held the name of slavery in no insult at all. 29.34. And the women (for they happened to have heard from their husbands that the enemy were great in body and superior in number), when they saw all of them sitting at the gate, spat in the faces of their husbands, all of them, and pointing with their hands at the victors, reproached them for their cowardice. 29.35. And Belisarius kept Wittigis in custody, not without honour, but ordered those of the barbarians who dwelt within the river Padus, who were going to their own fields, 29.36. to attend to them at their will. For he suspected that no enemy would arise there, nor would the Goths ever combine there, since he had previously established many of the Roman army in those regions. And they went off quickly and gladly. 29.37. And thus the Romans were now in safety; for they were no longer worsted by the Goths in Ravenna in numbers. And after this he took the goods in the Palatium, which he was to convey to the emperor. 29.38. For he himself plundered none of the Goths, nor permitted anyone else to plunder, but each of them preserved his property according to the agreements. 29.39. And when those of the barbarians who held the guard in the strongest of the places heard that Ravenna and Wittigis were held by the Romans, they sent envoys to Belisarius, seeing fit to surrender both themselves by agreement and what they guarded. 29.40. And he, providing pledges to all most readily, won over Tarbesion and any other fortification there was in Venetia. For Caesena alone in Aemilia was left, which he had previously won over together with Ravenna. 29.41. And all the Goths who commanded these places, as soon as they received pledges, came to Belisarius and remained there; but Ildibadus, a man of repute, who commanded the garrison in Verona, sent envoys indeed to Belisarius on the same terms as the others, since Belisarius had found and held his children in Ravenna, yet he neither came to Ravenna nor became subject to Belisarius. For a certain fortune befell him which I shall presently make plain.

About this time an army of Sclaveni, crossing the river Ister, wrought irreparable deeds upon all the Illyrians as far as the people of Epidamnus, killing and enslaving all who fell in their way, even to manhood, and plundering their goods. 29.2. And now they were able to take even many forts there which had seemed strong before, no one defending them, and went about everywhere searching them out at their will. 29.3. And the commanders of the Illyrians, having an army of fifteen thousand, followed, yet by no means dared to go anywhere near the enemy. 29.4. At that time, too, earthquakes often occurred in the winter season, exceedingly hard and prodigious, both in Byzantium and in other places, all by night. 29.5. And those who dwelt there, suspecting that they would be buried, were in great fear, yet nothing base befell them to suffer from this. 29.6. At that time too the river Nile, rising more than eighteen cubits, both flooded Egypt and watered the whole of it; but in the Thebaid, which is higher up, it gave its waters subsiding and withdrawing at the appropriate times to those who dwelt there to sow the land and attend to the other things, as was wont; 29.7. but from the land lower down, when it had once overflowed, it no longer departed, but, troubling it, passed the whole time of sowing—a thing which had not happened before in all eternity—and there were places where, the water having abated, it flooded again not long afterward. 29.8. And thus all the seed rotted, as much as had happened to be thrown into the land in the meantime. And the men were gripped by much helplessness at the strangeness of the calamity, and of the other animals the most were destroyed by want of food. 29.9. At that time too the sea-monster which the Byzantines called Porphyrius was taken. This sea-monster had troubled Byzantium and the regions about it for more than fifty years, not continuously, however, but leaving off, as it chanced, for a long time in between. 29.10. And it sank many ships, and threw the crews of many into confusion and forced them, carrying them very far off. It had been a care, then, to the emperor Justinian to master this beast. But he was by no means able to accomplish his purpose. How it now befell to be taken 29.11. I shall make plain. There happened to be great calm holding the sea, and a very great multitude of dolphins gathered somewhere close to the mouth of the Euxine Sea. 29.12. And these, suddenly seeing the monster, fled as each was able, but the most came to the outlets of the Sagaris. Some of them, then, the monster, overtaking, was straightway able to swallow. 29.13. And whether still gripped by hunger or by rivalry, it none the less pursued, until it fell, unawares, somewhere close to the land. 29.14. And there, meeting exceedingly deep mud, it forced and moved everything, in order that it might depart from there as quickly as possible, but was by no means able to escape this shoal, but became still more in the mire. 29.15. And when this came to all the dwellers around, going against it at once at a run, they cut at it with axes most continually on all sides, yet not even so did they kill it, but dragged it off with certain stout ropes. 29.16. And putting it into wagons they found it to be in length about thirty cubits, and in breadth ten. And there, tearing it apart in companies, some of them tasted of it at the moment, while others resolved to salt the portion that fell to them. 29.17. And the Byzantines, when they both perceived the earthquakes and learned what had befallen concerning the Nile and this monster, foretold straightway that whatever was pleasing to each of them would come to pass. 29.18. For men are wont, being at a loss before present things, to make wonders of the things to come, and, worn down by what troubles them, to conjecture for no reason what will befall. 29.19. But I, leaving the divinations and the interpretations of portents to others, know this well, that the staying of the Nile upon the land became the cause of great calamities at least for the present, but the disappearance of the monster appears to be a release from many evils. 29.20. And some say that this is not the monster of which I made mention, but another, which it befell to be taken. But I return to the point from which I made the digression of my account. 29.21. Totila, then, having accomplished these things which have been shown before, when he learned that the Romans in the fort at Ruscianae were running short of the necessities, thinking that he would take them as quickly as possible if they should not be able to bring in any of the provisions, encamped very close and, sitting down, set himself to a siege. And the winter was ending, and the thirteenth year of this war which Procopius has written was coming to a close.

For the Roman army, then, the matters of the journey were thus. But Totila, having now learned what had happened in Venetia, awaiting at first Teias and the army with him, remained quietly in the regions about Rome.

Then choosing out three hundred warlike Persians and setting over them Phabrizus, whom I just mentioned, he sends them there, whom he charged to make away with Gubazes as secretly as possible; for the rest he would take care of himself.

But when they were present, and only two thousand horsemen were still left, Totila did not wait for these, but, setting out with all the rest of the army, went to confront the enemy at a suitable place.

This wood, then, when it was conveyed to Lazica, chanced to be struck by lightning suddenly and reduced to ashes; and Phabrizus, coming with the three hundred to Lazica, set about how he might carry out concerning Gubazes the things enjoined by Chosroes.

And on this road, learning what had befallen Usdrilas and that the enemy had crossed Ariminum, he passed through all Tuscany, and, coming to be on the mountain called the Apennine, encamped there and remained near a village which the natives call Taginae.

There chanced to be one of the men of note among the Colchians, Pharsanses by name, who had offended Gubazes and had fallen into great hatred from him, and had no courage at all to come into the king's sight.

And the Roman army, with Narses leading, not long after, encamping themselves too on the mountain Apennine, remained, about a hundred stades distant from the camp of their opponents, in a place level, but encompassed close about with many hills, where once they say Camillus, a general of the Romans, destroyed a host of the Gauls, having conquered them in battle.
When Phabrizus learned this, sending for Pharsanses, he conferred with him and, bringing out the whole matter, inquired of the man how he should set about the deed.
And the place bears the name of this deed even to my time, and preserves in memory the calamity of the Gauls, being called Busta Gallorum; for the Latins call the remains from the funeral pyre busta.

It seemed, then, to them, taking counsel in common, that Phabrizus should be in the city of Petra, and should send for Gubazes there, that he might announce to him whatever might seem to the king to be expedient for the Lazi.

And there are here very many earthen mounds, tombs of those dead. At once, then, sending from there some of his intimates, Narses gave orders to make an exhortation to Totila, to lay down war and to take counsel for peace at some time, reckoning that he himself, ruling over a few men, and these gathered hastily by no law, could not contend for long against the whole Roman empire.
But Pharsanses secretly signified to Gubazes what was being done. Therefore Gubazes by no means came to Phabrizus, but openly looked to revolt.
And he said this too to them, that he, if they should see him wishing for war, would, with no delay, give command to fix some appointed day for the battle.

And Phabrizus charged the other Persians to take care of the garrison in Petra with all power and to prepare the matters of a siege most securely, but he himself with the three hundred withdrew home unsuccessful.

When, then, these envoys came into the presence of Totila, they did what was ordered. And he, talking big, made the boast that they must fight in every way; but they, taking it up, said, "But, good sir, set some fixed time for the engagement." And he at once said, "In eight days let us join battle."

And Gubazes, referring to the Emperor Justinian their present situation, begged him to be forgiving of what the Lazi had formerly done, and to defend them with all power, as they wished to be rid of the rule of the Medes. For the Colchians by themselves would not be able to repel the power of the Persians.
The envoys, then, returning to Narses, reported the agreement made with them; and he, suspecting that Totila was contriving deceits, made ready as if to fight on the morrow.
When the Emperor Justinian heard this, he was overjoyed and sent seven thousand men and Dagisthaeus as commander, and a thousand Tzani, to the aid of the Lazi.

And indeed he hit upon the enemy's thought. For on the following day Totila, of his own announcing, was present with all his army. And already both sides faced one another, distant no more than two bow-shots apart.
And these, coming to the land of Colchis, together with the Lazi and Gubazes, encamping about the wall of Petra, undertook a siege.

Now there was a certain small mound there, which both sides were eager to seize, thinking it to lie in a position suitable for them, both that they might be able to strike their opponents from above, and because, since wooded places, as I have shown, were somewhere there, it was impossible for any to encircle the Roman camp, going behind, except by a single path,
And the Persians there defending themselves most vigorously from the wall, much time was spent in the siege, since the Persians had chanced to store provisions enough for themselves.

which happened to be beside the mound. Wherefore it was necessary for both to make much account of it, for the Goths, that, encircling the enemy in the engagement, they might place them between two fires, and for the Romans, that they might not suffer this.

Disturbed by these things, Chosroes sent against them a great army of horse and foot, over whom he set Mermeroes as commander. When Gubazes perceived this, taking counsel in common with Dagisthaeus, he did as follows.
But Narses, getting the start, picking out fifty foot-soldiers from a register, sent them in the dead of night to seize and hold it.

The Boas river issues very near the borders of Tzanica in Armenia, where they dwell about the Pharangium. And at first it flows for a great extent on the right, going small and becoming crossable for all with no trouble, up to a place where on the right are the borders of the Iberians, and over against it the Caucasus mountain ends.
And they, with none of the enemy standing in their way, coming to be there, remained quiet.
There many other nations dwell, both Alani and Abasgi, Christians and friends of the Romans from of old, and Zechi, and after them Huns,

And there is a certain torrent-bed before the mound, beside the path which I have just mentioned, and opposite the place where the Goths were encamped, where the fifty stood, coming close to one another and drawn up into a phalanx as in a narrow space.

who are called Sabiri. And when this river comes to where the borders of the Caucasus and Iberia are, there, other waters coming to it, it becomes far greater, and is called Phasis instead of Boas from there, having become navigable as far as the so-called Euxine Sea, where its outlets chance to be, and on either side of it is Lazica.
And by day, seeing what had happened, Totila was eager to push them off. And he at once sent a squadron of horsemen against them, ordering them to drive them out from there as quickly as possible.
But on the right the whole country for a great extent is inhabited by the men there as far as the borders of Iberia.
The horsemen, then, with much tumult and shouting rushed against them, as if to take them at the first onset; but they, drawn up in a small space and fencing themselves with their shields,

For the villages of the Lazi are all within the river there, and towns have been made for them there from of old, among which Archaeopolis, being most strong, and there are Sebastopolis and the fortress of Pityus, and Scanda and Sarapanis by the borders of Iberia. The most notable cities there, however, are Rhodopolis and Mochiresis.

holding their spears extended, stood. Then the Goths, advancing eagerly, drove against them in confusion; but the fifty, by the pushing of their shields and the most close-packed and in no way disordered presenting of their spears, beat off the assailants most stoutly, and on purpose made a clatter with their shields, in this way ever frightening the horses, and the men with the points of their spears.

On the left of the river is the border of Lazica up to a day's journey for an unencumbered man, and the country chances to be empty of men. Bordering this country are the Romans who are called Pontic.

And the horses reared, distressed exceedingly by the difficult ground and the clatter of the shields and having no way out, and the men were worn down, fighting with men packed so close together and yielding in no way, and urging on horses that by no means obeyed. And, beaten off the first time, they retreated backward.
In the borders of Lazica, then, where men in no way dwelt, the Emperor Justinian in my time built the city of Petra.
And, making trial again and suffering the same things, they drew back. And often having departed thus, they no longer harassed them, but Totila set another squadron to this work.
Where John, surnamed Tzibus, establishing the monopoly, as I have said in the foregoing, became the cause of the revolt to the Lazi.
And these too departing like the former, others were set to the task. And Totila, having thus changed many squadrons, and after all of them having accomplished nothing, then desisted.

And going straight from the city of Petra toward the south wind the borders of the Romans receive one, and there are populous places there, the so-called Rhizaeum and Athenae and certain others up to the Trapezuntines.

The fifty, then, won great fame for valour, and two of them especially distinguished themselves in this struggle, Paul and Ansilas, who, leaping out from the phalanx, made a display of valour above all others.

When, then, the Lazi brought in Chosroes, crossing the Boas river and keeping the Phasis on the right, they came to Petra, in word to provide that they should not be compelled to ferry across the Phasis river with much time and toil, but in fact not wishing to display their own dwellings to the Persians.
For, drawing their daggers, they laid them on the ground, and, drawing their bows, shot, aiming most effectively at the enemy.
And yet Lazica is everywhere difficult of access, both within and outside the Phasis river.

And many men and many horses they dispatched, so long as their quivers still had shafts for them. And when all the missiles had now failed them, they, taking up their swords and holding their shields before them, defended themselves singly against the assailants.
For extraordinary crags on either side of the country make very long narrows there; the Romans call such roads clisurae, hellenizing the word.
And whenever some of their adversaries came riding against them with their spears, they, striking with their swords, at once cut off the points of the spears.
But since Lazica then chanced to be unguarded, the Persians most easily came to Petra with the leaders of the Lazi.
