And often, as they thus checked the attacks of the enemy, it befell the sword of one of them (this man's name was Paul) to be bent by continual cutting against the wood and to be altogether useless. Which he at once dashed to the ground,

Now Gubazes, learning of the Persian inroad, charged Dagisthaeus to send some to guard most strongly the narrows which is outside the Phasis river, but by no means to break up the siege, until they should be able to take both Petra and the Persians there.

and, laying hold with both hands of the spears, kept taking them from the assailants. And, taking thus manifestly four spears from the enemy, he became most of all the cause of their giving up the enterprise.
And he himself with the whole Colchian army came to the extremities of Lazica, to guard the narrows there with all power.
Wherefore Narses thenceforth appointed him his own private shield-bearer for this deed.

And he chanced much before to have brought the Alani and Sabiri into alliance, who had agreed for three centenaria not only to guard the land unravaged for the Lazi, but also so to make Iberia empty of men that the Persians could no longer go thence. This money Gubazes promised the emperor would give them.
He himself, then, referring to the Emperor Justinian the things agreed, besought him to send the barbarians this money and to grant some consolation to the Lazi, much afflicted.

And he said that the treasury owed him too his pay of ten years, since, being ranked among the silentiarii in the palace, he had received nothing thence from the time Chosroes came to the land of Colchis.
And the Emperor Justinian purposed to carry out the request, but some occupation coming on him, he did not send the money at the fitting time. Gubazes, then, did these things.
But Dagisthaeus (for he was a youth by no means worthy to carry through a Median war) used the present circumstances unsuitably.

For when he ought to have sent the greater part of the army to the narrows, and perhaps even himself to be present at this work, he sent only a hundred men, as though disposing of some by-task; and he himself, besieging Petra with the whole army, accomplished nothing, although the enemy were few. For at first there were not fewer than fifteen hundred,
but, by the Romans and Lazi storming the wall for a long time and being shot at and displaying valour most of all whom we know, many died, and it befell them to be reduced to very few.
The Persians, then, fallen into despair and helplessness, remained quietly, while the Romans made a trench about the wall in a small space, and the wall there at once fell.
But it befell that within this place there was a building standing no distance from the wall, which reached along the whole fallen part;
and this, becoming for the besieged instead of the wall, set them in safety no less.
Which by no means disturbed the Romans. For knowing well that, doing this same thing elsewhere, they would most easily take the city, they became much more of good hope.

Therefore Dagisthaeus declared to the emperor what had befallen, and held out that the prizes of victory should be in readiness for him, signifying with how many things it was needful for the emperor to gift both him and his brother; for they would take the Persian fortress not long after.
The Persians, then, withstood the Romans and Tzani, storming the wall most vigorously, beyond expectation, although left exceedingly few.

And when the Romans, storming the wall, accomplished nothing, they turned again to digging. And they came to such a point of this work that the foundations of the wall were no longer on the ground, but stood for the most part on emptiness, about to fall, as is likely, very soon.

And if Dagisthaeus had at once wished to set fire to the foundations, I think the city would have been taken straightway; but as it was, awaiting the hopes from the emperor and ever delaying and spending the time, he remained quietly. So these things were being done in the Roman camp here.

But Mermeroes, when he had passed the borders of Iberia with the whole army of the Medes, went forward, keeping the Phasis river on the right; for he by no means wished to go through the places of Lazica, lest some hindrance there should meet him.

Some of the commanders of the Roman army, having envy toward Belisarius, slandered him to the emperor, bringing against him a charge of tyranny that in no way belonged to him. 30.2. But the emperor, not so much persuaded by these slanders, but because the Median war was now pressing upon him, summoned Belisarius as quickly as possible, in order that he might march against the Persians; and he ordered Bessas and John with the others to take care of Italy, and instructed Constantianus to go from Dalmatia to Ravenna. 30.3. And the Goths who were settled beyond the river Padus and Ravenna, hearing that the emperor was summoning Belisarius, at first regarded the matter as unreasonable, supposing that Belisarius would never set the kingship of Italy below his loyalty to Justinian. 30.4. But when they learned that the preparation for his departure was great, taking counsel together, whatever was still uncorrupt among them, they went to Ticinum to Uraïas the nephew of Wittigis, and after first weeping much with him, spoke as follows: 30.5. “No other has been more responsible for the present evils to the nation of the Goths than you. For we should long ago have removed your uncle, who led us so basely and unfortunately, from his rule, as we did Theudatus the nephew of Theoderic, had we not, out of respect for your seeming energy, resolved to concede to Wittigis the name of the kingship, but in deed to hand over to you alone the rule of the Goths. 30.6. But the goodwill that then seemed ours has turned about, now appearing as folly and the cause of these our misfortunes. 30.7. For of the Goths, as you know, O dear Uraïas, it befalls that most and the best have died in the war, and of the survivors, whatever best is left, Belisarius will go off taking, together with Wittigis and all the goods. 30.8. And that this same thing will befall us too a little later, being few and exceedingly pitiable, no one would gainsay. 30.9. With such terrors, then, standing about us, it will be more profitable to die with good repute than to behold our children and wives being led off by the enemy to the ends of the earth. 30.10. And we shall do something, as is likely, worthy of valour, if we have you as leader of our deeds.” The Goths said so much. 30.11. And Uraïas answered as follows: “That in the present terrors we ought to choose danger before slavery, it befalls me to think the same as you. 30.12. But for me to set myself in the kingship of the Goths I think altogether inexpedient; first, because, being the nephew of Wittigis, a man so unfortunate, I should seem contemptible to the enemy, since men think that like fortunes are always passed on to kinsmen; 30.13. and second, I should seem to be doing what is unholy, mounting to the rule of my uncle, and on this account I should, as is likely, have most of you distressed at me. 30.14. But I say that we ought to set Ildibadus into this danger as ruler of the Goths, a man who has come to the height of valour and is exceedingly energetic. 30.15. And it is not unlikely that Theudis, who is his uncle and the ruler of the Visigoths, will join in the war because of the kinship. Wherefore we shall carry on the contest against our opponents with better hope.” 30.16. Having said so much, Uraïas too seemed to all the Goths to be speaking what was advantageous. And Ildibadus came to them immediately, summoned from Verona. 30.17. And throwing the purple about him, they proclaimed him king of the Goths and begged him to set their present affairs well in order. Thus Ildibadus came into power. 30.18. And a little later, calling together all the Goths, he spoke as follows: “I know that all of you, fellow-soldiers, are experienced in many wars, so that we shall never with reason go straight to making war. For experience, bringing reckoning, is least wont to be bold. 30.19. And it is worth while for you, remembering all that has happened before, thus now to deliberate about the present. 30.20. For forgetfulness, coming upon many men of what has already gone before, has lifted up their thoughts not as it ought, through ignorance, 30.21. and has sufficiently tripped them up in the greatest matters. Wittigis, then, not against your will nor while you resisted, gave himself into the hands of the enemy, but having then given up before the oppositions of fortune, you thought it most advantageous for yourselves to sit at home and obey Belisarius, rather than to risk your bodies endlessly. 30.22. But now, having heard that he is being sent to Byzantium, you have resolved to undertake a revolution. And yet each of you ought to reckon that not all things turn out for men as they think, but the issue of affairs has often gone contrary to expectation, in the opposite direction to what was resolved. 30.23. For fortune and repentance are wont for the most part to set things right from the unexpected; and that this will happen now too to Belisarius is in no way unlikely. 30.24. It is better, then, first to inquire of him, and to try to set the man back to the agreements made before, and thus for you to proceed to the second course in your actions.” 30.25. When Ildibadus had said this, he seemed to the Goths to have deliberated well, and he sent envoys to Ravenna quickly. And these, coming into the sight of Belisarius, reminded him of the agreements made with them and reviled him as a breaker of what had been agreed, calling him a self-chosen slave, and reproaching him because he did not blush at choosing slavery before kingship, and saying many other such things, exhorted him to the rule. 30.26. For thus, they affirmed, Ildibadus too would come of his own accord, to lay down the purple at his feet and do obeisance to Belisarius as emperor of both Goths and Italians. 30.27. The envoys said these things, thinking that the man would draw to himself the name of kingship without any delay at once. 30.28. But he, contrary to their expectation, openly refused, saying that Belisarius would never, while the emperor Justinian lived, mount to the name of kingship. 30.29. And they, hearing this, departed as quickly as possible and reported the whole matter to Ildibadus. 30.30. And Belisarius went off toward Byzantium; and the winter was ending, and the fifth year of this war which Procopius has written was coming to a close.

And the emperor Justinian sent foot-soldiers, no fewer than two thousand, to Sicily in ships, and ordered Valerianus to go to Belisarius with no delay. 30.2. And he, ferrying across, sailed down to Dryus, where he found Belisarius with his wife. 30.3. About this time Antonina the wife of Belisarius was sent to Byzantium to beg the empress to fit out the war with greater preparation. 30.4. But the empress Theodora, having fallen sick, was removed from among men, having survived for the empire twenty-one years and three months. 30.5. In the meantime those besieged in the fort at Ruscianae, hard pressed by the want of necessities, came to a parley with the enemy, and agreed to give over the fort about the middle of the summer season, if no help should come to them in the meantime, on condition that all should remain unharmed. 30.6. Now there were in this fort many notable Italians, and Deopheron the brother of Tullianus, and of the Roman army three hundred Illyrian horsemen, whom John had happened to establish there, setting over them Chalazar the spearman, a Massagete by race, exceedingly good in matters of war, and Gudilas a Thracian, and a hundred foot-soldiers sent by Belisarius for the guard of the fort. 30.7. At that time too the soldiers whom Belisarius had ranged for the guard of Rome killed their commander Conon, bringing against him as a charge his trafficking in grain and the other provisions to their own harm. 30.8. And sending some of the priests as envoys, they affirmed that, unless the emperor should grant them amnesty for this charge and pay within a fixed time the allowances which the public treasury owed them, they would, with no delay, come over to Totila and the Goths. And the emperor fulfilled their request. 30.9. And Belisarius, summoning John to Dryus, and gathering a large fleet with him and Valerianus and the other commanders, sailed quickly straight to Ruscianae, being eager to help the besieged. 30.10. And those in the fort, observing this fleet from on high and becoming hopeful, no longer resolved to come over to the enemy, although the day agreed upon for them had now arrived. 30.11. And at first, a prodigious storm falling upon them, and the shore there being altogether without a harbour, it befell that all the ships were scattered as far as possible from one another; 30.12. and in this way it befell that a length of time was wasted for them. And again, gathering in the harbour of the people of Croton, they put out for Ruscianae. When the barbarians saw them, leaping onto their horses they came about the beach, intending to prevent the landing of the enemy. 30.13. And Totila stationed them along the most of the shore facing the prows of the ships, some holding spears, others with bows drawn. 30.14. When the Romans saw this, they were dismayed and by no means dared to go near, but for some time, holding the ships at a distance, remained quiet; and afterward, despairing of the landing, all backed water and, setting out, put in again at the harbour of the people of Croton. 30.15. There, deliberating in common, it seemed best to them that Belisarius, going to Rome, should both settle matters there as well as possible and bring in provisions, while John and Valerianus, landing the men and horses and journeying by the road, should go to Picenum, to throw into confusion those of the enemy who were besieging the towns there. 30.16. For thus they had hope that Totila, breaking off the siege, would follow them. 30.17. John, then, with his followers, who were a thousand, did so; but Valerianus, fearing the danger, sailed with his ships around the Ionian Gulf straight for Ancon. For he thought that thus he would be in Picenum in safety and would join John. 30.18. But Totila by no means resolved even so to break off the siege, but himself sat there, while, selecting two thousand horsemen from the camp, he sent them to Picenum, in order that, joining the barbarians there, they might repel John and Valerianus. 30.19. And those besieged in the fort at Ruscianae, when the necessities had now altogether failed them and they had no longer any hope of help from the Romans, sending Gudilas the spearman and Deopheron the Italian to Totila, made an embassy concerning their safety, begging him to be forgiving toward them for what had been done. 30.20. And Totila announced that he would carry out the punishment on no other than Chalazar, as having disregarded what had previously been agreed, but that he would remit the charge to all the others. 30.21. Thus, then, he received the fort. And cutting off both the hands and the privy parts of Chalazar, he straightway killed him, and of the soldiers those who wished to remain he ordered to keep their own goods, on condition that for the future they should array themselves with the Goths on equal and like terms—which indeed he was wont to do in the other forts that were taken; 30.22. but those to whom remaining was by no means pleasing, these he ordered to depart wherever they wished, stripped, so that none of all men might campaign with him unwillingly. 30.23. Eighty of the Roman army, then, leaving their goods, came to Croton, but the others remained there with their goods. 30.24. From the Italians, however, he took away all their goods, but left their bodies altogether unharmed. 30.25. And Antonina the wife of Belisarius, the empress having died, coming to Byzantium begged the emperor to summon her husband there. And she accomplished this most easily. For the Median war, now pressing most strongly, was urging the emperor Justinian to this.

These things, then, went thus. And both sides made ready for battle-array. And Narses, gathering the army into a small space, exhorted them as follows: "For those who set themselves to the contest against the enemy with a power equally matched, perhaps there would be need of much exhortation and of urging to eagerness, so that thereby, having the advantage over their opponents, they might come off from the battle-array most according to their wish; but for you, men, for whom both in valour and in numbers and in all other equipment, by a great difference, the battle is against inferiors, I think there is need of nothing else than to enter upon this engagement with God propitious.
For he was eager to save the city of Petra and the Persians there, although a part of the wall had fallen suddenly.

Calling Him most assiduously to your alliance by prayer, then, with great contempt go for the mastery against these robbers, who, being slaves of the great emperor from the beginning, and having become runaways, and having set up for themselves a vulgar tyrant out of the rabble, were able, in a more thievish fashion, for a certain occasion, to throw the Roman empire into confusion.
For it was suspended, as I have said; and men of the Roman army to the number of fifty, going of their own will into the city, cried out for the Emperor Justinian as gloriously victorious.
And yet one would suspect that these men, reckoning what was likely, would not now even array themselves against us.
And there led them a certain young man, Armenian by race, John by name, son of Thomas, whom they called by the surname Gouzes.

But they, courting death by some senseless boldness and displaying a mad rashness, dare to take up manifest death, not putting forward good hope, nor awaiting what may come to them from the unexpected and the unlooked-for, but being expressly led by God to the punishments of their political deeds. For those who are doomed from above to suffer something go of their own accord to their chastisements.
This Thomas built many of the strongholds about Lazica, the emperor having charged him, and commanded the soldiers there, and seemed prudent to the emperor.

Apart from this, you set yourselves to this engagement contending for a lawful state, while they struggle on behalf of innovating against the laws, not expecting to hand on anything of their possessions to any successors, but knowing well that everything will perish together with them, and living with a hope that lasts but a day.
John, then, when the Persians came to blows with them, being struck, at once withdrew with his followers to the camp, since no other of the Roman army came to defend him;

So that they are most of all worthy to be despised. For from those who set themselves up not by law and a good state all valour has departed, and victory has been discerned, as is likely, not being wont

but a Persian man, Mirranes by name, who commanded the garrison in Petra, fearing for the city, charged all the Persians to keep guard most exactly, and himself, sent to Dagisthaeus, held out flattering and deceitful words, agreeing with no trouble to hand over the city not long after. And by this he was able to get round him, so that the city was not at once entered by the Roman army.

to set itself against the virtues." Such an exhortation Narses made. And Totila too, seeing his followers amazed at the Roman army, called them together and himself spoke to them all as follows: "To make to you a last exhortation, fellow-soldiers, I have gathered you here.
And those under Mermeroes, when they came to the narrows, there the Roman garrison, being a hundred, met them, and defended themselves vigorously, and checked those who made trial of the entrance.
For there will, I think, be no need of any other exhortation after this engagement, but the war will altogether be decided in a single day.
But the Persians by no means withdrew, but, others ever receiving those who were killed, went forward, forcing the entrance with all might.

For so has it befallen both us and the emperor Justinian to be unnerved and stripped of all our powers, having met with toils and battles and hardships for a vast length of time, and having grown weary of the necessities of war, that, if we get the better of our opponents in the present engagement, they will by no means henceforth recover, but if we stumble in this battle, no hope will be left to the Goths of renewing the fight, but each side will have the defeat sufficiently as a specious pretext for quiet.
There die of the Persians more than a thousand, and the Romans, killing, gave up, and, the throng forcing them, withdrew and, running up to the heights of the mountains there, were saved.

For men, despairing of the worst of their affairs, no longer dare to return to them, but even though need, perhaps very strongly, thrust them toward these, they are held back in their resolves, the memory of their evils frightening their souls.
When Dagisthaeus learned this, he at once broke up the siege, charging the army nothing, and drove to the Phasis river; and all the Romans followed, leaving their own things in the camp.
Having heard this much, men, play the man with all your might, putting off the valour of your soul to no other time, and toil with all your strength, not husbanding your bodies for any other danger.
And the Persians, seeing what was being done, opened the gates and, coming out, went to the huts of the enemy, as though to take the camp.
And let there be for you no sparing of arms and horses, as they will no longer be useful to you. For fortune, having worn out all else beforehand, has kept the very head of hope for this day alone.
But the Tzani (for they had not chanced to follow Dagisthaeus) came to the rescue there at a run, and routing the enemy with no trouble killed many.
Practise, then, good courage and prepare yourselves for daring. For those whose hope stands upon a hair, as now yours does, even the briefest moment of time it does not profit to be slack.

The Persians, then, fleeing, got within the wall, but the Tzani, having plundered the Roman camp, went straight to Rhizaeum. And thence, coming to Athenae, through the Trapezuntines they were conveyed home.

For when the height of the opportunity has passed, eagerness thenceforth becomes profitless, even though it be exceedingly excessive, the nature of things not admitting a stale valour, since, the need being past, what comes after must of necessity be out of season too.

And Mermeroes and the army of the Medes came there on the ninth day after the retreat of Dagisthaeus; where they found left of the Persian garrison, wounded and become unfit for fighting, three hundred and fifty, and unharmed a hundred and fifty only; for all the rest had died.
I think, then, that it befits you to take the struggle in hand most effectively, that you may also be able to use its good things. And you know well that in the present case flight is most deadly.

Of whom the survivors had by no means thrown the bodies outside the wall, but, choking with the foulness of the smell, held out beyond expectation, that they might give the enemy no eagerness for besieging, since most of them had perished.

For men flee, leaving their array, for no other reason than that they may live; but if flight is likely to bring manifest death, he who has undergone the danger will be much more in safety than the fugitive.

And Mermeroes, mocking, said that the state of the Romans was worthy of tears and lamentations, for whom affairs had come to such a point of weakness that they had been unable by any device to take a hundred and fifty Persians without walls.

And the throng of the enemy is worth despising, gathered as it is from nations the most numerous possible. For an alliance contributed from many quarters carries neither faith nor power secure, but, being torn apart in its races, is divided also in its purposes, as is likely.
And he was eager to rebuild as much of the wall as had fallen; but since he had neither lime for the moment nor any other of the things suitable for building in readiness, he devised the following.
For do not think that Huns and Lombards and Heruls, hired for I know not how much money, will ever risk their lives for them unto death.

Filling linen sacks, in which the Persians had brought provisions for themselves to the land of Colchis, with sand, he set them in the place of the stones, which, being thrown there, became instead of the wall.

For their souls are not so cheap that they should hold even their lives second to silver; but I know well that, making the matters of battle a thing for the eyes, they will very straightway play the coward, either having received their wages, or having fulfilled the command of their own commanders.

And choosing out three thousand of the warlike he left them there, for whom he stored provisions not for a length of time, charging them to take care of the building of the wall; and he himself with all the rest of the army rode back.

For to men, even what seem to be the most delightful of things—not to say warlike—if they be not done according to their wish, but under compulsion or for hire or constrained by something else, no longer turn out to their liking, but, through necessity, appear grievous. Considering these things, with all eagerness let us go against the enemy."

And since on the road as he went thence he had no provision of necessaries, having left in Petra all that the army chanced to be bringing from Iberia, he purposed to go by some other journey through the mountains there, where he learned men dwelt,

that they might be able to live by plunder. On this journey one of the men of note among the Lazi, Phubelis by name, ambushed the Persians as they bivouacked, bringing with him Dagisthaeus and two thousand Romans, who killed by a raid some of the Persians pasturing horses, and plundering horses made their withdrawal in a short time. Thus Mermeroes went thence with the army of the Medes.

And Gubazes, learning what had befallen the Romans both in Petra and in the narrows, was not even so afraid, nor did he leave the guard in the narrows over against him, thinking the head of their hope was there.

For he knew well that, even if the Persians, having forced the Romans outside the Phasis river to cross the narrows and to get to Petra, were able, they would from thence fasten no harm on the country of the Lazi, having no device to cross the Phasis, especially as no ships were present to them.
For this river has depth, if any other, most sufficiently, and extends in breadth for a great extent.

And its current has such force that, casting itself into the sea, it goes for a very long way by itself, in no way mingling there. And indeed drinkable water is at hand for those sailing there to draw in the midst of the open sea.
And the Lazi have made guard-posts within the river everywhere, that the enemy, even ferrying with ships, may have no landing onto the land.
And the Emperor Justinian sent to the nation of the Sabiri the money agreed, and gifted Gubazes and the Lazi with other money.

And he chanced much before to have sent another considerable army to Lazica, who had not yet arrived there. Rhecithancus from Thrace led them, a man intelligent and good in war. So these things stood thus.

And Mermeroes, having come into the mountains, as I have said, was eager to fill Petra thence with provisions. For he thought the provisions which they had chanced to bring in with them would by no means suffice the garrison there, being three thousand.

But since what came to their hands barely sufficed for the expense of this army, being not fewer than thirty thousand, and from this they were not able to send anything worth account to Petra, reckoning, he found it better for them that the greater part of the army should depart from the land of Colchis, but that some few should remain there, who were to bring much of the provisions they should meet into the garrison in Petra, and to use the rest themselves sufficiently;
choosing out, then, about five thousand men, he left them there, and set over them three other commanders and Phabrizus.
For it seemed not necessary to him to leave more there, no enemy being anywhere about. And he himself with the rest of the army, coming to Persarmenia, remained quietly in the places about Doubios.
And the five thousand, when they came nearer the extremities of Lazica, all encamped by the Phasis river, and thence, going about in small bands, plundered the places there.
When Gubazes perceived this, he charged Dagisthaeus to come to the rescue there with haste; for the enemy would be able to do them some great harm.
And he did accordingly, and went forward with the whole Roman army, keeping the Phasis river on the left, until he came to a place where the Lazi were encamped on the other bank of the river.

And there the Phasis chanced to be crossable, which the Romans and Persians, through inexperience of the places there, by no means suspected, but the Lazi, knowing it, crossed there suddenly and mingled with the Roman army; and the Persians, choosing out a thousand of the notable among them, sent them, lest anyone should go to do mischief to the camp.
Of whom two, going first on a reconnaissance and beyond expectation falling among the enemy, reported the whole matter.

Therefore the Romans and Lazi fell suddenly upon the thousand, and none of them was able to escape, but the most were destroyed, and some of them they took alive, by whom those under Gubazes and Dagisthaeus were able to learn both the measure of the army of the Medes and the length of the road, and how their present circumstances stood.
Setting out, then, with the whole army, they went against them, reckoning so that they might fall upon them far on in the night; and they were fourteen thousand.
The Persians, then, having nothing hostile in mind, slept a long sleep; for they thought the river uncrossable, and that the thousand, no one having met them,

were going somewhere very far by the road. But the Romans and Lazi, falling unexpectedly upon them at deep dawn, found some still taking sleep, and some just roused from sleep and lying naked on their bedding.

Therefore it befell none of them to look to defence, but the most, being overtaken, died, and some the enemy took alive, among whom it chanced was one of the commanders, and a few, escaping in the dark, were saved.
And the Romans and Lazi take the camp and all the standards, and plundered many arms and great wealth, and a great quantity of horses and mules.
And making the pursuit for a very long way, they came far into Iberia. There too, meeting some other Persians, they killed many.

Thus the Persians departed from Lazica, and the Romans and Lazi, finding there the rest of the provisions and a very great quantity of flour, burned all that the barbarians had brought from Iberia to bring into Petra.
And they left many of the Lazi in the narrows, that the provisions might no longer be able to be brought in to the Persians in Petra, and with the rest of the booty and the captives they turned back.
And the fourth year was ending of the Romans' armistice with the Persians, in the twenty-third year of the Emperor Justinian holding the supreme rule.
And John the Cappadocian had come summoned by the emperor to Byzantium a year before. For at that time there came upon Theodora the empress the day that ends life.
He recovered, however, none at all of his former dignities, but on his unwilling honour remained a priest; and yet a phantom had often come to the man that he would attain the kingship.
For the demon, which is wont to glamour men, loves to hang from greater and loftier hopes those whose mind chances not to stand on a firm nature.
And to this John, then, wonder-telling visions ever foretold many other things, and that he must put on the garb of Augustus.
Now there was a certain priest in Byzantium, Augustus by name, who had the guard of the treasures of the church of Sophia.

When, then, John, having had his hair shorn, was thought worthy of the priesthood by force—for he had no garment befitting a priest—from this Augustus, being near at hand, he was compelled by those set over the work to put on the chasuble and the tunic, and to this, I think, the prophecy was for him fulfilled.

About this time certain men plotted an attack against the emperor Justinian. How they came to this plan, and in what manner, being thwarted, they by no means came to the deed, 31.2. I shall now make plain. To Artabanes, who had overthrown the tyrant Gontharis, as has been said by me in the previous narrative, there came a prodigious desire to make Praejecta the niece of the emperor, whom he held betrothed, 31.3. his wife. And this was very much her wish too, not led to it by love of the man, but because she acknowledged that she owed him much gratitude, since he had avenged the murder of her husband Areobindus, and saved her and snatched her up when she was captive and not long after about to come unwillingly to the bed of the tyrant Gontharis. 31.4. And when both wished these things, Artabanes sent Praejecta to the emperor, but he himself, although established general of all Libya, needed the emperor, having invented certain unsound pretexts, 31.5. that he should summon him to Byzantium. For the hope of the marriage led him to this, showing forth many other good things from it, and that for the future he would not be far from the throne. 31.6. For men, having unexpectedly laid hold of prosperity, cannot keep their mind there, but await further things, and always go forward in their hopes, until they are deprived even of the good fortune that had befallen them, which they ought not. The emperor, however, fulfilled his request and summoned Artabanes to Byzantium, 31.7. establishing another general of Libya in his place, as has been related by me. 31.8. And when Artabanes came to Byzantium, the people marvelled at what he had done and otherwise loved him. 31.9. For he was tall in body and handsome, and his character was liberal and he uttered few words. And the emperor honoured him among the foremost. 31.10. For establishing him general of the soldiers in Byzantium and commander of the foederati, he enrolled him in the dignity of the consuls. 31.11. But to dwell with Praejecta he was by no means able. For he had a wife previously, who was a kinswoman and had come to him in marriage from boyhood. 31.12. Whom he had long before happened to put off himself, having perhaps fallen upon some cause for which it befalls wives to give offence to husbands. 31.13. This woman, so long as the affairs of Artabanes did not stand well, sat at home in all quietness, bearing the present in silence. But when Artabanes had now become both brilliant in his deeds and great in his fortunes, the woman, no longer bearing the dishonour, came to Byzantium. And becoming a suppliant of the empress, she saw fit to recover her husband. 31.14. And the empress (for she was by nature always inclined to favour unfortunate women) resolved that he should dwell, much against his will, with her, and Praejecta John the son of Pompeius the son of Hypatius made his wedded wife. 31.15. This calamity Artabanes did not bear gently, but grew savage and said that, having done such good for the Romans... no one allowed him, willing as he was, to lead in marriage the woman willingly betrothed to him, while he was compelled to be with the woman most hostile of all to him for all time; a thing which by nature most distresses the soul of a man. 31.16. Wherefore, indeed, not long afterward, as soon as the empress had been removed from among men, he gladly sent this wife away immediately. 31.17. Now the emperor happened to have his cousin Germanus, who had a brother Boraïdes. This Boraïdes the brother of Germanus had lately died, leaving the most of his goods to his brother and the children of that brother. 31.18. And though he had a wife and one daughter, he ordered the daughter to have only so much as the law compelled. Wherefore the emperor saw fit rather to support the daughter; a thing which especially galled Germanus.

Totila too said this much. And the armies came together for battle and were drawn up as follows. Front to front, all on both sides stood, intending to make the front of the phalanx as deep and as long as possible.
And of the Romans, the left wing Narses and John held, about the mound, and with them whatever was best in the Roman army;
for each of them, apart from the other soldiers, was followed by a multitude of bodyguards and shield-bearers and barbarian Huns, gathered for their valour;
while on the right Valerian and John the Glutton with Dagisthaeus and all the rest of the Romans were drawn up.

And foot-archers from the register-soldiers, about eight thousand, they set on both wings. And in the middle of the phalanx Narses set the Lombards and the Herul nation and all the other barbarians, dismounting them from their horses and making them foot-soldiers, in order that, if they should prove cowards in the work or play the malingerer, if it should so happen, they might not be the quicker to flight.
And the end of the left wing of the Roman front Narses set at an angle, stationing there one thousand five hundred horsemen.

And it had been ordered to five hundred of them, whenever any of the Romans should happen to be routed, to bring them aid in haste, and to the thousand, whenever the foot-soldiers of the enemy should begin the work, to come at once behind them and place them between two fires.
And Totila too in the same manner set the whole army opposite the enemy. And, going round his own array, he encouraged the soldiers and called them to daring by countenance and word.
And Narses too did this same thing, raising on poles bracelets and necklaces and golden bridles and certain other incitements to eagerness for the danger.
And for some time neither began the battle, but both remained quiet, awaiting the attack of their opponents.

But afterwards one from the Gothic army, Coccas by name, having a sufficient reputation for energy, riding out his horse, came near the Roman army and challenged, if anyone wished to come out against him to single combat.
Now this Coccas happened to be one of the Roman soldiers who had earlier deserted to Totila.
And at once one of the bodyguards of Narses stood opposite him, an Armenian by race, Anzalas by name, himself too mounted on a horse.
Coccas, then, rushing first as if to strike with his spear, came at his enemy, aiming at his belly.
But Anzalas, suddenly swerving his horse, made him fail of his own rush. And thereby, coming himself to the flank of the enemy, he thrust his spear into his left side.
And he, falling from his horse, lay a corpse on the ground; and an extraordinary outcry rose from the Roman army, yet not even so did either side begin any battle.

But Totila alone came into the no-man's-land, not to fight a single combat, but to baulk this opportunity for his opponents. For, learning that the two thousand Goths who had been left were coming up close by, he was putting off the engagement until their arrival, and did the following.

First he did not disdain to show the enemy who he was. For both the equipment of his arms, thickly overlaid with gold, he was wearing, and the adornment of his cheek-pieces and from his cap and his spear hung purple and otherwise kingly, a marvel how great.

And he himself, mounted on a surpassing horse, skilfully played the war-dance in the no-man's-land. For wheeling his horse in a circle, and turning him again to the other side, he made circular courses.

And, as he rode, he hurled his spear into the air, and, snatching it as it quivered from there, then passing it from hand to hand frequently on either side, and shifting it skilfully, he prided himself on his practice in such things, leaning back and bending sideways and inclining to either side, like one accurately taught from boyhood the matters of the dance.

And, doing these things, he wore away all the early morning. And, wishing to prolong the postponement of the battle to the utmost, he sent to the Roman camp, saying that he wished to confer with them. But Narses maintained that he was playing a trick, since, if he had wished to fight earlier, when there was opportunity to put forward proposals, now, having come into the no-man's-land, he would proceed to discussions.

So matters about Artabanes and Germanus stood thus for the emperor. Now there was a certain man, Arsaces by name, in Byzantium, an Armenian by race, an Arsacid man, related by birth to Artabanes. 32.2. He had been detected a little before doing mischief to the state, and was plainly convicted of treachery, as acting in concert with Chosroes the king of the Persians for a revolution against the Romans. 32.3. And the emperor did him no other harm, but, scourging him a few times on the back, exposed him to public derision, mounted on a camel through the city, yet took from him nothing either of his body or of his substance, 32.4. nor indeed punished him with exile. But Arsaces, none the less being distressed at what had befallen, began to devise plots against both Justinian and the state. 32.5. And when he saw Artabanes distressed, as his kinsman, he provoked him still more, and, catching the man with the ambushes of words, reviled him, relaxing neither night nor day, and reproached him as one who had become brave and unmanly by turns. 32.6. For toward the evils of others he had become noble and a destroyer of tyranny, when, being a friend and a guest, he had taken Gontharis with his own hand and killed him for no reason. 32.7. But at the present time, having played the coward, he sat there so unmanfully, while his country was most continually held in guard and worn down by unaccustomed taxes, and his father had been slain on the pretext of agreements and a treaty, and all his kindred had been enslaved and were always scattered everywhere over the Roman empire. 32.8. But these things being so, Artabanes thinks it enough if he be general of the Romans and be called consul only. ‘And you,’ he said, ‘being my kinsman and having suffered irreparable things, in no way share my grief; but I pity you, most excellent man, for your fortune in both your women, both her of whom you have been deprived, which you ought not, and her with whom you have been compelled to dwell. 32.9. And yet it is not likely that anyone who has even a little spirit should shrink from the murder of Justinian, neither through shrinking nor through any dread, who sits unguarded for ever in some hall at an unseasonable hour of the night, together with the oldest of the priests, eager to turn over the oracles of the Christians. 32.10. But indeed,’ he said, ‘none of the kinsmen of Justinian will set himself against you. Germanus, however, the most powerful of all, I think, will help you eagerly together with his children, who are youths boiling with both their age and their spirit against him, whom I have hope of bringing of their own accord to the deed. 32.11. For they happen to have already been wronged by him in such things as neither we nor any other of the Armenians have.’ With such things Arsaces, always bewitching Artabanes, when at some time he saw that he had given in, brought the matter to another Persarmenian, 32.12. Chanaranges by name. Now this Chanaranges was a youth, handsome in body, but not in earnest, but for the most part childish. 32.13. So when Arsaces had joined both him and Artabanes in purpose and in words, he departed, promising that he would make Germanus and his children of one mind with them for the deed. 32.14. Now Justinus the elder of the children of Germanus was a youth and just growing his first beard, but energetic and keen toward action; 32.15. so that he had mounted into the chair of the consuls not long before. And coming to him, Arsaces said that he wished to meet him secretly in a certain church. 32.16. And when both came into the church, Arsaces first saw fit that Justinus should affirm by oaths that he would never report his words to any of all men except only to his father. 32.17. And when the man had sworn this, he reproached him because, being a nearest kinsman to the emperor, he saw market men and common men, who had no right to them, holding the magistracies of the state, while he himself, being already of such age that affairs were managed by him, overlooked not only himself but also his father, although he had come to the height of valour, and his brother Justinian, sitting in the position of a private man for all time. 32.18. And it had not even befallen him to come into the substance of his uncle, of which he had become heir, at least so far as Boraïdes had resolved, and then had been deprived of it, which he ought not, for the most part. 32.19. And yet it was likely that they would be overlooked still far more immediately, as soon as Belisarius should come from Italy. For he was reported to be already somewhere in the midst of the Illyrians. 32.20. Saying so much, Arsaces urged the youth to the plot against the emperor, revealing the agreements between himself and Artabanes and Chanaranges concerning this deed. 32.21. When Justinus heard this, he was thrown into confusion, and, being seized with dizziness, openly refused Arsaces, saying that these things ought never to be done either by himself or by Germanus his father. 32.22. And Arsaces reported what had befallen to Artabanes, while Justinus carried the whole account to his father. And he, taking counsel with Marcellus, who commanded the guards in the Palatium, deliberated about the matter, whether it was advantageous for them to report it to the emperor. 32.23. Now this Marcellus was most weighty in character and for the most part given to silence, doing nothing for the sake of money, nor enduring jests in words or deeds, nor otherwise rejoicing in a slack mode of life, but always having a hard life and alien to pleasure, yet an exact guardian of justice and a most ardent lover of the truth. 32.24. He, then, would not let the account be carried to the emperor. ‘For,’ he said, ‘it is inexpedient that you become the informer of this. For if you should wish to say anything secretly to the emperor, Artabanes and his men will immediately suspect that it has been reported, and if Arsaces should be able to escape unseen, the charge will remain unproved. 32.25. And I am by no means wont, unless I have inquired most exactly, either to believe myself or to report to the emperor. 32.26. I wish, then, either to be a hearer of the words myself, or that one of my friends, by your preparation, should hear the man saying something clear about these things.’ 32.27. When Germanus heard this, he ordered Justinus his son to act so that Marcellus' instruction might be carried out. 32.28. And he was no longer able to say anything about this to Arsaces, since he had openly refused him, as has been said by me. 32.29. But he inquired of Chanaranges whether Arsaces had come to him lately by the resolve of Artabanes. ‘For I would never,’ he said, ‘have dared to leave any of the secret things to him, being such as he is. 32.30. But if you should wish to tell me anything to the purpose, deliberating in common we might perhaps 32.31. do some good.’ Concerning these things Chanaranges, having taken counsel with Artabanes, carried everything to Justinus, all that Arsaces had previously happened to tell him. 32.32. And when Justinus agreed both to accomplish everything himself and to provide his father of one mind, it seemed best to Germanus to bring Chanaranges into conversation, and a fixed day was agreed upon for the dialogue. 32.33. Germanus, signifying this to Marcellus, saw fit that he should provide one of his friends to them, 32.34. who should be a hearer of the words of Chanaranges. And he provided Leontius, the son-in-law of Athanasius, a man who laid claim to the account of justice and exceedingly understood how to tell the truth. 32.35. Him Germanus, bringing into his house, seated in a chamber, where a thick curtain hung as a screen of the couch on which he was wont to feast. 32.36. And hiding Leontius within this curtain, he himself with Justinus his son remained outside. 32.37. There, when Chanaranges came, Leontius clearly heard him saying everything which had been deliberated by him and Artabanes and Arsaces. 32.38. Among which this also came into the discussion, that if they should kill the emperor while Belisarius was still on his way to Byzantium, nothing of what had been deliberated would proceed for them; since they wished to establish Germanus as emperor, but it was likely that Belisarius would gather a multitude of an army from the regions of Thrace, and thus, the man coming against them, they would by no means be able to thrust him off. 32.39. It would be needful, then, to put off the deed until the coming of Belisarius, and, as soon as the man should come to Byzantium and be with the emperor in the Palatium, then, it being late evening somewhere, bearing daggers, to come there unexpectedly, and to kill both Marcellus and Belisarius together with the emperor. 32.40. For thus they would for the future manage matters more fearlessly as they wished. When Marcellus learned this from Leontius, not even so did he resolve to carry the account to the emperor, but was still gripped by much shrinking, lest he should bring about the ruin of Artabanes unconsidered with much haste. 32.41. Germanus, however, carried everything to Buzes and Constantianus, fearing, as happened, lest from the delay he should incur some suspicion. 32.42. And many days later, when Belisarius was reported to be already somewhere close, Marcellus carried the whole account to the emperor, and he immediately ordered that Artabanes and his men be led off to prison, and entrusted the examination concerning them to some of the magistrates. 32.43. And when the whole plot had now come to light and was expressly in writing, the emperor seated all those of the senate in the Palatium, where they are wont to make their judgements about disputed matters. 32.44. And these, having read over everything which had happened to be told by those examined, none the less brought the charge against Germanus and Justinus his son, until Germanus, providing the testimony of Marcellus and Leontius, was able to dissolve the suspicion. 32.45. For both they and Constantianus and Buzes affirmed on oath that Germanus had hidden nothing whatever of these things on their account, but that everything had befallen just as has been related by me. 32.46. So those of the senate immediately voted to acquit both him and his son, as having done no wrong against the state. 32.47. And when all came inside before the emperor, the emperor himself, sharply angered, was vexed and grew prodigiously savage against Germanus, charging him with the slowness of the disclosure; and two of the magistrates, flattering him, agreed with his opinion and seemed to share his vexation; and in this way they greatly raised the emperor's anger, being eager to gratify him with the calamities of others. 32.48. But the others, cowering, kept silence, by not opposing yielding to him whatever he wished. But Marcellus alone, speaking uprightly, was able to save the man. 32.49. For drawing the charge upon himself and forcing it with all his might, he said that Germanus had reported what was being done most opportunely, but that he himself, searching too exactly, had disclosed it rather slowly. 32.50. And thus he stopped the emperor's anger. And great fame this Marcellus girt himself with among all men, as one who laid claim to valour in the most necessary matters. 32.51. And the emperor Justinian removed Artabanes from the office which he held, but did him no other harm, nor indeed any of the others, except indeed that he held them all in custody not without honour, in the Palatium, however, not in the public prison.

And meanwhile the two thousand too came to the Goths; and Totila, learning that they had come to the stockade, since the time also was leading toward the midday meal, both went himself to his own tent and the Goths, breaking up the battle-array, returned backward.

And coming to be in his own halting-place, Totila found the two thousand already present. And, ordering all to take their meal, and changing the whole equipment of his arms, he armed himself accurately in the manner of a soldier, and at once led the army against the enemy, thinking to fall upon them unexpectedly and thereby to take them.

But not even so did he find the Romans unprepared. For Narses, fearing—which happened—lest the enemy should fall upon them unexpectedly, had forbidden all to take their meal or to sleep or even to take off their cuirasses, no one of them all, or to let his horse loose from the bridle.

Yet he did not leave them altogether without food, but ordered them to breakfast in their array and in the equipment of their arms, and thus, continually on the watch, to await the attack of the enemy.
In the same manner, however, they were no longer drawn up, but for the Romans the wings, on which the foot-archers stood by four thousands, turned to a crescent shape, by the counsel of Narses.

And the foot-soldiers of the Goths all stood in a mass behind the horsemen, in order that, if it should befall the horsemen to be routed, the fugitives, turning back upon them, might be saved, and both together at once advance. And it had been ordered to all the Goths to use neither bow nor anything else at all in this engagement except their spears.

Wherefore it befell Totila to be outgeneralled by his own imprudence; for he, setting himself to this battle, persuaded by I know not whom, presented to his opponents his own army opposing them neither in arms nor balanced in array nor matched in any other respect, since the Romans, each, used whatever was most effective in the work, either shooting, or thrusting with spears, or handling swords, or doing some other of the things ready to their hand and serviceable for the moment, some riding, others setting themselves on foot in the array, according to what was profitable to the need, and in some places effecting an encirclement of the enemy, in others receiving them as they came on and beating off the attack with their shields.

But the horsemen of the Goths, their foot-soldiers being left behind them, trusting in their spears alone, advanced with an inconsiderate rush, and, coming to be in the toil, reaped the fruit of their imprudence.

For rushing against the middle of the enemy, they unwittingly came to be in the midst of the eight thousand foot-archers, and, being shot at by them on both sides, they straightway gave up, since the archers were turning both wings of the front gradually to the crescent, as I have said before.

Many men, then, and many horses the Goths lost in this toil, before they had yet come to close quarters with their opponents, and, having made trial of many irreparable evils, late and with difficulty came to the array of the enemy.
Here I cannot single out any of the Romans or of the barbarian allies with them for wonder above the rest.
For there was one eagerness and valour and contending spirit in all, and each, as their opponents came on, receiving the onset most stoutly, beat it off.
And it was now toward evening, and both camps were suddenly set in motion, the Goths to retreat, the Romans to pursuit.
For when the Romans rushed against them, the Goths did not hold out against the enemy, but yielded as they advanced and turned in headlong flight, terrified by their throng and their good order.
And they looked to no defence, as if phantoms had fallen upon them, fearing them, or as if warred upon from heaven.
And in a little, when they came to their own foot-soldiers, the evil was raised much higher and went forward.

For not in order making their withdrawal did they come to them (to recover breath and to renew the fight with them, as is the custom, or to push off the pursuers, or to make a counter-pursuit or some other form of war), but so disorderly that some of them even were destroyed, the cavalry falling upon them.

Wherefore the foot-soldiers neither, opening their ranks, received them, nor stood firm to save them, but together with them all fled headlong, and there indeed they destroyed one another, as in a battle by night.

And the Roman army, enjoying their terror, with no sparing kept ever killing those in their path, who neither defended themselves nor dared to look them in the face, but offered themselves to the enemy to do with as they wished; so much did the terrors weigh upon them and the fear prevail.

And six thousand of them died in this work, and many gave themselves up to their adversaries. These the Romans for the moment took alive, but not long after killed. And not only Goths were slain, but very many too of the old Roman soldiers, those who had earlier renounced the Roman army and deserted, as I have said in the earlier books, to Totila and the Goths.

But those of the Gothic army to whom it befell neither to perish nor to come into the hands of the enemy were able to escape notice and to flee, as each of them had of horse or of foot or of fortune (or as occasion or place served to attain this).

This battle, then, ended thus, and it was now altogether growing dark. And as Totila fled in the darkness with men no more than five, of whom Scipuar happened to be one, some of the Romans pursued, not knowing that it was Totila; among whom Asbadus the Gepid happened to be.
He, when he came very close to Totila, set upon him as if to strike him on the back with his spear.

But a Gothic youth from the household of Totila, following his master as he fled, and indignant at the fortune then present, cried out loudly, "What is this, you dog? Are you rushing to strike your own master?" Asbadus, then, thrust his spear with all his might against Totila, but he himself, struck in the foot by Scipuar, remained there.
And Scipuar himself, struck by one of the pursuers, stood still, and those who had made the pursuit with Asbadus, being four, no longer pursued, in order to save him,

but turned back with him. But those who followed Totila, thinking the enemy were still pursuing them, none the less drove forward, although they were bringing along the man mortally struck and most surely fainting, necessity controlling their violent course.
And, having accomplished eighty-four stades, they came to a place named Caprae. There, keeping quiet thenceforth, they tended Totila's wound; and he not long after measured out his life.

And there those who had followed him, hiding him in the earth, withdrew. This was the end of the rule and the life of Totila, who had ruled the Goths eleven years, an end not coming worthily upon his former deeds, since both the affairs of the man had earlier gone forward, and his death came not according to reason upon his deeds.

But now too fortune, plainly displaying her charms and mocking human affairs, both the unaccountable that is her own and the unpleadable of her will, gave Totila prosperity, of itself, for a length of time, from no cause, but then, in this stubborn way, allotted the man cowardice and ruin.

from no fitting cause at the present time. But these things, I think, are neither comprehensible to man, nor ever will be later; yet they are forever spoken of and held in opinion, whispered abroad for all time, as is dear to each, the seemingly probable account consoling the ignorance. But I return to the former account.
The Romans, then, did not know that Totila had thus vanished from among men, until a certain woman, a Goth by race, told them and pointed out the tomb.

And they, hearing it, thinking the account not sound, came to the place, and, digging up the grave with no hesitation, brought out Totila a corpse from there, and, recognizing him, as they say, and having filled their desire with this sight too, hid him again in the earth, and at once reported the whole matter to Narses.
But some say that the matters concerning Totila and this battle did not happen thus, but in some other manner; which it has seemed to me not inappropriate to record.

For they say that the retreat of the Gothic army did not come about without cause or contrary to reason, but that, some of the Romans skirmishing, an arrow from a bow fell suddenly upon Totila, not by the forethought of the one who sent it, since Totila, armed in the manner of a soldier and arrayed somewhere in the phalanx unregarded, stood, not wishing to be plain to the enemy, nor in any way offering himself to a plot, but some fortune contriving these things for him and guiding the shaft to the man's body; and that he, mortally struck, becoming, so far as possible, in great pain, went out of the phalanx and, with a few, went backward little by little.
And as far as Caprae he drove his horse, enduring the hardship, but there, fainting, remained thenceforth to tend the wound, and not long after the appointed day of life came upon him.

And the Gothic army, being neither otherwise a match for their opponents, and their commander too having become, contrary to expectation, incapable of fighting, fell into amazement, that Totila alone, not from a plot of the enemy, should be mortally struck, and from this, becoming exceedingly fearful and dispirited, fell into a terror that had no bound and into a retreat thus shameful. But concerning these things let each man say as he knows.

About the time of this war the barbarians became expressly masters of the whole West. And the Gothic war for the Romans, although at first they had conquered by force, as has been said by me before, came to such a pass that not only did much of their money and many of their men perish for no benefit, but Italy too was lost in addition, and they beheld nearly all the Illyrians and Thracians being ravaged and destroyed in no order by the barbarians, who had become neighbours to them. And it came about thus. 33.2. The Goths gave the whole of the Gauls that were subject to them, at the beginning of this war, to the Germans, thinking that they would not be able to array themselves against both, as has been said by me in the previous narrative. 33.3. And this deed not only could the Romans not prevent, but the emperor Justinian even strengthened it for them, so that no obstacle from these barbarians, were they made hostile, might meet him. 33.4. For the Franks never thought that they held the Gauls in safety unless the emperor set his seal on this very thing. And from this the rulers of the Germans held both Massalia, the colony of the Phocaeans, and all the regions by the sea, and mastered the sea there. 33.5. And they sit in Arelate watching the chariot-contest, and have made a gold coin from the metals in the Gauls, not putting on this stater the stamp of the Roman emperor, as is the custom, 33.6. but their own image. And yet the king of the Persians is wont to make a silver coin in whatever way he wishes, but to put his own stamp on a gold stater is lawful neither for him nor for any other king of all the barbarians, and this though he be lord of more gold, since they are not even able to pass this coin on to those who deal with them, even if it befalls that those who deal with them are barbarians. So matters went for the Franks thus. 33.7. And when the affairs of the Goths and Totila became superior in the war, the Franks made the most of Venetia their own for no reason, the Romans being no longer able to defend it nor the Goths able to carry on the war against both. 33.8. And the Gepaedes took and held the city of Sirmium and almost all the Dacias, as soon as the emperor Justinian had taken them from the Goths; and they enslaved the Romans there, and going still ever forward on their way they plundered, doing violence to the Roman empire. 33.9. Wherefore the emperor no longer gave them the allowances which they had from of old been wont to receive from the Romans. 33.10. And the Lombards the emperor Justinian presented with the city of Noricum and with the forts on Pannonia and many other places and very great sums of money. 33.11. On account of this the Lombards, setting out from their ancestral abodes, settled thence beyond the river Ister, not far from the Gepaedes. 33.12. And they plundered and enslaved the Dalmatians and Illyrians as far as the borders of Epidamnus; and when some of the captives, fleeing from there, were able to be conveyed home, these barbarians, going about the Roman empire, as being in treaty with the Romans, whenever they recognized any of those who had fled, laid hold of them as of their own slaves who had run away, and dragging them off from their parents, conveyed them with themselves to their own homes, no one withstanding them. 33.13. And the Eruli too held other places of Dacia, the emperor giving them, about the city of Singidunum, where they are settled now, overrunning the Illyrians and the regions of Thrace and plundering them for the most part. And some of them became Roman soldiers, ranged among those called foederati. 33.14. So whenever envoys of the Eruli were sent to Byzantium, these men, who plundered the subjects of the Romans, having received all their allowances from the emperor, departed with no toil.
And Narses, exceedingly delighted at what had happened, ceased not referring all things to God, which indeed was the true account, and managed the matters at hand.

And first, wishing to be rid of the absurdity of the Lombards who followed him (who, in addition to their other lawlessness in their manner of life, burned the buildings they fell in with, and forcibly approached the women who took refuge in the sanctuaries), he, having welcomed them with great sums, let them go to their ancestral homes, ordering Valerian and Damian his nephew, with their followers, to lead them on their way as far as the Roman borders, so that they should harm no one in their withdrawal.
And when the Lombards had departed from the land of the Romans, Valerian encamped about the city of Verona, intending to besiege it and bring it over to the emperor.
And the guards there, becoming afraid, came to a conference with Valerian, as about to hand over both themselves and the city by agreement.

But when the Franks who held the garrison in the regions of Venetia learned this, they hindered it with all eagerness, thinking fit to lay claim to the country as belonging to them. And from this Valerian withdrew from there with his whole army, accomplishing nothing.
And the Goths, all those who had fled from the engagement and been saved, crossing the river Po, held the city of Ticinum and the regions there, and appointed Teias as their ruler.

And he, finding all the money which Totila had happened to lay up in Ticinum, planned to bring the Franks into alliance, and disposed and arranged the Goths as well as he could from the present circumstances, gathering them all about him in haste.

Hearing this, Narses ordered Valerian, with all his followers, to keep guard about the river Po, so that the Goths might not be able more fearlessly to combine, while he himself, with all the rest of the army, went against Rome.

And, coming to be in Tuscany, he took Narnia by agreement, and to the people of Spoletium, who were unwalled, he left a garrison, ordering them to rebuild as quickly as possible such parts of the circuit-wall as the Goths had happened to throw down.

And he sent also some to make trial of the garrison in Perusia. And those who commanded the guards in Perusia were two Romans who had become deserters, Meligedius and Ulifus, who, having been a bodyguard of Cyprian before, persuaded by Totila who promised him much, then killed Cyprian by treachery, who at that time commanded the garrison there.
Meligedius, then, accepting the proposals of Narses, planned, with his Roman followers, to hand over the city; but those about Ulifus, perceiving what was being done, combined openly against them.

And Ulifus with those of his mind was destroyed, while Meligedius at once handed over Perusia to the Romans. To Ulifus, however, it befell that vengeance from God, clearly, fell upon him, in that he was destroyed in the very place where he had killed Cyprian. These things, then, went forward thus.
And the Goths who held the guard in Rome, when they learned that Narses and the Roman army were coming against them and were very close, prepared to confront them with what they could.

Now Totila had happened to burn many of the buildings of the city, when he first took it. . . . And at last, reckoning that the Goths, being reduced to a few, could no longer guard the whole circuit-wall of Rome, he, fencing off a small portion of the city about the tomb of Hadrian with a short wall and fastening it to the former wall, set up the shape of a fort.
And there, laying up their most precious possessions, the Goths guarded this fort accurately, but the rest of the wall of the city they neglected and disregarded.

Leaving, then, a few of themselves as guards in this place at that time, all the rest, coming to be about the battlements of the wall of the city, were eager to make trial of the enemy as they assaulted the wall.
Now the whole circuit of Rome, through its excessive size, neither could the Romans, attacking, surround, nor the Goths guard.

But, scattered, the one party attacked where they happened to come, the others defended as best they could from the present circumstances. And Narses, bringing along a great number of archers, made an attack upon a certain portion of the circuit-wall, while elsewhere John the son of Vitalian with his followers assaulted.
And Philemuth and the Heruls harassed at another part, and very far from them the rest followed. And they all assaulted the wall, being as far as possible from one another.

And against them the barbarians, gathering, received the attack. But the rest of the circuit-wall, where the Romans made no assault, was altogether empty of men, the Goths all gathering wherever the enemy should attack, as I have said.

And meanwhile, by the counsel of Narses, Dagisthaeus, having a great multitude of soldiers and bringing along both the standard of Narses and that of John and many ladders, suddenly attacked a portion of the circuit-wall altogether bereft of guard.
And at once setting all the ladders against the wall, with no one defending, with no toil he came inside the circuit-wall with his followers, and they opened the gates at will.
And the Goths, perceiving this at once, no longer looked to defence, but all fled wherever it became possible for each. And some leaped into the fort, while others went at a run to Portus.

And here a thought has come to me in my account, in what manner fortune mocks human affairs, not always going to men in the same way, nor regarding them with equal eyes, but changing with time and place, and plays a sort of game against them, by varying the worth of the wretched men according to the occasion or the place or the manner, if indeed Bessas, who earlier lost Rome, not long after recovered for the Romans Petra in Lazica, while conversely Dagisthaeus, having given up Petra to the enemy, recovered Rome for the emperor in a short time.
But these things have been from the beginning and will always be, so long as the same fortune is with men. And Narses then went with all his army to make war upon the fort.

And the barbarians, becoming terrified and having received pledges concerning their lives, surrendered to him at once both themselves and the fort, in the twenty-sixth year of the reign of the emperor Justinian.
And thus, under the reign of this emperor, Rome was taken for the fifth time; and Narses at once sent the keys of its gates to the emperor.

Thus the barbarians divided up the Roman empire among themselves. And some time later the Gepaedes and the Lombards, since they dwelt somewhere near one another, became exceedingly at variance. 34.2. And being eager for war with all eagerness against one another, both sides were keen to come to battle with the enemy, and a fixed time was set for the engagement. 34.3. But the Lombards, thinking that they would not be a match for the Gepaedes by themselves (for it befell that they were inferior in numbers to the enemy), resolved to bring in the Romans to alliance. 34.4. So sending envoys to the emperor Justinian, they begged him to send them an army. When the Gepaedes learned this, they too sent envoys to Byzantium to beg for the same things. Now at that time Thorisin commanded the Gepaedes, and the other people Auduin. 34.5. And the emperor Justinian resolved to hear the words of both, not coming together, however, but coming to him separately. 34.6. First, then, the Lombards, coming into the emperor's sight, spoke as follows: “We are dismayed, O emperor, at the impropriety of the Gepaedes, who, having transgressed against your empire in matters so great in multitude and so great in magnitude, now come to you bringing you the greatest of insults. 34.7. For these men alone would do the utmost outrage to their neighbours, who, thinking them too easy to deceive, came to them to enjoy the simplicity of the wronged. 34.8. And we ask you to consider so much, in what state of mind are the affairs of friendship for the Gepaedes. For thus you would work out what is advantageous most safely for the Roman empire, since men are able with safety to judge of what is to be from what has always gone before. 34.9. If, then, it befell that the nation of the Gepaedes had displayed its thanklessness only toward certain others, we should have needed much argument and time and outside testimony, wishing to convict the character of these men; but now it is possible to take the example near at hand from you yourselves. 34.10. For consider: the Goths held the land of the Dacians in payment of tribute in earlier times, and the Gepaedes all dwelt at the first on the other side of the Ister, so cowed by the power of the Goths that they were never able even to make trial of crossing the river, but being in treaty and most friendly with the Romans, and receiving many gifts in the name of friendship each year both from those who reigned before, 34.11. and from you none the less. We would gladly inquire what good these men have ever wrought toward the Romans in return for these things. But they would not be able to say either great or small; 34.12. so long, then, as they had nothing on which to wrong you, not by any purpose, but compelled by inability, they kept quiet. 34.13. For you saw fit to lay no claim to the regions beyond the Ister, while the fear from the Goths drove them back from this side. 34.14. And who would ever call inability good will? What confirmation of friendship will arise in the impossibility of doing wrong? It is not so, O emperor, it is not. For power alone displays the nature of a man, bringing forth into public the character of all by the license to act. 34.15. For behold: as soon as the Gepaedes saw the Goths driven out of all Dacia, and you held in occupation with the enemy, the most abominable of them dared everywhere to mount upon your land.” 34.16. “How could one reach in words the impropriety of the matter? Did they not despise the Roman empire? Did they not break the ordinances of treaties and alliances? 34.17. Did they not insult those whom they ought least? Did they not do violence to an empire of which they would pray to be slaves, if any leisure should arise for you against them? The Gepaedes, O emperor, hold Sirmium and enslave Romans, and boast that they lay claim to the whole of Dacia; 34.18. having conquered what war on your behalf, or with you, or against you yourselves? Or having made this land the prize of what contest? And this though they have often been hired by you and have received money, as has been said, for time we know not how far back. 34.19. And yet of their present embassy there has been no act more abominable in all time. For when they saw us eager for war against them, they took heart to come to Byzantium and to come into the sight of an emperor so greatly insulted. 34.20. Perhaps, too, in the abundance of their shamelessness, they will invite you to alliance against us, who are so earnestly your friends. 34.21. And indeed if they come intending to give back what they have mounted upon, which in no way belongs to them, the Lombards must be reckoned by the Romans most responsible for the benefit arising from this, since, compelled by fear, they belatedly clothe themselves in unwilling good will. 34.22. For he who has obtained a kindness will, as is natural, know the gratitude to him who has made the necessity. But if they have not even now resolved to give up what does not belong to them, what could be the excess of this their evil character?” 34.23. “Let these things, then, be said by us with barbaric simplicity, sparing of words, in no way worthy of the matters. 34.24. But do you, O emperor, considering all that has been said by us more meagrely than the need, do what will be advantageous both to the Romans and to your Lombards, considering this above all else, that to us, who are of one mind with you about God, the Romans will at the first justly be arrayed in alliance, but to those who are Arians, and for this very reason, they will go in opposition.” 34.25. The Lombards said so much. And coming on the following day to the emperor, the envoys of the Gepaedes too spoke as follows: “It is just, O emperor, that those who come to their neighbours at a request for alliance should first show that they come to beg for things both just and advantageous to their allies, and thus make the speeches for which they make their embassy. 34.26. That we have been wronged by the Lombards, then, is plain at once; for we are eager to dissolve our differences by justice, 34.27. and it in no way belongs to those who are eager to do violence to plead at law. 34.28. And that in multitude and valour the Gepaedes happen to be by far superior to the Lombards, 34.29. why should one speak at length among those who know? But to go to a contest ranged with the inferior is to go to a manifest evil, when it is possible, ranging with the more powerful, to have the victory without danger; which we think none even of those who have a little prudence would choose. 34.30. So that, going against certain others, the Gepaedes too will for the future be arrayed with you, owing you gratitude for what has been done, and from the abundance of their power providing, as is natural, the mastery over the enemy. 34.31. And indeed it would befit you to reckon this also, that the Lombards have lately become friends to the Romans, while it befalls the Gepaedes to have been from above in treaty and known to you. 34.32. And a friendship interwoven by length of time has its dissolution not easy. So that you will obtain allies not only powerful but also firm. 34.33. These, then, are the pleas we have toward you for the alliance. But behold what the Lombards are in character. 34.34. To dissolve their differences by justice, though we challenge them often, they by no means resolved, being gripped by unreasoning boldness; but when the war is now somewhere at hand, and they, going back behind affairs because they share knowledge of their own weakness, come to you, seeing fit that the Romans take up the contest on their behalf, which they ought not. 34.35. By all means these robbers put forward to you Sirmium and certain other places in Dacia as the pretext of this war. 34.36.
